# 15. Use In-Memory Events Bus
Date: 2019-07-15

## Status
Accepted
## Context
As we want to base inter-modular communication on asynchronous communication in the form of event-driven architecture, we need some "events bus" to do that.
## Possible solutions
### 1. In Memory Events Bus
In memory Publish/Subscribe implementation without any external component.
#### Pros
- very easy to implement
- no network communication needed
- performance (it depends)
- no need to learn anything
- simple solution
#### Cons
- does not support more advanced integration scenarios, everything needs to be implemented
- does not have configuration
- does not have other features (who have messaging brokers)
### 2. Message Broker
External middleware component. It could be a low-level broker (like RabbitMQ) or a high-level broker (like MassTransit, NServiceBus).
#### Pros
- only integration with platform code needed
- more advanced integration scenarios
- richness of configuration
- a lot of features
#### Cons

# Orchard Core Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from the real Orchard Core codebase, for one specific learner: a **junior fullstack engineer** (CRUD web dev — .NET/C#, React/Node/TS or similar) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, when it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is
Orchard Core (v3.0.1) is an open-source, **modular, multi-tenant application framework and CMS for ASP.NET Core**, maintained by the Orchard Core team under the .NET Foundation. It is two products in one repository: a framework for building modular multi-tenant ASP.NET Core apps (`src/OrchardCore/*`), and a full CMS built on that framework as ~95 pluggable modules (`src/OrchardCore.Modules/*`). Each tenant gets its **own dependency-injection container and request pipeline**, built lazily from that tenant's enabled features. Persistence is **YesSql** — a document store over SQL Server/SQLite/MySQL/Postgres where documents are JSON and queries run against explicit *index tables*. UI is rendered through a **display-management** system (drivers produce "shapes", placement files position them, templates can be overridden per theme). It is one of the most instructive large .NET codebases in the wild: real multi-tenancy, real modularity, real versioned-content invariants, real background scheduling — all things interviews probe.
## The learning tracks
| Track | Directory | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cartography | `01-codebase-cartography/` | Maps: system, reading order, glossary, tooling, key flows |
| Stack mastery | `02-stack-and-language-mastery/` | C#/.NET/ASP.NET Core/YesSql mental models anchored to real files |
| Architecture | `03-architecture-and-patterns/` | Boundaries, persistence, authz, async/reliability, pattern catalog, critique |
| Reading gym | `04-code-reading-gym/` | Annotation drills, trace tables, fake-code contrasts, review katas |
| Quality | `05-quality-engineering/` | Testing, debugging, performance, security, observability |
| Contribution | `06-contribution-practice

# Getting started with Orchard Core as a NuGet package
In this article, we are going to see how easy it is to create a CMS Web application using the NuGet packages provided by Orchard Core.
!!! tip
Do you just want to test drive Orchard Core, without creating a .NET application? Check out [this guide](test-drive-orchard-core.md).
## Create an Orchard Core CMS application
!!! note
This guide follows a manual process so you can have a deeper understanding of what's happening. You can also use our [code generation templates](templates/README.md) for a quicker start if you create a brand-new application. Check out [this guide](../guides/create-cms-application/README.md).
In Visual Studio (or [any other .NET IDE](../getting-started/development-tools.md)), create a new empty .NET web application, e.g. `Cms.Web`. Do not check "Place solution and project in the same directory", because later when you create modules and themes you will want them to live alongside the web application within the solution.
!!! note
If you want to use the `preview` packages, [configure the OrchardCore Preview URL in your Package sources](preview-package-source.md).
To add a reference to the package, right-click on the project and click on `Manage NuGet packages...`, check `Include prerelease` if required. If you added the preview source above, select this from the `Package Source` selection in the top right.  In the `Browse` tab, search for `OrchardCore.Application.Cms.Targets` and `Install` the package.
### Getting Started with `Program.cs` Only Using .NET 6 and later?
!!! tip
When starting a new project using .NET 6, you'll notice that the created project does not have a `Startup` class as it did in previous versions of .NET.
Open `Program.cs` file. Remove the following line "if exists"
```csharp
builder.Services.AddRazorPages();
```
Add the following line
```csharp
builder.Services.AddOrchardCms();
```
Additionally, remove the following lines
```csharp
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseRouting();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapRazorPages();

# 01 — Codebase Cartography
You can't reason about a system you can't locate yourself in. This track builds your map of Orchard Core before you form opinions about it.
| File | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| [01-system-map.md](01-system-map.md) | The three-layer shape: host → framework libs → modules; ownership map |
| [02-file-reading-order.md](02-file-reading-order.md) | 28 files in reading order, junior/mid/senior paths |
| [03-domain-glossary.md](03-domain-glossary.md) | Tenant, shell, content item, part, field, shape, recipe… with code locations |

| [05-key-flows.md](05-key-flows.md) | **The core asset**: 8 end-to-end flows with trace tables and drills |
Suggested order: 01 → 03 (skim) → 05 (deep) → 02 (as a guided tour) → 04 (reference).
Interview note: "walk me through a large codebase you know" is a standard mid-level screen question. The system map + one key flow, told concretely, is a complete answer.

# 02 — Stack and Language Mastery
The stack here is **C# 13 / .NET 10, ASP.NET Core, YesSql, Liquid (Fluid), and a Yarn-managed JS asset layer**. This track builds mental models from first principles, then shows where this repo uses them well and where the sharp edges are.
| File | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| [01-language-runtime-model.md](01-language-runtime-model.md) | async/await & the task model, AsyncLocal, threading, exceptions, disposal |
| [02-framework-mental-models.md](02-framework-mental-models.md) | ASP.NET Core DI lifetimes, middleware, MVC binding, hosted services |
| [03-type-system-and-contracts.md](03-type-system-and-contracts.md) | generics, JSON-backed dynamic models, interfaces-as-contracts, versioned abstractions |
| [04-tooling-and-build-system.md](04-tooling-and-build-system.md) | slnx, central package management, assets-manager, CI |
Every concept anchors to a real file. Every file ends with an **Interview angle** listing the questions this material answers, cross-linked into [08-interview-prep/](../08-interview-prep/).
If you come from Node/TS: the biggest mental shifts are (1) real threads — concurrency bugs exist that Node can't have, (2) DI lifetimes as a first-class design axis, (3) exceptions instead of error values as the dominant style.

samples.opening:
# Upskill: The Expense Management Training Lab
This is a self-directed curriculum that turns **this** repository — a small ASP.NET Core
(C#) + React expense-management system — into a training lab. It teaches two things at
once:
1. **This codebase specifically** — where things live, how a request flows, why each
pattern was chosen.
2. **Transferable engineering judgment** — runtime fundamentals, framework mental models,
architecture, testing, debugging, performance, security, code review, and how to
contribute to a real project.
## Repo identity (read this first)
This is a learning clone of Ramp / Expensify / Brex expense workflows. An **employee**
creates an expense, attaches a receipt, and submits it; a **manager** approves or rejects
it; **finance** reimburses it (payment completes asynchronously). The backend is an
ASP.NET Core 8 Web API with **zero NuGet dependencies** — everything (auth, hashing,
background queue, JSON) uses the bundled framework, by design, so the moving parts are
visible rather than hidden in libraries. Persistence is an **in-memory store** (a
singleton of `ConcurrentDictionary`s) that resets on restart; this keeps the focus on the
domain (a state machine, a policy engine, role-scoped authorization) instead of a
database. The frontend is a Vite + React SPA that talks to the API over `fetch` with a
bearer token. The whole thing is intentionally readable in an afternoon — which is exactly
what makes it a good lab.
> ⚠️ **Status caveat (verify before trusting):** at the time these docs were written the
> code had **not been compiled or run** in this environment (no .NET SDK installed). The
> code is complete and written to be correct, but treat "it builds / it runs" as
> *unverified* until you run it yourself. See [08-reference/verification-log.md](08-reference/verification-log.md).
## Who this is for
A junior engineer who wants to reach mid-level (and start thinking like a senior). It also
works for a mid-level engineer who is new to ASP.NET Core, React, or to this repo.

# 04 — Code Reading Gym
Reading code well is a trainable skill. These are reps. Do them with the files open; resist
reading the answers first.
| Page | Reps |
| --- | --- |
| [01-annotation-drills](01-annotation-drills.md) | 10 — annotate a real snippet's inputs/outputs/invariants/failure modes |
| [02-trace-tables](02-trace-tables.md) | 6 — fill in a step-by-step value trace |
| [03-fake-code-contrasts](03-fake-code-contrasts.md) | 10 — bad vs better, tied to real patterns |
| [04-review-katas](04-review-katas.md) | 10 — review a fake PR diff and find the issues |
Self-grade everything **Basic / Solid / Strong**.

# 05 — Quality Engineering
The repo currently has **no tests, no CI, and no observability** — which makes it a perfect
place to *build* those skills rather than just admire them.
| Page | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| [01-testing-strategy](01-testing-strategy.md) | What to test where, and what not to |
| [02-writing-tests-here](02-writing-tests-here.md) | 7 concrete test recipes for this code |
| [03-systematic-debugging](03-systematic-debugging.md) | A method + 5 repo-specific scenarios |
| [04-performance-thinking](04-performance-thinking.md) | Where the hotspots are (and will be) |
| [05-security-checklist](05-security-checklist.md) | Threats tied to real lines + a pre-merge list |
| [06-observability-and-operations](06-observability-and-operations.md) | "How would I know this broke?" |

# Expense Management System
A learning-oriented clone of Ramp / Expensify / Brex expense workflows, built with
**ASP.NET Core (C#)** and **React**. It demonstrates file uploads, validation,
background processing, a state machine, security, and reporting — with a deliberately
small dependency footprint.
> **Status:** the source is complete but has not been compiled/run in this environment
> (the .NET SDK isn't installed here). Install the .NET 8 SDK to build and run.
---
## What it does
- **Employees** create expenses, attach receipts, and submit them for approval.
- **Managers** approve or reject their direct reports' expenses.
- **Finance** reimburses approved expenses (payment completes in the background).
- **Policy checks** flag or block expenses (receipt required over $25, category limits,
future dates, high-value spend).
- **Reports** summarise spend by status and category, scoped to your role.
### Expense state machine
```
Draft ──submit──▶ Submitted ──approve──▶ Approved ──reimburse──▶ Reimbursing ──(system)──▶ Reimbursed
▲                   │
│                   └──reject──▶ Rejected ──submit──▶ Submitted
└──────── edit (while Draft or Rejected)
```
All transitions go through a single `ExpenseStateMachine` that enforces both the legal
edges and which **role** may trigger each one. Every change is recorded in an audit trail.
---
## Architecture
```
backend/                 ASP.NET Core Web API (.NET 8) — ZERO NuGet packages
Domain/                Entities, enums, the state machine, domain exceptions
Storage/               In-memory DataStore (singleton) + demo seeding
Security/              PBKDF2 hashing, token sessions, custom auth handler
Services/              PolicyEngine, ExpenseService, ReceiptService, Reporting, mappings

the pieces relate before you change one.

| [02-file-reading-order](02-file-reading-order.md) | 25 files in the order that builds understanding fastest |

| [04-runtime-and-tooling-map](04-runtime-and-tooling-map.md) | SDK/build/runtime boundaries, config, secrets |
| [05-key-flows](05-key-flows.md) | 6 end-to-end traces — **the most important page here** |
Start with the system map, then read [05-key-flows](05-key-flows.md) with the code open.

# 02 — Stack & Language Mastery
Every concept here points to a real line in this repo. The goal is not "learn C#/React" in
the abstract, but to understand the exact features this code relies on — and the failure
modes that bite when you don't.
| Page | Teaches |
| --- | --- |
| [01-dotnet-runtime-model](01-dotnet-runtime-model.md) | CLR, GC, async/await, Task vs ValueTask, cancellation, IDisposable |

Concept → why it matters → real code → failure mode → drill, throughout.

# Upskill Training Lab
This curriculum turns the subscription billing sample into a training lab for moving from junior toward senior engineering judgment. The repo is a C#/.NET 8 minimal API plus a React/Vite client: the API registers services, CORS, idempotency middleware, hosted workers, and `/api` endpoints in [Program.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Program.cs#L7-L37); the client renders one dashboard shell from [App.tsx](../../src/Billing.Web/src/App.tsx#L27-L395). The core domain is billing: customers, plans, coupons, subscriptions, usage, invoices, payments, and webhook events are immutable records in [BillingModels.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Domain/BillingModels.cs#L3-L123). Money uses integer minor units in [Money.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Domain/Money.cs#L5-L57), which is a transferable production habit. Persistence is intentionally in-memory behind [BillingStore.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Infrastructure/BillingStore.cs#L5-L264), so persistence, transaction, EF Core, and migration lessons are taught as missing boundaries and migration exercises. Background behavior exists through hosted services registered in [Program.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Program.cs#L19-L20) and implemented in [PaymentWorker.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Infrastructure/PaymentWorker.cs#L6-L36) plus [WebhookDeliveryWorker.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Infrastructure/WebhookDeliveryWorker.cs#L6-L56). Security is partial: CORS and signed webhooks exist, but app authentication/authorization is not configured in [Program.cs](../../src/Billing.Api/Program.cs#L21-L35).
Use this over a weekend, two weeks, eight weeks, or as an ongoing code-review gym. Every codebase claim should point to a path and line anchor. Fake code is labeled `// Illustrative fake code: not from this repo`. Drills ask you to annotate inputs, outputs, dependencies, invariants, side effects, and failure modes before you change anything.

Before you can change a system safely, you need a map: what the major parts are, who owns what, the
order to read files in, the vocabulary, the tooling, and how a request actually flows. This module
builds that map for the Subscription Billing Dashboard.
| File | What it gives you |

# Subscription Billing Dashboard
A learning-oriented Stripe Billing / Chargebee style dashboard built with C#, .NET minimal APIs, and React.
The implementation focuses on enterprise billing fundamentals:
- Customer, plan, subscription, coupon, invoice, usage event, and webhook domain models.
- Money represented as integer minor units to avoid floating point drift.
- Idempotent write APIs via `Idempotency-Key`.
- Background processing for queued payments and outbound webhook dispatch.
- Signed inbound webhook endpoint using HMAC SHA-256.
- Usage-based billing simulator with metered plans.
## Prerequisites
This workspace was generated without installing anything. To run it elsewhere, install the normal toolchains:
- .NET SDK 8 or later
- Node.js 20 or later
## Run
Backend:
```powershell
dotnet run --project src/Billing.Api
```
Frontend:
```powershell
cd src/Billing.Web
npm install
npm run dev
```
The React app expects the API at `http://localhost:5088` by default. Override with `VITE_API_BASE_URL`.
## API Highlights
- `GET /api/dashboard`
- `GET /api/customers`
- `POST /api/customers`
- `GET /api/plans`
- `POST /api/plans`
- `GET /api/invoices`

# Codebase Cartography
Use this section to build the map before touching behavior. The API composition lives in [Program.cs](../../../src/Billing.Api/Program.cs#L7-L37), the domain records in [BillingModels.cs](../../../src/Billing.Api/Domain/BillingModels.cs#L3-L123), the in-memory store in [BillingStore.cs](../../../src/Billing.Api/Infrastructure/BillingStore.cs#L5-L264), and the React app in [App.tsx](../../../src/Billing.Web/src/App.tsx#L27-L395).
Read in this order:
1. [01-system-map.md](01-system-map.md)
2. [02-file-reading-order.md](02-file-reading-order.md)
3. [03-domain-glossary.md](03-domain-glossary.md)
4. [04-runtime-and-tooling-map.md](04-runtime-and-tooling-map.md)
5. [05-key-flows.md](05-key-flows.md)
Verification note: no controllers, EF Core migrations, auth handlers, or test projects were found in `rg --files`; the API uses minimal endpoint mapping in [Program.cs](../../../src/Billing.Api/Program.cs#L39-L250).

# 03 — Architecture & Patterns
This is where you stop describing the code and start *judging* it. Boundaries, persistence, auth,
reliability — then a catalog of the patterns worth stealing, an honest critique, and the comparison
cards that train the core senior skill: choosing between viable designs and knowing what each
commits you to.
| File | What it builds |
| --- | --- |
| [01-boundaries-and-layers.md](01-boundaries-and-layers.md) | What each layer owns and must not own; the leaks. |
| [02-data-model-and-persistence.md](02-data-model-and-persistence.md) | Entities, relationships, the (missing) indexes, "transaction" boundaries, safe schema change. |
| [03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md](03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md) | The validation layers, and the gaping absence of authn/authz/tenant isolation. |
| [04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md](04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md) | Queues, workers, webhooks; idempotency, retries, outbox, timeouts, failure visibility. |
| [05-pattern-catalog.md](05-pattern-catalog.md) | 9 pattern cards — the transferable shapes. |
| [06-architecture-critique.md](06-architecture-critique.md) | Strongest choices, real risks, "if I owned this for 3 months". |
| [07-comparative-implementations.md](07-comparative-implementations.md) | 3 comparison cards incl. a migration drill — **the senior skill**. |

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line across which things are decoupled: code on one side can change without forcing changes on the other. A **layer** owns a responsibility and depends only inward. Finding boundaries — and spotting where they *leak* — is the core architecture skill.
## The four layers
| Layer | Project | Owns | Must NOT own |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Domain | `ApplicationCore` | Entities, invariants, use-case services, query specs, the interfaces it needs | EF, ASP.NET, HTTP, JSON |
| Infrastructure | `Infrastructure` | EF mappings, migrations, Identity, email, concrete `IRepository` | Business rules |
| Presentation | `Web`, `PublicApi`, `BlazorAdmin` | HTTP, view models/DTOs, auth wiring, rendering | Domain invariants, direct SQL |
| Contracts | `BlazorShared` | Shapes shared client↔API | Behavior |
The dependency rule: **arrows point inward.** `Infrastructure` and the UIs depend on `ApplicationCore`; `ApplicationCore` depends on nothing internal. Proof: [ApplicationCore.csproj](../../src/ApplicationCore/ApplicationCore.csproj) references only small helper libraries (Ardalis.*), never EF Core or ASP.NET.
## Where the boundaries are clean (good examples)
- **Domain ↔ persistence:** the domain declares `IRepository<T>` ([IRepository.cs](../../src/ApplicationCore/Interfaces/IRepository.cs)); `Infrastructure` implements it ([EfRepository.cs](../../src/Infrastructure/Data/EfRepository.cs)). Swap SQL for in-memory by changing one registration ([Dependencies.cs:19-38](../../src/Infrastructure/Dependencies.cs#L19-L38)).
- **Domain ↔ UI shape:** `CatalogViewModelService` explicitly calls itself "a UI-specific service … does not contain any business logic" ([CatalogViewModelService.cs:14-17](../../src/Web/Services/CatalogViewModelService.cs#L14-L17)) and maps entities to view models — keeping presentation concerns out of the domain.
- **Network boundary:** BlazorAdmin runs in the browser and *cannot* reach the DbContext; it must call the API over HTTP ([HttpService.cs](../../src/BlazorAdmin/Services/HttpService.cs)). The compiler + runtime enforce this boundary.
- **Client ↔ API contract:** shared DTOs live in `BlazorShared` so both sides compile against the same shapes without sharing domain internals.
## Where boundaries leak or bend (teachable weak spots)
- **UI decides a domain value:** the checkout's shipping address is constructed in the *page* ([Checkout.cshtml.cs:57](../../src/Web/Pages/Basket/Checkout.cshtml.cs#L57)) and handed to the domain. Address *should* be user input flowing into the domain, not a presentation-layer

This module is first-class, not an afterthought. Target: **mid-level fullstack interviews** (.NET/C# primary; the transferable concepts map to any stack). At least 60% of the question cards here are anchored to real code in this repo, so you practice answering with concrete evidence — "in eShopOnWeb, the `OrderService` does X at line Y" — instead of reciting definitions.
## How mid-level fullstack loops are usually structured

## The golden rule
**Answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff, and a failure mode — not a definition.**
- Weak: "Clean Architecture separates concerns."
- Strong: "In this repo, `ApplicationCore` defines `IRepository<T>` and `Infrastructure` implements it, so I can unit-test `BasketService` with a fake repo — the tests do exactly that. The cost is more mapping code and indirection; for a thin CRUD app I'd skip it."
The second answer proves you've read and reasoned about real code. That's the mid-level signal.

samples.opening:
# eShopOnWeb Upskill Curriculum
A codebase-to-curriculum training lab built on Microsoft's **eShopOnWeb** reference application. It teaches two things at once, always paired:
1. **This repo**: where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill**: why these patterns exist, when they fail, how to recognize them in any codebase — and how to articulate them in a mid-level fullstack interview.
## Who this is for
A junior fullstack engineer (CRUD web dev in .NET/C#, or React/Node/TS moving to .NET) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
## What this repo is (identity in 7 sentences)
eShopOnWeb is Microsoft's official reference application for the free eBook *Architecting Modern Web Applications with ASP.NET Core and Azure* ([README.md](../README.md#L18)). It is a deliberately **monolithic** e-commerce store — catalog, basket, checkout, orders, admin — built on .NET 8 ([global.json](../global.json)). It demonstrates **Clean Architecture**: a dependency-free domain project (`ApplicationCore`), an EF Core data layer (`Infrastructure`), and three UI surfaces — a Razor Pages storefront (`Web`), a JWT-secured minimal-API backend (`PublicApi`), and a Blazor WebAssembly admin panel (`BlazorAdmin`). Persistence is SQL Server via EF Core with two separate DbContexts (catalog vs. identity). It is a *teaching* app: some things are intentionally simplified or deliberately flawed (hardcoded JWT secret, hardcoded checkout address, a `Task.Delay(1000)` in an API endpoint), which makes it an outstanding lab for developing senior judgment — you get to find real flaws in a professionally structured codebase. Development moved to [dotnet/eShop](https://github.com/dotnet/eShop); this repo is stable and safe to dissect. Everything here was verified against the code on 2026-07-16; see the [verification log](09-reference/verification-log.md).

# NetCalendy — Upskill Curriculum
## What This Is
A structured training lab that uses the NetCalendy codebase as the vehicle to move a learner from junior through mid-level and toward senior engineer. Every concept is anchored to a real file in this repo. The curriculum teaches transferable judgment, not just "here is where the thing lives."
## The Repo in 8 Sentences
NetCalendy is a Calendly-style booking SaaS: hosts define event types (e.g., "30-minute chat"), publish scheduling links, and invitees book slots without creating an account. It is built on **.NET 9 / ASP.NET Core** with **React + Vite + TypeScript** on the frontend. The backend follows **Clean Architecture** — Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and API layers that form a strict inward dependency cone. Business logic lives in the **Domain** layer as aggregates with enforced invariants and domain events; commands and queries live in the **Application** layer using **CQRS via MediatR**. All writes are validated by **FluentValidation** injected as a MediatR pipeline behavior. Persistence uses **EF Core 9 + PostgreSQL** (Npgsql), with tenant isolation enforced per-row by `TenantId` columns. **Multi-tenancy** is resolved from the `X-Tenant-Slug` HTTP header or subdomain, added to the JWT, and read back by `ICurrentTenantService`. The test suite spans three layers: pure domain unit tests, application handler tests with NSubstitute mocks, and full integration tests using `WebApplicationFactory` + **Testcontainers** (a real Postgres instance).
## Learning Stages
| Stage | Mental Question | Observable Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **Orientation** | "Can I run it and name the parts?" | Boot app, call one endpoint, trace one request |
| **Junior** | "How do I make this work?" | Add a field, add a handler, copy existing pattern |
| **Mid-level** | "Is this the right pattern?" | Design cross-layer change, write integration tests, debug from logs |
| **Senior** | "What does this commit us to? Who pays? How do we reduce risk?" | Critique boundaries, identify latent bugs, propose migrations, write RFCs |
Senior mindset line: **a junior ships it; a mid-level asks if it's correct; a senior asks what breaks three months later and whether there's a cheaper way to find out.**

# NetCalendy
A production-grade Calendly-style booking SaaS built with C# / .NET 9 and React.
## Architecture
```
src/
NetCalendy.Domain/        # Aggregates, Value Objects, Domain Events, Repository interfaces
NetCalendy.Application/   # CQRS commands & queries (MediatR), validators (FluentValidation)
NetCalendy.Infrastructure/ # EF Core + PostgreSQL, repository implementations, services
NetCalendy.Api/           # ASP.NET Core controllers, JWT auth, middleware
tests/
NetCalendy.Domain.Tests/        # Pure domain unit tests (xUnit + FluentAssertions)
NetCalendy.Application.Tests/   # Handler unit tests (NSubstitute mocks)
NetCalendy.Integration.Tests/   # End-to-end API tests (WebApplicationFactory + Testcontainers)
web/                        # React + TypeScript + Vite frontend
```
### Key design decisions
| Concern | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture | Clean Architecture / DDD | Domain is dependency-free; infra depends inward |
| CQRS | MediatR | Decoupled handlers, pipeline behaviors for cross-cutting concerns |
| Multi-tenancy | Tenant ID per row | Simple, performant, no schema management overhead |
| Validation | FluentValidation pipeline behavior | Validated before handlers execute; clean error surface |
| Domain events | `IHasDomainEvents` + MediatR `IPublisher` | Events dispatched after `SaveChanges` succeeds |
| Auth | JWT Bearer | Stateless; tenant + user claims in token |
| Integration tests | Testcontainers (real Postgres) | No mock/real divergence risk |

# Architecture
Netgum uses a clean architecture style that keeps business rules independent from HTTP, SQL Server, and vendor integrations.
## Dependency Direction
```text
Netgum.Api -> Netgum.Application -> Netgum.Domain
Netgum.Infrastructure -> Netgum.Application + Netgum.Domain
```
The API hosts the process and maps HTTP requests. The application layer defines use cases and ports. Infrastructure implements those ports with EF Core, logging, fake payments, and fake email. The domain owns marketplace rules.
## Main Use Cases
- Register a creator with a unique slug.
- Create and publish a digital product after at least one asset is attached.
- Add coupons with percentage or fixed-amount discounts.
- Create checkout sessions for published products.
- Complete fake payments and fulfill orders with generated license keys.
- Guard downloads behind a paid order status.
## Extension Points
- Replace `FakePaymentGateway` with a Stripe or Adyen adapter.
- Replace `ConsoleEmailSender` with a transactional email provider.
- Add authentication and require creator ownership on product management endpoints.
- Add webhook endpoints and verify signatures before completing orders.
- Add EF Core migrations once the SDK is available.

# Netgum
Netgum is a learning-oriented, production-shaped clone of Gumroad built with C# and .NET 8. It is not a real commerce product and intentionally uses fake payment and email adapters so you can study the code without vendor accounts.
## What Is Included
- Clean architecture layout: Domain, Application, Infrastructure, API, Tests.
- Creator registration and profile primitives.
- Digital product listings with slugs, prices, assets, variants, publishing, archiving, and coupons.
- Checkout flow with platform fee calculation, fake payment intent creation, order fulfillment, license key generation, and purchase receipt email abstraction.
- EF Core SQL Server persistence mappings, repositories, health checks, Swagger, rate limiting, CORS, structured logging, and RFC7807-style errors.
- xUnit tests for domain rules and the checkout flow.
## Projects
```text
src/Netgum.Domain          Business model and invariants
src/Netgum.Application     Use cases, DTOs, and ports
src/Netgum.Infrastructure  EF Core, repositories, fake payment/email adapters
src/Netgum.Api             Minimal API endpoints and hosting
tests/Netgum.Tests         Focused unit/integration-style tests
```
## Run Locally
This machine currently does not have the `dotnet` CLI on PATH, so I generated the code without restoring or building it. On a machine with the .NET 8 SDK:
```powershell
dotnet restore
dotnet test
dotnet run --project src/Netgum.Api
```
The API will expose Swagger at:
```text
https://localhost:7042/swagger
```

# NetTrello
NetTrello is a Trello-style kanban starter built with C#, ASP.NET Core, React, and TypeScript. It is intentionally structured as a teaching codebase: the app is small enough to read in one sitting, but it uses patterns that scale into production systems.
## What Is Included
- ASP.NET Core API with domain entities, application services, typed contracts, endpoint mapping, centralized errors, security headers, CORS, health checks, and optimistic concurrency.
- React client with TypeScript contracts, a dedicated API client, a board orchestration hook, reusable components, card editing, card archiving, board creation, column creation, and drag/drop card movement.
- In-memory persistence seeded with sample data so the product can run before a database is introduced.
- Production-oriented defaults: nullable C#, warnings as errors, code style enforcement, Dockerfile, environment example, and architecture docs.

Domain/          Business rules and entities

# Fable — Code Review of AtlasWork (PeblClone)
Review date: 2026-07-01. Scope: full repo — .NET backend (Domain / Application / Infrastructure / Api), React frontend (PeblClone.Web), tests, solution/build files, CI.
## Contents
| File | What's in it |
|---|---|
| [issues.md](issues.md) | Concrete bugs and defects, ordered by severity, with file/line references |
| [improvements.md](improvements.md) | Design and quality improvements — not bugs, but things worth changing |
## Overall verdict
The codebase is well-shaped for its stated teaching purpose. The layering is honest (Domain has no dependencies, Application owns use cases and ports, Infrastructure adapts, controllers stay thin), records are immutable, central package management and `TreatWarningsAsErrors` are on, and the frontend keeps API typing and fallback behavior in one place as the README promises.
That said, the review found **one build-blocking defect** (a malformed project-type GUID in `PeblClone.sln` that prevents the solution from loading), **a cluster of correctness bugs around the frontend mock fallback** (it silently bypasses backend validation and business rules), and **a systemic looseness around money** (currencies are echoed, summed, and compared inconsistently — the `Money` type exists but its one safety guarantee is never used where it matters).
## Findings at a glance
| # | Severity | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| I-1 | Blocker | Invalid project-type GUID in `PeblClone.sln` — solution fails to parse |
| I-2 | High | `createQuote` mock fallback bypasses backend validation and availability rules |
| I-3 | High | `formatDate` has a UTC/local off-by-one-day bug for all date-only strings |
| I-4 | High | Dashboard payroll total sums `Money.Amount` across unchecked currencies |
| I-5 | Medium | Quote calculator echoes request currency without conversion; flat USD fees mislabeled |
| I-6 | Medium | `QuoteBuilder` submit has no error handling — unhandled rejection path |
| I-7 | Medium | `npm run lint` is broken — no ESLint 9 flat config exists |
| I-8 | Medium | Unhandled exceptions return bare 500s — `UseExceptionHandler` never wired |
| I-9 | Low | Seed "Today" frozen at process start in a singleton |
| I-10 | Low | `Money` equality vs `Add` treat currency casing inconsistently |
| I-11 | Low

AtlasWork is a teaching-oriented, production-shaped clone of the core product surface behind modern global workforce platforms such as Velocity Global / Pebl: hire, pay, and manage international employees and contractors from one dashboard.

# C# Bootcamp — offline, test-graded, self-paced
A personal coding bootcamp for levelling up C# and .NET fundamentals. Built
to run **fully offline** — every exercise is a single self-contained file
graded by its own tests, runnable with nothing but the .NET SDK.
**Start here → [`FLIGHTPLAN.md`](FLIGHTPLAN.md)** — the ten-hour schedule.
## Quick start (30 seconds)
```bash
dotnet run bootcamp/01-language-core/exercises/01-count-vowels.cs   # any exercise
dotnet run bootcamp/progress.cs                                     # your scoreboard
```
An exercise file is a prompt in comments, a stub that throws, and tests
underneath. You write the code and re-run the file until:
```
✔ counts lowercase vowels
✔ is case-insensitive
✔ handles the empty string
6 passed
all green — next file!
```
No test runner to install, no `.csproj`, no NuGet restore, no watcher —
`dotnet run <file>.cs`, that's the whole workflow. (`☐ todo` = not written
yet · `✘` = failing · `✔` = done · `🐛` = a hunt-module bug you haven't
caught yet.)
### How it works with no project file
.NET 10 runs a **file-based app**: a `.cs` file with top-level statements is
a program. The only thing an exercise needs from outside is the test
harness, and it asks for that with a single directive at the top:
```csharp

They are not a test you pass; they are a retrieval exercise. **Say the

# GPT Code Review Findings
Review date: 2026-07-25
Scope: `apps/api`, `apps/redirect`, `apps/web`, `packages/shared`, `packages/analytics`, Prisma schema/migrations, tests, and CI configuration.
## Executive summary
The project has a solid foundation: tenant and role checks are consistently applied to protected API routes, input schemas cover most write operations, postbacks use raw-body HMAC verification, payout creation uses a database advisory lock, uploaded images are inspected by content, and the codebase has meaningful unit and integration coverage.
The highest-priority risks are:
1. Long-lived refresh tokens are readable by browser JavaScript.
2. The installed production dependency tree contains five high-severity vulnerable packages.
3. A fraud rule calculates IP concentration across an entire affiliate/campaign instead of the cookie being scored, allowing suspicious traffic to evade that signal.
4. Concurrent conversion reversals can apply the same paid-commission clawback more than once.
No application code was changed as part of this review.
## Findings
### CR-01 — High: refresh tokens are exposed to any same-origin script
Evidence:
- [`apps/web/src/lib/api.ts`](../apps/web/src/lib/api.ts) stores both the access token and the 30-day refresh token in `localStorage`.
- [`apps/api/src/services/auth.service.ts`](../apps/api/src/services/auth.service.ts) accepts the same refresh token repeatedly until it expires or the user's global `tokenVersion` changes.
Impact:
Any XSS, compromised third-party script, or malicious browser extension with page access can extract a credential that remains useful for up to 30 days. Because refresh tokens are not rotated, stealing one once is enough to mint new access tokens repeatedly. Logging out revokes every session for the user, but there is no per-session revocation or stolen-token reuse detection.
Recommendation:
- Put the refresh token in a `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, appropriately scoped `SameSite` cookie.
- Keep the access token in memory rather than persistent browser storage.
- Rotate refresh tokens on every use and persist a hashed session/token-family record.
- Revoke the token family when an already-rotated token is reused.
- Add CSRF protection if the final cookie and cross-site deployment configuration requires

# Upskill Curriculum
This curriculum turns the Agentic Help Desk repository into a training lab for a junior engineer growing toward mid-level and senior judgment. It is for learners who want to read real code, make safe changes, explain tradeoffs, and practice interview-ready engineering thinking using this exact codebase.
## Repo Identity
This is a TypeScript modular monolith for an internal help desk and incident intelligence platform. The web app lives in `apps/web`, and shared packages live in `packages/*` through npm workspaces (`package.json:6-9`). The product surface includes tickets, incidents, structured logs, background jobs, audit events, and deterministic mock agents. Persistence is modeled in Prisma (`packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:111-281`). Mutations happen mostly through Next.js server actions (`apps/web/lib/actions.ts:41-530`). Business invariants live in `packages/domain`, especially ticket transitions and SLA rules (`packages/domain/src/tickets.ts:34-89`). # Five-Sprint Feature Roadmap
This roadmap turns the Agentic Help Desk app into a realistic training project for a junior software engineer. The point is not just to add features. The point is to practice how real product work moves from user stories to design, implementation, tests, review, release, and retrospective learning.
The app is already a TypeScript modular monolith with Next.js App Router pages, Prisma persistence, domain packages, deterministic agents, audit events, and Vitest coverage. The sprint docs below build on those existing boundaries instead of inventing a new architecture.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sprint One](sprint-one/README.md) | Support Triage and Ownership | Support agents can find, claim, assign, and explain ticket changes faster. | UI filters, server actions, domain rules, audit events, permissions, focused tests. |

# Codebase Cartography
Cartography is the skill of forming a reliable map before changing code. In this repo, the important move is to distinguish product surfaces from ownership boundaries:
- UI pages: `apps/web/app/*`
- server actions: `apps/web/lib/actions.ts`
- domain rules: `packages/domain/src/*`
- persistence: `packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma`
- deterministic agents: `packages/agents/src/*`
- reusable UI: `packages/ui/src/*`
- tests: `tests/*.test.ts`
Use this module before making contributions. Do not start by changing the first file that looks relevant.

# Mission Learning Path Suite
Welcome to the Mission Learning Path. This suite is not documentation to be read passively; it is an active training campaign. You are not reading—you are executing missions to build your muscle memory and intuition within this specific codebase.
## How to Use This Suite
Each mission forces you to trace code, answer questions, review logic, debug issues, or explain patterns.

# 🎓 EduOps Platform: Architecture Manual & Training Laboratory
Welcome to the **Agentic Education Operations & LMS** architecture guide. This codebase is designed as an upskilling platform and learning laboratory for software engineers. It models a production-grade enterprise system utilizing a modern, decoupled **Modular Monolith** structure in TypeScript.
---
## 1. System Topology & Architectural Monolith
Rather than a tangled web of imports, this project organizes the application into distinct virtual packages inside `src/packages/`. This mimics a highly scalable corporate ecosystem while keeping the deployment profile local and simple.
```mermaid
graph TD
UI[App router Pages & Server Actions] --> |Invokes| Agents[packages/agents - Mock AI Orchestration]
UI --> |Invokes| Observability[packages/observability - Logs & Jobs]
UI --> |Validates| Domain[packages/domain - Pure Business Rules]
Agents --> |Calculates| Domain
Agents --> |Persists| DB[packages/db - Cached Prisma DB]
Observability --> |Triggers Recalcs| Domain
Observability --> |Persists Logs| DB
Domain --> |Zero Dependencies| PureRules[Pure TypeScript functions]
```
### Decoupled Packages
1. **`@/db` (Database Access)**: A centralized, singleton instance of the Prisma Client, configured to prevent SQLite resource leaks during Next.js Hot Module Replacement (HMR).
2. **`@/domain` (Core Business Rules)**: Zero-dependency, pure mathematical and logical formulas. Contains no knowledge of database models, SQL, ORM, or Next.js layout configurations.
3. **`@/observability` (Telemetry & Jobs)**: Manages structured log aggregation, error fingerprint calculations, transactional audit event logging, and the background job execution loop.
4. **`@/agents` (Mock Heuristic AI Engine)**: Standardizes simulated AI prompts. Houses 5 deterministic reasoning engines that generate structured findings, data limitations, and sequential Chain-of-Thought logs.
5. **`@/shared` (Common Utilities)**: Shared enums, types, date-formatting tools, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) permission maps.
---

# 🎓 EduOps Platform
A school operations cockpit built as a **software engineering training laboratory**.
Students, teachers, courses, sections, enrollments, assignments, grades, attendance and
counselling interventions — wrapped in a production-shaped observability layer (structured
logs, audit events, a background job queue) and an **agent layer** of five deterministic
analysts that read the database, reason in traceable steps, and persist reports you can
inspect.

```

## Why this repo exists
Two things are being taught here at once.
**1. How a real application is structured.** This is a *modular monolith*: five virtual
packages with an enforced dependency direction, business rules isolated as pure functions,
mutations that audit themselves, and slow work pushed to a queue.
**2. How real engineering work is delivered.** Every feature in this repo arrived through
a branch, a series of explained commits, and a pull request. The git history is not
exhaust — it is the curriculum. Read it:
```bash
git log --oneline --graph --all
```
Start with [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md), which documents the exact workflow every
commit here follows and why each convention exists.

# Tier 1: Junior Missions
Welcome to Tier 1. Your goal is to map the physical terrain of the codebase. You are not building anything yet; you are learning how to read the map.
---
### Mission 1: The App's Heartbeat
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 10 minutes
**Goal:** Prove that you know how the server determines "who" is looking at the screen.
**The Concept:** Every interaction in this app requires a "badge scan." The server must know who you are before it shows you data or lets you change it. In a normal app, this is a complex JWT validation middleware. Here, it is drastically simplified for training.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:**
We expect to find a function that reads a cookie from the incoming request, looks up a user in the database matching that cookie, and returns their profile. If they don't have a cookie, it should probably default to someone safe so the app doesn't crash during local dev.
**Find It In The Code:**
Open `src/packages/shared/auth.ts`.
Read the `getActiveUser` function (Lines 18-51).
*Annotations to follow:*
- Notice `cookies().get('mock_user_id')`. This relies heavily on Next.js server context.
- Notice the fallback: `where: { username: 'admin' }`. This is a deliberate choice to make local onboarding frictionless, avoiding login screens entirely.
**The Aha Moment:** The server *pretends* someone is logged in if they don't have a cookie, ensuring the developer can immediately see the UI.
**Socratic Checkpoint:**
1. What happens if the `admin` user is deleted from the SQLite database?
2. Does this function run in the user's browser, or on the server?
3. What is the return type of `getActiveUser`?
*How to self-grade:*
1. The app will throw a fatal error: `❌ Critical Setup Error: No admin user found`.
2. It runs entirely on the server. `cookies()` from `next/headers` is a server-only API.
3. It returns a Promise resolving to `ActiveSession`, which contains the `UserRole` and `profileId`.
**Connects To:** Mission 2 (Your First React Component) heavily relies on calling `getActiveUser()`.
---
### Mission 2: Your First React Component
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 15 minutes
**Goal:** Understand how a page fetches data and renders it without any loading spinners.
**The Concept:** Imagine going to a restaurant where the chef already knows what you want, cooks it before you sit down, and hands you the plate the second you pull out your chair. That's a React Server Component.

# Agentic Education Operations
Agentic Education Operations is a TypeScript modular-monolith learning project that emulates the start of a realistic internal education operations and LMS platform.
It includes teacher, student, course, section, term, guardian, enrollment, assignment, rubric, submission, gradebook, attendance, intervention, approval, notification, logs, jobs, audit, and deterministic mock-agent workflows. No Tailwind, no real LLM APIs, and no external API keys are used.

- Zod validation and domain rules in `packages/domain`
- Local deterministic mock agents in `packages/agents`
- Structured logging and audit helpers in `packages/observability`

# Architecture Overview
This project is an internal education operations and learning management platform. It models records and workflows for teachers, students, courses, class sections, enrollments, assignments, submissions, grades, attendance, support notes, intervention plans, jobs, structured logs, audit events, and mock agent analysis.
## Major Modules
- `apps/web`: Next.js App Router UI, route handlers through server actions, layout, pages, and application workflows.
- `packages/db`: Prisma schema, Prisma Client singleton, and deterministic seed data.
- `packages/domain`: business rules, validations, calculations, and risk scoring.
- `packages/agents`: deterministic local mock agent framework and initial agent implementations.
- `packages/observability`: structured log helpers, audit metadata helpers, and anomaly scoring utilities.
- `packages/ui`: small reusable UI primitives and CSS-variable design system.
- `packages/shared`: shared enums, labels, role helpers, and formatting utilities.
## Modular Monolith
The app is intentionally one deployable system with clear internal module boundaries. That makes it easier to learn than microservices while still teaching production ideas:
- domain logic is isolated from React
- data access is centralized through Prisma
- agents are replaceable components with stable interfaces
- UI pages compose services rather than owning business rules
- audit, logs, and jobs are first-class operational concepts
## Data Flow
Typical write flow:
1. User submits a form in `apps/web/app/**`.
2. A server action in `apps/web/lib/actions.ts` parses form data.
3. Zod schemas and domain rules validate the request.
4. Prisma writes to PostgreSQL.
5. Audit events are written for important actions.
6. Next.js revalidates affected routes.
## Request Flow
Pages are React Server Components. They query Prisma directly for read-heavy views and call pure domain functions for derived values such as grade summaries, risk scores, attendance summaries, and workload scores.
## Where Logic Lives
- Business logic: `packages/domain/src`
- Agent logic: `packages/agents/src`
- Database schema and seed: `packages/db/prisma`
- Database client: `packages/db/src/index.ts`

# Junior-To-Mid-Level Learning Plan

Day 1: Read the README and architecture overview. Run the app and seed data.
Day 2: Read `schema.prisma`. Draw the entity relationship map.
Day 3: Read `seed.ts`. Explain the Maya scenario in your own words.
Day 4: Study `grades.ts`, `attendance.ts`, and `risk.ts`. Run tests.
Day 5: Modify one grade rule and update tests.
Day 6: Trace enrollment from UI to `decideEnrollment`.
Day 7: Add one validation test and one domain edge-case test.
Day 8: Study `agents/src/types.ts` and `registry.ts`.
Day 9: Run every agent from the UI and inspect `/agent-runs/[id]`.
Day 10: Add a small field to an agent trace and test it.
Day 11: Debug a failed job using `/jobs`, `/logs`, and `/audit-events`.
Day 12: Add a new dashboard card using existing domain logic.
Day 13: Review server actions and list where audit events are written.
Day 14: Present the architecture, risks, and extension plan as if in an interview.

# Phase 1: Architecture Stabilization
Phase 1 was about making the existing MVP easier to extend safely. The product surface stayed mostly the same, but the internal architecture changed from "pages and one giant server-action file orchestrate everything" to a cleaner request path:
`page -> server action -> application service -> domain rule/db/audit`
## Why This Phase Matters
The original codebase had good package boundaries for domain logic and agents, but `apps/web/lib/actions.ts` had become a large coordination file. That is common in early Next.js apps: server actions start small, then slowly absorb validation, authorization, database writes, audit logging, agent orchestration, and redirect behavior.
That pattern is fine for a prototype, but it becomes harder to evolve because:
- authorization is easy to forget
- multi-write operations are not consistently transactional
- pages duplicate read-model calculations
- agent persistence is mixed with UI concerns
- tests have fewer stable seams
- future features require editing one central file too often
Phase 1 creates those seams.
## What Changed
### Added `packages/application`
New package:
```text
packages/application
src/context.ts
src/errors.ts
src/audit.ts
src/services/*
src/queries/*
```
This package owns application use cases. It is intentionally different from `packages/domain`:
- `domain` decides business rules using pure functions.
- `application` coordinates workflows using domain rules, Prisma, permissions, transactions, audit events, and agents.
This is still a modular monolith. Nothing became a microservice.
## Service Layer
The previous `actions.ts` implementation contained all write workflows. These now live in services:
- `teacherService`
- `studentService`

# Architecture
## Modular Monolith
GlobalWorkforce OS is built as a **Modular Monolith**. Instead of splitting the application into microservices, we keep all business logic within a single deployable backend (NestJS). This approach is chosen because:
1. **Reduced Operational Complexity**: Easier to deploy, test, and run locally.
2. **Data Consistency**: Easy to manage transactions across domains (e.g., completing an onboarding task automatically updates the worker's status).
3. **Refactoring**: Easier to refactor code and boundaries before network boundaries are introduced.
## Directory Structure
The repository is a Monorepo managed with npm workspaces:
- `apps/web`: React SPA built with Vite.
- `apps/api`: NestJS REST API.
- `packages/shared`: Shared TypeScript types, enums, and Zod schemas.
## Backend (NestJS + Prisma)
- **Controllers**: Handle incoming HTTP requests, route them to services, and format responses.
- **Services**: Contain the core business logic.
- **Prisma**: Acts as our ORM. It provides a strongly typed database client and handles migrations.
- **Guards**: `JwtAuthGuard`, `RolesGuard`, and `TenantGuard` protect routes and enforce authorization at the request level.
## Frontend (React + Vite)
- **Component-Driven**: UI is built with reusable React components.
- **State Management**: React Query handles server state (caching, fetching, mutating). Local state is handled via React hooks.
- **Routing**: React Router handles SPA navigation.
- **Forms**: React Hook Form combined with Zod for robust client-side validation.
## Database (PostgreSQL)
A relational database is crucial for an EOR platform due to complex relationships (Tenants -> Companies -> Workers -> Contracts) and strict data integrity requirements. Prisma handles schema modeling and migrations.

# GlobalWorkforce OS
A production-minded, multi-tenant Employer of Record (EOR) operations platform built as a learning resource for software engineers.
## Features
- **Multi-Tenancy**: Data is strictly isolated between client organizations.
- **Role-Based Access Control**: 5 distinct roles (`PLATFORM_ADMIN`, `INTERNAL_OPS`, `CLIENT_ADMIN`, `CLIENT_HR`, `WORKER`).
- **Domain Logic**: Complex state transitions for Contracts, Onboarding, and Payroll.
- **Audit Logging**: Automatic tracking of critical actions.
- **Monorepo**: Shared validation and types between frontend and backend.
## Tech Stack
- **Frontend**: React, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, React Query, React Hook Form, Zod.
- **Backend**: Node.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL.
- **Testing**: Jest, Playwright.
## Setup Instructions
1. **Prerequisites**: Node v18+, Docker.
2. **Install**: `npm install`
3. **Database**: `docker-compose up -d` (Requires Docker Desktop running)
4. **Migrate & Seed**:
```bash
npm run prisma:migrate
npm run prisma:seed
```
5. **Start**: `npm run dev`
*(Note: If Docker is not running, the application cannot connect to the database. You will need to install PostgreSQL locally or start the Docker daemon).*
## Demo Accounts
Use password: `Password123!`
- `platform.admin@example.com` (All access)
- `ops@example.com` (Internal Operations)
- `client.admin@acme.example.com` (Client Admin)

# Learning Guide for Junior to Mid-Level Engineers
Welcome to GlobalWorkforce OS! If you are a junior engineer looking to level up your architectural understanding, this project is designed for you.
## How to Read This Codebase
Don't read it top-to-bottom. Start with the data model (`apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma`). Understand the relationship between `Tenant`, `Company`, and `Worker`.
Next, look at the authentication flow: `apps/api/src/auth`. Understand how a user logs in and receives a JWT.
Then, pick one feature (like `Workers`) and trace a request from the frontend UI (`apps/web/src/pages/Workers`), to the API Client, to the NestJS Controller, down to the Service, and finally to the Prisma query.
## Key Concepts to Master
1. **Multi-Tenancy**: How do we ensure Client A cannot see Client B's data? Look at `TenantGuard` and how `tenantId` is passed into Prisma `where` clauses.
2. **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**: How do we prevent a `WORKER` from approving a payroll cycle? Look at `RolesGuard`.
3. **Validation Boundary**: Where is data validated? Look at the Zod schemas in `packages/shared` and how they are used by React Hook Form (frontend) and validation pipes (backend).
## 10 Learning Tasks to Modify the App
1. **Add a new field**: Add a `middleName` field to the Worker model. Update the DB, backend DTOs, and frontend forms.
2. **Enhance Audit Logs**: Currently, audit logs might only trigger on a few actions. Add an interceptor to automatically log whenever an entity is updated.
3. **Build a Workflow Engine**: When a contract is signed, automatically mark the associated onboarding task as DONE.
4. **Implement Soft Delete**: Instead of deleting workers, implement a `deletedAt` field and update queries to ignore deleted records.
5. **Add Pagination**: The worker list currently returns all workers. Add limit/offset parameters to the API and a paginated table component on the frontend.
6. **Feature Flags**: Introduce a simple feature flag service to hide the "Benefits" tab from certain tenants.
7. **File Uploads**: Replace the simulated document upload with a real integration to AWS S3.
8. **Email Notifications**: Add an event emitter when a support case is created, and simulate sending an email.
9. **Extract a Microservice**: The `SupportCases` domain is fairly isolated. Try extracting it into a separate NestJS app.
10. **Write an E2E Test**: Add a new Playwright test for the payroll approval flow.
## 10 Interview Talking Points from this Project
If you study this project, you can confidently discuss:
1. "I built a multi-tenant architecture using

# Extension Roadmap
This MVP serves as a learning foundation. A real EOR platform would need the following extensions:
## 1. Real Document Storage
Currently, document uploads are simulated metadata updates. This needs to be integrated with AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage, along with pre-signed URLs for secure access.
## 2. Background Jobs & Workflow Engine
Payroll generation, report compilation, and sending bulk emails should not happen synchronously. A message queue (RabbitMQ, Redis + BullMQ, Kafka) is needed to process these jobs in the background.
## 3. Webhooks & Integrations
Client companies need to synchronize data with their internal HRIS (Workday, BambooHR). We need an outbound webhook system and public API keys.
## 4. Advanced Compliance Engine
Instead of static rules, the compliance engine should be a rule-based system (e.g., using a rules engine library) that evaluates worker country, visa status, and role to dynamically generate required documents.
## 5. Analytics & Reporting
Integrate a proper analytics pipeline (e.g., Snowflake, dbt, Looker) or build materialized views in PostgreSQL for complex payroll and workforce reporting.
## 6. Microservice Extraction
As the team grows, the `Payroll` module is the most likely candidate for extraction into a separate microservice, as it has high security and performance isolation requirements.

# Architecture
## Backend
The backend follows a clean architecture shape:
- `BuildAsana.Domain`: enterprise work-management concepts and business rules. Entities know how to protect their own invariants, such as invalid task estimates or self-dependencies.
- `BuildAsana.Application`: use cases, DTO contracts, access policy, dashboard aggregation, automation execution, and audit logging.
- `BuildAsana.Infrastructure`: current repository adapter. It is in-memory by design so the learning path stays clear, but the application layer only depends on `IWorkManagementRepository`.
- `BuildAsana.Api`: HTTP boundary. It extracts a demo user from headers, maps failures to problem responses, and groups work endpoints under `/api/work`.
This keeps business behavior away from ASP.NET details and makes persistence replaceable.
## Frontend
The frontend is organized by feature:
- `src/lib`: shared types, API client, mock seed data, and local optimistic state helpers.
- `src/features/dashboard`: portfolio and capacity views.
- `src/features/tasks`: operational board and task movement.
- `src/App.tsx`: shell, navigation, view composition, and top-level data orchestration.
The API client tries the .NET API first. If it is unavailable, it falls back to mock data with the same shape. That lets you learn React composition immediately, then study the backend integration separately.
## Production Upgrade Path
Good next steps:
- Replace `InMemoryWorkManagementRepository` with EF Core and PostgreSQL.
- Add real authentication using OpenID Connect, tenant-aware authorization, and signed audit identity.
- Add command validation with a validation pipeline.
- Introduce optimistic concurrency for task updates.
- Add domain events for automation execution and notifications.
- Add pagination, filtering, and saved views for larger workspaces.
- Add frontend tests for board interactions and API failure states.
- Add CI that runs `dotnet test`, `npm run build`, and linting on every pull request.

# BuildAsana
BuildAsana is an Asana-inspired work management system built for learning production-quality C#, .NET, and React patterns. It is intentionally scoped as a serious scaffold rather than a tiny clone: it models projects, tasks, capacity, goals, automations, approvals, RBAC, audit events, and executive portfolio health.
## Stack
- Backend: ASP.NET Core 8 minimal API, clean architecture, domain entities, application services, repository abstraction, in-memory infrastructure adapter.
- Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, typed API client, resilient mock fallback, responsive enterprise workspace UI.
- Tests: xUnit application-service tests.
## Features Modeled
- Project and task tracking with status, priority, due dates, estimates, tags, dependencies, comments, and approval requirements.
- Enterprise controls: role-aware writes, audit trail, explicit access policy, automation execution hooks.
- Portfolio dashboards: completion rate, blocked work, at-risk work, project health, workload/capacity utilization.
- Goals/OKRs with progress tracking.
- Automation rules for trigger/action workflows.
- Frontend fallback data so you can study and iterate on UI patterns without running the API.

# MarketForge
MarketForge is a production-style multi-vendor marketplace codebase. It models a buyer storefront, seller operations portal, and platform admin console with shared domain rules, typed API routes, Prisma persistence, Redis-backed security primitives, and Stripe Connect payment boundaries.
This repository is intentionally scaffolded without installing dependencies or running services. The code is written as if it were a corporate production application, but Docker, npm install, database provisioning, and third-party credentials are left to the learner.
## Stack
- Next.js App Router with React Server Components
- TypeScript with strict compiler settings
- Prisma with PostgreSQL
- Redis for rate limits, refresh-token families, sessions, and cache
- Stripe Connect for marketplace payments and seller payouts
- Zod-style request validation
- Pino-style structured logging
- Vitest and Playwright test targets
## Project Layout
- `app/`: Next.js routes, route handlers, and web entry points.
- `src/components/`: reusable UI components for marketplace, seller, admin, and shell surfaces.
- `src/domain/`: pure business rules: checkout splitting, order state machines, seller approval rules, RBAC.
- `src/server/`: infrastructure adapters for database, auth, payments, cache, validation, logging, and API responses.
- `prisma/`: production-grade relational data model.
- `tests/`: unit, integration, and E2E test targets.
- `docs/`: architecture notes, ADRs, and the older static prototype.
## Learning Order

This curriculum turns BuildJira into a training lab for a junior engineer growing toward mid-level and senior engineering judgment. # Feature Walkthroughs
## Book Appointment
1. Frontend loads services, staff, and slots.
2. User chooses local time and timezone.
3. Backend converts local input to UTC.
4. Backend validates availability and conflicts.
5. Appointment, activity, audit, and notification records are created together.
## Cancel Appointment
1. Lifecycle endpoint validates the state transition.
2. Appointment is marked cancelled.
3. Future reminders are cancelled.
4. Cancellation notification is queued.
5. Activity and audit records are created.
## Reschedule Appointment
1. User provides a new local time and timezone.
2. Backend converts that local time to UTC.
3. Conflict detection re-runs on the new slot.
4. Reminder records are regenerated.
5. Activity and audit records capture the old and new time.
## Create Recurring Appointments
1. Series metadata is stored.
2. Concrete occurrences are generated in local time.
3. Each occurrence is converted to UTC for storage.
4. Any conflict fails the full series in the MVP design.

# Architecture
## Core Rules
- Store appointment timestamps in UTC.
- Preserve the original timezone for display and recurrence logic.
- Keep business logic in services, not controllers.
- Separate slot generation from booking confirmation.
- Recheck availability and conflicts inside a transaction when booking.
## Backend Shape
- `routes` parse HTTP concerns
- `controllers` translate requests into service calls
- `services` hold business logic
- `repositories` isolate persistence details where logic grows
- `middleware` handles auth, validation, and errors
- `shared/utils` centralizes timezone and scheduling helpers
## Frontend Shape
- `api/` wraps HTTP calls
- `features/` groups pages, hooks, and components by domain
- `auth.store.ts` keeps auth/session state in Zustand
- TanStack Query owns server-state fetching and mutation
- Route protection happens with `RequireAuth` and `RequireRole`
## Scheduling Design
- Availability windows define potential bookable ranges.
- Slot generation evaluates service duration, buffers, blocked windows, and existing appointments.
- Booking performs a second conflict check inside a transaction.
- Recurring appointments generate concrete appointment instances for later cancellation, reminders, and reporting.
## Appointment Lifecycle
- `REQUESTED -> CONFIRMED`
- `REQUESTED -> CANCELLED`

# Testing Guide
- Unit tests should cover overlap logic, timezone conversion, state transitions, slot generation, and recurrence.
- Integration tests should cover slot generation, booking conflicts, cancellation, rescheduling, and authorization.
- E2E tests should validate the scheduling flow through the UI.
Suggested backend integration scenarios:
1. Create service, staff profile, and availability window.
2. Generate slots for a date and timezone.
3. Book an appointment into one of those slots.
4. Attempt a conflicting booking and expect `409`.
5. Reschedule to an open slot and verify reminder regeneration.
6. Cancel and verify pending notifications move to `CANCELLED`.
Suggested frontend scenarios:
1. Login as scheduler.
2. Visit dashboard and ensure summary widgets render.
3. Open booking flow, choose service/staff/date, and submit.
4. Open appointment detail and cancel or reschedule.
5. Switch calendar timezone and verify rendering changes.

# Learning Guide
Scheduling systems look simple until timezone, daylight saving time, overlap detection, and race conditions enter the picture.
Study this codebase in this order:
1. Prisma schema
2. RBAC permissions
3. Timezone utilities
4. Overlap detection
5. Slot generation
6. Booking transaction
7. Recurrence generation
8. Notification job flow
What to watch for while studying:
- Slot generation is advisory. Booking is authoritative.
- UTC storage solves only storage and comparison, not recurrence intent.
- Back-to-back appointments are not overlaps unless buffers extend them into each other.
- Reminder scheduling is a separate concern from booking confirmation.
- Calendar pages become state-heavy quickly because timezone, filters, and range selection all interact.

# Scheduling + Appointment Platform
Full-stack scheduling platform scaffolded with React, TypeScript, Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Redis, BullMQ, JWT auth, RBAC, and scheduling-focused backend architecture.
## What This Project Covers
This codebase is intentionally broad and architecture-heavy so it can be studied like a realistic production project. It covers:
- Authentication with access and refresh token flows
- RBAC-oriented route protection
- User, staff, customer, and service management
- Staff-service assignments
- Availability windows and blocked time
- Timezone-safe slot generation
- Transactional appointment booking
- Appointment lifecycle actions: cancel, reschedule, complete, no-show
- Recurring appointment series with concrete generated instances
- Notification and reminder records plus BullMQ worker structure
- Calendar and dashboard endpoints
- Frontend feature slices for dashboard, booking, appointments, calendar, availability, staff, customers, and services
- Test scaffolds and documentation for study
## Quick Start
```bash
cp .env.example backend/.env
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d
npm install
npm --workspace backend run prisma:generate
npm --workspace backend run prisma:migrate
npm run dev
```
Backend: `http://localhost:4000`
Frontend: `http://localhost:5173`

1. [backend/prisma/schema.prisma](C:/Users/Owner/Desktop/buildScedulingPYJS/backend/prisma/schema.prisma)
2. [backend/src/shared/utils/timezones.ts](C:/Users/Owner/Desktop/buildScedulingPYJS/backend/src/shared/utils/timezones.ts)

# System Architecture Overview
## High-Level Structure
- Framework: Next.js App Router with server route handlers under `src/app/api` and UI pages/components under `src/app` and `src/components`.
- Storage: SQLite via Prisma ORM; data model lives in `prisma/schema.prisma`.
- Client cache: React Query handles read caching and invalidation after mutations.
- Offline writes: Dexie (IndexedDB) queues mutations, replayed through `/api/sync`.
## Core Data Domains
- Identity/session: User, Session, UserSettings.
- Planning hierarchy: Area -> Project -> Task.
- Daily execution: DayPlan, DayTask, ScheduleBlock, TimeEntry.
- Tracking goals: Goal + DashboardWidget.
## Request and Mutation Flow
- UI issues reads with `apiFetch` + React Query (`TodayClient` is the main orchestrator).
- UI issues writes through `useOfflineMutation`.
- If online: write goes directly to route handlers.
- If offline: write payload is queued in IndexedDB.
- On reconnect: `useOfflineSync` sends queue to `POST /api/sync`.
- Server replays each mutation in `src/lib/sync.ts` with last-write-wins checks.
## Auth and User Resolution
- Shared auth helpers in `src/lib/auth.ts`.
- Routes call `withUser` from `src/lib/api.ts` for user-scoped access.
- Current behavior supports no-sign-in usage by resolving/creating a local default user.
## Today Page Composition
- Container: `src/components/today/today-client.tsx`.
- Checklist row: `TaskRow`.
- Schedule row: `ScheduleBlockRow`.
- Offline visibility: `OfflineBanner` in `AppShell`.
- Timer actions hit `/api/time-entries`, which delegates invariants to `src/lib/timer.ts`.

Master Life Plan is a personal planning web app for organizing long-term structure and daily execution:

- Daily checklist-first workflow with timers and manual time editing
- Locked 30-minute schedule blocks (no auto-shift)

# Feature: Prerequisites and Learning Paths
## Goal
Support ordered learning journeys and course dependencies.
## Impacted Areas of the Codebase
- Prisma models: `LearningPath`, `LearningPathItem`, `CoursePrerequisite`.
- Catalog course detail includes prerequisites.
## Implementation Approach
Learning paths are ordered collections of courses. Prerequisites connect a course to required prior courses.
## Design Considerations
Prerequisites are graph-like data; future work should detect cycles and enforce completion before enrollment.
## Build Journal
Implemented schema support and API include for prerequisites.
A junior developer should learn to separate roadmap structure from course content itself.

# Code Walkthroughs for Important Files
These walkthroughs cover the most architecturally important files in the first codebase. Read them in this order when learning the system.
## `apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma`
### What the File Does
Defines the product database model: organizations, users, memberships, courses, versions, modules, lessons, enrollments, progress, quizzes, assignments, certificates, reporting support, audit logs, events, and operational records.
### Why It Exists
In a business application, the schema is a large part of the architecture. The API and frontend are easier to understand after you understand the nouns and relationships.
### Connections
- Seed data in `apps/api/prisma/seed.ts` creates realistic rows for this schema.
- API routes query and mutate these models.
- Domain helpers assume the same conceptual boundaries: content is separate from progress, definitions are separate from attempts/submissions.
### Important Sections
- `Course` and `CourseVersion`: stable course identity versus published/draft content.
- `Enrollment` and `LessonProgress`: learner state.
- `Quiz`, `QuizQuestion`, `QuizAttempt`: assessment definition versus attempt history.
- `Certificate`: generated artifact and verification record.
- `DomainEvent` and `OutboxMessage`: async integration boundary.
### Senior-Level Concepts
The schema protects historical truth. Learners enroll in a course version, so later authoring changes do not rewrite what they completed.
### How to Read It
Start with `Organization`, `User`, and `Membership`, then follow one course through `CourseVersion`, `Module`, `Lesson`, `Enrollment`, `LessonProgress`, `QuizAttempt`, `AssignmentSubmission`, and `Certificate`.
## `packages/domain/src/authorization.ts`
### What the File Does
Provides shared authorization helpers for role checks and sensitive actions.
### Why It Exists
Permissions are business rules. They should not be scattered across controllers and UI components.
### Connections
- API middleware uses these helpers.

# Final System Design
## Repository Structure
- `apps/api`: Express modular monolith API with Prisma.
- `apps/web`: Next.js SaaS frontend.
- `apps/worker`: BullMQ worker process.
- `packages/domain`: shared business rules and tests.
- `docs/architecture`: architecture planning, journal, and final design.
- `docs/features`: feature plans and build journals.
- `docs/code-walkthroughs`: guided reading for important files.
- `docs/backlog`: phased product backlog.
## Major Modules
### Identity and Authorization
Users belong to organizations through memberships. Membership roles are `LEARNER`, `INSTRUCTOR`, `ORG_ADMIN`, and `ADMIN`. API middleware loads the current user and checks organization-scoped roles.
### Content and Authoring
Courses are stable product records. Course versions hold publishable learning content. Modules and lessons belong to versions. This separation lets instructors draft future versions without changing what learners already enrolled in.
### Learner Activity
Enrollments connect users to course versions. Lesson progress, quiz attempts, assignment submissions, and certificates are separate records so the system can report and audit learning history.
### Assessment
Quizzes have definitions, questions, options, attempt policies, randomized question order, and attempts. Assignments have definitions, submissions, rubrics, grading state, score, and feedback.
### Certification
Certificates are generated artifacts with verification codes and revocation status. They are issued after completion rules are met.
### Reporting and Administration
Admin routes expose dashboards, organization reports, transcripts, audit logs, bulk import, CSV export requests, feature flags, impersonation, and API key management.
### Async Platform
Domain events and outbox messages record asynchronous work. The worker processes certificates, notifications, video assets, and outbox dispatch with retry policies.
## Key Workflows
1. Instructor creates a course and draft course version.
2. Instructor adds modules, lessons, quizzes, assignments, and rubrics.

The initial architecture uses a TypeScript monorepo with a modular monolith backend. - Course content lives under `CourseVersion`.
- Learner state lives under `Enrollment`, `LessonProgress`, `QuizAttempt`, and `AssignmentSubmission`.

## 2026-05-03 - Project Framing
We are building a fictional Employer of Record platform called GlobalWork. An EOR platform lets client companies hire workers in countries where the client may not have a local legal entity. That domain is useful for growth because it contains many real production concerns:
- Multi-tenant data access: one client must never see another client's workers, payroll, documents, or invoices.
- Workflow state: hires, documents, payroll cycles, expenses, and invoices all move through controlled states.
- Sensitive data: identity documents, compensation, tax details, and bank details require careful permissions and auditing.
- Operational queues: internal teams need dashboards for work that is pending, blocked, overdue, or risky.
- Background work: notifications, payroll cycle generation, invoice creation, document reminders, and email retries cannot all happen inline in HTTP requests.

The project is intentionally a modular monolith. That means one deployable backend application, but code is organized into domain modules with explicit boundaries. This gives us the learning benefits of enterprise architecture without the accidental complexity of microservices.
