# Plane Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from the Plane codebase for one learner: a **junior fullstack JS engineer** (React/Node/TS CRUD background) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles. Every module teaches two things at once: *where things live in this repo* and *the transferable pattern you can name in any repo — and in an interview*.
## What this repo is
Plane (v1.3.1, AGPL-3.0) is an open-source project management platform — work items, cycles (sprints), modules, pages, intake, and public publishing — positioned against Jira/Linear. It is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo with three React Router 7 + Vite + MobX SPAs (`apps/web` the main app, `apps/admin` instance admin, `apps/space` anonymous/public site), a Django REST Framework API with Celery background workers (`apps/api`), and a Node.js real-time collaboration server built on Hocuspocus/Yjs for collaborative page editing (`apps/live`). Sixteen shared packages carry the TipTap editor, typed API clients, UI kit, types, and i18n. Persistence is Postgres (plus Redis/Valkey for cache + pubsub, RabbitMQ for Celery, MinIO/S3 for files, optional Mongo for webhook logs). A Caddy proxy fronts everything (`apps/proxy`). One codebase spans two languages, five runtimes, and every architectural boundary a mid-level interview can ask about — that's why it makes a good gym.
Unusual for its size: the frontend is a client-only SPA (no SSR data loading), the Django API disables CSRF for its session-cookie REST endpoints (`apps/api/plane/authentication/session.py:8-11` — studied in the security module), and CE/EE editions are split by module aliasing rather than branches.

# Payload CMS — Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from the Payload CMS monorepo (`payload-monorepo` v4.0.0-beta.0) for one specific learner: a **junior fullstack JS engineer** (React/Node/TS CRUD experience) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every module teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, its failure modes, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is
Payload is an open-source, TypeScript-first headless CMS and application framework that installs natively into a Next.js app. A single **config object** (collections, globals, fields, access functions, hooks) drives everything: the database schema, REST API, GraphQL API, a typed Local API, and a React Server Components admin panel. It is a pnpm/Turbo **monorepo**: the core engine lives in [packages/payload](../../packages/payload), the admin UI in [packages/ui](../../packages/ui), the Next.js binding in [packages/next](../../packages/next), and databases are pluggable adapters ([packages/db-mongodb](../../packages/db-mongodb), [packages/db-postgres](../../packages/db-postgres), [packages/drizzle](../../packages/drizzle)) behind one `payload.db` interface. Auth (JWT + sessions + API keys), document versioning/drafts, uploads with image processing, a job queue, localization, and a rich-text editor (Lexical) are all first-party subsystems — which makes this one repo a tour of nearly every backend and frontend concept a mid-level interview covers.
## How to use it

| One weekend | [00-fast-track.md](00-fast-track.md) |

# Feature 01: Feed Cost Allocation Per Batch
## What This Feature Adds
Batch profit now includes an estimated feed cost. Before this change, the app could calculate global feed purchase cost, but a single batch's profit only subtracted pig purchase cost and batch-specific expenses. That meant the batch detail and batch performance report could look more profitable than reality because feed usage was not represented as a batch cost.
The feature lives mostly in `src/utils/calculations.ts`, with UI usage in:
- `src/screens/batches/BatchListScreen.tsx`
- `src/screens/batches/BatchDetailScreen.tsx`
- `src/screens/reports/ReportsScreen.tsx`
- `tests/calculations.test.ts`
## Senior Engineer Rationale
The important design choice was to keep feed-cost allocation in the calculation layer instead of putting it directly in screens. Screens should mostly answer, "What do I render?" The calculation file should answer, "What does this business number mean?"
That means if Dashboard, Reports, and Batch Detail all need the same batch profit formula, they can call the same helper. This prevents three slightly different versions of "profit" from drifting apart.
## Core Idea
Feed purchases tell us how much feed was bought and what it cost:
```ts
{
feedType: "Starter Feed",
quantity: 10,
unit: "sack",
costPerUnit: 1200
}
```
Feed usage tells us which batch consumed feed:
```ts
{
batchId: "batch-a",
feedType: "Starter Feed",
quantityUsed: 4,
unit: "sack"

## What this repo is
This is the **shadcn/ui monorepo** — the source of ui.shadcn.com and the `shadcn` npm CLI. It is *not* a component library you install from npm; it is a **code distribution system**. Components live as source files in a registry; the CLI fetches JSON descriptions of them, transforms the code with AST tooling to match *your* project (import aliases, icon library, RTL, Tailwind prefix), and writes the files into your codebase so you own them. Three workspaces matter: [`packages/shadcn`](../../packages/shadcn) (the CLI: commands, registry client, transformers, updaters, an MCP server), [`apps/v4`](../../apps/v4) (Next.js 16 site: docs, component previews, and the build pipeline that generates the static registry JSON), and [`packages/tests`](../../packages/tests) (integration tests that run the real CLI binary against fixture projects and a local registry). # Spree Storefront
A production-ready, headless ecommerce storefront for [Spree Commerce](https://spreecommerce.org), built with Next.js 16, React 19, and the [Spree REST API](https://spreecommerce.org/docs/api-reference). Open source (MIT) and free to fork and customize.
[Live Demo](https://demo.spreecommerce.org) | [Quickstart Docs](https://spreecommerce.org/docs/developer/storefront/nextjs/quickstart) | [TypeScript SDK](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@spree/sdk)
## Why This Storefront
**TypeScript SDK.** [@spree/sdk](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@spree/sdk) is an official typed client for every Store API endpoint (OpenAPI 3.0 documented). Autocomplete and type safety in your editor, no codegen step to maintain.
**Multi-region out of the box.** Country, currency, and language switching via URL segments (`/us/en/`, `/de/de/`, `/uk/en/`), powered by Spree [Markets](https://spreecommerce.org/docs/developer/core-concepts/markets). Distinct selling regions bundling geography, currency, and locale in a single store.
**One-page checkout.** Guest and authenticated users, multi-shipment, coupon codes, gift cards, and store credit. Stripe, PayPal, and Adyen via Payment Sessions. Card data never touches your server. [Swap providers](https://spreecommerce.org/docs/developer/core-concepts/payments) easily.
**Transactional emails.** Order confirmation, shipping notification, password reset. Built with react-email, sent via Resend, triggered by Spree webhooks.
**MIT licensed.** Open source and free to use.
## Performance
The live demo at [demo.spreecommerce.org](https://demo.spreecommerce.org) scores 98/100 on desktop and 88/100 on mobile for Performance on Google's Lighthouse audit, with five language versions served from the same deployment.
| Lighthouse metric | Mobile | Desktop |
|-------------------|--------|---------|
| Performance | 88 | 98 |
| Accessibility | 100 | 100 |
| Best Practices | 100 | 100 |
| SEO | 100 | 100 |
No external performance plugins. No edge-side rendering hacks. The architecture is Next.js 16 App Router with React 19 Server Components, server-side data fetching via `@spree/sdk`, and Tailwind CSS 4.

### Mission 9: State Has a Home and a Reason
**Tier:** Mid-Level
**Time Estimate:** 45 minutes
**Goal:** Decide where each kind of state belongs.
**The Concept:** Storefront state is like inventory paperwork: Spree owns the official order, cookies hold the claim ticket, React Context shows the clerk's current screen, and URLs label the aisle.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:** Read cart context, cart cookies, and listing params. Poor state placement causes stale carts, broken back buttons, or wrong market prices.
**Find It In The Code:** Open `src/contexts/CartContext.tsx:39-184`, `src/lib/spree/cookies.ts:43-60`, and `src/lib/utils/listing-search-params.ts:1-13`.
```ts
const [cart, setCart] = useState<Cart | null>(null); // Browser session view.
const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false); // Pure UI state.
const itemCount = useMemo(() => cart?.items?.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.quantity, 0) ?? 0, [cart]); // Derived state.
```
**The Aha Moment:** Bugs shrink when you can name the rightful owner of every value.

# Teable Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from this repository for one specific learner: a **junior fullstack JS engineer** (React/Node/TS CRUD experience) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how Teable's real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill** — why these patterns exist, their failure modes, and how to recognize and articulate them in *any* repo and in an interview.
## What this repo is
Teable (v1.10.0, AGPL-3.0) is an open-source **Airtable alternative**: a no-code spreadsheet-database hybrid on top of real Postgres tables. It is a pnpm/Turbo-style monorepo with two apps — a **NestJS backend** ([apps/nestjs-backend](../../apps/nestjs-backend)) and a **Next.js frontend** ([apps/nextjs-app](../../apps/nextjs-app)) — plus shared packages: Zod API contracts ([packages/openapi](../../packages/openapi)), a React SDK with realtime hooks ([packages/sdk](../../packages/sdk)), core domain logic ([packages/core](../../packages/core)), and Prisma schemas for Postgres and SQLite ([packages/db-main-prisma](../../packages/db-main-prisma)). Realtime collaboration runs on **ShareDB** (operational transformation) with optional Redis pub/sub. Its most distinctive engineering feature: a second-generation core in [packages/v2](../../packages/v2) — a hexagonal/CQRS rewrite being rolled out **behind canary flags** while v1 still serves traffic. You are watching a live strangler-fig migration, which is rare and valuable to study.

# Adding actions
ToolJet supports several actions that can be invoked as the handler for any `event` that is triggered in an application.
## To add actions
To attach an action for component events, click on the component's handle, and then click on the `Add handler` button on the
inspector panel available on the right side.
To attach an action for query events, select the query, go to the `advanced` tab and then click on the `Add handler` button.
## Available actions
Some of the actions that ToolJet Support are
Action| Description|
----| -----------  |
Show alert | Show an alert message as a bootstrap toast           |
Run query | Run any of the data queries that you have created           |
Open webpage | Go to another webpage in a new tab          |
Goto app | Go to another ToolJet application          |
Show modal | Open any modal that you've added          |
Close modal | Close any modal that you've added if its already open          |
Copy to clipboard | Copy any available text that you see on the application to clipboard          |
Set localStorage | Set a key and corresponding value to localStorage          |
Generate file | Construct file using data available in your application and let the user download it          |

---
id: row-level-security
title: Setup Row Level Security
---
Row-level security in ToolJet lets you control which records a user can see or interact with, even when multiple users access the same table. This is useful when you want to restrict access to specific rows based on [custom groups](/docs/user-management/role-based-access/custom-groups/) or [default user roles](/docs/user-management/role-based-access/user-roles#default-user-roles). Row-level security is applied on the server side, ensuring the logic is secure and hidden from the client.
The below syntax fetches the groups for the current user from the server side. Groups include both custom groups and default user roles like `admin` and `end-user`.
```bash
{{globals.server.currentUser.groups}}
```
*The above syntax will work with all data sources except Run Javascript and Run Python.*
## Example: Department-Specific View Using a PostgreSQL Data Source
If you're using PostgreSQL, you can filter records by referencing the user’s group(s) directly in your SQL query. This ensures each user only sees data relevant to them.
Suppose you're building an internal issue tracking tool for your company. Each department (like “Engineering”, “HR”, "Marketing") logs and manages its own issues in a shared table with the below structure:
- Table name: **issue_reports**
- Columns: **id**, **title**,	**status** and **department**
- Access control: Each user is assigned to department-based Custom Groups matching department names in the database.
To ensure users only see reports from their own department(s), you can use the following SQL query:
```SQL
SELECT * FROM issue_reports
WHERE department = ANY (
string_to_array('{{globals.server.currentUser.groups}}', ',')
);
```
**How This Works:**
- `{{globals.server.currentUser.groups}}` fetches the user’s groups securely from the server.
- `string_to_array(...)` converts the comma-separated string containing groups into a usable array.
- `department = ANY (...)` ensures users only see issues filed under their own departments.

# Twenty CRM — Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built on this repository for one learner: a **junior fullstack JS engineer** (React/Node/TS CRUD experience) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles. Every module teaches two things at once: how **this** codebase works (with exact file anchors) and the **transferable pattern** you can recognize and articulate in any other repo — including in an interview room.
## What this repo is
Twenty is an open-source CRM (a Salesforce/HubSpot alternative) built as an Nx monorepo managed with Yarn 4. The backend is NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL + Redis, exposing a **metadata-driven GraphQL API**: the schema is not written by hand but *generated per workspace* from object/field metadata stored in the database ([workspace-schema.factory.ts](../../packages/twenty-server/src/engine/api/graphql/workspace-schema.factory.ts#L23-L68)). The frontend is React 18 + Jotai + Apollo + Linaria, driven by the same metadata so users can define custom objects and fields at runtime. Multi-tenancy is per-workspace, enforced down at the ORM layer where a custom query builder injects permission checks and row-level predicates before any SQL runs ([workspace-select-query-builder.ts](../../packages/twenty-server/src/engine/twenty-orm/repository/workspace-select-query-builder.ts#L342-L352)). Background work (webhooks, workflows, email sync) runs on BullMQ workers. This is a production-grade system with real reliability tradeoffs worth studying — and worth talking about in interviews.

# 01 — Architecture: the metadata engine and the shape of everything else
## What it is and why it exists
Twenty is a CRM where customers define their own data model. A workspace admin can
create a "Property Listing" object with a "Commission Rate" currency field at 2pm
on a Tuesday, and by 2:00:05 that object has a Postgres table, a GraphQL API with
filtering and aggregation, REST endpoints, permissions, and UI views. That single
product requirement — **user-defined schema at runtime** — is the gravitational
center of this codebase. Almost every architectural oddity you'll find is a
consequence of it.
Concretely, the server is two applications wearing one NestJS trench coat:
1. **The core app** — auth, billing, workspaces, users, files, feature flags.
Ordinary NestJS + TypeORM code against fixed tables. Lives in
`packages/twenty-server/src/engine/core-modules/` (look at `auth/`, `billing/`,
`workspace/`, `feature-flag/`).
2. **The metadata engine** — the machinery that stores *descriptions* of objects
and fields (`src/engine/metadata-modules/`, see `object-metadata/`-style modules
like `field-metadata/` and the whole family of `flat-*` modules), turns those
descriptions into real DDL (`src/engine/workspace-manager/workspace-migration/`),
and serves records through a runtime-built API (`src/engine/api/` and
`src/engine/twenty-orm/`).
The monorepo around it is an Nx workspace (`nx.json`, `tsconfig.base.json`) with
~20 packages. The ones you'll live in: `twenty-server`, `twenty-front` (React 18 +
Jotai + Linaria), `twenty-shared` (types shared across the wire — build this first),
and `twenty-ui`.

# Onboarding: Welcome to Twenty (from the person who has the most scar tissue)
Hey. I'm the principal engineer on this codebase, and this doc pack is what I wish
someone had handed me. It's not the marketing tour — you can get that from the
website. This is the candid version: why things are shaped the way they are, which
decisions I'd defend in front of a review board, and which ones I'd quietly redo if
I had a free quarter.
## How to read this
Six sections, in dependency order. Read 01 first no matter what — everything else
in this system is downstream of the metadata engine, and nothing will make sense
until you internalize that **the CRM's data model does not exist at compile time**.
| Doc | Subsystem |
| --- | --- |
| [01-architecture.md](01-architecture.md) | The metadata engine, the monorepo, and why the server is really two applications |
| [02-api-design.md](02-api-design.md) | Runtime-generated GraphQL, the REST facade, and the Zapier coupling I'm not proud of |
| [03-data-access.md](03-data-access.md) | twenty-orm, per-workspace schemas, dynamic DDL migrations |
| [04-testing-strategy.md](04-testing-strategy.md) | Why we test against a real Postgres and what the sync queue driver hides from you |
| [05-error-handling.md](05-error-handling.md) | Exception taxonomy, filters, and the webhook delivery incident |
| [06-observability.md](06-observability.md) | Logger, metrics, audit events, Sentry — and the fire-and-forget problem |
Each section ends with three questions. Take them seriously — they're the questions
I'll ask you in our 1:1 before I let you review PRs in that area. If you can't
answer them from the code, go back and read the files cited. Every file path in
these docs is real; open them side by side with the prose.
## Ground rules while you ramp
- **Never touch a workspace schema table with raw TypeORM.** Always go through
`WorkspaceRepository` (`packages/twenty-server/src/engine/twenty-orm/repository/workspace.repository.ts`).
Section 03 explains why this rule exists and what happened when someone broke it.
- **Run `npx nx typecheck twenty-server` before you believe anything works.**
Half our safety net is the type system; the other half is integration tests
against a real database.
- **When you change entity files, generate an instance command**
(`npx nx run twenty-server:database:migrate:generate --name <name> --type <fast|slow>`).
Committed migration `up`/`down` logic is append-only. No exceptions.

# Tier 1 Junior Missions
### Mission 1: The App's Heartbeat
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 25 minutes
**Goal:** Identify how the builder app wraps every page.
**The Concept:** The app shell is the factory floor: every worker station receives power, identity, translations, theme, data cache, and workspace context before doing specialized work.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:** `apps/builder/src/pages/_app.tsx` owns global providers. If provider order is wrong, hooks deeper in the tree fail or render without required context.
**Find It In The Code:** Open [apps/builder/src/pages/_app.tsx](../../apps/builder/src/pages/_app.tsx:57).
```tsx
// lines 57-79
<TolgeeProvider tolgee={ssrTolgee}> // translation context
<NuqsAdapter> // URL query-state context
<ThemeProvider attribute="class"> // theme class on DOM
<QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}> // server-state cache
<SessionProvider session={pageProps.session}> // auth session
<UserProvider> // current user abstraction
<TypebotProvider typebotId={typebotId}> // current bot draft
<WorkspaceProvider typebotId={typebotId}> // current workspace
<Component {...pageProps} /> // page finally runs here
```
**The Aha Moment:** Most builder pages are not standalone; they assume this provider stack exists.
**Socratic Checkpoint:** 1. Which provider gives ORPC/TanStack Query cache? 2. Which provider gives auth? 3. Why is `typebotId` read from the router? 4. Why are toasts outside the page component? 5. What breaks if `TypebotProvider` is removed? How to self-grade: strong answers cite lines 55-79, name the provider, and describe one hook that would lose context.
**Connects To:** Mission 2 because folder ownership makes more sense after the app shell; Mission 9 because state ownership starts here.
### Mission 2: The Folder Mental Map
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 30 minutes
**Goal:** Separate app folders from shared package folders.

# Umami Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built on the **Umami** codebase (`umami` v3.1.0 — `package.json:3`), a privacy-focused, self-hostable web analytics platform. This is not documentation *for* Umami; it is a curriculum that uses Umami as a real, production-grade specimen to take a junior fullstack JS engineer to solid mid-level and prepare them for mid-level fullstack interviews.
Every page teaches two things at once:
- **This repo**: where things live, how its real flows work, what its authors decided.
- **The transferable skill**: why the pattern exists, its alternatives and failure modes, and how to recognize and explain it in *any* codebase — and in an interview.
## Why Umami is a good teaching specimen
1. It is a **real product**, not a toy. Analytics collection is a genuine high-throughput write path with genuine tradeoffs (privacy vs. accuracy, cost vs. detail).
2. It has a **clean layered shape**: Zod validation → auth → permission → query layer → dispatch to Postgres *or* ClickHouse. You can see each boundary.
3. It exercises the exact topics interviewers probe: async data flow, an event loop hot path, SQL and schema design, caching, authz/IDOR, multi-tenancy, and a real system-design story ("design an analytics platform").
4. It has a **polymorphic persistence layer** — the same logical write targets a relational DB or a columnar analytics DB — which is a rare and impressive thing for a junior to be able to explain.
5. It ships a **vanilla-JS tracker** and a **React 19 dashboard** in one repo, so you get both the client edge and the server core.
6. It has **honest sharp edges** (fire-and-forget Kafka, a latent `orderBy` injection surface, no app-level rate limiting) that make excellent "what would a senior inspect first?" material.
Read the repo's identity in one paragraph: *Umami receives anonymous events from a tiny tracker script over an unauthenticated `POST /api/send`, derives a cookieless visitor identity by hashing IP + user-agent + a rotating salt, and writes each event to either Postgres (via Prisma) or ClickHouse (optionally through Kafka). A Next.js 16 App Router dashboard, guarded by bearer tokens and per-entity permission checks, reads aggregated metrics back through a hand-written parameterized SQL layer. Teams, shares, reports,

# Mission Learning Path
This suite is a training campaign. Each mission asks you to trace real files, annotate real code, answer questions, and self-grade immediately.
Recommended pacing:
- Tier 1: one mission per sitting, 30 to 60 minutes each.
- Tier 2: one mission every one or two days, with a scratch branch open.
- Tier 3: one mission per week, ideally while reviewing a real or hypothetical change.
How to self-grade:
1. Read the exact file ranges.
2. Explain the flow without looking.
3. Compare your answer to the rubric.
4. Re-read the lines you could not explain.
This differs from normal documentation because you are not trying to memorize the codebase. # Zulip Upskill Curriculum
This curriculum turns this repository into a serious training lab for a new Python/Django engineer who wants to become productive in Zulip and also develop transferable engineering judgment. It is written for learners who need both codebase-specific orientation and reusable mental models for Python, Django, TypeScript, testing, debugging, performance, security, and open source collaboration.
Zulip is a large monorepo-style application, even though it ships as one server product. The core Django app lives in `zerver/`, startup and settings live in `zproject/`, long-poll/event delivery uses Tornado code in `zerver/tornado/`, background jobs live in `zerver/worker/`, the web client lives in `web/src/`, and extensive contributor docs already live under `docs/`. The codebase is opinionated about typed Python, broad automated testing, explicit permission boundaries, and careful backwards compatibility. It also carries real complexity: old API names are preserved for compatibility, the event system spans multiple runtime surfaces, and the message-send path has a lot of side effects. That makes Zulip a very strong study repo for moving from junior implementation to senior judgment.

# Jeopardy Game Architecture
This document describes the current and target architecture for the Jeopardy web app, with the no-auth, friends, sharing, and admin-whitelisted public games requirements.
## Overview
The app is a React + Vite frontend backed by a Node.js/Express API and a PostgreSQL database managed through Prisma. The system is split into two apps:
- `frontend/`: SPA UI, routing, and API client.
- `backend/`: REST API, data access, and gameplay logic.
## Goals (Target)
- No traditional authentication (no passwords, no OAuth).
- Lightweight user identity (username profile stored locally) to enable friends and sharing.
- Public games are only visible if the game owner is whitelisted by an admin.
- Admin can grant or revoke public publishing access for any user.
## Runtime Topology
- Browser (React) talks to Express API at `/api`.
- Express uses Prisma to read/write PostgreSQL.
```
Browser (React) -> /api -> Express routes -> Services -> Prisma -> PostgreSQL
```
## Frontend Architecture
### Entry and Routing
- `frontend/src/main.jsx`: App bootstrap, router, context providers.
- `frontend/src/App.jsx`: Route definitions and page wiring.
### State Management
- `GameContext`: session/gameplay state (current session, players, active question).
- `UserContext` (target): current user identity stored in localStorage, shared across pages.
### API Client
- `frontend/src/api/client.js`: Axios client, base URL `/api`.
- Adds `X-User-Id` header when a local user is selected.
- Exposes typed API wrappers in `frontend/src/api/*`.

# Training Doc: Database Schema (`src/lib/db/schema.ts`)
## Purpose
This file defines the **entire data model** for the Reps application using Drizzle ORM. Every table, column, relationship, and constraint in the SQLite database is declared here. If you want to understand what data the app stores and how entities relate to each other, this is the single source of truth.
## Prerequisites
- Basic understanding of relational databases (tables, columns, primary keys, foreign keys)
- Familiarity with TypeScript syntax
- Concept of an ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) — a library that lets you define database tables using code instead of raw SQL
---
## Line-by-Line Walkthrough of Key Code
### Line 1 — Imports from Drizzle ORM
```typescript
import { sqliteTable, text, integer, real, primaryKey } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core";
```
**Why this matters:** Drizzle provides builder functions specific to each database engine. Since we use SQLite, we import from `sqlite-core`. Each import serves a specific purpose:
- `sqliteTable` — creates a new table definition
- `text`, `integer`, `real` — column type builders (string, whole number, decimal number)
- `primaryKey` — creates composite primary keys (primary keys made of multiple columns)
These functions don't execute SQL immediately — they produce a JavaScript object that Drizzle uses later to generate SQL when the app queries the database.
---

```typescript
export const categories = sqliteTable("categories", {
id: text("id").primaryKey(),
name: text("name").notNull(),
description: text("description").notNull().default(""),
icon: text("icon").notNull().default(""),
sortOrder: integer("sort_order").notNull().default(0),
});

# `src/lib/db/schema.ts` — The Database Schema
**What this file does:** Defines every table in the database using Drizzle ORM's TypeScript API. This is the single source of truth for the shape of all data in the app.
**Why it matters:** If you understand this file, you understand the app's data model. Every API route, every query, every component ultimately reads from or writes to the structures defined here.
---
## How Drizzle Schema Definitions Work
Each `sqliteTable()` call maps to a SQL `CREATE TABLE` statement. The first argument is the table name in SQL (snake_case by convention), and the second is an object defining columns.
```ts
export const categories = sqliteTable("categories", {
id: text("id").primaryKey(),
name: text("name").notNull(),
// ...
});
```
This produces a SQL table like:
```sql
CREATE TABLE categories (
id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
name TEXT NOT NULL
);
```
The key insight: Drizzle uses these definitions at *runtime* to build queries **and** at *compile time* for TypeScript type inference. When you write `db.select().from(schema.categories)`, TypeScript knows the result has `id: string`, `name: string`, etc.
---
## The Tables, Explained
### `categories` — Problem Groupings
Simple lookup table. Five rows: Strings, Arrays, Objects/Maps, Recursion, Sorting/Searching. The `sortOrder` column controls display order so we don't rely on alphabetical sorting.
### `patterns` — Reusable Problem-Solving Strategies
Patterns are the teaching core of the app. "Two Pointer," "Hash Map Lookup," "Accumulator," etc. The `slug` field is a URL-safe identifier (`two-pointer`) — it's unique because we use it in URLs and references. The `explanation` field is a longer teaching text shown when a user clicks to learn more.
### `problems` — The Coding Challenges

# `src/lib/db/index.ts` — Database Connection
**What this file does:** Creates a single, shared database connection that every API route uses. It's only 14 lines, but every line matters.
---
## Line by Line
```ts
const dbPath = path.join(process.cwd(), "reps.db");
```
`process.cwd()` returns the project root directory (where `package.json` lives). The database file lives right there. This is a SQLite-specific pattern — the database is literally a file on disk.
```ts
const sqlite = new Database(dbPath);
```
`better-sqlite3` is a synchronous SQLite driver for Node.js. Unlike most database libraries that return Promises, this one returns results immediately. This is actually a *feature* — SQLite is an embedded database (no network calls), so synchronous access is faster and simpler.
```ts
sqlite.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");
```
**WAL = Write-Ahead Logging.** This is important. SQLite's default journal mode locks the entire database during writes, blocking all readers. WAL mode allows concurrent reads while a write is happening. Since Next.js may process multiple API requests at once, WAL prevents them from blocking each other.
```ts
sqlite.pragma("foreign_keys = ON");
```
SQLite has foreign key support but it's **OFF by default** (for backwards compatibility). Without this line, you could insert an attempt referencing a non-existent problem ID and the database wouldn't complain. With it on, the database enforces referential integrity — exactly what we want.
```ts
export const db = drizzle(sqlite, { schema });
```
This wraps the raw SQLite connection with Drizzle ORM, passing in our schema definitions so Drizzle knows the table structure. The resulting `db` object is what every API route imports to run queries.
---
## Why a Module-Level Singleton?
The connection is created at module load time (not inside a function). In Node.js, modules are cached after first import — so `import { db } from "@/lib/db"` in 10 different API routes all get the **same** `db` instance. This is intentional. Opening a new SQLite connection per request would be wasteful. One connection handles everything.
**Note for later:** If you ever switch to PostgreSQL or another network database, this file is the only place that changes. Everything else imports `db` and doesn't care what's behind it.

# `src/types/index.ts` — Shared Type Definitions
**What this file does:** Defines TypeScript types that are shared across the client (components), server (API routes), and libraries. This is the "contract" between all layers of the app.
**Why it matters:** When a component expects a `SessionProblem` and an API returns a `SessionProblem`, they both reference this file. Change the type here, and TypeScript will flag every place in the codebase that needs updating.
---
## The Types, Grouped by Purpose
### Test Execution Types (`TestCase`, `TestResult`, `ExecutionResult`)
```ts
export type TestCase = {
input: unknown[];    // Arguments passed to the user's function
expected: unknown;   // What the function should return
description: string; // Human-readable name like "handles empty array"
isEdgeCase: boolean; // Used by error classifier to detect "edge-case-miss"
};
```
`input` is `unknown[]` (an array of unknowns) because function arguments can be any type — numbers, strings, arrays, objects. Same for `expected`. We use `unknown` instead of `any` because `unknown` forces you to check the type before using the value, which is safer.
`ExecutionResult` wraps the full output of running all test cases:
```ts
export type ExecutionResult = {
allPassed: boolean;       // Quick check — did everything pass?
results: TestResult[];    // Per-test-case results
errorType: string | null; // Classified error or null if all passed
};
```
### Session Types (`SessionProblem`, `DrillPhase`)
`SessionProblem` is what the API returns to the client. It's a denormalized view — the database stores `categoryId` (a foreign key), but the API enriches it with `categoryName` so the client doesn't need a separate fetch. Same for `patterns` — the join table is resolved server-side.
```ts
export type DrillPhase =
| "approach"    // Writing the approach text
| "coding"      // Writing code
| "running"     // Tests are executing (brief)
| "results"     // Seeing test results
| "post-solve"; // Seeing patterns, feedback

### `patterns` — Reusable Problem-Solving Strategies
Patterns are the teaching core of the app. "Two Pointer," "Hash Map Lookup," "Accumulator," etc. The `slug` field is a URL-safe identifier (`two-pointer`) — it's unique because we use it in URLs and references. The `explanation` field is a longer teaching text shown when a user clicks to learn more.
### `problems` — The Coding Challenges

# `src/lib/db/index.ts` — Database Connection
**What this file does:** Creates a single, shared database connection that every API route uses. It's only 14 lines, but every line matters.
---
## Line by Line
```ts
const dbPath = path.join(process.cwd(), "reps.db");
```
`process.cwd()` returns the project root directory (where `package.json` lives). The database file lives right there. This is a SQLite-specific pattern — the database is literally a file on disk.
```ts
const sqlite = new Database(dbPath);
```
`better-sqlite3` is a synchronous SQLite driver for Node.js. Unlike most database libraries that return Promises, this one returns results immediately. This is actually a *feature* — SQLite is an embedded database (no network calls), so synchronous access is faster and simpler.
```ts
sqlite.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");
```
**WAL = Write-Ahead Logging.** This is important. SQLite's default journal mode locks the entire database during writes, blocking all readers. WAL mode allows concurrent reads while a write is happening. Since Next.js may process multiple API requests at once, WAL prevents them from blocking each other.
```ts
sqlite.pragma("foreign_keys = ON");
```
SQLite has foreign key support but it's **OFF by default** (for backwards compatibility). Without this line, you could insert an attempt referencing a non-existent problem ID and the database wouldn't complain. With it on, the database enforces referential integrity — exactly what we want.
```ts
export const db = drizzle(sqlite, { schema });
```
This wraps the raw SQLite connection with Drizzle ORM, passing in our schema definitions so Drizzle knows the table structure. The resulting `db` object is what every API route imports to run queries.
---
## Why a Module-Level Singleton?
The connection is created at module load time (not inside a function). In Node.js, modules are cached after first import — so `import { db } from "@/lib/db"` in 10 different API routes all get the **same** `db` instance. This is intentional. Opening a new SQLite connection per request would be wasteful. One connection handles everything.
**Note for later:** If you ever switch to PostgreSQL or another network database, this file is the only place that changes. Everything else imports `db` and doesn't care what's behind it.

# `src/types/index.ts` — Shared Type Definitions
**What this file does:** Defines TypeScript types that are shared across the client (components), server (API routes), and libraries. This is the "contract" between all layers of the app.
**Why it matters:** When a component expects a `SessionProblem` and an API returns a `SessionProblem`, they both reference this file. Change the type here, and TypeScript will flag every place in the codebase that needs updating.
---
## The Types, Grouped by Purpose
### Test Execution Types (`TestCase`, `TestResult`, `ExecutionResult`)
```ts
export type TestCase = {
input: unknown[];    // Arguments passed to the user's function
expected: unknown;   // What the function should return
description: string; // Human-readable name like "handles empty array"
isEdgeCase: boolean; // Used by error classifier to detect "edge-case-miss"
};
```
`input` is `unknown[]` (an array of unknowns) because function arguments can be any type — numbers, strings, arrays, objects. Same for `expected`. We use `unknown` instead of `any` because `unknown` forces you to check the type before using the value, which is safer.
`ExecutionResult` wraps the full output of running all test cases:
```ts
export type ExecutionResult = {
allPassed: boolean;       // Quick check — did everything pass?
results: TestResult[];    // Per-test-case results
errorType: string | null; // Classified error or null if all passed
};
```
### Session Types (`SessionProblem`, `DrillPhase`)
`SessionProblem` is what the API returns to the client. It's a denormalized view — the database stores `categoryId` (a foreign key), but the API enriches it with `categoryName` so the client doesn't need a separate fetch. Same for `patterns` — the join table is resolved server-side.
```ts
export type DrillPhase =
| "approach"    // Writing the approach text
| "coding"      // Writing code
| "running"     // Tests are executing (brief)
| "results"     // Seeing test results
| "post-solve"; // Seeing patterns, feedback

## Codex Watchdog Agent
This repo includes a watchdog agent that checks every 5 minutes if Codex appears stuck and then triggers a restart from the latest steps.
### Run Once
```bash
npm run watchdog:once
```
### Run Continuously
```bash
npm run watchdog
```
### What It Does
- Reads latest Codex session activity from `~/.codex/sessions`.
- If activity is stale long enough, writes restart context to:
- `.watchdog/restart-from-last-steps.txt`
- Sends a restart command:
- `codex exec --cd <workspace> "Watchdog detected Codex inactivity ..."`
- Logs checks and actions to:
- `.watchdog/watchdog.log`
### Environment Variables
- `WATCHDOG_CHECK_MS` (default `300000`)
- `WATCHDOG_STUCK_MS` (default `900000`)
- `WATCHDOG_STALE_CHECKS` (default `2`)
- `WATCHDOG_RESTART_COOLDOWN_MS` (default `1800000`)
- `WATCHDOG_AUTO_RESTART` (default `true`)
- `WATCHDOG_STEP_LINES` (default `12`)
- `CODEX_WATCHDOG_WORKSPACE` (default current directory)
- `CODEX_SESSIONS_DIR` (default `~/.codex/sessions`)
### Windows Task Scheduler (Every 5 Minutes)

```powershell
schtasks /Create /SC MINUTE /MO 5 /TN "CodexWatchdog" /TR "powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command \"cd C:\Users\Owner\Desktop\jstrain2; npm run watchdog:once\"" /F

# 25 · Codebase Debug Hunts
Module 24 taught you to find the lying line in one file. This module
removes the comfort you didn't know you had: **the whole bug in front of
you**. Here every exercise is a small app spread over several files, the
failing test points at the entry point, the stack trace points at an
innocent bystander, and each file — read alone — is defensible. That is
what inheriting a codebase feels like, and it's what a real ticket hands
you: a symptom in one place, a cause in another.
The format: each exercise is a runner file plus an app directory —
```
exercises/01-shipping-quote.js          ← run this; prompt + the tests
exercises/01-shipping-quote-app/        ← the app; the bug lives in here
rates.js   cart.js   quote.js       ← you edit ONE of these
```
Run the runner, read red, then go read the app. Fix the app file that is
wrong — the runners and their tests are not yours to edit.
## The mental model
Single-file hunting is about lines. Multi-file hunting is about
**contracts**: what each file promises (its top comment, its function
names, its parameter names) and what each caller assumes. When every
file is locally correct, the bug is a disagreement between a promise and
an assumption — so stop reading bodies and start diffing boundaries.
The three disagreements that cover most of them, one per exercise:
| boundary bug | how it reads | file that owns the fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| broken promise | a doc says "throws / never null / already sorted"; the body stopped doing that | the file that made the promise |
| wrong pipeline order | every step is right; the composer calls them in an order one step documented away | the file that composes |
| unit mismatch | a bare number changes meaning across an import — seconds→ms, dollars→cents | the sender who mislabeled it |

# Intern to mid-level engineer learning path
This curriculum uses the three applications in the parent directory as a working textbook. It teaches the difference between “I can make the happy path work” and “I can own a change across UI, API, domain rules, SQL, failure handling, tests, and operations.”
## What “mid-level” means here
A mid-level engineer can take a bounded product outcome and:
1. Find the correct ownership boundary before editing.
2. State invariants and hostile cases in plain language.
3. Validate runtime input instead of trusting TypeScript.
4. Enforce authorization against the target resource.
5. make multi-write behavior atomic and retry-safe.
6. Build usable loading, empty, error, permission, and conflict states.
7. Select tests that prove the risky behavior at the right boundary.
8. Operate the result: configuration, logs, health, shutdown, migration, rollback, and recovery.
9. Explain tradeoffs and limitations without exaggerating.
## Recommended ten-week route
| Week | Read | Practice | Exit evidence |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [How to learn](./00-HOW-TO-LEARN.md), [architecture tour](./01-ARCHITECTURE-TOUR.md) | Trace one request through every layer | Hand-drawn or Mermaid sequence plus teach-back |
| 2 | [TypeScript and validation](./02-TYPESCRIPT-AND-VALIDATION.md) | Add one rejected boundary case | Parser test fails before implementation and passes after |
| 3 | [HTTP, identity, authorization](./03-HTTP-AUTHORIZATION.md) | Add a negative permission test | Same denial for missing and forbidden private resource |
| 4 | [SQL and transactions](./04-SQL-TRANSACTIONS.md) | Inject a failure between two writes | Database remains unchanged after rollback |
| 5 | [Concurrency and idempotency](./05-CONCURRENCY.md) | Run and mutate a race test | Explain why the test is deterministic |
| 6 | [React product engineering](./06-REACT-PRODUCT-ENGINEERING.md) | Build a visible conflict/retry state | Accessible component test |
| 7 | [Workers and operations](./07-WORKERS-AND-OPERATIONS.md) | Force retry and dead-letter recovery | Logs and database evidence |
| 8 | [Inventory tour](./projects/01-INVENTORY-CODE-TOUR.md) | Lab 1 or 2 | Small vertical change and review note |
| 9 | [Project-management tour](./projects/02-PROJECT-MANAGEMENT-CODE-TOUR

# Hands-on labs
Each lab is a bounded mid-level ticket. Work in a branch. Do not modify all three projects at once. Before coding, write the contract, riskiest assumption, non-goals, and first failing test.
## Lab workflow
1. Read the named source and tests.
2. Write a one-page change plan.
3. Predict one likely regression.
4. Add the smallest critical failing test.
5. Implement a vertical slice.
6. Run focused tests, then the project’s full gate.
7. Review the diff for validation, authorization, concurrency, failure behavior, logs, and documentation.
8. Complete a five-minute teach-back without source open.
## Lab 1: Inventory cycle count
### Outcome
An administrator can start a count, record a counted quantity, inspect variance, and approve an adjustment. Variance above a configurable threshold requires a second authorized approval.
### Constraints
- A count snapshots expected quantity/version.
- Approval is a named command, not arbitrary state update.
- Approval creates a compensating immutable movement and audit record.
- A stale count conflicts; it cannot overwrite intervening stock activity.
- Duplicate approval is idempotent.
### Proof
- domain transition table;
- real SQL rollback test;
- stale-version and cross-tenant denial tests;
- React form with validation/conflict state;
- migration blank/repeat test.
### Non-goals
Barcode hardware and recurring count scheduling.

# Bootcamp — offline, test-graded, self-paced
A personal coding bootcamp for leveling up software engineering
fundamentals, in two languages. Built to run **fully offline** — every
exercise is a single self-contained file graded by its own tests,
runnable with nothing but Node or the .NET SDK.
**JavaScript / TypeScript — start here →
[`FLIGHTPLAN.md`](FLIGHTPLAN.md)** — the 10-hour core-JS schedule.
Flight 2 (Node + TypeScript) →
[`FLIGHTPLAN-NODE-TS.md`](FLIGHTPLAN-NODE-TS.md).
**C# / .NET (web-focused) — start here →
[`csbootcamp/FLIGHTPLAN.md`](csbootcamp/FLIGHTPLAN.md).** Same format,
same harness philosophy, weighted toward ASP.NET Core: 29 modules, 147
exercises, 1,292 tests. Every web exercise runs a real Kestrel server over
real HTTP. Needs the .NET 10 SDK and nothing else.
## Quick start (30 seconds)
```bash
node bootcamp/01-language-core/exercises/01-*.js   # run any exercise
node bootcamp/progress.js                          # your scoreboard
```
An exercise file looks like this: a prompt in comments, a function that
throws `TODO`, and tests underneath. You write the code and re-run the
file until:
```
✔ counts lowercase vowels
✔ is case-insensitive
✔ handles the empty string
3 passed
all green — next file!
```
No test runner to install, no config, no watcher — `node <file>`, that's
the whole workflow. (`☐ todo` = not written yet · `✘` = failing · `✔` = done
· `🐛` = a debug-hunt bug you haven't caught yet.)

# Guide: package.json
## Purpose
`package.json` is the contract for how this project runs. It defines runtime dependencies (what the app needs to execute), dev dependencies (what helps build/lint it), and script commands (`dev`, `build`, `start`, `lint`). For a junior developer, this file explains the stack before reading any code.
## Line-by-line walkthrough
### Basic metadata
- `name`, `version`, `private`: package identity. `private: true` prevents accidental publish to npm.
### `scripts`
- `dev`: starts Next.js development server with hot reload.
- `build`: creates production build artifacts.
- `start`: runs production server from built output.
- `lint`: runs ESLint checks.
Control-flow idea:
- These are command aliases. Running `npm run dev` triggers `next dev`.
### `dependencies`
- `next`, `react`, `react-dom`: core app framework.
- `zustand`: global client state store.
- `better-sqlite3`: server-side SQLite access.
- `nanoid`, `uuid`: unique IDs.
- `fuse.js`: fuzzy text search.
- `@dnd-kit/*`: drag-and-drop engine.
- `react-icons`: icon components.
- `yjs`, `y-websocket`: collaborative editing libs (currently not wired fully).
- `prisma`, `@prisma/client`, `date-fns`, `lucide-react`: currently mostly unused or lightly used in this codebase.
Design observation:
- Having some unused deps is common during prototyping, but production cleanup is recommended.
### `devDependencies`
- `eslint`, `eslint-config-next`: code quality checks.
- `tailwindcss`, `@tailwindcss/postcss`: styling toolchain.

# Guide: src/app/page.js
## Purpose
`page.js` is the home route (`/`). It delegates all UI behavior to `WorkspaceApp`. This keeps route files thin and pushes real logic into reusable components.
## Line-by-line walkthrough
### Import
- `WorkspaceApp` from `@/components/WorkspaceApp`.
Why:
- Route should render the main product UI component.
### `Home()` component
- Returns `<WorkspaceApp />`.
Control flow:
- Next.js calls `Home` when user visits `/`.
- `WorkspaceApp` handles all interaction from there.
State/closures:
- No local state; this file is intentionally minimal.
Side effects:
- None directly.
TypeScript notes:
- No types. In TS, this would likely be `export default function Home(): JSX.Element`.
## Concepts taught by this file
- Thin route component pattern
- Separation of routing vs feature logic
## Common mistakes
- Putting large business logic directly in route file.
- Adding duplicate state here and in `WorkspaceApp`.
## Mini exercises
1. Wrap `<WorkspaceApp />` with a feature-flag condition.
2. Add a temporary banner above `WorkspaceApp` and remove it cleanly.

# Master Architecture Guide
## 1) What This App Is
This project is a Notion-style workspace where a team can create nested pages, edit block content, add inline databases, comment on blocks, search content, and export/import documents. It is aimed at small teams and learners who want a single place to manage notes and lightweight project knowledge.
The app is currently a strong MVP, not a fully hardened production system. It has many production-like patterns (API routes, persistence, offline queue, version history), but also intentional shortcuts (single workspace seed, no auth, full-state saves).
## 2) Who It Is For
- End users: small teams that need shared docs and task tables.
- Developers: juniors learning full-stack React + Next.js architecture.
- Product stage: advanced prototype / MVP.
## 3) System Overview
High-level responsibilities:
- `src/components/WorkspaceApp.js`: main UI shell and behavior orchestration.
- `src/lib/workspaceStore.js`: client-side app state and state mutation actions.
- `src/app/api/**/route.js`: server endpoints for save/load/search/import/export/versioning.
- `src/lib/sqlite.js`: SQLite bootstrap, schema creation, data read/write helpers.
- `src/lib/offlineStore.js`: IndexedDB queue + draft storage for offline mode.
- `src/lib/defaultWorkspace.js`: initial seeded workspace data.

# Guide: package.json
## Purpose
This is the project's manifest file. It tells npm (Node Package Manager) what this project is called, what scripts you can run, and what libraries it depends on. Every Node.js project has one. Think of it as the project's resume — it lists everything the project needs to function.
## Line-by-Line Walkthrough
### Lines 1-4: Project Identity
```json
{
"name": "jstrain2.4",
"version": "0.1.0",
"private": true,
```
- `name` — the project name. Used if you ever publish this as a package (we won't).
- `version` — follows semantic versioning (major.minor.patch). `0.1.0` means "first minor version, pre-release."
- `private: true` — prevents accidentally publishing to the npm registry. Always set this for internal apps.
### Lines 5-14: Scripts
```json
"scripts": {
"dev": "next dev",
"build": "next build",
"start": "next start",
"lint": "eslint",
"db:generate": "prisma generate",
"db:migrate": "prisma migrate dev",
"db:seed": "node prisma/seed.js",
"db:setup": "node scripts/setup-db.js"
},
```
Scripts are shortcuts you run with `npm run <name>`. For example, `npm run dev` runs `next dev`.

Orbit Deploy Console is an **internal developer platform** (IDP) — think of it as a mini Heroku or Vercel that a company would run internally. It lets engineering teams:

# Guide: `drizzle.config.ts`
## Purpose
This config tells Drizzle where schema definitions live, where SQL migrations should be generated, and how to connect to Postgres. It is a bridge between TypeScript schema code and DB migration files.
## Line-by-line walkthrough
- `const drizzleConfig = { ... }` defines a plain config object.
- `schema: "./src/lib/db/schema.ts"` points to schema source.
- `out: "./src/lib/db/migrations"` is migration output folder.
- `dialect: "postgresql"` selects SQL dialect.
- `dbCredentials.url` pulls `DATABASE_URL` from env with empty fallback.
- `export default drizzleConfig` exports for Drizzle CLI to consume.
## Concepts taught by this file
- Tooling configuration
- Environment-driven configuration
- Migration generation pipeline
## Common mistakes
- Using wrong schema path so migrations generate nothing.
- Missing `DATABASE_URL` and silently connecting nowhere.
- Assuming this file means DB is already wired at runtime (it is not).
## Mini exercises
1. Point `out` to `./drizzle` and explain what else must change.
2. Add a runtime guard that throws if `DATABASE_URL` is empty.
3. Change dialect to mysql and list what in this project would break.
## Further reading
- Search: `drizzle orm config schema out`
- Search: `database migrations why`

# Guide: `worker/index.js`
## Purpose
This is a placeholder worker entrypoint. It marks where background jobs (email sending, SLA checks, indexing) would run in a separate process from the web app.
## Line-by-line walkthrough
- `console.log(...)` prints startup confirmation.
- There are no imports or job loops yet, so this file is intentionally incomplete.
## Concepts taught by this file
- Background process separation
- Worker vs web process architecture
## Common mistakes
- Running heavy background work inside API routes instead of workers.
- Assuming this placeholder already executes queues.
## Mini exercises
1. Add a timer that logs every 30 seconds and explain why timers are usually not enough for production jobs.
2. Add graceful shutdown handling (`SIGTERM`) and explain why containerized apps need it.
## Further reading
- Search: `node worker process architecture`
- Search: `bullmq worker basics`

# OpsForge Training Docs (fable-docs)
A nine-chapter course that teaches production web engineering using **this actual
codebase** — OpsForge, an internal operations dashboard built with Next.js 14, TypeScript,
Drizzle, and BullMQ. It assumes you know basic JavaScript/React syntax but have never
worked in a production codebase.
These docs replace file-by-file reading with **concept-and-flow chapters**: each one gives
you a mental model, teaches from real files in this repo (all paths are clickable), names
the mistakes juniors actually make, and ends with exercises — because reading informs, but
only doing trains.
> Looking for the old per-file guides? They still live in [`_learning/`](../_learning) and
> remain useful as reference *after* you understand a chapter. The review that shaped this
> set is in [`docs-review.md`](docs-review.md).
## How to read this
- **In order, one chapter per sitting.** Concepts compound; Chapter 7 assumes Chapters 3–5.
- **With the repo open and running.** Do the "Try it yourself" exercises as you hit them —
several ask you to break things on purpose and watch the failure. That's where the
learning is. (Setup: `cp .env.example .env`, `npm install`,
`docker compose up -d postgres redis`, `npm run dev` — details in Chapter 2.)
- **With a coding agent nearby.** Every chapter ends with an "Ask your agent" exercise;
Chapter 9 is entirely about that workflow.
- **Glossary on the side.** Any wobbling term is in the [Glossary](GLOSSARY.md), linked
back to the chapter that develops it.
## The path
| # | Chapter | You'll be able to… |
|---|---|---|

# Guide: Database Connection Setup
**Source file:** `src/lib/db/index.ts`
---
## Purpose
This file is the single point of entry for talking to the database. Every time your application needs to read from or write to PostgreSQL, it goes through the `db` object exported here. The file does three things:
1. Makes sure this code only ever runs on the server (never in a browser).
2. Creates a connection pool to PostgreSQL.
3. Wraps that pool with Drizzle ORM so you can write type-safe queries.
Think of it as the "front door" to your database. Every other file in the project that needs the database imports `db` from this file.
---
## Line-by-Line Walkthrough
```typescript
import "server-only";
```
This is a Next.js convention. The `server-only` package does not export any code. It exists solely as a build-time guard: if any client-side bundle accidentally tries to import this file, the build will fail with a clear error message. Without this line, you could accidentally leak your database connection string into the browser JavaScript -- a serious security problem.
```typescript
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/node-postgres";
```
Drizzle ORM is a lightweight TypeScript ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). It lets you write database queries in TypeScript instead of raw SQL strings. The `drizzle-orm/node-postgres` import tells Drizzle to use the `node-postgres` (`pg`) driver under the hood. Drizzle supports many drivers (MySQL, SQLite, etc.), and this line picks the PostgreSQL one.
```typescript
import { Pool } from "pg";
```
`pg` (also called `node-postgres`) is the most widely-used PostgreSQL client for Node.js. `Pool` is a connection pool -- more on that below.
```typescript
import * as schema from "@/lib/db/schema";
```
This imports every table and enum definition from the schema file. The `* as schema` syntax bundles them all into a single `schema` object. Passing this to Drizzle is what makes the relational query API work -- Drizzle needs to know about your table shapes to give you type inference and autocompletion.
The `@/` prefix is a path alias configured in `tsconfig.json` that points to the project root. So `@/lib/db/schema` resolves to `src/lib/db/schema.ts`.
```typescript
const connectionString = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
```
`process.env` gives you access to environment variables -- key-value pairs set outside your code (usually in a `.env` file or in your hosting platform's settings). `DATABASE_URL` is a standard convention for database connection strings. A typical value looks like:

# Bulletproof React 🛡️ ⚛️ A simple, scalable, and powerful architecture for building production ready React applications. ## Introduction React is an excellent tool for building front-end applications. It has a diverse ecosystem with hundreds of great libraries for literally anything you might need. However, being forced to make so many choices can be overwhelming. It is also very flexible, you can write React applications in any way you like, but that flexibility comes with a cost. Since there is no pre-defined architecture that developers can follow, it often leads to a messy, inconsistent, and over-complicated codebase. This repo attempts to present a way of creating React applications using some of the best tools in the ecosystem with a good project structure that scales very well. Based on my experience working with a lot of different codebases, this architecture turns out to be the most effective. The goal here is to serve as a collection of resources and best practices when developing React applications. It is supposed to showcase solving most of the real-world problems of an application in a practical way and help developers write better applications. Feel free to explore the sample app codebase to get the most value out of the repo. > 🤝 **Looking for help implementing these patterns at your company?** [Get in touch](mailto:alan2207@live.com) ## What makes a React application "bulletproof"? This repo doesn't aim to be a silver bullet for all React applications as there are many different use cases, but it tries to provide a solid foundation for building applications based on the following principles: - Easy to get started with - Simple to understand and maintain - Uses the right tools for the job - Clean boundaries between different parts of the application - Everyone on the team is on the same page when it comes to how things are done - Secure - Performant - Scalable in terms of codebase and team size - Issues detectable as early as possible #### Disclaimer: This is not supposed to be a template, boilerplate or a framework. It is an opinionated guide that shows how to do some things in a certain way. You are not forced to do everything exactly as it is shown here, decide what works best for you and your team and stay consistent with your style. To get most out of it, do not get limited by the technologies used in this sample app, but rather focus on the principles and the concepts that are being presented here. # FastAPI RealWorld Up-skilling Suite
Welcome to the **FastAPI RealWorld Up-skilling Suite**. This comprehensive, custom-tailored curriculum transforms this repository into a live codebase training laboratory. It is specifically designed for working JavaScript/TypeScript developers learning Python who want to successfully target mid-level backend CRUD roles at enterprise and Fortune-500-style companies.
---
## 🗺️ Codebase Identity
This codebase implements the RealWorld "Conduit" API spec using a modern, asynchronous FastAPI backend. Built on Python >= 3.14, it utilizes SQLAlchemy 2.0 as its Object-Relational Mapper (ORM), Pydantic 2.0 for request/response serialization and validation, and Alembic for schema migrations. Instead of relying on synchronous database drivers, it employs an asynchronous PostgreSQL engine via `psycopg` to handle high-concurrency connections efficiently. The repository adheres to clean architecture principles by isolating routing logic from data access through a dedicated Repository pattern (located under `app/crud/`). By studying this codebase, you will see how production-ready Python applications structure asynchronous loops, manage transaction scopes, run integration test fixtures, and secure API endpoints.
---
## 📈 The Senior-Mindset Framework
In enterprise engineering, the difference between skill levels is not just syntax fluency—it is how you think about code ownership and risk:
*   **Junior Mindset ("Make it work"):** Focuses entirely on the happy path. The goal is to get the local ticket done, write code that compiles, and pass the tests. "It works on my machine" is the metric of success.
*   **Mid-Level Mindset ("Is this the right pattern"):** Focuses on clean code, reusability, and maintainability. They ensure that new changes adhere to existing repository designs (e.g., using `Depends` in FastAPI correctly, segregating routing from queries).
*   **Senior Staff-Level Mindset ("What does this commit us to, who pays, and how do we reduce blast radius"):** Looks at the long-term trade-offs of code changes. A senior engineer asks: *What database lock will this migration acquire and for how long? Does splitting database reads to a read-only replica (`SessionLocalRo`) introduce synchronization lag bugs? # Request Flow Deep-Dive: Article Creation
This module breaks down the end-to-end request lifecycle of creating an article in this FastAPI application. We will trace how a client request traverses the HTTP route boundary, triggers schema validation, runs dependency injections, executes database queries, inserts child relationships (tags), commits the transaction, and returns the serialized JSON response.
---
## Flow: Article Creation (`POST /api/articles`)
**Why this flow matters:** This is the most complex write operation in the system. It handles nested child relations (tags) that must be upserted (found or created) within a single database transaction, demonstrating FastAPI's asynchronous flow, dependency injection layers, and SQLAlchemy 2.0 ORM operations.
**Bridge equivalent:** A POST endpoint in Express/NestJS using a Zod validation middleware and a Prisma/TypeORM transaction to execute `prisma.article.create({ data: { ..., tags: { connectOrCreate: ... } } })`.

headings: # Lesson 01: JavaScript Foundations and Mental Models
samples.opening:
# Lesson 01: JavaScript Foundations and Mental Models
## Goals
- Understand what JavaScript is and where it runs.
- Build a strong mental model for values, variables, expressions, and types.
- Learn why JavaScript feels different from many other languages.
## Prerequisites
- Basic comfort with programming concepts like variables and conditionals.
## Concepts
JavaScript is a general-purpose language used in browsers, servers, tooling, and build systems. A useful first mental model is this: JavaScript spends most of its time evaluating expressions, storing values in variables, and passing values into functions.
JavaScript values include strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, `undefined`, objects, arrays, and functions. Some of these are primitive values. Some are objects. This distinction matters because primitives behave like self-contained values, while objects are reference values.
`undefined` usually means "a value is missing right now." `null` usually means "we intentionally set this to no value." The language does not always enforce these meanings, but disciplined developers do.
## Worked Example
```js
const price = 19.99;
const taxRate = 0.08;
const total = price + price * taxRate;
console.log(total);
```
This code stores numeric values in `price` and `taxRate`, evaluates an arithmetic expression, and stores the result in `total`. JavaScript executes the right-hand side before assigning the final value.
Now compare that to object references:
```js
const user = { name: "Avery", role: "student" };
const sameUser = user;
sameUser.role = "junior developer";
console.log(user.role); // "junior developer"
```
## Explaining The Code
`sameUser = user` does not clone the object. It copies the reference. Both variables point at the same object in memory, so mutating through one variable changes what the other sees. This is one of the earliest JavaScript ideas that creates real bugs in app code.

- Shift from feature-level thinking to system-level thinking.
- Understand how architecture choices affect reliability, performance, maintainability, and team velocity.
- Practice framing design tradeoffs the way stronger mid-level and senior engineers do.
- Build a practical study path for system design interviews and real-world architecture conversations.
## Prerequisites
- Comfort with the junior track in this repository or equivalent experience building small full-stack apps.
- Familiarity with APIs, databases, async work, frontend state, and debugging.
## Why This Track Exists
Getting to a junior level usually means you can implement features with guidance. Moving toward mid-level and senior work means you start owning how systems are shaped, not just how one function or screen is written.
That shift includes questions like:
- What are the most important quality attributes for this system?
- Where should the boundaries between modules, services, or teams live?
- What breaks first when usage grows?
- Which failures are acceptable, and which are business-critical?
- How do we design for change instead of only for the current feature request?
System design is not about drawing random boxes and arrows. It is structured reasoning under constraints.
## The Mental Shift
Junior-level implementation questions often sound like:
- How do I build this form?
- Why is this API call failing?
- How should I structure this component?
Mid/senior architecture questions often sound like:
- Should this capability live in the frontend, backend, or both?
- What contracts must remain stable if multiple teams depend on this service?
- Should this system be synchronous or event-driven?
- Where do we cache, and what staleness is acceptable?

samples.opening:
# JavaScript Job-Readiness Course
This repository is a docs-first JavaScript training course for a learner who already understands basic programming ideas but needs stronger JavaScript skills to become competitive for a junior software engineering role.
The course is designed as a 12-16 week path. It starts with core language fluency, moves into browser and server work, layers in testing and TypeScript, and finishes with a portfolio-quality capstone.
After the junior track, the repository also includes an advanced continuation section for mid-level and senior-oriented growth in system design and architecture.
## Who This Is For
- You can read code and write simple logic in at least one language.
- You understand variables, loops, and functions at a basic level.
- You do not yet feel confident building real JavaScript applications.
- You want a path that explains both the "how" and the "why".
## What You Will Be Able To Do
By the end of this course, you should be able to:
- read and write idiomatic JavaScript in both browser and Node.js environments
- understand scope, closures, objects, prototypes, classes, modules, and async code
- build interactive browser features with the DOM and browser APIs
- create and consume JSON APIs
- build a simple backend with Node.js and Express-style routing
- test small units of code and debug common issues
- add TypeScript to a JavaScript project without panic
- explain your decisions clearly in a junior-level interview
## Suggested Pace
- `Weeks 1-2`: Lessons 1-2
- `Weeks 3-4`: Lessons 3-4
- `Weeks 5-6`: Lessons 5-6
- `Weeks 7-8`: Lessons 7-8
- `Weeks 9-10`: Lessons 9-10
- `Weeks 11-16`: Capstone planning, implementation, polish, and reflection
Move slower if you need to. The goal is durable understanding, not speed-running syntax.
## How To Use This Course
1. Read the lesson goals first.
2. Type out the code examples yourself instead of only reading them.
3. Pause after each section and predict what the code will do.
4. Complete the embedded labs before reading the solution guide.

# Course Overview
## Summary
This course teaches JavaScript as a working language, not a trivia topic. The main idea is simple: junior developers become effective when they can reason about values, functions, state, asynchronous behavior, and program structure with confidence. Everything in this course points back to that.
The main path in this repository is a junior job-readiness track. After that, the docs extend into an advanced track focused on system design and architecture for mid-level and senior growth.
## Learning Strategy
The curriculum moves in a deliberate order:
1. Learn how JavaScript thinks about values and execution.
2. Learn how to structure logic using functions, scope, and data.
3. Learn how larger programs organize behavior with objects and modules.
4. Learn how JavaScript interacts with browsers and servers.
5. Learn how real apps handle async work, APIs, validation, and failures.
6. Learn how teams use tooling, tests, TypeScript, and frameworks without losing the core language.
## What "Job Ready" Means Here
Job ready does not mean expert. It means you can:
- take a small task ticket and break it down
- read existing JavaScript without freezing
- add features with reasonable structure
- ask good questions when blocked
- test and debug your work
- explain tradeoffs clearly enough for code review and interviews
## Study Workflow
Use the same workflow for every lesson:
1. Read the goals and prerequisites.
2. Work through examples slowly.
3. Re-type the code and change one thing at a time.
4. Write down predictions before running code.
5. Complete the lab without looking at solutions.
6. Compare your code to the solution and note what you missed.
7. Summarize the lesson in plain English.
## Required Habits
- Keep a running `questions.md` file for topics that still feel fuzzy.
- Commit small checkpoints if you place exercises into a practice repo.

# Codebase Map
This project is a real-time collaborative Kanban-style board app built on Next.js App Router with Socket.IO and PostgreSQL. The codebase is structured as a small service-oriented frontend/backend monolith:
UI renders and handles user interaction.
Server routes and Socket.IO handlers receive requests/events.
Service modules enforce domain behavior and permissions.
Database schemas define shared contracts between persistence and business logic.
Background jobs handle async side effects (webhook/outbox dispatch).
## Major Architectural Layers
## UI Layer
- `src/app/...` and `src/components/...` define page entry points and board interactions.
- State orchestration for optimistic updates and presence lives in `BoardSurface` and `useBoardSocket`.
## API and Realtime Boundary
- HTTP API routes (for board snapshots and audit queries) are in `src/app/api/...`.
- Long-lived realtime coordination is in `src/lib/socket/actions.ts`.
- Both currently assume a session-like auth model built via request headers and DB user lookup.
## Domain and Integration Layer
- `src/lib/services/board-service.ts` contains the main command/invariant logic: create cards, move cards, update details, archive/restore, role changes, and event emission.
- `src/lib/outbox/dispatcher.ts` persists webhook work items and retries on failures.
- `src/lib/presence/manager.ts` handles in-memory collaborative presence.
## Persistence Layer
- `src/lib/db/index.ts` creates the Drizzle DB client.
- `src/lib/db/schema.ts` defines entities, enums, relationships, and event history.
## Runtime Boundaries
1. Browser client sends drag or edit intents through the socket hook.
2. Socket handlers run checks, mutate data through services, and broadcast board events.
3. Services write domain state and append audit/outbox records.
4. Clients receive board events and apply local state transitions, sometimes optimistically.
5. Background interval sends outbox records to external webhook targets.

# `server.ts`
## What This File Is For
This file is the runtime bootstrap for the app. It wires Next.js request handling, starts Socket.IO, optionally enables Redis adapter for multi-instance scaling, schedules background work, and starts the HTTP server.
## Why This File Matters
It defines how HTTP and realtime transport coexist in one process. Most architecture discussion depends on this topology: API routes are Next handlers, while realtime events arrive through Socket.IO on the same server socket.
## Key Exports / Main Units
- `start()` (internal async bootstrap)
- Builds the app, creates HTTP server, wires Socket.IO, registers handlers, starts background loops.
- `app`, `handler`, `io`, `httpServer`
- Internal instances for request handling and realtime channels.
## How It Works
- `next({ dev })` prepares Next.
- `createServer` wraps the Next request handler.
- `new SocketIOServer(httpServer, { path: "/api/socket.io", transports: [...] , cors })` enables browser connections from the app.
- If `REDIS_URL` exists, it creates pub/sub adapters so socket rooms can be shared across processes.
- On each socket connection, `registerBoardSocket(socket)` installs all board event handlers.
- `startPresencePurgeLoop(io)` begins periodic presence inactivity sweeps.
- `setInterval(..., OUTBOX_DISPATCH_INTERVAL_MS)` runs outbound webhook dispatch in the background.
## How It Connects To Other Files
- Imports and calls `registerBoardSocket` and `startPresencePurgeLoop` from `src/lib/socket/actions.ts`.
- Imports `dispatchOutboxEvents` from `src/lib/outbox/dispatcher.ts`.
- Relies on Next route handlers already defined in `src/app/*`.
- Reads runtime env vars used by multiple layers (PORT, SOCKET_PORT, REDIS_URL, OUTBOX_DISPATCH_INTERVAL_MS).
## Important Design Choices
- One process handles both SSR/API and socket I/O, which reduces infra complexity for development and small deployments.
- Redis adapter is conditional, preserving local simplicity while allowing horizontal scaling.
- Periodic dispatch loop in-process keeps architecture simple but introduces process-level coupling.
## Things A Junior Dev Should Notice

# `src/hooks/useBoardSocket.ts`
## What This File Is For
This hook creates a Socket.IO client for a board, subscribes to server events, tracks a local board version, and exposes a typed `emit` helper.
## Why This File Matters
It demonstrates how client state integrates with realtime and why version tracking matters for conflict recovery.
## Key Exports / Main Units
- `useBoardSocket(boardId, handlers)`
- Connects socket, emits join payload, listens for state/event/error messages.
- `emit(event, payload)`
- Appends current `boardVersion` automatically to outgoing payloads.
- Handler map:
- `onBoardState`, `onPresence`, `onEvent`, `onConflict`.
## How It Works
- On mount (or board change), creates a socket with path `/api/socket.io`.
- Sets up a heartbeat interval (15s) with null cursor and column markers.
- On `connect`, emits `board:join` with latest known version.
- Receives:
- `board:state` to replace local snapshot and version.
- `board:event` and `board:events-delta` to apply remote changes.
- `presence:change` to update collaborator list.
- `board:error` to surface conflict details.
- Cleans up listeners, emits `board:leave`, disconnects, and clears heartbeat on unmount.
## How It Connects To Other Files
- Socket server counterpart is `src/lib/socket/actions.ts`.
- Uses types from `src/lib/types.ts`.
- Consumed in `src/components/board/BoardSurface.tsx`.
- Supports route-level pages that provide boardId context.
## Important Design Choices
