# FluxGrant Learning Platform
FluxGrant is a grant and funding lifecycle management platform built as a learning artifact for backend-oriented product engineering. It supports separate grantor and grantee portals, tracks opportunities, applications, awards, budgets, reporting periods, compliance requirements, subawards, documents, notifications, and closeout workflows, and keeps auth, validation, services, and repositories explicitly separated.
## What is in this repo
- `src/app`: Next.js pages and REST route handlers
- `src/components`: Thin UI components that call the API
- `src/lib/auth`: Signed-cookie auth and RBAC boundary
- `src/lib/validation`: Request validation modules

- `docs/architecture`: System-level architecture notes
- `docs/learning`: Guided code-reading material, flow traces, build journal, and testing rationale
## Stack choice
This build keeps the default Next.js + React + TypeScript + Tailwind foundation, but intentionally does not add Prisma, PostgreSQL, Zod, or React Query because the project was requested as a no-new-installs learning exercise. The code is still structured so those tools could replace the in-memory store and handwritten validators later.

# Auth And Permissions
Session cookies are signed in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` by `createSessionCookieValue()` and verified by `verifySessionCookieValue()`. The Next-specific page bridge is `src/lib/auth/page-context.ts`, where `getPageRequestContext()` reads cookies through `next/headers` and passes them into `getRequestContextFromCookieHeader()` from `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts`.
API routes authenticate through `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts` - `requireAuthorizedContext(cookieHeader, action)`. That function first builds a `RequestContext`, then calls `assertCan()` in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. If there is no valid session, `AuthenticationError` from `src/lib/http/api-errors.ts` is thrown with status `401`. If the role does not have the named action, `AuthorizationError` is thrown with status `403`.
Role rules live in one place: `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` - `permissionMatrix`. That file maps actions like `opportunity:manage`, `application:review`, `award:manage`, and `report:submit` to roles such as `GRANTOR_ADMIN`, `GRANTOR_REVIEWER`, `GRANTEE_ADMIN`, and `GRANTEE_MANAGER`. Route handlers never hard-code roles directly; they call `requireAuthorizedContext()` with an action name.
Portal access is separate from action access. The grantor page in `src/app/grantor/page.tsx` calls `assertGrantorPortalAccess()` from `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts` after loading the page context. The grantee page in `src/app/grantee/page.tsx` calls `assertGranteePortalAccess()` the same way. This keeps the UI boundary explicit before the dashboards render.
Authorization is also rechecked at the service layer when resource ownership matters. Example: `src/services/grantorOpportunityService.ts` - `publishGrantOpportunity()` verifies the opportunity belongs to the current grantor organization before checking status. Example: `src/services/granteeApplicationService.ts` - `submitGrantApplication()` verifies `application.granteeOrganizationId === context.organization.id` before allowing submission. Example: `src/services/reportingService.ts` - `approveAwardReport()` authorizes against `award.grantorOrganizationId`, not the report submitter.
Data isolation is explicit but not multi-tenant in the SaaS `tenantId` sense. This version uses organization ownership fields such as `grantorOrganizationId` and `granteeOrganizationId` in `src/types/domain.ts`, and repositories filter on those fields. Example: `src/repositories/opportunityRepository.ts` - `listGrantorOpportunities()` scopes by `grantorOrganizationId`. Example: `src/repositories/applicationRepository.ts` - `listG

# Architecture Overview
This project is a multi-tenant learning management system focused on backend-oriented product engineering. The core workflow is: a request enters an App Router route in `src/app/api/*`, auth is resolved in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, payload validation happens in `src/lib/validation/*`, business rules live in `src/services/*`, and Prisma queries stay in `src/repositories/*`.
Top-level folders:
- `src/app` contains UI entry points and REST route handlers. Examples: `src/app/api/courses/route.ts` and `src/app/dashboard/manager/page.tsx`.
- `src/components` contains presentation components that call hooks rather than embedding business logic. Examples: `src/components/assignments/ComplianceOverview.tsx` and `src/components/courses/CourseCatalog.tsx`.
- `src/hooks` contains React Query hooks that talk to the API through `src/lib/api/client.ts`.
- `src/lib` contains cross-cutting boundaries: `src/lib/auth/session.ts` for session resolution, `src/lib/permissions/requirePermission.ts` for RBAC enforcement, `src/lib/api/route.ts` for request parsing, and `src/lib/validation/*` for Zod schemas.
- `src/services` is the business layer. `src/services/assignmentService.ts` owns assignment fan-out into enrollments, and `src/services/enrollmentService.ts` owns completion and certification rules.
- `src/repositories` owns all database access. `src/repositories/courseRepository.ts` and `src/repositories/enrollmentRepository.ts` are good starting examples of tenant-scoped queries.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the persistent domain model.
- `tests` contains focused tests for auth, validation, state transitions, and tenant isolation.
- `docs/architecture` explains structure and request movement. `docs/learning` explains how to read the code like a stronger engineer.
The architectural center of gravity is the service layer, not React. The reason is visible in `src/services/assignmentService.ts` and `src/services/enrollmentService.ts`: the hard problems here are permissions, tenant scoping, state transitions, and transaction boundaries, which need to stay server-side and reviewable.

**What to trace:** `src/lib/api/route.ts` calls `getSessionFromRequest()`, and pages like `src/app/page.tsx` call `getServerSession()`.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Services never parse headers directly; once they do, your core business logic becomes HTTP-coupled.

ClosingHub is a Next.js App Router application for real estate transaction and deal management. The product shape is centered on one shared transaction record that changes visibility depending on whether the viewer is an agent, broker, buyer, or seller. The top-level design goal is to keep auth, validation, workflow rules, and persistence boundaries explicit so a reviewer can see where each responsibility lives.

The project models partner onboarding, deal registration approvals, MDF decisions and reimbursements, certification tracking, partner-visible data scoping, and leaderboard reporting with a small async job system.
This codebase intentionally does **not** use full multi-tenancy. Instead, it models a single vendor deployment with partner-owned records. Internal users can see all data, while partner users are scoped to their own `partnerOrgId` through `src/lib/auth/visibility.ts` and the repository methods that call it.

SignalDesk is a Next.js App Router application that keeps request handling, business logic, and persistence boundaries explicit. The UI lives in `src/app/page.tsx` and the components under `src/components`, but user actions leave the browser through client hooks such as `src/hooks/use-account-detail.ts` and land in REST route files like `src/app/api/accounts/[accountId]/playbook-runs/route.ts`. Those route files stay thin because `src/lib/middleware/with-route-contract.ts` owns auth, permission checks, and Zod parsing before the request reaches services.
The service layer in `src/services` owns product behavior. `src/services/health-score-config-service.ts` updates versioned configs and immediately triggers recalculation through `src/services/health-score-service.ts`; `src/services/playbook-service.ts` owns workflow transitions; `src/services/renewal-forecast-service.ts` owns attribution rules. Services call repository contracts from `src/repositories/contracts.ts`, and the active adapter is chosen once in `src/repositories/repository-factory.ts`.
Persistence is split into two realistic paths. `src/repositories/prisma/*` shows the production-style PostgreSQL/Prisma boundary backed by `prisma/schema.prisma`, while `src/repositories/mock/mock-repository-factory.ts` keeps the project runnable in learning mode with deterministic data from `src/repositories/mock/mock-data.ts`. This is a deliberate architecture choice: the app teaches real repository and tenant-scoping patterns even when the default runtime uses mock data.
Cross-cutting concerns stay centralized. Auth and session resolution live in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, RBAC lives in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`, request validation lives in `src/lib/validation/*`, and scoring math lives in `src/lib/scoring/health-score-engine.ts`. SignalDesk is a learning-oriented customer success and health scoring platform built with Next.js, TypeScript, React Query, Zod, and Prisma-style repository boundaries. It aggregates account signals, computes a configurable weighted health score, drives playbook execution, tracks renewal forecasts, and keeps auth, RBAC, tenant scoping, and business rules explicit in the codebase.

Session creation starts in `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, where `withRouteContract()` validates the request body with `loginSchema` from `src/lib/validation/auth-schemas.ts`. The route then calls `createSessionForCredentials()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, which looks up the user through `getRepositoryBundle().users.getByEmail()` and persists the session token through `getRepositoryBundle().sessions.createSession()`. The HTTP-only cookie name is `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`.
Session verification happens in `getCurrentSessionFromRequest()` inside `src/lib/auth/session.ts`. That function reads the cookie, looks up the server-side session record, rejects expired sessions, and hydrates the user record before returning an `AuthenticatedSession`. Routes do not re-implement that logic; they rely on `withRouteContract()` in `src/lib/middleware/with-route-contract.ts`, which resolves the session before the handler runs.
Role-based access control is centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. The `rolePermissions` map is the single source of truth for what `PLATFORM_ADMIN`, `ORG_ADMIN`, `CSM`, and `LEADERSHIP` can do. When a route supplies `permission: "health-config:write"` or any other permission string to `withRouteContract()`, the wrapper calls `hasPermission()` before the route handler executes. Example: `src/app/api/admin/health-score-config/route.ts` requires `health-config:write` for `POST`, while `src/app/api/accounts/route.ts` requires `accounts:read` for `GET`.
Tenant isolation is first-class. After auth, those routes construct a `TenantScopedContext` from `session.tenantId` and `session.user.id`. That context then flows into services and repositories rather than letting routes pass raw tenant IDs around ad hoc.
Repository-level tenant scoping is explicit in both adapters. # Auth And Permissions
Session resolution starts in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`. `getSessionFromHeaders()` reads `x-demo-user-email` and `x-active-tenant-id`, validates them with Zod, and rejects unknown or invalid tenant switches before a request reaches the service layer. `requireTenantContext()` then turns that session into a request context with a concrete `tenantId`.
Role-based access control is centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. `assertCan()` checks the `AppAction` requested by a route against the role matrix in `rolePermissions`. Route files do not embed their own role logic; instead they declare the needed action in `src/lib/http/with-route-context.ts`, which calls `getSessionFromHeaders()`, `assertCan()`, and `requireTenantContext()` before invoking the handler.
Examples of permission enforcement:
- Quote creation is guarded in `src/app/api/quotes/route.ts` by `withRouteContext(request, "quote:create", ...)`.

- Payment application is guarded in `src/app/api/invoices/[invoiceId]/apply-payment/route.ts` by `withRouteContext(request, "invoice:applyPayment", ...)`.
- Additional resource-level authorization happens in `src/services/quote-service.ts` inside `decideQuoteApproval()`, where the service verifies that the caller's role actually has a pending approval row on that specific quote.

- Session-level tenant selection happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`. Platform admins must still choose an active tenant, so downstream repository code always receives one tenant context instead of branching on cross-tenant access.

# Architecture Overview
Locksmith Dashboard is a Next.js application that teaches distributed coordination with a database-backed lock manager, explicit RBAC, and an operational dashboard. The codebase is organized so each layer has a narrow job and real file examples you can trace.
## Top-level folders
- `src/app/`
App Router pages and REST endpoints live here. Examples: `src/app/dashboard/page.tsx`, `src/app/api/locks/acquire/route.ts`, and `src/app/api/simulations/run/route.ts`.
- `src/components/`
React UI composition stays here, with the main orchestration container in `src/components/dashboard/DashboardShell.tsx` and presentational widgets like `src/components/dashboard/LockTable.tsx`.
- `src/hooks/`
Browser-side data access and mutation wiring live in `src/hooks/useLockDashboard.ts`.
- `src/lib/`
Cross-cutting boundaries live here:
`src/lib/auth/session.ts` resolves the current user.
`src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` enforces RBAC.
`src/lib/validation/lockSchemas.ts` and `src/lib/validation/simulationSchemas.ts` enforce request shapes.
`src/lib/http/responses.ts` standardizes API responses.
`src/lib/db/prisma.ts` owns Prisma client creation.
- `src/services/`
Business logic lives here. `src/services/lockCoordinatorService.ts` owns acquisition, renewal, release, and stale expiry. `src/services/dashboardService.ts` builds role-aware dashboard data. `src/services/simulationService.ts` runs concurrency simulations.
- `src/repositories/`
Database access is isolated here. `src/repositories/lockScopeRepository.ts` handles row-level scope locking and version state. `src/repositories/lockLeaseRepository.ts` writes lease rows and audit events. `src/repositories/simulationRunRepository.ts` stores simulation history.
- `src/data/`
Demo-only seed-like constants live here, such as `src/data/demoUsers.ts`.
- `prisma/`
`prisma/schema.prisma` defines the durable coordination model and its relations.
- `tests/`
Small but purposeful tests live under `tests/unit/` and `tests/integration/`.
- `docs/`
Architecture and learning notes are in `docs/architecture/` and `docs/learning/`.

- Schema/model file: `prisma/schema.prisma` - `model LockScope`

- Role in the system: represents a scoped coordination target such as `RESOURCE:invoice:123` or `JOB:nightly-reconciliation`.
- Why it exists separately from leases: `LockScope.version` supports optimistic concurrency, while `activeLeaseId` and `activeLeaseExpiresAt` track the current pessimistic holder.
### LockLease
- Schema/model file: `prisma/schema.prisma` - `model LockLease`

## Session flow
Session resolution starts in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` - `getSessionFromRequest()`. That function reads `x-demo-user-id`, then the `demo-user-id` cookie, then falls back to `DEMO_SESSION_USER_ID`. The important security boundary is that the request only supplies a user id; the role comes from `src/data/demoUsers.ts`, not from client-provided JSON.
Routes that require authentication call `src/lib/auth/session.ts` - `requireSession()`. Examples:
- `src/app/api/locks/route.ts` calls `requireSession()` before reading dashboard data.
- `src/app/api/locks/acquire/route.ts` calls `requireSession()` before parsing the acquire body.
- `src/app/api/simulations/run/route.ts` calls `requireSession()` before allowing a simulation run.
## Role enforcement
RBAC rules are centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`.
- `assertPermission(session, "locks:view")` is used in `src/app/api/locks/route.ts`.
- `assertPermission(session, "locks:manage")` is used in `src/app/api/locks/acquire/route.ts`, `src/app/api/locks/[lockId]/renew/route.ts`, and `src/app/api/locks/[lockId]/release/route.ts`.
- `assertPermission(session, "locks:expire")` is used in `src/app/api/locks/expire-stale/route.ts`.
- `assertPermission(session, "simulations:run")` is used in `src/app/api/simulations/run/route.ts` and again inside `src/services/simulationService.ts` so the service can defend itself even if another caller reuses it later.

Role checks alone are not enough for lock mutation. `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` - `assertCanManageLease()` adds per-record ownership rules:
- Admins and operators can manage any lease.
- Viewers can only manage their own lease rows.
That ownership check runs inside `src/services/lockCoordinatorService.ts` in both `renewLock()` and `releaseLock()`, after the lease is loaded from `src/repositories/lockLeaseRepository.ts` - `findLeaseById()`. It then passes that filter into `src/repositories/lockScopeRepository.ts` - `listScopes()`, `src/repositories/lockLeaseRepository.ts` - `listVisibleLocks()` and `listRecentEvents()`, plus `src/repositories/simulationRunRepository.ts` - `listRecentSimulationRuns()`. Requests enter through Next.js route handlers like `src/app/api/platform/customer-profiles/route.ts`, move through shared request context in `src/lib/http/api-context.ts`, hit validation in `src/lib/validation/customer-profile-schemas.ts`, then flow into services such as `src/services/customer-profile-service.ts` and repositories such as `src/repositories/customer-profile-repository.ts`.
Top-level folder map:
- `src/app` contains the HTTP surface and UI entry points. The versioned API lives under `src/app/api/platform/**`, while the dashboard shell starts in `src/app/page.tsx`.
- `src/lib` contains cross-cutting boundaries. Auth lives in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` and `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`; request setup lives in `src/lib/http/api-context.ts`; version metadata and rollout logic live in `src/lib/versioning/version-registry.ts` and `src/lib/versioning/version-rollout.ts`.
- `src/services` contains business logic. `src/services/customer-profile-service.ts` owns profile rules like invalid lifecycle transitions, and `src/services/api-version-service.ts` owns rollout updates and usage summaries.
- `src/repositories` contains database access. `src/repositories/customer-profile-repository.ts` scopes profile reads by owner, `src/repositories/version-catalog-repository.ts` persists rollout overrides, and `src/repositories/usage-metric-repository.ts` records per-version usage.
- `prisma` contains the relational model in `prisma/schema.prisma`.
- `docs` contains architecture and learning guides that point back to concrete code paths such as `docs/architecture/request-lifecycle.md` and `docs/learning/flow-traces.md`.
- `tests` contains focused examples of the system boundaries: route auth in `tests/routes/version-rollout-route.test.ts`, validation in `tests/validation/customer-profile-schemas.test.ts`, and service-layer invariants in `tests/services/customer-profile-service.test.ts`.

# Auth And Permissions
Authentication flow:
- Session extraction happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `requireSession()`. The check is at the top of the file and throws `UNAUTHORIZED` before routes proceed if `x-user-id`, `x-user-role`, or `x-client-id` are missing.
- Request setup happens in `src/lib/http/api-context.ts` inside `buildApiContext()`. The middle of that file calls `requireSession()`, resolves the requested version, merges rollout overrides through `services.apiVersions.getEffectiveVersionDefinition()`, and then applies `assertVersionAccess()`.
Authorization flow:
- Role checks are centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. `assertRole()` is the generic guard used by `CustomerProfileService.listProfiles()`, `CustomerProfileService.createProfile()`, and `ApiVersionService.updateRollout()`.
- Ownership checks are also centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. `assertCanMutateProfile()` enforces that only `ADMIN`, `SUPPORT`, or the owning `CLIENT` can modify a profile.
- Read isolation is enforced lower in the stack in `src/repositories/customer-profile-repository.ts`. `buildVisibilityWhere()` scopes client reads by `ownerUserId`, so `findByIdForSession()` and `listForSession()` never fetch another client's rows in the first place.
Role matrix in this codebase:
- `ADMIN`
Can list profiles, read any profile, create profiles, update profiles, and change rollout state through `ApiVersionService.updateRollout()` in `src/services/api-version-service.ts`.
- `SUPPORT`
Can list profiles, read any profile, create profiles, and update profiles through `src/services/customer-profile-service.ts`, but cannot change rollout because `ApiVersionService.updateRollout()` only accepts `ADMIN`.
- `ANALYST`
Can list and read profiles through `CustomerProfileService.listProfiles()` and `CustomerProfileService.getProfile()`, but cannot mutate profiles or rollout.
- `CLIENT`
Can list and read only owned profiles because `src/repositories/customer-profile-repository.ts` scopes queries by `ownerUserId`.
Can update only owned profiles because `assertCanMutateProfile()` checks `profile.ownerUserId === session.userId`.
Cannot change rollout because `assertRole(session, ["ADMIN"])` rejects inside `ApiVersionService.updateRollout()`.
Version access:
- `src/lib/versioning/version-rollout.ts` contains `assertVersionAccess()`. This runs before validation or service logic and gates `CLIENT` access by percentage rollout and allowlist.
- Internal roles bypass rollout checks in that file so support and admin tooling can inspect versions that are not fully rolled out

# S3-lite Architecture
This project is a production-style learning scaffold for a distributed file storage system with tenant isolation, multipart uploads, retries, signed downloads, quota tracking, and duplicated chunk storage. The runtime core is intentionally dependency-light so it can execute in this no-install environment, while the app shell still mirrors a Next.js + React + Prisma stack.
Top-level folders map to clear layers:
- `src/app/` contains the framework edge. For example, `src/app/api/files/route.ts` accepts REST requests and immediately delegates to services, while `src/app/files/page.tsx` renders the demo dashboard.
- `src/services/` owns business rules and state transitions. `src/services/uploadService.ts` decides when a file can move from `UPLOADING` to `READY`, and `src/services/accessService.ts` owns signed URL and download logic.
- `src/repositories/` owns persistence-shaped access. `src/repositories/fileRepository.ts` performs tenant-scoped file/chunk reads and writes, and `src/repositories/uploadSessionRepository.ts` owns idempotency-keyed upload-session state.
- `src/lib/auth/`, `src/lib/validation/`, and `src/lib/http/` hold cross-cutting boundaries. `src/lib/auth/session.ts` resolves tenant-aware sessions, `src/lib/auth/guards.ts` enforces centralized authorization, and `src/lib/validation/fileSchemas.ts` rejects malformed request bodies before services run.
- `src/lib/storage/` contains the blob storage adapter. `src/lib/storage/localReplicaStorage.ts` writes each chunk to both `storage/replica-a/` and `storage/replica-b/`.
- `src/server/` wires the app together. `src/server/container.ts` creates the repositories, services, storage adapter, and config in one place.
- `prisma/` captures the production-target relational schema. `prisma/schema.prisma` models tenants, memberships, files, chunks, and upload sessions even though the demo runtime uses `src/lib/db/inMemoryDatabase.ts`.
- `tests/` covers load-bearing failures. `tests/auth-permissions.test.ts`, `tests/state-transition.test.ts`, and `tests/data-isolation.test.ts` focus on security and correctness instead of broad happy-path coverage.
The most important architectural split is: metadata and workflow state live in repositories/services, while chunk bytes live in the storage adapt

This project is a notification delivery platform built as a single TypeScript application with a separate background worker process. The web app owns auth, CRUD-style operational APIs, and dashboards. The worker in `src/workers/notificationWorker.ts` owns async delivery, retry scheduling, and rate-limit enforcement.

Example files: `src/app/api/notifications/route.ts`, `src/app/notifications/page.tsx`

Production-style Next.js application for sending queued notifications over email, SMS, and push with retry logic, delivery history, user preferences, rate limiting, and an admin monitoring surface.

# Architecture Overview
This project is a Next.js + React + TypeScript learning build for employer-of-record operations. The backend is organized around `prisma/schema.prisma`, `src/repositories/prisma/*.ts`, and `src/services/*.ts`, with `src/app/api/*/route.ts` acting as the thin HTTP boundary. The UI lives in `src/app/(app)/*` and uses React Query hooks from `src/hooks/*.ts` to talk to the API.
Top-level structure:
- `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the tenant-owned data model and workflow enums.
- `src/lib/auth/*` holds session parsing, tenant context, and permission guards.
- `src/lib/validation/*` holds the Zod schemas that reject bad input before service logic runs.
- `src/repositories/prisma/*` owns database access and tenant-scoped query shapes.
- `src/services/*` owns business logic, transition rules, duplicate checks, and audit writes.
- `src/app/api/*/route.ts` authenticates, validates, and delegates to services.
- `src/hooks/*` owns the browser-side request flow with React Query.
- `src/app/(app)/*` owns the visible screens that exercise the routes.
Why this layout matters:
- A junior engineer can follow one request from page to hook to route to service to repository without guessing where logic lives.
- A mid-level engineer should notice that write rules are not hidden in the UI.
- A senior engineer should notice that tenant scoping is repeated at the service and repository boundaries, which is deliberate defense in depth.

# Guided Reading Path
## Step 1 — `prisma/schema.prisma`
**Why read this:** This is the domain contract for the entire app. Every repository and workflow service assumes these models and enums are correct.
**What to look for:** The tenant-owned tables, the workflow enums, and the fact that `tenantId` appears on every operational model.
**What to trace:** `src/repositories/prisma/*.ts` reads these models; `src/services/*.ts` depends on their status fields.
**What a junior would likely miss:** The schema is not just persistence. It is also the first place the project decides what counts as a state machine.
## Step 2 — `src/lib/auth/session.ts`
**Why read this:** This is where request identity starts.
**What to look for:** `verifySessionFromHeaders()` and how the demo headers become a typed `SessionUser`.
**What to trace:** `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts` calls this file; every route handler eventually depends on the session it returns.
**What a junior would likely miss:** The session parser is security-sensitive even in a learning project because bad parsing can turn into a bad permission decision.
## Step 3 — `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts`
**Why read this:** This file resolves the active tenant and blocks tenant mismatches before services run.
**What to look for:** `buildRequestContext()` and the `requireTenant` branch.
**What to trace:** `src/app/api/*/route.ts` calls it; `src/lib/auth/guards.ts` consumes the returned context.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Tenant selection is not the same thing as authentication.

**Why read this:** This is the actual role matrix.

Role checks are centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` and `src/lib/auth/guards.ts`. `hasPermission()` maps `PlatformRole` and `TenantRole` to the action list, while `assertPermission()` throws `ForbiddenError` before the request reaches business logic. `requireTenantContext()` makes tenant scope a first-class value, not an optional afterthought.
Examples from the route layer:
- `src/app/api/workers/route.ts` calls `buildRequestContext()` and then `workerService.listWorkers()` or `workerService.createWorker()`.
- `src/app/api/contracts/[contractId]/route.ts` uses the same context flow before `contractService.changeContractStatus()`.
- `src/app/api/jobs/compliance-scan/route.ts` still requires tenant context even though it is a background-style workflow.

- Repository methods in `src/repositories/prisma/workerRepository.ts`, `src/repositories/prisma/contractRepository.ts`, `src/repositories/prisma/complianceRepository.ts`, and the other Prisma repositories always include `tenantId` in their `where` clauses.
- Services in `src/services/workerService.ts`, `src/services/contractService.ts`, `src/services/complianceService.ts`, and related files call `requireTenantContext()` before they ask the repository to read or write.
What would need to change to add a second isolation layer:
- The session would need a real auth provider instead of demo headers.
- `buildRequestContext()` would need to read tenant membership from the auth provider and possibly an active-tenant session claim.
- Every tenant-owned Prisma query would still need the `tenantId` filter, so the repository contract would stay the same.
Senior concern:
- `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts` is the last place to stop a tenant mismatch before the repository layer sees it. If this file drifts, the rest of the code can become technically “correct” and still unsafe.

# Architecture Overview
Flagship is a Next.js control plane for runtime feature rollout. The web app lives in `src/app/**`, request auth and HTTP helpers live in `src/lib/http/**` and `src/lib/auth/**`, business rules live in `src/services/**`, and database access is isolated in `src/repositories/**`.
Top-level layers:
- `src/app` contains the UI pages and REST routes. Examples: `src/app/flags/page.tsx` renders the flag console, and `src/app/api/flags/route.ts` handles list/create requests.
- `src/components` contains client-side control plane surfaces. `src/components/flags/FlagConsole.tsx` is the main admin UI for versioned flag operations.
- `src/hooks` wraps the REST API for React Query consumers. `src/hooks/useFeatureFlags.ts` is the main read/write client boundary for flags.
- `src/lib` contains cross-cutting concerns. `src/lib/http/route-context.ts` owns route protection, `src/lib/auth/session.ts` resolves user/service identity, and `src/lib/validation/featureFlagSchemas.ts` owns write contracts.

- `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the relational model and `prisma/seed.ts` seeds example users, segments, flags, and service credentials.
The architectural center of gravity is the evaluator path:
1. `src/app/api/sdk/evaluate/route.ts`
2. `src/lib/http/route-context.ts`
3. `src/lib/auth/session.ts`
4. `src/lib/validation/sdkSchemas.ts`
5. `src/services/evaluationService.ts`
6. `src/repositories/featureFlagRepository.ts`
7. `src/services/exposureMetricService.ts`
8. `src/repositories/exposureMetricRepository.ts`

- `flags:write` allows `ADMIN`, `OPERATOR`

- `segments:write` allows `ADMIN`, `OPERATOR`
- `services:write` allows `ADMIN`

Environment scoping is the main isolation boundary for machine callers in this project. `src/app/api/sdk/evaluate/route.ts` checks `serviceAccount.allowedEnvironments.includes(body.environment)` and rejects with `ForbiddenError` if not. The test in `tests/isolation/sdk-environment-scope.test.ts` covers that rejection path.

# Architecture Overview
Workspace Wire is a Slack-like messaging platform built around a strict server-side boundary: route handlers validate input, services apply business rules, repositories own database queries, and the websocket layer only fans out already-authorized workspace events. The top-level shape is meant to be easy to read as a backend-oriented product app rather than a tutorial scaffold.
`src/app/` contains the UI routes and REST handlers. Examples: `src/app/workspace/[workspaceId]/channel/[channelId]/page.tsx` server-renders an authorized channel view, while `src/app/api/workspaces/[workspaceId]/channels/[channelId]/messages/route.ts` is the HTTP boundary for channel history and message creation.
`src/services/` contains the business logic. `src/services/messageService.ts` owns thread rules, notifications, read-state updates, and sync-event creation; `src/services/channelService.ts` owns channel creation and private-channel access rules.

# StayBound Architecture
StayBound is a Next.js App Router application for searching listings, requesting bookings, approving stays, capturing mock payments, applying cancellation policies, and creating post-stay reviews. The backend is intentionally service-led: route handlers in `src/app/api/**/route.ts` validate input and resolve the actor, services in `src/services/*.ts` own workflow rules, and repositories in `src/repositories/*.ts` own Prisma access.
The stack stays close to the requested default: `Next.js + React + TypeScript + PostgreSQL + Prisma + Tailwind + Zod + React Query + REST`. Prisma was chosen over Drizzle because `src/services/bookingService.ts` relies on explicit transactions, relational includes, and a readable generated client while teaching service/repository boundaries. # Appointment Booking System
This is a Next.js + TypeScript booking app with PostgreSQL, Prisma, Zod, and React Query. The code is split around request boundaries and business boundaries: `src/app/api/*` handles HTTP, `src/services/*` owns business rules, `src/repositories/*` owns database reads and writes, and `src/components/*` plus `src/hooks/*` keep the UI thin.
Top-level map:
- `src/app` contains routes and pages.
- `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts` and `src/app/api/auth/logout/route.ts` handle session creation and teardown.
- `src/app/api/appointments/route.ts` and `src/app/api/appointments/[appointmentId]/cancel/route.ts` handle booking and cancellation.
- `src/services/appointmentService.ts` and `src/services/availabilityService.ts` own the calendar and appointment rules.
- `src/repositories/appointmentRepository.ts`, `src/repositories/staffRepository.ts`, and `src/repositories/userRepository.ts` own Prisma queries.
- `src/lib/auth/*`, `src/lib/validation/*`, and `src/lib/data/*` hold shared guards, schemas, and query scopes.
- `src/components/*` and `src/hooks/*` drive the React UI and data fetching.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the domain model, and `prisma/migrations/0001_initial/migration.sql` adds the PostgreSQL exclusion constraint that prevents overlapping bookings.
Why this split matters:
- `src/app/api/*` stays focused on request parsing and response codes.
- `src/services/*` is where a reviewer checks the actual product rules.
- `src/repositories/*` is where you verify the app is not leaking data or querying too broadly.
- `src/lib/data/appointmentScopes.ts` keeps owner scoping central so the same filter is reused everywhere.
If multi-tenancy is added later, the first places to change would be `prisma/schema.prisma`, `src/lib/data/appointmentScopes.ts`, `src/repositories/*.ts`, and `src/services/authService.ts`.

# Guided Reading Path
## Step 1 — `prisma/schema.prisma`
**Why read this:** This is the canonical domain model.
**What to look for:** The `Role` and `AppointmentStatus` enums, plus the `StaffProfile` and `Appointment` relations.
**What to trace:** `src/repositories/*.ts` reads from this schema, and `src/services/*` uses the generated model shapes.
**What a junior would likely miss:** The model can look simple while still requiring a separate database-level overlap constraint.
## Step 2 — `prisma/migrations/0001_initial/migration.sql`
**Why read this:** It shows the real database guarantee behind double-booking prevention.
**What to look for:** The exclusion constraint on `Appointment`.
**What to trace:** `src/services/appointmentService.ts` checks conflicts first, but PostgreSQL is the last line of defense.
**What a junior would likely miss:** App-level conflict checks are not enough under concurrency.
## Step 3 — `src/lib/auth/session.ts`
**Why read this:** This defines the session token contract.
**What to look for:** Cookie name, TTL, token generation, and hashing.
**What to trace:** `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts` sets the cookie, and `src/services/authService.ts` reads it.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Never store or compare the raw token in the database.
## Step 4 — `src/services/authService.ts`
**Why read this:** This is the session and login workflow.
**What to look for:** `login()`, `logout()`, and `getActorFromRequest()`.
**What to trace:** `src/lib/auth/with-auth.ts` calls into this file before any protected handler runs.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Auth is a server concern, not a UI concern.
## Step 5 — `src/lib/auth/with-auth.ts`
**Why read this:** This is the reusable authentication guard.
**What to look for:** How it converts missing sessions into a 401 response.
**What to trace:** It wraps `src/app/api/me/route.ts`, `src/app/api/appointments/route.ts`, and `src/app/api/staff/route.ts`.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Every protected route should use the same guard shape.
## Step 6 — `src/lib/auth/with-role.ts`
**Why read this:** This is where admin-only access is enforced.

# Domain Model
```mermaid
erDiagram
User ||--o{ Session : has
User ||--o| StaffProfile : may_have
StaffProfile ||--o{ WorkingHoursRule : owns
StaffProfile ||--o{ TimeOffBlock : owns
StaffProfile ||--o{ Appointment : receives
User ||--o{ Appointment : books
```
Entity ownership and logic:
- `User`
- Schema: `prisma/schema.prisma`
- Primary service: `src/services/authService.ts`
- Important repository: `src/repositories/userRepository.ts`
- `Session`
- Schema: `prisma/schema.prisma`
- Primary service: `src/services/authService.ts`
- Important repository: `src/repositories/sessionRepository.ts`
- `StaffProfile`
- Schema: `prisma/schema.prisma`
- Primary service: `src/services/availabilityService.ts`
- Important repository: `src/repositories/staffRepository.ts`
- `WorkingHoursRule`
- Schema: `prisma/schema.prisma`
- Primary service: `src/services/availabilityService.ts`
- Important repository: `src/repositories/availabilityRepository.ts`
- `TimeOffBlock`

# Auth and Permissions
Session creation starts in `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, which validates the payload with `loginSchema` from `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts` and then calls `login()` in `src/services/authService.ts`. That service hashes the supplied password with `verifyPassword()` in `src/lib/auth/password.ts`, creates a session token in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, stores the hashed token through `src/repositories/sessionRepository.ts`, and returns the user payload for the cookie-setting response.
Session lookup happens in `src/services/authService.ts` inside `getActorFromRequest()`. It reads `appointment_session` from the request cookie, hashes the token, and loads the active session from `src/repositories/sessionRepository.ts`. If the session is missing, revoked, or expired, the request never reaches the handler body because `src/lib/auth/with-auth.ts` converts that into a 401 response.
Role checks are centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` and enforced in the route guards:
- `src/lib/auth/with-role.ts` calls `requireRole()` before an admin route handler runs.
- `src/lib/auth/with-auth.ts` blocks anonymous requests before a protected handler runs.
- `src/app/api/admin/staff/route.ts`, `src/app/api/admin/working-hours/route.ts`, and `src/app/api/admin/time-off/route.ts` use `withRole(["ADMIN"], ...)`.
Ownership checks are not scattered through React components. Instead:
- `src/lib/data/appointmentScopes.ts` builds the Prisma `where` filters for admin, staff, and client views.
- `src/repositories/appointmentRepository.ts` uses those filters in `listAppointmentsForActor()` and `findScopedAppointmentById()`.
- `src/services/appointmentService.ts` still performs a second explicit cancellation check so the state transition is enforced before the update write happens.
Current role model:
- `ADMIN` can manage staff, working hours, and time off through the admin routes.
- `CLIENT` can book and cancel their own appointments.
- `STAFF` can view their scoped calendars and appointments, but the booking endpoint rejects them.
No multi-tenancy is included. If the product later needs org boundaries, the changes would be:
- Add `tenantId` to `User`, `Session`, `StaffProfile`, `WorkingHoursRule`, `TimeOffBlock`, and `Appointment` in `prisma/schema.prisma`.
- Load `tenantId` in `src/services/authService.ts` and include it in the `RequestActor`.
- Add tenant filters to `src/lib/data/appointmentScopes.ts`.
- Update every repository query in `src/repositories/*.ts` to include `tenantId` alongside the ownership filter.

This project is a single-store inventory reservation app. It manages product stock, converts active holds into released or completed reservations, and keeps low-stock alerts in sync with stock changes.
The stack stays close to the default recommendation:

REST was chosen over tRPC because the request boundaries are part of the teaching artifact; the route handlers in `app/api/*` make auth, validation, and service delegation very easy to trace.

# Architecture Overview
This app is a small-store inventory reservation system built around three core workflows: create a hold, release a hold, and keep low-stock alerts in sync when inventory changes. The backend shape is intentionally production-style even though persistence is mocked in-memory for a no-install learning build.
Top-level folders map to the system like this:
- `src/app` contains the request entrypoints and the page shell. `src/app/api/reservations/route.ts` and `src/app/api/items/route.ts` are the server boundaries, while `src/app/page.tsx` renders the dashboard shell.
- `src/components` contains the client workbench. `src/components/dashboard/inventory-workbench.tsx` is the only interactive UI and it exercises the actual API routes with mock session headers.
- `src/lib` contains shared infrastructure: `src/lib/auth/session.ts` reads the fake session, `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts` enforces auth and roles, `src/lib/validation/*.ts` defines the Zod boundary, and `src/lib/http/api.ts` turns errors into JSON responses.
- `src/services` contains business logic. `src/services/reservationService.ts` owns hold/release rules, `src/services/inventoryService.ts` owns item changes and stock math, and `src/services/alertService.ts` keeps low-stock alerts aligned with item state.
- `src/repositories` contains the persistence boundary. `src/repositories/inventoryRepository.ts` defines the contract and `src/repositories/inMemoryInventoryRepository.ts` provides the current in-memory implementation.
- `src/domain` contains pure entities and helpers. `src/domain/inventory.ts` defines the item, reservation, and alert shapes plus derived stock helpers.
- `src/data` contains seed data for learning and demo use. `src/data/seed.ts` keeps the starting inventory consistent with the alert state.
- `tests` contains focused behavior tests. `tests/inventory.test.ts` pins the auth rejection, validation, state transition, and data-scoping rules.
The important architectural choice is that all request handlers call into services instead of touching the repository directly. That is why the route files stay small and the stateful rules live in `src/services/*.ts`.

# Guided Reading Path
## Step 1 — `src/app/page.tsx`
**Why read this:** This is the entry shell for the app and shows how little page code should do in a backend-shaped frontend.
**What to look for:** The page only composes the workbench and the headline copy; it does not own business rules.
**What to trace:** It renders `src/components/dashboard/inventory-workbench.tsx`.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Putting fetch logic or permission checks here instead of in the route/service layers.
## Step 2 — `src/components/dashboard/inventory-workbench.tsx`
**Why read this:** It shows how the UI exercises the actual API routes instead of faking the data locally.
**What to look for:** The `fetchJson()` helper and the session header builder.
**What to trace:** It calls `src/app/api/items/route.ts`, `src/app/api/reservations/route.ts`, `src/app/api/alerts/route.ts`, and the mutation routes.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Assuming UI controls are enough to enforce permissions.
## Step 3 — `src/lib/auth/roles.ts`
**Why read this:** This file defines the role vocabulary the rest of the app uses.
**What to look for:** The permission helpers like `canManageInventory()` and `canViewAllReservations()`.
**What to trace:** It is consumed by `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts`, `src/services/inventoryService.ts`, and `src/services/reservationService.ts`.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Re-encoding the same role rules in multiple routes.
## Step 4 — `src/lib/auth/session.ts`
**Why read this:** It shows how request identity is created from headers in this learning build.
**What to look for:** The `getSessionFromRequest()` header parsing and null rejection path.
**What to trace:** Called by `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts`.

The app models a single store, so the core entities are inventory items, reservations, and low-stock alerts.

# Auth and Permissions
Auth is intentionally explicit and header-based in this learning build. `src/lib/auth/session.ts` reads `x-user-id`, `x-user-name`, and `x-user-role` from the incoming request and turns them into a `Session` object. If the headers are missing or the role is invalid, the request never reaches the business logic.
Permission enforcement is centralized in `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts` and `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts`. The route wrappers call `withAuth()` first, which rejects unauthenticated requests with `401` and blocks forbidden roles with `403` before the handler body runs. The actual role rules live in `src/lib/auth/roles.ts` as helpers such as `canManageInventory()`, `canCreateHold()`, and `canViewAllReservations()`.
Concrete examples from the code:
- `src/app/api/items/route.ts` uses `withAuth(... { roles: ['owner', 'manager'] })` so only managers and owners can create items.
- `src/app/api/items/[itemId]/adjust-stock/route.ts` uses the same role gate because stock adjustments are inventory mutations, not UI-only actions.
- `src/services/reservationService.ts` checks `canViewAllReservationAction()` and the reservation owner before releasing a hold, so clerks can only release their own reservations.
- `src/services/reservationService.ts` also scopes `listReservations(session)` to `createdByUserId` for non-manager roles, which is the data-isolation rule this app uses instead of multi-tenancy.
Multi-tenancy is not included because the product requirement describes one small store, not multiple organizations or tenants. If we added tenants later, we would need to thread `tenantId` through `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, all route contexts, `src/repositories/inventoryRepository.ts`, and every repository method that currently reads or writes items, reservations, or alerts. The important thing would be making tenant scoping impossible to forget, not sprinkling `tenantId` checks in the UI.
The senior concern in this design is that the auth headers are only a learning substitute. In a real deployment, `src/lib/auth/session.ts` would become an adapter over a real session source, but `withAuth.ts` and the service-layer authorization checks should stay in place.

# Architecture Overview
Atlas Support is a Next.js App Router application with a thin UI, REST API routes, a service layer for business rules, and Prisma-backed repositories for data access. The code is deliberately split so request handling, validation, permissions, and persistence are easy to trace in separate files.
## Top-Level Map
- `src/app/` holds pages and API routes.
- Example page: `src/app/page.tsx` renders the dashboard shell.
- Example route: `src/app/api/tickets/route.ts` handles list/create ticket requests.
- `src/components/` holds client components that only orchestrate hooks and forms.
- Example: `src/components/dashboard/Dashboard.tsx` renders the ticket console.
- Example: `src/components/auth/LoginPanel.tsx` renders the sign-in form.
- `src/hooks/` holds React Query wrappers over the REST API.
- Example: `src/hooks/useTickets.ts` centralizes ticket queries and mutations.
- `src/services/` holds business logic.
- Example: `src/services/ticketService.ts` owns ticket lifecycle, assignment, and comment rules.
- Example: `src/services/escalationService.ts` owns the cron-style escalation sweep.
- `src/repositories/` holds Prisma adapters and query boundaries.
- Example: `src/repositories/ticketRepository.ts` scopes ticket reads and writes.
- Example: `src/repositories/assignmentRuleRepository.ts` resolves routing rules.
- `src/lib/` holds shared technical primitives.
- Example: `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts` verifies the session cookie.
- Example: `src/lib/validation/ticketSchemas.ts` defines request payload boundaries.
- `src/domain/` holds pure policy helpers that are easier to test than database code.
- Example: `src/domain/ticketDomain.ts` defines valid lifecycle transitions.
- Example: `src/domain/ticketVisibility.ts` builds the visibility filter used by ticket lists.
- `prisma/` holds schema and seed data.
- Example: `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the data model.
- Example: `prisma/seed.ts` seeds users, groups, SLAs, and automation rules.
- `docs/` contains the code-anchored learning material you are reading now.
## How A Request Moves

# Guided Reading Path
## Step 1 — `prisma/schema.prisma`
**Why read this:** This is the contract between the domain and the database, so it explains the whole shape of the system.
**What to look for:** The `Role`, `TicketPriority`, and `TicketStatus` enums plus the relationships among `User`, `SupportGroup`, `Ticket`, and the rule tables.
**What to trace:** `src/repositories/*Repository.ts` reads and writes these models; `src/services/ticketService.ts` and `src/services/ruleService.ts` consume them.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Compound uniqueness on `SlaPolicy` and the support-group relationships that make the app scope-aware.
## Step 2 — `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`
**Why read this:** It is the central permission vocabulary for the app.
**What to look for:** The `roleCapabilities` map and the `hasCapability()` / `mayReadTicket()` helpers.
**What to trace:** `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts` calls `hasCapability()`, and `src/services/ticketService.ts` calls `mayReadTicket()`.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Role checks are not enough by themselves; some data reads still need ownership or group checks.
## Step 3 — `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts`
**Why read this:** It is the session boundary for every protected route.
**What to look for:** Cookie extraction, session hash lookup, expiry verification, and user loading.
**What to trace:** `src/app/api/auth/me/route.ts`, `src/app/api/tickets/*/route.ts`, and `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts` all depend on it.
**What a junior would likely miss:** The raw cookie value never becomes the database key; only the hash does.
## Step 4 — `src/domain/ticketVisibility.ts`
**Why read this:** It shows how a visibility rule becomes a Prisma filter.
**What to look for:** The branch that returns `{}` for admins, `supportGroupId` for staff, and `createdById` for customers.
**What to trace:** `src/repositories/ticketRepository.ts` calls `buildVisibleTicketWhere()`, and `src/tests/dataIsolation.test.ts` asserts it.
**What a junior would likely miss:** A query helper is often the real security boundary, not just a service method.
## Step 5 — `src/repositories/contracts.ts`
**Why read this:** It explains the service/repository boundary and the minimum surface each layer is allowed to use.
**What to look for:** The reposito

# Domain Model
The schema lives in `prisma/schema.prisma`, and the business rules for each entity live in the service files listed below. The model is intentionally support-group scoped rather than multi-tenant, so the authorization boundary is explicit but simpler than a full tenant model.
```mermaid
erDiagram
User ||--o{ Session : has
User ||--o{ Ticket : creates
User ||--o{ Ticket : assigned_to
User ||--o{ TicketComment : writes
User ||--o{ AuditLog : performs
SupportGroup ||--o{ User : contains
SupportGroup ||--o{ Ticket : owns
SupportGroup ||--o{ AssignmentRule : routes
SupportGroup ||--o{ SlaPolicy : governs
SupportGroup ||--o{ EscalationRule : escalates
SupportGroup ||--o| SlaPolicy : default_policy
Ticket ||--o{ TicketComment : has
Ticket ||--o{ AuditLog : records
Ticket ||--o| SlaPolicy : uses
SlaPolicy ||--o{ Ticket : applies_to
AssignmentRule }o--|| SupportGroup : source_group
EscalationRule }o--|| SupportGroup : source_group
```
## Entities
- `User`
- Schema/model file: `prisma/schema.prisma`
- Primary service owner: `src/services/authService.ts` for login/session issuance, and `src/services/ticketService.ts` for actor-aware ticket operations.
- Notes: the `role` and `supportGroupId` fields drive permission and visibility decisions.
- `Session`

# Auth and Permissions
Session auth starts in `src/services/authService.ts` and is verified on every protected request in `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts`. Role capability checks happen in `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts` and are backed by the role-to-capability map in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`.
## Session Flow
- `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts` calls `loginSchema.safeParse()` from `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts`, then `AuthService.login()` in `src/services/authService.ts`.
- `AuthService.login()` verifies the password in `src/lib/auth/password.ts`, creates a raw session token, hashes it with `hashSessionToken()`, and stores the hash through `src/repositories/sessionRepository.ts`.
- The login route writes the raw token into the `ticket_session` cookie with `serializeSessionCookie()` from `src/lib/auth/session.ts`.
- `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts` reads the cookie, hashes it, looks up the session row, verifies expiry, then loads the user row.
## Permission Flow
- `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` maps `Role.ADMIN`, `Role.MANAGER`, `Role.AGENT`, and `Role.CUSTOMER` to capabilities like `ticket:assign`, `rule:write`, and `sla:write`.
- `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts` calls `withAuth()` first, then rejects the request with `403` if `hasCapability()` returns false.
- `src/app/api/tickets/[ticketId]/assign/route.ts` uses `withRole(..., "ticket:assign")` before it ever reaches `TicketService.assignTicket()`.
- `src/app/api/rules/assignment/route.ts` and `src/app/api/slas/route.ts` use `withRole(..., "rule:write" | "sla:write")` so only operations roles can change routing or SLA policy.
## Ticket Visibility
- `src/domain/ticketVisibility.ts` builds the Prisma `where` clause for list queries.
- `src/repositories/ticketRepository.ts` calls `buildVisibleTicketWhere()` inside `listVisible()` so the scope decision stays centralized.
- `src/services/ticketService.ts` calls `mayReadTicket()` inside `getTicket()` before returning a single ticket.
## Multi-Tenancy
Multi-tenancy is not included. The app is scoped by support group and ownership, not by tenant.
If we added multi-tenancy later, the minimum changes would be:
- add `tenantId` to the Prisma models in `prisma/schema.prisma`
- carry `tenantId` through `AuthContext` in `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts`
- include `tenantId` in `buildVisibleTicketWhere()` and every repository query that touches tenant-owned data
- separate platform-level roles from tenant-level roles, rather than reusing the current role map as-is

WorkGrid is a production-style Jira-like work management platform built to teach backend-oriented product engineering. It includes multi-tenant organizations, DB-backed auth sessions, centralized RBAC, projects, issues, workflows, comments, custom fields, saved filters, boards, audit activity, and queued automation jobs.

- Vitest

2. Start PostgreSQL and create the database in `DATABASE_URL`
3. Install dependencies
`npm install`
4. Generate the Prisma client
`npm run db:generate`
5. Push the schema
`npm run db:push`
6. Seed demo data

7. Start the app
`npm run dev`

WorkGrid uses cookie-backed server-side sessions plus explicit organization and project authorization contexts.

- Login payload is validated in `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts` with `loginSchema`.
- `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts` parses the payload and calls `authService.login()`.

- Session lookup happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `getSessionContext()`. The cookie token is hashed, resolved back to a `Session` row through `authRepository.findSessionByTokenHash()`, and refreshed with `authRepository.updateSessionHeartbeat()`.
- `src/lib/auth/session.ts` deletes orphaned or expired sessions before the request continues. That means a stale cookie is not enough to stay authenticated.
## Organization Membership
- Organization access starts in `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts` with `requireOrganizationContext(organizationId)`.
- That function loads the current session from `src/lib/auth/session.ts` and then checks whether the authenticated user has a matching organization membership in `session.organizations`.
- If the organization is missing, `requireOrganizationContext()` throws `NotFoundError`, which `src/lib/http/responses.ts` converts into a JSON 404 response.

- Project access is resolved in `src/lib/auth/request-context.ts` with `requireProjectAccess()`.
- `requireProjectAccess()` first checks org membership, then calls `projectRepository.findProjectAccess()` in `src/repositories/projectRepository.ts`.
- The tenant guard is in `src/repositories/projectRepository.ts` inside the `where` clause for `findProjectAccess()`: both `id` and `organizationId` must match before the project can resolve.
- Project roles are loaded from the project’s `projectMemberships` include and converted into `ProjectAccessContext`.

- The permission matrix lives in `src/lib/permissions/permissions.ts`.
- Org-wide admin behavior is defined by `isOrganizationAdmin()`, which treats `ORG_OWNER` and `ORG_ADMIN` as bypass roles for all project-level permissions.
- `assertOrganizationCanCreateProject()` in `src/lib/permissions/permissions.ts` protects project creation in `src/services/projects/projectService.ts`.
- `assertProjectPermission()` in `src/lib/permissions/permissions.ts` protects i

# Architecture Overview
This project is a single-platform job board admin dashboard built for backend-oriented CRUD learning. Employers submit job postings, internal staff review and moderate them, and staff can persist owner-scoped saved searches that run manually or through an internal digest path.
The top-level folders map to clear layers:
- `src/app` holds the Next.js entry points. API handlers such as `src/app/api/admin/job-postings/route.ts` stay thin and pages such as `src/app/admin/job-postings/page.tsx` compose UI panels.
- `src/lib` holds cross-cutting boundaries. `src/lib/auth/guards.ts` owns route guards, `src/lib/validation/jobPostingSchemas.ts` owns request validation, and `src/lib/http/handle-route.ts` standardizes JSON error responses.
- `src/services` owns business workflows. `src/services/jobPostingService.ts` controls submission and review transitions, `src/services/moderationService.ts` owns flag lifecycle rules, and `src/services/savedSearchService.ts` owns saved search CRUD plus execution.
- `src/repositories` owns Prisma reads and writes. `src/repositories/jobPostingRepository.ts` issues queue queries, `src/repositories/savedSearchRepository.ts` enforces owner-scoped saved search reads and writes, and `src/repositories/sessionRepository.ts` resolves hashed sessions.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the database model and relationships. `prisma/seed.ts` creates demo users and a sample submitted job posting for the dashboard flow.
- `src/components` and `src/hooks` form the thin frontend layer. `src/hooks/useAdminJobPostings.ts` calls the REST endpoints, while components such as `src/components/admin/AdminJobPostingsPanel.tsx` render data and trigger mutations without owning business rules.
- `tests` contains focused boundary tests. `tests/auth-authorization.test.ts` verifies role rejection, and `tests/job-posting-state-transition.test.ts` verifies workflow enforcement in the service layer.
Why Prisma over Drizzle matters here:
- Prisma makes the entity graph in `prisma/schema.prisma` easy to scan for a learner who is still building instinct for relational modeling.
- The repository layer in `src/repositories/*.ts` can stay compact, which keeps the teaching surface focused on service boundaries, auth, and workflow transitions instead of SQ

**What to look for:** The `JobPosting`, `ModerationFlag`, `SavedSearch`, `Session`, and `AuditLog` models plus the enums that drive workflow state.

## Step 2 — `src/lib/constants/permissions.ts`
**Why read this:** This is the single place where role capability is defined.
**What to look for:** The `permissions` object and `permissionMatrix`.
**What to trace:** `src/lib/auth/guards.ts` calls `roleHasPermission()`, and route files such as `src/app/api/admin/job-postings/[jobPostingId]/approve/route.ts` depend on it.
**What a junior would likely miss:** If a route bypasses this file and checks role strings directly, authorization drift starts immediately.

**What to trace:** `src/lib/auth/session.ts` feeds this file, and API handlers in `src/app/api/**/route.ts` call it before services execute.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Ownership checks are separate from role checks; `requireEmployerMembership()` exists because role alone is not enough.
## Step 4 — `src/lib/auth/session.ts`
**Why read this:** It is the narrow bridge from a cookie to a typed application user.
**What to look for:** `getRequestSessionUser()` and how it hashes the cookie token before querying storage.
**What to trace:** `src/app/api/auth/session/route.ts` writes the cookie, and `src/repositories/sessionRepository.ts` resolves it.
**What a junior would likely miss:** Expiration belongs in the repository lookup, not just in browser cookie metadata.
## Step 5 — `src/lib/validation/jobPostingSchemas.ts`
**Why read this:** It shows the request validation boundary for the core domain.
**What to look for:** `employe

# Domain Model
```mermaid
erDiagram
Organization ||--o{ User : has
Organization ||--o{ JobPosting : owns
User ||--o{ Session : authenticates
User ||--o{ SavedSearch : owns
User ||--o{ SavedSearchRun : triggers
User ||--o{ JobPosting : submits
User ||--o{ JobPosting : reviews
User ||--o{ ModerationFlag : raises
User ||--o{ ModerationFlag : resolves
JobPosting ||--o{ ModerationFlag : has
SavedSearch ||--o{ SavedSearchRun : records
User ||--o{ AuditLog : writes
```
## Organization
- Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model Organization`
- Primary service owner: `src/services/jobPostingService.ts` because organization ownership is applied when `submitEmployerJobPosting()` creates a job posting and when `getEmployerJobPosting()` resolves organization-scoped reads.
## User
- Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model User`
- Primary service owner: `src/services/authService.ts` because `signIn()` resolves a user record and issues a session tied to that identity.
## Session
- Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model Session`
- Primary service owner: `src/services/authService.ts` because `signIn()` writes the session and `src/lib/auth/session.ts` later resolves it into a `SessionUser`.
## JobPosting
- Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model JobPosting`
- Primary service owner: `src/services/jobPostingService.ts` because `submitEmployerJobPosting()`, `approveJobPosting()`, and `rejectJobPosting()` own the posting lifecycle.

# Auth And Permissions
Session creation starts in `src/app/api/auth/session/route.ts` inside `POST()`. The request body is validated by `signInSchema` from `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts`, then `authService.signIn()` in `src/services/authService.ts` looks up the user through `userRepository.findByEmail()` and writes a hashed session through `sessionRepository.create()`. The raw token is only written to the cookie in the route file; the database stores the hash created by `hashSessionToken()` in `src/lib/auth/session-cookie.ts`.
Session verification happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `getRequestSessionUser()`. That function reads the `job-board-session` cookie, hashes it, and calls `sessionRepository.findActiveByTokenHash()`. Expiration is enforced in the repository query, not just at the cookie layer, so stale browser cookies do not become valid sessions.
Route-level auth is centralized in `src/lib/auth/guards.ts`:
- `requireSessionUser()` rejects unauthenticated requests with `ApiError(401, ...)`.
- `assertPermissionForUser()` and `requirePermission()` enforce role-based access with `ApiError(403, ...)`.
- `requireEmployerMembership()` adds the extra ownership rule that an `EMPLOYER` must also have an `organizationId`.
- `requireInternalJobToken()` protects the background digest route in `src/app/api/internal/saved-search-digests/run/route.ts`.

This project is a Next.js App Router application that keeps transport, business rules, and database access in separate layers so request flow is easy to read. Production-style multi-tenant SaaS starter built with Next.js, TypeScript, Prisma, Tailwind, Zod, React Query, and REST APIs.
This repo is organized around explicit backend boundaries:
- `src/app/api/` holds the HTTP layer, for example [src/app/api/organizations/[organizationId]/projects/route.ts](src/app/api/organizations/[organizationId]/projects/route.ts).
- `src/lib/middleware/` holds auth and tenant access guards, for example [src/lib/middleware/require-organization-access.ts](src/lib/middleware/require-organization-access.ts).
- `src/services/` holds business rules, for example [src/services/project-service.ts](src/services/project-service.ts).
- `src/repositories/` holds Prisma queries, for example [src/repositories/project-repository.ts](src/repositories/project-repository.ts).
- `prisma/schema.prisma` defines the domain model and tenant-owned tables.
## Stack
The app uses the requested default stack except for one deliberate deviation:
- `Next.js`, `React`, `TypeScript`, `Node.js`
- `Prisma`
- `Tailwind`
- `Zod`
- `React Query`
- `REST APIs`
- `SQLite` instead of PostgreSQL for this starter
SQLite is used here so the project stays runnable in one workspace with no Docker or hosted database dependency. The architecture is still Postgres-ready because tenant scoping lives in `src/lib/middleware/require-organization-access.ts` and the repository layer, not in SQLite-specific behavior.
## Quick Start

pnpm dev
```

# Auth And Permissions
## Auth flow
Sign-in starts in `src/app/api/auth/sign-in/route.ts` in `POST()`. The request body is parsed in `src/lib/http/parse-request.ts` by `parseJsonBody()` and validated by `src/lib/validation/auth-schemas.ts` with `signInSchema`.
Credential verification lives in `src/services/auth-service.ts` inside `signIn()`. That function calls `src/repositories/user-repository.ts#findUserByEmail()`, compares the password with `src/lib/auth/password.ts#verifyPassword()`, creates an opaque token in `src/lib/auth/session.ts#buildSessionPayload()`, persists the hashed token with `src/repositories/session-repository.ts#createSession()`, and writes the cookie with `src/lib/auth/session.ts#setSessionCookie()`.

# Admin Analytics Dashboard
Production-style Next.js application for event ingestion, daily aggregation jobs, and protected analytics views.
## Stack
- Next.js App Router + React + TypeScript
- PostgreSQL + Prisma
- Tailwind CSS
- Zod
- React Query
- REST APIs
## Why Prisma and REST
- Prisma fits this project better than Drizzle because the app has a broad relational surface area: sessions, users, raw events, rollups, jobs, metric views, and audit logs. The generated client keeps service and repository code readable for junior-to-mid engineers.
- REST fits better than tRPC here because the product naturally exposes multiple boundary types: browser clients, operator tooling, and machine ingestion. Explicit route files make request flow, RBAC, validation, and docs easier to trace.
## Quick Start
1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env`.
2. Point `DATABASE_URL` at a PostgreSQL database.
3. Run `npm install`.
4. Run `npm run db:push`.
5. Run `npm run db:seed`.
6. Run `npm run dev`.
## Demo Credentials
- `admin@example.com`
- `analyst@example.com`
- `ingestor@example.com`
- `viewer@example.com`
Password for every seeded user: `password123`
## Project Docs
- [Architecture README](docs/architecture/README.md)
- [Domain model](docs/architecture/domain-model.md)
- [Auth and permissions](docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md)
- [Request lifecycle](docs/architecture/request-lifecycle.md)
- [Guided reading path](docs/learning/guided-reading-path.md)
- [Flow traces](docs/learning/flow-traces.md)

# Auth And Permissions
## Auth flows
- Browser session auth starts in `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts` when `POST` parses `loginSchema`, then `src/services/auth-service.ts` runs `loginUser()` to verify the password and create a hashed session record. The cookie name comes from `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`.
- Session verification happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `getRequestSession()` for APIs and `requirePageSession()` for pages. Both paths resolve the cookie token, hash it with `hashSessionToken()`, and look up the stored record through `src/repositories/session-repository.ts`.
- Event ingestion does not use browser sessions. `src/app/api/events/route.ts` validates the payload, then `src/services/event-ingestion-service.ts` runs `findActiveEventSourceByKey()` from `src/repositories/event-source-repository.ts` before any raw event write occurs.
## RBAC
- The role and permission vocabulary lives in `src/types/auth.ts`.
- The role-to-permission map is centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` inside `rolePermissions`.
- API authorization is enforced in `src/lib/http/route-guards.ts` inside `withRouteGuard()`. The route guard rejects missing sessions with `401 UNAUTHENTICATED` and insufficient roles with `403 FORBIDDEN` before service code runs.
- Page-level permission gating happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `requirePageSession(permission)`. The page redirects to `/dashboard` if the session exists but the role lacks the requested permission.
## Role matrix
- `ADMIN`
Can view metrics, view raw events, create metric views, manage jobs, manage users, and perform ingestion-capable operations.
- `ANALYST`
Can view metrics, inspect raw events, and create metric views.
- `INGESTOR`
Can manage jobs and perform ingestion-related work, but cannot see metric dashboards.
- `VIEWER`
Can view metrics and create personal/shared metric views, but cannot inspect raw events or admin jobs.
## Ownership and data isolation
- Private saved metric views are scoped in `src/repositories/metric-view-repository.ts` inside `listMetricViewsVisibleToSession()`. For non-admin users the Prisma `where` clause only allows `ownerUserId = session.userId` or `visibility = "SHARED"`.
- Ownership for new saved views is derived in `src/services/metric-view-service.ts` inside `createSavedMetricView()`, which always sets `ownerUserId` from `session.userId` instead of trusting client input.
- Last-admin protection lives in `src/services/user-service.ts` inside `updateDashboardUserRole()`. Before demoting an admin, it calls `countActiveAdmins()` from `sr

This project is a single-tenant CRM lead pipeline built around explicit backend boundaries. Requests enter through `src/app/api/**/route.ts`, pass through auth and validation helpers in `src/lib/`, execute business rules in `src/services/`, and hit Prisma-backed repositories in `src/repositories/`.
Top-level folders and how they relate:
- `src/app/` contains App Router pages and REST endpoints. For example, `src/app/api/leads/[leadId]/route.ts` turns HTTP input into `getLeadDetail()` or `updateLeadRecord()` service calls, while `src/app/leads/[leadId]/page.tsx` renders the authenticated lead workspace.
- `src/components/` contains client-facing UI composition. `src/components/dashboard/dashboard-page.tsx` coordinates the dashboard query and passes data into presentation-focused children like `src/components/dashboard/pipeline-board.tsx`.
- `src/hooks/` contains React Query hooks that speak HTTP, not business logic. `src/hooks/use-lead-detail.ts` owns the client cache and mutation invalidation strategy for `/api/leads/[leadId]`.

- `src/repositories/` owns Prisma query shapes. `src/repositories/leadRepository.ts` builds lead filters, keeps include trees consistent, and scopes lead reads via the `LeadVisibilityScope`.

- `docs/architecture/` explains how requests and layers fit together.
- `docs/learning/` is the code-reading guide anchored to specific files and functions in this repo.

Production-style CRM lead pipeline built with Next.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Prisma, Zod, Tailwind, React Query, and REST APIs.
## What’s inside
- Lead stages with controlled transitions
- Explicit ownership and role-based permissions

## Local setup
1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local`
2. Start PostgreSQL with `docker-compose up -d`
3. Generate Prisma client with `npx prisma@6.7.0 generate`
4. Push the schema with `npx prisma@6.7.0 db push`
5. Seed demo data with `npm run db:seed`
6. Start the app with `npm run dev`

## Learning docs

# Auth And Permissions
Authentication flow:
- Credentials are parsed in `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts` with `loginSchema` from `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts`.
- `authenticateUser()` in `src/services/authService.ts` loads the user through `findUserByEmail()` in `src/repositories/userRepository.ts`, checks `isActive`, and verifies the bcrypt hash through `verifyPassword()` in `src/lib/auth/password.ts`.
- `createSession()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` signs the cookie payload and writes the `crm_session` HTTP-only cookie.
- Server-rendered pages call `requirePageSession()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` before they render `src/app/page.tsx` or `src/app/leads/[leadId]/page.tsx`.
- API routes call `withAuth()` in `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts`, which reads the session with `getRequestSession()` from `src/lib/auth/session.ts` and rejects unauthenticated requests with a 401 `ApiError`.
Role model:
- Roles live in `prisma/schema.prisma` as `enum UserRole` with `ADMIN`, `MANAGER`, and `REP`.
- Role capabilities are centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` inside `rolePermissions`.
- `hasPermission()` is the base capability check, while `canAccessLead()`, `canEditLead()`, `canReassignLead()`, and `canManageFollowUp()` convert role data into lead-specific authorization rules.
- `withRole()` in `src/lib/middleware/withRole.ts` rejects elevated-only actions with a 403 before business logic runs. One concrete use is `src/app/api/dashboard/route.ts`, where a rep trying to query `ownerId` for another user is rejected before `getDashboardData()` executes.
Ownership and data isolation:
- Lead visibility is computed in `src/services/dashboardService.ts` and `src/services/leadService.ts` by `getLeadVisibility()`. For reps, it returns `{ ownerId: user.id }`; for managers and admins, it returns `{}`.
- The repository scoping happens in `src/repositories/leadRepository.ts` inside `buildLeadWhere()`. When `visibility.ownerId` is present, the query adds `{ ownerId: visibility.ownerId }` to the Prisma `AND` list.
- The current app is not multi-tenant. Isolation is owner-based and role-based, not tenant-based. To add multi-tenancy later, `tenantId` would need to be added to `prisma/schema.prisma`, injected into the session shape in `src/lib/types/auth.ts`, applied inside `buildLeadWhere()` in `src/repositories/leadRepository.ts`, and mirrored in follow-up and note repositories. The service boundaries already pass explicit visibility objects, so this is additive rather than a rewrite.

```mermaid
erDiagram
User ||--o{ Lead : owns
User ||--o{ Lead : creates
User ||--o{ Note : authors
User ||--o{ FollowUp : owns
User ||--o{ FollowUp : creates

Lead ||--o{ Note : has

Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model User`
Primary service owner: `src/services/authService.ts` — `authenticateUser()` for login and `src/services/dashboardService.ts` — `getAssignableUsersForViewer()` for assignment visibility
- `Lead`
Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model Lead`
Primary service owner: `src/services/leadService.ts` — `createLeadRecord()`, `getLeadDetail()`, and `updateLeadRecord()`

Schema/model: `prisma/schema.prisma` — `model FollowUp`
Primary service owner: `src/services/followUpService.ts` — `addLeadFollowUp()` and `changeFollowUpStatus()`

- `Lead.ownerId` and `Lead.createdById` are separate in `prisma/schema.prisma`, which lets the system distinguish who currently owns pipeline execution from who originally entered the lead.

This project is a zero-install learning build of a marketplace order management system. It keeps the production-style boundaries the prompt asked for, but replaces PostgreSQL, Prisma, Zod, and React Query with a local in-memory store, manual runtime validation, and a thin fetch hook because the user explicitly asked not to install anything.

Session is created in `src/app/api/session/route.ts` when `POST` calls `parseLoginInput()` from `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts`, then `authService.login()` in `src/services/authService.ts`, then `writeSessionCookie()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`.

Protected API routes verify session with `requireActor()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` before reaching business logic. Examples:
- `src/app/api/orders/route.ts`
- `src/app/api/orders/[orderId]/cancel/route.ts`
- `src/app/api/orders/[orderId]/fulfillment/route.ts`

- `src/app/api/refunds/[refundId]/approve/route.ts`
