# ADR 0001: Client-rendered teaching boundary
## Status
Accepted in Sprint 1.
## Context
The course needs React lifecycle, browser state, accessible interaction, and API-boundary lessons to remain visible. A full-stack framework could productively solve many of those concerns, but it would also combine routing, rendering, data loading, and deployment before the learner has models for each.
## Decision
Use a Vite-powered React application, a separate Fastify API, and a pure TypeScript core package. Packages share strict compiler and quality configuration but own their runtime boundaries.
## Consequences
The learner can trace browser, transport, and domain state independently. The repository must make loading and error behavior explicit, and it does not claim server rendering or framework-level production optimizations.

# FormForge
FormForge is a complete, schema-driven form builder and response analytics platform built as a fifteen-sprint React and TypeScript teaching repository. A junior engineer studies the issues, ordered commits, pull-request reviews, architecture decisions, counterexamples, and tests that produced the product.
Version `1.0.0` includes typed authoring, seven field variants, validation, conditional logic, multi-page branching and resume, immutable publishing, retry-safe submissions, response filtering and CSV export, analytics, comments, version diffs, accessibility checks, autosave recovery, and operational readiness boundaries.
## Run the release candidate
```bash
pnpm install
pnpm seed
pnpm dev
```
`pnpm seed` verifies the canonical demo scenario and prints a deterministic fingerprint. The development command starts the Vite application and Fastify API. No database, Docker daemon, or external service is required.
Run the complete local evidence gate with:
```bash
pnpm gate
```
## Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
Browser[React 19 + Vite] --> Core[@formforge/core\ntyped domain rules]
Browser --> API[Fastify API\nruntime boundaries]
API --> Core
API --> Data[@formforge/data\nrepository contracts + in-memory adapters]
Data --> Core
CI[GitHub Actions] --> Checks[lint + typecheck + tests + build\nsecret scan + bundle budget]
```
The browser owns interaction and presentation state. `@formforge/core` owns pure schemas, reducers, validation, branching, response queries, analytics, and diffs. The API validates untrusted HTTP data and authorization context. `@formforge/data` demonstrates versioned repository contracts with deterministic in-memory adapters; durable deployment storage remains an explicit production integration, not a claim made by this repository.
## Implemented stack
- React 19, strict TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Router, and TanStack Query;
- Fastify with Zod-backed domain parsing at HTTP boundaries;

# Using Hermes to Upskill Toward Mid and Senior SWE
The fastest way to grow is not just to write more code. It is to improve how you read systems, make tradeoffs, communicate decisions, reduce risk, and help other engineers move faster. Hermes can help you practice those habits deliberately.
## Skill Ladder
Junior-to-mid growth usually means:
- You can finish scoped tasks independently.
- You understand the surrounding code before editing.
- You write tests that protect behavior.
- You ask better questions earlier.
- You communicate blockers clearly.
- You can debug without thrashing.
Mid-to-senior growth usually means:
- You reason across systems, not just files.
- You reduce ambiguity for others.
- You make tradeoffs explicit.
- You spot long-term maintenance risks.
- You mentor through clear feedback.
- You turn vague product goals into executable plans.
## Weekly Upskilling Loop
Use this loop every week.
1. Pick one project or feature area.
2. Ask Hermes to map the system.
3. Choose one small improvement or bug.
4. Implement with tests.
5. Ask Hermes for a senior-style review.
6. Write a short reflection on what you learned.
Prompt:
```text
Act as a senior SWE coach. Help me turn this task into a learning loop. Identify what concepts I should practice, what good execution looks like, and how I can verify I understood it.

Quiz me on the architecture we just mapped. Rules:

- Six questions total, escalating: 2 on structure, 2 on data flow and failure modes, 2 on "what would you change and what breaks."

- After question six, output: my weakest area, the misconception behind it, and one concrete 20-minute exercise in this repo to fix it.

# Orchard Core Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from the real Orchard Core codebase, for one specific learner: a **junior fullstack engineer** (CRUD web dev — .NET/C#, React/Node/TS or similar) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, when it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is
Orchard Core (v3.0.1) is an open-source, **modular, multi-tenant application framework and CMS for ASP.NET Core**, maintained by the Orchard Core team under the .NET Foundation. It is two products in one repository: a framework for building modular multi-tenant ASP.NET Core apps (`src/OrchardCore/*`), and a full CMS built on that framework as ~95 pluggable modules (`src/OrchardCore.Modules/*`). Each tenant gets its **own dependency-injection container and request pipeline**, built lazily from that tenant's enabled features. Persistence is **YesSql** — a document store over SQL Server/SQLite/MySQL/Postgres where documents are JSON and queries run against explicit *index tables*. UI is rendered through a **display-management** system (drivers produce "shapes", placement files position them, templates can be overridden per theme). It is one of the most instructive large .NET codebases in the wild: real multi-tenancy, real modularity, real versioned-content invariants, real background scheduling — all things interviews probe.

If you added the preview source above, select this from the `Package Source` selection in the top right. !!! tip

Open `Program.cs` file. Remove the following line "if exists"
```csharp

```
Add the following line
```csharp
builder.Services.AddOrchardCms();
```
Additionally, remove the following lines
```csharp
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseRouting();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapRazorPages();

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line across which things are decoupled: code on one side can change without forcing changes on the other. A **layer** owns a responsibility and depends only inward. Finding boundaries — and spotting where they *leak* — is the core architecture skill.
## The four layers
| Layer | Project | Owns | Must NOT own |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Domain | `ApplicationCore` | Entities, invariants, use-case services, query specs, the interfaces it needs | EF, ASP.NET, HTTP, JSON |
| Infrastructure | `Infrastructure` | EF mappings, migrations, Identity, email, concrete `IRepository` | Business rules |
| Presentation | `Web`, `PublicApi`, `BlazorAdmin` | HTTP, view models/DTOs, auth wiring, rendering | Domain invariants, direct SQL |
| Contracts | `BlazorShared` | Shapes shared client↔API | Behavior |
The dependency rule: **arrows point inward.** `Infrastructure` and the UIs depend on `ApplicationCore`; `ApplicationCore` depends on nothing internal. Proof: [ApplicationCore.csproj](../../src/ApplicationCore/ApplicationCore.csproj) references only small helper libraries (Ardalis.*), never EF Core or ASP.NET.
## Where the boundaries are clean (good examples)
- **Domain ↔ persistence:** the domain declares `IRepository<T>` ([IRepository.cs](../../src/ApplicationCore/Interfaces/IRepository.cs)); `Infrastructure` implements it ([EfRepository.cs](../../src/Infrastructure/Data/EfRepository.cs)). Swap SQL for in-memory by changing one registration ([Dependencies.cs:19-38](../../src/Infrastructure/Dependencies.cs#L19-L38)).
- **Domain ↔ UI shape:** `CatalogViewModelService` explicitly calls itself "a UI-specific service … does not contain any business logic" ([CatalogViewModelService.cs:14-17](../../src/Web/Services/CatalogViewModelService.cs#L14-L17)) and maps entities to view models — keeping presentation concerns out of the domain.
- **Network boundary:** BlazorAdmin runs in the browser and *cannot* reach the DbContext; it must call the API over HTTP ([HttpService.cs](../../src/BlazorAdmin/Services/HttpService.cs)). The compiler + runtime enforce this boundary.
- **Client ↔ API contract:** shared DTOs live in `BlazorShared` so both sides compile against the same shapes without sharing domain internals.
## Where boundaries leak or bend (teachable weak spots)
- **UI decides a domain value:** the checkout's shipping address is constructed in the *page* ([Checkout.cshtml.cs:57](../../src/Web/Pages/Basket/Checkout.cshtml.cs#L57)) and handed to the domain. Address *should* be user input flowing into the domain, not a presentation-layer

## The golden rule
**Answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff, and a failure mode — not a definition.**
- Weak: "Clean Architecture separates concerns."
- Strong: "In this repo, `ApplicationCore` defines `IRepository<T>` and `Infrastructure` implements it, so I can unit-test `BasketService` with a fake repo — the tests do exactly that. The cost is more mapping code and indirection; for a thin CRUD app I'd skip it."
The second answer proves you've read and reasoned about real code. That's the mid-level signal.
## How to use this repo as your portfolio of talking points
You may not be able to discuss your employer's proprietary code in an interview. You *can* discuss a public reference app you studied deeply. Treat eShopOnWeb as a shared codebase you can point at: it gives you concrete anchors for architecture, auth, caching, testing, and at least one real security bug you found ([the Flow 7 IDOR](../01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md#flow-7-view-my-order-details-read--the-idor-lesson)).

# eShopOnWeb Upskill Curriculum
A codebase-to-curriculum training lab built on Microsoft's **eShopOnWeb** reference application. It teaches two things at once, always paired:
1. **This repo**: where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill**: why these patterns exist, when they fail, how to recognize them in any codebase — and how to articulate them in a mid-level fullstack interview.
## Who this is for
A junior fullstack engineer (CRUD web dev in .NET/C#, or React/Node/TS moving to .NET) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
## What this repo is (identity in 7 sentences)
eShopOnWeb is Microsoft's official reference application for the free eBook *Architecting Modern Web Applications with ASP.NET Core and Azure* ([README.md](../README.md#L18)). It is a deliberately **monolithic** e-commerce store — catalog, basket, checkout, orders, admin — built on .NET 8 ([global.json](../global.json)). It demonstrates **Clean Architecture**: a dependency-free domain project (`ApplicationCore`), an EF Core data layer (`Infrastructure`), and three UI surfaces — a Razor Pages storefront (`Web`), a JWT-secured minimal-API backend (`PublicApi`), and a Blazor WebAssembly admin panel (`BlazorAdmin`). Persistence is SQL Server via EF Core with two separate DbContexts (catalog vs. identity). It is a *teaching* app: some things are intentionally simplified or deliberately flawed (hardcoded JWT secret, hardcoded checkout address, a `Task.Delay(1000)` in an API endpoint), which makes it an outstanding lab for developing senior judgment — you get to find real flaws in a professionally structured codebase. Development moved to [dotnet/eShop](https://github.com/dotnet/eShop); this repo is stable and safe to dissect. Everything here was verified against the code on 2026-07-16; see the [verification log](09-reference/verification-log.md).
## Learning tracks
| Track | Folder | You'll be able to... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cartography | [01-codebase-cartography](01-codebase-cartography/README.md) | Navigate any layered .NET repo in hours, not weeks |

samples.opening:
# Learner guide
For each sprint:
1. Read the milestone and issues before opening code.
2. Read commits in order: model, service/storage, API, tests, documentation.
3. Run the focused test and change one rule to see a useful failure.
4. Follow one request from JSON through the service into the model and back.
5. Explain the code in plain language before adding an abstraction.
6. Read review comments and state what you would change differently.
Ask: what fact must remain true, which class owns it, and what is the simplest test that proves it?

# BorrowBox curriculum specification
## Product
BorrowBox helps a fictional college catalog equipment, register borrowers, check items out and in, manage reservations, inspect damage, enforce simple limits, and report inventory status.
## Simple business rules
- Equipment has one current status and cannot be checked out twice.
- A borrower must be active and below their loan limit.
- A loan records checkout and due dates; a return records a UTC event.
- Reserved equipment can be collected only by the reservation owner before expiry.
- Damaged equipment requires inspection before becoming available.
- Public API models do not expose database entities directly.
## Fifteen sprints
| Sprint | Outcome | New skill |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | Create and retrieve equipment | classes, records, DI, HTTP |
| 02 | Update and retire equipment | CRUD, validation, status codes |
| 03 | Search and paginate inventory | LINQ, query parameters |
| 04 | Register borrowers | relationships and DTOs |
| 05 | Check equipment out; `v0.5.0` | services and business rules |
| 06 | Return equipment | dates and transitions |
| 07 | Store data with SQLite | EF Core and migrations |
| 08 | Reserve equipment | competing states |
| 09 | Expire reservations | clocks and background services |
| 10 | Damage and inspections | workflow and history |
| 11 | Borrower limits | configuration and policy |
| 12 | Authentication/roles concept | authorization boundaries |
| 13 | Reports and CSV | projections and export |
| 14 | Three-bug harvest | regressions and concurrency |
| 15 | Operations and `v1.0.0` | health, logging, deployment judgment |

# API integration guide
Base path: `/api/v1`. JSON is the default representation; errors use `application/problem+json` with a stable `code` extension for business errors.
## Identity in this course
Send `X-Demo-Role: Student` for borrowing operations or `X-Demo-Role: Staff` for administrative operations. Replace this scheme in any deployment; it provides no identity assurance.
## Compatibility
- Additive response fields may appear within v1; clients should ignore unknown fields.
- Enum values are strings in API responses; handle unknown future values safely.
- Send a unique `X-Correlation-ID` of at most 100 characters and record the echoed response value.
- There is no idempotency-key support yet. Do not blindly retry mutating requests after an ambiguous timeout.
## Typical flow
1. Staff creates equipment and a borrower.
2. A student or staff identity creates a loan or reservation using returned IDs.
3. Staff completes returns and inspections.
4. Staff reads inventory summary or CSV export.
Use the Development OpenAPI document at `/openapi/v1.json` as the machine-readable contract. Contract changes require tests and changelog notes.

# BorrowBox
BorrowBox is a beginner-friendly fifteen-sprint C#/.NET teaching repository for lending campus equipment such as laptops, cameras, calculators, and lab kits.
The repository is designed for a new graduate with limited .NET experience. It starts with plain C# and one HTTP slice, then gradually introduces validation, LINQ, dependency injection, SQLite, background work, authorization concepts, testing, and operations.
## Deliberately small architecture
```text
BorrowBox.Api             HTTP routes and request/response models
BorrowBox.Core            equipment, borrowers, loans, and simple services
BorrowBox.Infrastructure  in-memory and SQLite storage
```
BorrowBox does not use microservices, MediatR, CQRS, generic repositories, AutoMapper, or a message broker.
```powershell
dotnet restore BorrowBox.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/BorrowBox.Api
dotnet test BorrowBox.slnx
```
## Run it
Requires the .NET 10 SDK.
```powershell
dotnet restore BorrowBox.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/BorrowBox.Api
```
OpenAPI is available at `/openapi/v1.json` in Development. Inventory reads and health endpoints are public. Mutating inventory uses the teaching header `X-Demo-Role: Staff`; borrowing accepts `Student` or `Staff`. This header is not production authentication.
## Course map
| Sprints | Theme | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–3 | C# and HTTP foundations | equipment CRUD, validation, search, pagination |
| 4–6 | Business workflows | borrowers, checkout, return, v0.5 release |
| 7–10 | Data and state | SQLite adapter, reservations, expiry, inspections |
| 11–13 | Policies and API design | lending limits, authorization, reports |
| 14–15 | Engineering judgment | bug harvest, threat model, operations, v1.0 |
Each sprint has a focused lesson in [`docs/sprints`](docs/sprints). Start with the [learner guide](LEARNER-GUIDE.md) and [course specification](docs/curriculum/SPEC.md). Then use [TESTREADME.md](TESTREADME.md) to practice testing and [OEReadMe.md](OEReadMe.md) to discuss which complexity is justified.
## Useful commands

headings: ## What a learner should now be able to do
samples.opening:
# Course retrospective
## Progression
The course began with one class, one store, and one endpoint slice. Each later concept answered a problem already visible: SQLite answered persistence, policies answered lending limits, an injected clock answered nondeterministic time, and atomic checkout answered a reproduced race.
## What a learner should now be able to do
- Trace an HTTP request through a use case into an adapter.
- Place business rules in objects or services rather than controllers.
- choose unit, integration, or API tests based on the boundary being proved.
- Read a CI failure, create a regression test, and make a scoped repair.
- Explain 401 versus 403, persistence versus memory, and liveness versus readiness.
- Push back on speculative architecture while naming evidence that would justify it.
## Suggested capstone
Choose one production-readiness gap, write an architecture decision record, implement the smallest vertical slice, and demonstrate it with tests and an updated runbook. Good options are durable loan persistence, idempotent checkout, or real token validation in a local identity test environment.

# Junior → Mid-Level SWE Fast-Track Plan
**Stack:** C# / ASP.NET Core / EF Core / SQL / React (light) · **Tools:** VS Code, Claude Code, Codex · **Timeline:** 10 weeks aggressive (15–20 hrs/wk) · **Goal:** pass practical interviews for mid-level CRUD web dev roles
## TL;DR
- **The engine is a 4-step AI loop, not AI generation:** attempt each feature yourself first (45-min cap), use Claude Code as a strict reviewer/quizzer rather than an author, use Codex only for completions you could have typed yourself, and rebuild one feature from memory every Saturday with AI off.
- **Two projects instead of courses:** a ticket-tracker API (weeks 1–3) whose feature ladder forces out every classic screener topic, then a real product with one deliberately hard problem — e.g. concurrent booking slots — plus CI, deployment, and a decisions-focused README (weeks 4–7). The hard problem becomes the 10-minute interview deep-dive story.
- **Interview training targets the 4 practical formats:** timed take-home simulations (AI-generated and AI-graded against a mid-level rubric), pair-programming mocks with narration practice, rapid-fire technical Q&A, and system-design-lite with a repeatable script.
- **Daily SQL drills and a STAR story bank are non-negotiable** — raw SQL and vague behavioral answers are the two most common junior→mid rejection reasons.
- **Applications start at week 6–7,** before "ready" — real interviews are the best study guide.
- **Two highest-leverage drills:** the Friday "plant 3 bugs and let me find them" debugging exercise, and the Saturday from-memory rebuild.
---
---
## What "mid-level" actually means to an interviewer
Interviewers don't test juniors vs. mids on syntax. They test on these five signals — everything in this plan feeds one of them:
1. **Can ship a feature end-to-end unsupervised** — DB migration → API endpoint → validation → tests → PR.
2. **Debugs systematically** — reads stack traces, reproduces bugs, uses logs/breakpoints, doesn't guess.
3. **Knows why, not just how** — can explain why async/await, why an index, why DTOs instead of entities.
4. **Writes reviewable code** — small PRs, meaningful names, tests, handles the unhappy path.
5. **Talks about tradeoffs** — "I chose X over Y because…" in every design conversation.
---
## The AI learn

## Concepts to close out this week (checklist items 1–4)
samples.opening:
# Week 1 Guide — CRUD, REST Semantics, DTOs, Validation
**Ships:** Rungs 1–2 of the [project spec](01-project1-spec.md). **Concepts unlocked:** HTTP semantics, DTOs, model binding/validation, DI basics.
## Day-by-day
### Mon — Rung 1, part 1
- Solution skeleton from setup day. Create `Ticket` model + `TicketsController` with POST and GET (list + by id) against a static in-memory list.
- Attempt-first: write the controller before asking anything. Then task-breakdown prompt if flailing.
- Build a `tickets.http` file as you go — every endpoint gets a request the moment it exists.
- **Trap you should hit on purpose:** return the wrong status code somewhere, then ask Claude to review — see if it catches it.
### Tue — Rung 1, part 2
- PUT, DELETE. Decide: 204 vs 200-with-body on update (either defensible — *write your reasoning in the PR description*, that habit is the point).
- 404 handling for every `{id}` route. GET-after-DELETE returns 404.
- Strict-review prompt on the full controller → fix → ownership quiz → merge PR #1.
### Wed — Rung 2, part 1 (DTOs)
- Before coding, concept deep-dive prompt: **"why DTOs instead of exposing entities"**. You want three reasons minimum (over-posting, coupling/API stability, serialization cycles later with EF).
- Create request/response DTOs, hand-map (no AutoMapper — hand-mapping makes the boundary visible while you're learning).
### Thu — Rung 2, part 2 (validation)
- Data annotations on request DTOs; observe `[ApiController]` auto-400 behavior. Inspect the error response shape in your `.http` output — you'll be asked "what does a validation failure look like to the client" in take-home debriefs.
- Edge cases: empty body, wrong types (`"priority": "banana"`), extra unknown fields. Know what happens for each.
- PR #2: review → quiz → merge.
### Fri — Drill day
- Debugging drill starts next week; today instead: **status-code oral exam** — quiz prompt: "rapid-fire me on HTTP: when 200 vs 201 vs 204, 400 vs 404 vs 409 vs 422, 401 vs 403, PUT vs PATCH vs POST, what idempotent means and which verbs are."
- SQL drill as every day (days 1–5 of the plan).
### Sat — Rebuild drill #1
- Blank file, AI off: `Ticket` CRUD controller with correct status codes + one DTO, from memory, ≤45 min. Rules in [../drills/rebuild-drills.md](../drills/

headings: # Weeks 4–5 Guide — Core Domain + The Hard Problem
## Week 4 — foundations at speed, then the interesting part
### Wed–Thu — Feature 4 (slot computation) — the domain-logic showpiece
samples.opening:
# Weeks 4–5 Guide — Core Domain + The Hard Problem
**Ships:** Features 1–7 of the [Bookable spec](01-project2-spec.md), including the concurrency centerpiece.
## Week 4 — foundations at speed, then the interesting part
### Mon — Feature 1–2 (auth + provider/services)
- This is Phase-1 material again on purpose. Target: both features in one day. If auth takes more than ~2 hours, that's signal — note it and drill the rebuild.
- New wrinkle: **ownership** — a provider edits only their own services. Enforce from claims in the service layer; add the 403 test.
### Tue — Feature 3 (availability windows)
- Overlap validation between windows is a warm-up for booking overlaps: half-open intervals `[start, end)`, two windows overlap iff `aStart < bEnd && bStart < aEnd`. Get this predicate right today with unit tests — you reuse it for the real invariant.
### Wed–Thu — Feature 4 (slot computation) — the domain-logic showpiece
- Pure function: `(windows, duration, existingBookings, date, timeZone) → slots`. No DB, no HTTP in the core — this is your best unit-testing material and a great "how do you make code testable" interview exhibit.
- Design note in PR: why slots are computed, not stored (stored slots = state to sync = bugs; computed = always consistent).
- Timezone discipline: compute in provider-local, return UTC. Test a DST transition date. **This test will probably fail the first time. Perfect — log the story.**
- Edge tests: window shorter than duration, booking mid-window splitting it, request for a past date.
### Fri — Drill day
- Planted-bug drill now runs on Bookable. New twist from this week: one of the 3 bugs should be a *domain* bug (wrong boundary in the overlap predicate, off-by-one in slot math).
- SQL drills: days 22–26.
### Sat — Rebuild
- From memory: the slot-computation core function + 3 of its unit tests. Pure logic rebuilds are the best kind — this one doubles as live-coding practice.
## Week 5 — the hard problem
### Mon — Feature 5 (naive booking)
- Check-then-insert, knowingly racy. Write the correctness tests that don't involve concurrency (fits in window, no overlap with *committed* bookings, 24h cancel rule can wait).
- **Branch `naive-booking` stays in history** — your before/after evidence.
### Tue — Prove the race
- The parallel test: N=20

# Learning Log
One entry per day, minimum one line. Honest > polished. By week 8 this file is the raw material for your behavioral story bank and take-home retros.
**Entry format:**
```
## YYYY-MM-DD (Week N, Day)
- Built: <what you shipped today>
- Broke: <what went wrong / what confused you>
- Learned: <the thing you'd explain differently now>
- Flag: <anything to revisit — becomes Saturday rebuild or quiz material>
```

# Learner guide
CampusOps targets a junior engineer moving toward mid-level ownership. Work through sprint documents in order, read the corresponding pull request, run the nearest tests, and explain each design choice in plain language.
For every sprint:
1. Read the outcome and acceptance criteria.
2. Draw the request path from contract to use case to adapter.
3. Predict failure cases before reading tests.
4. Run focused tests, then the whole solution.
5. Review what was deliberately not abstracted.
The goal is protecting business rules, publishing dependable contracts, and making changes with evidence.

# CampusOps curriculum specification
CampusOps manages university locations, assets, maintenance requests, work orders, technicians, parts, preventive maintenance, vendors, procurement, notifications, and reporting.
| Sprint | Outcome | Primary skill |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | Locations and API foundation | entities, contracts, HTTP |
| 02 | Asset lifecycle | invariants and state |
| 03 | Maintenance intake and triage | validation and prioritization |
| 04 | Work-order workflow | state machines |
| 05 | Technician skills and assignment | policies and relationships |
| 06 | Comments and audit history | append-only facts |
| 07 | SQLite persistence | EF Core and migrations |
| 08 | Parts and stock reservations | transactions and quantities |
| 09 | Preventive maintenance | clocks and background work |
| 10 | SLA clocks and escalation | configurable policy |
| 11 | Vendors and purchase requests | approval thresholds |
| 12 | Roles and campus permissions | authentication and authorization |
| 13 | React operations dashboard | TypeScript contracts and UI state |
| 14 | Webhooks and bug harvest | idempotency and concurrency |
| 15 | Reporting and operations | observability and release judgment |
Constraints: one backend deployment, explicit modules, stable v1 contracts, UTC timestamps, no real student data, and no claim of production readiness.

# API integration guide
Base path: `/api/v1`. JSON is default; business failures use Problem Details with a stable `code` extension.
- Ignore additive response fields and handle unknown future enum values.
- Send a unique `X-Correlation-ID` of at most 100 characters and record the echoed value.
- Work-order commands require the version last read; reload after `work_order.version_conflict`.
- Webhook event IDs are idempotency keys. Reusing one intentionally produces no new delivery.
- Webhook endpoints must be HTTPS. Secrets are referenced by name and resolved by deployment infrastructure.
- Do not blindly retry other mutations after an ambiguous timeout; general idempotency keys are not implemented.
Development OpenAPI is available at `/openapi/v1.json`. Demo identity headers provide no security assurance.

# CampusOps
CampusOps is a fifteen-sprint teaching repository for learning business-heavy C#/.NET API development and React/TypeScript integration through a university facilities platform.
## Architecture
```text
CampusOps.Api             HTTP composition and security
CampusOps.Core            business modules and use cases
CampusOps.Infrastructure  in-memory, SQLite, and integration adapters
CampusOps.Contracts       stable public request/response contracts
CampusOps.Worker          scheduled maintenance and delivery work
CampusOps.Web             React and TypeScript operations console
```
The backend is a modular monolith. Module boundaries organize code without adding network calls, distributed transactions, or separate deployments.
```powershell
dotnet restore CampusOps.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/CampusOps.Api
npm ci --prefix web/CampusOps.Web
npm run build --prefix web/CampusOps.Web
```
## Course map
| Sprints | Theme | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–5 | Operational foundations | locations, assets, requests, work orders, technicians |
| 6–10 | Reliability and time | audit history, SQLite, stock, worker scheduling, SLAs |
| 11–13 | Integration surfaces | procurement, authorization, React dashboard |
| 14–15 | Engineering ownership | idempotency, concurrency, reporting, operations, release |
Development OpenAPI is at `/openapi/v1.json`. Mutations use teaching-only `X-Demo-Role` and `X-Demo-Campus` headers. The API default is non-durable; `/health/ready` reports that fact.
Read [LEARNER-GUIDE.md](LEARNER-GUIDE.md), the [curriculum specification](docs/curriculum/SPEC.md), [TESTREADME.md](TESTREADME.md), and [OEReadMe.md](OEReadMe.md).

headings: # ADR-001: start as a modular monolith
samples.opening:
# ADR-001: start as a modular monolith
CampusOps uses one backend deployment with module-oriented code inside `CampusOps.Core`. Facilities workflows share transactions and evolve together. In-process calls keep failure modes visible to a learner.
Revisit only when a module has independent ownership and release cadence, measured scaling needs, and a clear data boundary that outweighs network and operational costs.

# Curriculum retrospective
CampusOps begins with one vertical slice and introduces complexity only after a visible need: SQLite for persistence, a worker for scheduled work, `IClock` for deterministic time, policies for permissions, React for an actual consumer, and idempotency/concurrency controls for reproduced integration failures.
A learner finishing the course should be able to trace requests across layers, model state and policy, choose an appropriate test boundary, publish compatible contracts, diagnose CI, review security and operational gaps, and argue against speculative architecture with concrete evidence.
Suggested capstone: choose one production-readiness gap—durable outbox, token validation, or transactional work-order persistence—write an ADR, implement one tested vertical slice, and update the runbook.

samples.opening:
# Onboarding: The Honest Version
Welcome. I built most of this. I'm going to tell you the truth about it, which is not the same story you'll get from the marketing page or the conference talk.
## What this codebase actually is
It's a **.NET 10 Clean Architecture solution template** — the thing behind `dotnet new ca-sln`. The sample domain is deliberately tiny (todo lists and todo items) because the *architecture* is the product, not the features. That has a consequence you need to internalize on day one: **a lot of the "why" here is about teaching a pattern cleanly, not about running a business.** Some of the decisions I'll defend below are the right call for a template and the *wrong* call for the app you'll eventually deploy on top of it. I'll flag those every time.
The other consequence: you'll see conditional-compilation directives everywhere — `#if (UseApiOnly)`, `#if (UsePostgreSQL)` in C#, `<!--#if ... -->` in XML, `//#if` in the scaffolding templates. Those are `dotnet new` template switches, not normal code. This checkout compiles as the **SQLite + full-stack (Angular default)** variant because none of those symbols are defined. When you read a file, always ask "which variant am I looking at?" — see [src/Web/Program.cs L40-L49](../src/Web/Program.cs#L40-L49) and [src/Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs L26-L74](../src/Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs#L26-L74).
## How to read this document
Six sections, each about one subsystem. Every section follows the same shape, because I want you to build the same reflexes I use:
1. **What it does and why it exists** — the honest purpose, not the slogan.
2. **The 2–3 hardest decisions** — including the alternatives I rejected and the tradeoffs that *still* bother me.
3. **Evidence** — exact files and classes. Don't take my word for anything; open them.
4. **One incident** — a real failure mode this design caused or prevented. War stories stick better than principles.
5. **Three questions** — you should be able to answer all three before moving to the next section. If you can't, you skimmed.

| 1 | [Architecture & layering](01-architecture.md) | The dependency rule is real; the "Domain has zero dependencies" ideal is a comfortable lie. |

# Reverse-Engineered Architecture Decision Records
This folder reconstructs the **ten most significant architecture decisions** the authors of this codebase made — most of them *implicitly*, i.e. embodied in code without a written ADR. Each is written in standard ADR format (Context, Decision, Alternatives Considered, Consequences, Status) and grounded in specific files and classes you can open.
## Method and honesty notes
- These are *reverse-engineered*. I inferred the decision and its rationale from the code; where the authors actually documented a decision themselves, I say so and mark the status accordingly rather than pretending I discovered it.
- The repo already contains three real ADRs in [docs/decisions/](../docs/decisions/README.md): ADR-001 (EF Core in the Application layer), ADR-002 (Aspire for orchestration/testing), ADR-003 (MediatR.Contracts in Domain). Two of my ten overlap those; I reverse-engineer them independently from code and then note the authors confirmed them. The other eight are genuinely undocumented.
- Anchors use `path#Lstart-Lend`. Line numbers were checked against the working tree (branch `main`, a clean checkout); if dependency-bump commits have since shifted lines, trust the path and symbol.
- This checkout compiles as the **SQLite + full-stack** template variant. `#if` blocks for other variants are inert here.
## The ten ADRs
| # | Decision | Category |
|---|---|---|
| [ADR-001](adr-001-clean-architecture-layering.md) | Four-layer Clean Architecture with dependency inversion via inward-owned interfaces | Layering / project structure |
| [ADR-002](adr-002-cqrs-lite-via-mediatr.md) | CQRS-lite: every use case is a MediatR command or query with one handler | Project structure |
| [ADR-003](adr-003-behaviour-pipeline.md) | Cross-cutting concerns as an ordered MediatR behaviour pipeline | App design / error handling |
| [ADR-004](adr-004-efcore-in-application-no-repository.md) | EF Core exposed via `IApplicationDbContext`; no repository layer | Data access |
| [ADR-005](adr-005-minimal-apis-reflection-registration.md) | Minimal APIs with convention/reflection endpoint registration | API design |
| [ADR-006](adr-006-contract-first-client-generation.md) | Contract-first typed clients; endpoint method name = OpenAPI operationId | API

# Clean Architecture Solution Template
The goal of this template is to provide a straightforward and efficient approach to enterprise application development, leveraging the power of Clean Architecture and ASP.NET Core. Using this template, you can effortlessly create a new app with Angular, React, or Web API only, powered by ASP.NET Core and Aspire. Getting started is easy - simply install the **.NET template** (see below for full details).
For full documentation, visit **[cleanarchitecture.jasontaylor.dev](https://cleanarchitecture.jasontaylor.dev)**.
If you find this project useful, please give it a star. Thanks! ⭐
## Getting started
### Prerequisites
- [.NET 10.0 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0) or later
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (LTS) — only required if you plan to use the Angular or React frontend
- [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) or [Podman](https://podman.io/) (or any OCI-compliant container runtime) — only required when using SQL Server or PostgreSQL. Not required when using SQLite (the default).
### Install the template
```bash
dotnet new install Clean.Architecture.Solution.Template
```
### Create a new solution
Create a new solution using the template. Specify the client framework using `--client-framework` (`-cf`) and the database provider using `--database` (`-db`):
```bash
dotnet new ca-sln --client-framework [angular|react|none] --database [postgresql|sqlite|sqlserver] --output YourProjectName
```
| Option | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--client-framework` | `angular`, `react`, `none` | `angular` |
| `--database` | `postgresql`, `sqlite`, `sqlserver` | `sqlite` |
**Examples:**
🅰️ Angular SPA with ASP.NET Core Web API and PostgreSQL:
```bash
dotnet new ca-sln -cf angular -db postgresql -o YourProjectName

⚛️ React SPA with ASP.NET Core Web API and SQL Server:

dotnet new ca-sln -cf react -db sqlserver -o YourProjectName

# fabledocs — A Training Lab Built From This Codebase
This is a learning curriculum generated from the code in this repository. It is written for one specific learner: **a junior fullstack engineer** (comfortable with CRUD web dev in .NET/C# and React/TypeScript or similar) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file-and-line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, what the alternatives are, how it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repository is
This is [jasontaylordev/CleanArchitecture](../README.md) — the source of the `Clean.Architecture.Solution.Template` NuGet template (`dotnet new ca-sln`). It is a **.NET 10 solution template** demonstrating Clean Architecture with:
- **Domain** layer: entities, value objects, domain events — almost no external dependencies ([ADR-003](../docs/decisions/ADR-003-MediatR-Contracts-In-Domain.md)).
- **Application** layer: CQRS use cases via MediatR, FluentValidation, AutoMapper, and a pipeline of cross-cutting behaviours (logging, exception handling, authorization, validation, performance).
- **Infrastructure** layer: EF Core 10 (`ApplicationDbContext`), ASP.NET Core Identity, save-changes interceptors for auditing and domain-event dispatch.
- **Web** layer: Minimal API endpoint groups, OpenAPI + Scalar, ProblemDetails error mapping, and two SPA clients (Angular 21 and React 19) whose API clients are **generated** from the OpenAPI spec by NSwag.
- **Aspire** orchestration: `AppHost` runs the full stack; `TestAppHost` runs just the database for functional tests ([ADR-002](../docs/decisions/ADR-002-Aspire-For-Orchestration-And-Testing.md)).
- Four test layers: domain unit tests, application unit tests, functional tests against a real database (Respawn resets), and Playwright/Reqnroll acceptance tests.
The sample domain is deliberately small — todo lists and todo items — so the architecture is the star. That makes it an ideal gym: every enterprise pattern is present, but no page of business logic gets in your way.
**One caveat you must internalize early:** this repo is a *template*. You will see `#if (UseApiOnly)` / `#if (UsePostgreSQL)` conditional blocks in C# and `<!--#if ... -->` in XML — these are template preprocessor directives, not normal code (e.g. [Program.cs](../src/Web/Program.cs#L40-L49), [DependencyInjection.cs](../src/Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs#L26-L32)). And i

# fabledocs4 — The Hands-On Workbook
The other three doc sets in this repo are things you *read*. This one is things you *do*.
- **fabledocs** — the full curriculum (maps, patterns, drills, interview prep).
- **fabledocs2** — the candid principal-engineer onboarding tour.
- **fabledocs3** — reverse-engineered architecture decision records.
- **fabledocs4 (this one)** — guided labs you build with your own hands, plus first-principles primers on the fundamentals this codebase quietly assumes you already know.
If you're a junior engineer and the other folders felt like drinking from a firehose, **start here.** You learn a codebase by changing it, breaking it, watching a test go red and then green — not by reading about it. This workbook is built around that.
## What's inside
| Part | What it is | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| [01-guided-labs/](01-guided-labs/README.md) | Five step-by-step labs. You edit real files, run real commands, verify real results. | Do these first, in order. This is the core. |
| [02-fundamentals-primers/](02-fundamentals-primers/README.md) | Five "from scratch" explainers: dependency injection, async/await, web auth, transactions, HTTP/REST. Each teaches the concept, then shows exactly where this repo uses it. | Read a primer when a lab or a file uses a concept you can't fully explain to someone else. |
| [03-syntax-decoder.md](03-syntax-decoder.md) | Every unfamiliar C# and TypeScript symbol in this codebase, decoded — `init`, `record`, `null!`, `=>`, `??`, `[]`, `static abstract`, and friends. | Keep it open while you read code. Look things up as you hit them. |
| [04-tooling-and-debugging.md](04-tooling-and-debugging.md) | How to actually run it, set a breakpoint, read a stack trace, see the SQL EF generates, and use the Aspire dashboard. | Before Lab 1, and whenever something breaks and you don't know why. |
| [05-workflow-and-habits.md](05-workflow-and-habits.md) | Branching, commits, PRs, breaking a task down, estimating, and — the most important junior skill — how to ask for help well. | Read once early; revisit before your first real PR. |
## The one rule
**Do the labs on a branch, and never be afraid to break things.** Nothing here can hurt the real project — you're working on your own copy, and in development this app *recreates its database from scratch on every run* ([evidence](../src/Infrastructure/Data/ApplicationDbContextInitialiser.cs#L44-L46)), so there's no precious state to lose. Breaking something and fixing it is the entire point. The engineer who's afraid to break things stays junior; the one who breaks thin

samples.opening:
# ADR 0001: Client-rendered teaching boundary
## Status
Accepted in Sprint 1.
## Context
The course needs React lifecycle, browser state, accessible interaction, and API-boundary lessons to remain visible. A full-stack framework could productively solve many of those concerns, but it would also combine routing, rendering, data loading, and deployment before the learner has models for each.
## Decision
Use a Vite-powered React application, a separate Fastify API, and a pure TypeScript core package. Packages share strict compiler and quality configuration but own their runtime boundaries.
## Consequences
The learner can trace browser, transport, and domain state independently. The repository must make loading and error behavior explicit, and it does not claim server rendering or framework-level production optimizations.

# FormForge
FormForge is a complete, schema-driven form builder and response analytics platform built as a fifteen-sprint React and TypeScript teaching repository. A junior engineer studies the issues, ordered commits, pull-request reviews, architecture decisions, counterexamples, and tests that produced the product.
Version `1.0.0` includes typed authoring, seven field variants, validation, conditional logic, multi-page branching and resume, immutable publishing, retry-safe submissions, response filtering and CSV export, analytics, comments, version diffs, accessibility checks, autosave recovery, and operational readiness boundaries.
## Run the release candidate
```bash
pnpm install
pnpm seed
pnpm dev
```
`pnpm seed` verifies the canonical demo scenario and prints a deterministic fingerprint. The development command starts the Vite application and Fastify API. No database, Docker daemon, or external service is required.
Run the complete local evidence gate with:
```bash
pnpm gate
```
## Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
Browser[React 19 + Vite] --> Core[@formforge/core\ntyped domain rules]
Browser --> API[Fastify API\nruntime boundaries]
API --> Core
API --> Data[@formforge/data\nrepository contracts + in-memory adapters]
Data --> Core
CI[GitHub Actions] --> Checks[lint + typecheck + tests + build\nsecret scan + bundle budget]
```
The browser owns interaction and presentation state. `@formforge/core` owns pure schemas, reducers, validation, branching, response queries, analytics, and diffs. The API validates untrusted HTTP data and authorization context. `@formforge/data` demonstrates versioned repository contracts with deterministic in-memory adapters; durable deployment storage remains an explicit production integration, not a claim made by this repository.
## Implemented stack
- React 19, strict TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Router, and TanStack Query;
- Fastify with Zod-backed domain parsing at HTTP boundaries;

samples.opening:
# Learner Guide
You are the audience of this repository. Nobody expects you to write Agora — you are here to
**read it the way a senior engineer would**, one sprint at a time. This guide tells you how.
## The unit of study: one merged PR per sprint
Each sprint is a single squash-merged Pull Request. Study them **in order** (PR list, oldest
first). For every sprint:
1. **Read the stakeholder issue** attached to the sprint milestone. It states the business need
in a persona's voice. Before reading any code, sketch how *you* would build it.
2. **Read the sprint playbook** (`docs/sprints/sprint-NN.md`) — goal, scope, teaching focus.
3. **Walk the commits in order** (the PR's Commits tab). The commit sequence is a story:
domain model → use cases → adapters → endpoints → web UI → docs. Some sprints deliberately
commit a naive implementation, then a RED failing test, then the fix — that arc is the
lesson. Commit bodies have `Why this way:` / `Notice:` / `See also:` sections; read them.
4. **Read the inline review comments** on the diff. They are tagged:
- 📘 **concept** — an idea worth studying on its own
- 🔍 **review-lens** — how a senior reads this code; what they check first
- ⚠️ **pitfall** — a trap this code avoids (or once contained)
- 🔗 **connects-to** — links to an ADR or an earlier sprint
Comments are authored under persona prefixes: `[Author]`, `[Reviewer]`, `[Stakeholder]`.
When `[Reviewer]` and `[Author]` argue, follow the whole thread — sometimes the Reviewer wins
and a later commit changes course.
5. **Read the design-debate comment** on the PR (one per sprint). It is the closest thing to
sitting in a real architecture review.
6. **Do the exercises** at the bottom of the PR body. They are small and pointed
("delete X and let the test suite tell you why it existed").
## How to read the codebase
Backend: start from the **inside** and move out — the same direction the commits are ordered.
1. `Agora.Domain` — entities, value objects, state machines, promotion policies. No framework

## The thesis: earn the abstraction three times
## How to read a single PR
samples.opening:
# Learner Guide — How to Study Folio (the Capstone)
Welcome to the capstone. **Folio is a course disguised as a codebase** — a from-scratch build of a
Notion-class collaborative document editor (block-based rich text, real-time multiplayer, offline merge,
comments, permissions, version history), delivered as 15 pull requests. But this course is different from
the five before it, and the difference is you.
This is **Course 6**, and its subject is the hardest thing in product engineering: **real-time
collaborative editing** — CRDTs, distributed consistency, presence, and a real rich-text document model.
It's taken *last on purpose*: every prior course's lessons converge here.
---
## What's different: you co-author
In the earlier courses you mostly *read* a senior's PRs. Here, **you write a substantial share of the
code** from Sprint 3 on, and the AI shifts toward **reviewer**. The teaching artifact flips: from "study
the senior's implementation" to "the senior reviews yours." A commit tagged `[L]` is yours; `[A]` is the
AI's. The AI proposes the design and reviews your work; you build it. By this course you're a near-peer —
act like one.
So the three active moves from earlier courses gain a fourth:
1. **Predict** before reading the design.
2. **Review** the diff yourself before reading the placed comments.
3. **Do the lab.**
4. **Author.** Write the `[L]` commits. The AI's review of your code — its questions, its "here's what a
senior catches" — is the most valuable thing in the repo.
---
## The thesis: earn the abstraction three times
The signature arc of the whole curriculum lands here, stated as a roadmap in **ADR-0002** (read it first):
- **Sprint 5 — build multiplayer WRONG on purpose.** Naive last-write-wins. It *will* lose data and feel
broken, and that's the point: you must feel the need before you understand the fix.
- **Sprint 6 — build a toy CRDT from scratch** (`packages/crdt-101`, a sequence CRDT, RGA/Logoot-style)
with a convergence fuzzer. Now you understand sequence CRDTs *in the bones* — causality, intention

headings: # ADR-0002: Add Storefront Cache Layers Only When Measured
samples.opening:
# ADR-0002: Add Storefront Cache Layers Only When Measured
- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-07-12
## Context
Catalog reads will eventually traverse CDN, Next.js ISR, Redis, and Postgres. Each
layer can reduce origin load, but every layer also creates a new place where a
price or availability value can become stale. Starting with all layers would hide
which one provides value and make invalidation failures difficult to teach.
## Decision
Start with the separate storefront read seam and add layers in measured stages:
1. Sprint 3 selects SSG, ISR, or dynamic rendering per route.
2. Sprint 5 adds Redis read-through caching and records hit rate, p95, and origin load.
3. Sprint 6 adds tag invalidation, TTL backstops, single-flight, and SWR.
4. Sprint 12 tunes keys and warming from measurements; Sprint 13 stress-tests them.
Every cached surface must name its audience and staleness tolerance. Storefront
catalog pages initially tolerate 60 seconds; cart, checkout, inventory mutation,
and all admin reads tolerate zero and never use the catalog page cache as truth.
## Consequences
Each layer arrives with a baseline and a removal criterion. Event invalidation will
provide precision, TTL will self-heal missed events, and transactional operations
will always revalidate price and inventory against the authoritative store.

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-07-10
- **Sprint:** S01
- **Deciders:** Folio authors (capstone)
## Context
Folio's defining hard problem is **conflict-free collaborative editing**: many people editing one rich
document at once, offline and reconnecting, and everyone converging to the same result. This is a research
area, not a weekend feature. The temptation is to reach for the production library (Yjs) on day one — but
you cannot *evaluate* or *operate* a CRDT you don't understand, and a team that adopts one as a black box
will misuse it and be unable to debug it. This ADR sets the roadmap that frames all 15 sprints, so the
build order is a deliberate teaching sequence, not accidental churn.
## Decision
**Earn convergence three times**, each phase teaching something the next depends on and then discarding
what it needs to:
1. **S05 — Naive last-write-wins, on purpose broken.** Real-time multiplayer where the whole document is
one string and the last save wins. It *will* lose data under concurrent edits, and it will feel wrong.
That failure is the investment: you must **feel the need** before the fix means anything. (Throwaway —
we delete it.)
2. **S06 — A toy CRDT from scratch** (`packages/crdt-101`, a sequence CRDT in the RGA/Logoot family) with a
**convergence fuzzer**. Hand-building it teaches sequence CRDTs *in the bones* — causality, tombstones,
intention preservation, why concurrent inserts converge. (Throwaway as production code — but the
understanding is permanent.)
3. **S07 — Adopt Yjs, knowingly** (the flagship). A hand-rolled CRDT for *rich text* (nested blocks,
formatting, undo) is a multi-year project; Yjs already solved it. We adopt it with `y-prosemirror` and a
**custom WebSocket provider** — and because we built a toy one, we know exactly what Yjs is doing, can
reason about its update log, and can debug it as a peer.
DocState is **plaintext** until S07, then becomes a **Yjs update log + periodic snapshots**. The name
`DocState` (not `content`) is chosen now to survive that change.
## Alternatives considered
- **Design for a CRDT from the start (S01).** No migration later — but premature: we don't yet understand
the shape a CRDT wants (that's literally S06's job), so we'd be designing for an abstraction we can't

# ADR-0002: The classic → sync migration roadmap
- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-07-09
- **Sprint:** S01
- **Deciders:** Tracer authors
## Context
Tracer's signature subject is real-time collaboration: a sync engine, offline-first clients,
and conflict resolution. This is genuinely hard, and teaching it cold — building a sync engine
in Sprint 1 — would overwhelm before the learner understands *why* each piece exists.
## Decision
We will build Tracer as a **classic REST + TanStack Query app first (Sprints 1–5)**, then
**migrate it to a local-first sync engine (Sprint 06 server spine, Sprint 07 offline-first
client)**. The classic architecture is a deliberate, planned throwaway — its replacement is the
core lesson of the course.
The endgame is named here so every early decision can be made with it in view: for example, we
choose a SPA (ADR-0001) and per-field mutation granularity precisely because the sync engine
will need them.
## Alternatives considered
- **Build the sync engine from day one.** Rejected: premature. Without first *feeling* the
limits of the classic approach (Sprint 05 will make invalidate-everything visibly laggy),
the learner can't appreciate what the sync engine buys. Building it cold also front-loads the
hardest material before the domain is understood.
## Consequences
- Some Sprint 1–5 code (notably the TanStack-Query data layer) is intentionally deleted in
Sprint 06–07. That is a feature, not waste: the migration *is* the curriculum, and doing it
under a live product is the most valuable thing in the course.
- Early sprints should keep their data layer at arm's length so the swap is clean.
- **Revisit:** never — this is a pedagogical decision, not a technical one that scale could
overturn. (See the recurring "build-once-badly-then-adopt" thesis across the whole curriculum.)
## Links
- ADR-0001 (SPA over Next), `docs/sprints/README.md` (the cross-sprint arc), `docs/sprints/sprint-06.md`, `docs/sprints/sprint-07.md`

# Learner guide
Study each sprint as a decision trail rather than reading only the final code.
1. Read the milestone and stakeholder issue to understand the outcome and constraints.
2. Read commits in order. Predict the next design pressure before opening the next commit.
3. Start with domain tests, then trace the application use case, adapter, endpoint, and contract.
4. Read inline review comments at the referenced lines and compare them with the ADR.
5. Recreate the design debate: state which option you would choose and what evidence could change your mind.
6. Run the focused test, alter one invariant, and make the failure explain the business risk.
7. Complete the sprint exercises without changing public contracts accidentally.
After Sprint 15, read the [flaw harvest](docs/quality/FLAW-HARVEST.md), [over-engineering review](OEReadMe.md), and [retrospective](docs/curriculum/RETROSPECTIVE.md) together. For each choice, separate business complexity from framework complexity and curriculum ceremony from product delivery.
## Review questions
- Which business fact must always remain true?
- Which aggregate owns the decision?
- Is this rule effective-dated, country-specific, tenant-specific, or currency-specific?
- Does the API contract expose a stable business concept or an internal storage shape?
- Can a retry duplicate money, state transitions, audit records, or integration messages?
- What is the narrowest interface that lets another system integrate safely?
- Which tests would survive replacing ASP.NET Core, EF Core, or an external provider?
- Which abstraction has at least two real consumers or implementations, and which exists only for a hypothetical future?
- What evidence is still missing before an operational or production claim is honest?

# GlobeHire product and curriculum specification
## Product statement
GlobeHire helps a client organization plan, hire, onboard, employ, pay, support, and offboard workers in countries where the client does not operate a legal entity. The platform acts as a fictional employer-of-record operations system and integration hub.
This is an educational domain model, not a legal, tax, payroll, immigration, or compliance product.
## Personas
- **Global HR partner:** initiates hires, chooses compensation and benefits, tracks onboarding, and requests employment changes.
- **Payroll operator:** closes payroll periods, validates inputs, resolves exceptions, and produces statements and client invoices.
- **Compliance specialist:** maintains effective-dated country policies, reviews classification risk, and manages immigration cases.
- **Finance approver:** reviews cost estimates, invoices, expenses, and compensation changes.
- **Worker:** supplies onboarding data, requests leave/expenses, reviews statements, and raises disputes.
- **Integration engineer:** synchronizes HRIS, finance, identity, and provider systems using APIs, webhooks, and bulk files.
- **Support auditor:** reconstructs who decided what, under which policy version, and when.
## Core capabilities
1. Client organizations, legal-employment countries, users, roles, and tenant boundaries.
2. Effective-dated country policy catalogs for notice, probation, leave, employer costs, currencies, and required onboarding steps.
3. Workforce planning and transparent cost estimates with explicit assumptions and policy versions.
4. Hire cases, offers, approval chains, contracts, onboarding tasks, and document metadata.
5. Employment agreements, compensation, benefits, leave, expenses, amendments, and offboarding.
6. Payroll calendars, typed payroll inputs, validation, simplified gross-to-net fixtures, statements, and client invoices.
7. Contractor classification, contracts, invoices, approvals, disputes, and conversion to employment.
8. Immigration cases and compliance-review checkpoints.
9. Search, reporting, audit timelines, bulk import/export, and operational reconciliation.
10. Versioned REST APIs, OpenAPI, idempotency, optimistic concurrency, webhooks, and replaceable integration adapters.
## Domain model
### Tenant an

# Integration guide
All teaching endpoints are under `/api/v1/clients/{clientId}`. Treat `clientId` as a security boundary, not a filter. Real authorization must derive and validate tenant access from the authenticated principal; a path value alone is not proof of access.
## Contract rules
- Send ISO country/currency codes, `DateOnly` values as `YYYY-MM-DD`, and timestamps in UTC.
- Use `Idempotency-Key` for retryable creates. Replaying the same logical operation with the same key must not create a second resource.
- Preserve `ETag` and send the expected version through `If-Match` for mutable resources. On conflict, fetch current state and ask the user to reconcile rather than silently overwrite.
- Parse Problem Details by HTTP status and stable `code`; display `detail` to a human but do not branch on its wording.
- Record `X-Trace-Id` in integration logs and support requests. Do not put secrets or PII in correlation values.
- Treat `404` for a resource outside the current tenant as intentional information minimization.
## Webhooks and bulk work
Webhook message and delivery IDs are stable across retry. Consumers must make processing idempotent before acknowledging. Signatures in this model demonstrate deterministic input only; production needs HMAC verification, timestamps, replay windows, secret rotation, endpoint validation, and SSRF defenses.
Bulk validation returns bounded, row-level outcomes so one invalid row need not erase valid findings. External row keys should be stable across resubmission. A real importer must define whether valid rows commit independently or the file is atomic, then expose reconciliation evidence.
## Compatibility
Changes within v1 should be additive: add optional fields or new endpoints without changing existing meanings. Removing/renaming fields, changing requiredness, altering enum meaning, or changing idempotency/version semantics requires a new API version and a consumer migration window. OpenAPI describes transport shape; examples and contract tests should protect behavior.

# GlobeHire
GlobeHire is a complete fifteen-sprint C#/.NET teaching repository for a fictional global workforce and employer-of-record platform. It focuses on changeable business logic, versioned API design, integration boundaries, and the engineering judgment a junior developer needs to grow.
It is an original educational project inspired by publicly described industry workflows. It does not copy Pebl/Velocity Global code, private behavior, wording, assets, or branding, and it is not affiliated with or endorsed by those companies.
## What you will learn
- model money, dates, policies, approvals, and lifecycle state machines independently of ASP.NET Core;
- keep HTTP contracts versioned and separate from domain and persistence shapes;
- design tenant-bound ports, idempotency, optimistic concurrency, outbox/webhook identities, and partial-failure results;
- test business risk at the lowest useful level, then sample public wiring through the API;
- recognize when architecture helps change and when ceremony becomes over-engineering;
- distinguish a green build from honest production readiness.
## Architecture
```text
HTTP / OpenAPI contracts
|
v
Application use cases -----> persistence, time, identity, and event ports
|
v
Domain aggregates, policies, value objects, and events
^
|
Infrastructure adapters (in-memory teaching adapters today)
```
Dependencies point inward. The domain has no ASP.NET Core, EF Core, serialization, or provider dependency. The API maps contracts explicitly. This is a modular monolith with seams for proven integration needs, not premature microservices.
## Course map
| Sprint | Outcome | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Workforce-plan vertical slice | [notes](docs/sprints/sprint-01.md) |
| 2 | Effective-dated country estimates | [notes](docs/sprints/sprint-02.md) |
| 3 | Hire-case state machine | [notes](docs/sprints/sprint-03.md) |
| 4 | Offers, approvals, contracts | [notes](docs/sprints/sprint-04.md) |
| 5 | Onboarding and activation (`v0.5.0`) | [notes](docs/sprints/sprint-05.md) |

# Fifteen-sprint retrospective
## What changed well
The architecture grew from one quote slice into hiring, offers, employment, payroll, people operations, contractors, lifecycle changes, integrations, bulk work, and compliance without moving business rules into controllers or binding the domain to storage. Typed tenant IDs, policy snapshots, idempotency identities, and state machines became stable integration concepts rather than framework conventions.
The five planted flaws were valuable because each counterexample changed a contract: exact money conservation, half-open effective dates, tenant-bound lookup, atomic versioned mutation, and stable retry identity. The fixes stayed local and produced tests that explain the risk.
## What was intentionally expensive
The issue, milestone, commit, PR, and review trail is much more ceremony than this codebase needs. It turns delivery history into course material. The source-project split also arrived earlier than many small products would need; [the over-engineering review](../../OEReadMe.md) identifies where to simplify without discarding important rules.
## What remains
A useful next exercise is a PostgreSQL adapter that passes the same use cases while atomically persisting aggregate state, audit evidence, and outbox messages. Follow it with authenticated tenant claims, a real webhook worker and contract test fixture, then load and restore drills. Do not implement country/payroll policy for real use without qualified legal, tax, payroll, and privacy owners.
## Questions for the learner
1. Which boundary would change first for a second HRIS provider, and which code should remain untouched?
2. Where must a transaction begin and end when state and an outbox message change together?
3. Which project boundaries still pay rent, and which would you merge on a three-person team?
4. What production evidence would turn each candidate SLO into a defensible target?
5. Which regression test would you keep if you could retain only one per harvested flaw?

# VT Code Architecture Guide
## Overview
VT Code follows a modular architecture designed for maintainability,
extensibility, and performance. Internally, VT Code uses Rust traits for
runtime composition. Externally, VT Code prefers protocol- and manifest-driven
extension seams such as MCP, skills, plugin manifests, and
`[[custom_providers]]` so third-party integrations do not need to land new Rust
impls in the core workspace. This is deliberate: Rust coherence and orphan-rule
constraints make public trait APIs a poor default extension boundary for an
ecosystem-style project.
For internal composition, prefer explicit provider selection over "clever"
trait resolution when a boundary starts depending on many overlapping impls,
associated types, or context-specific behavior. In practice, VT Code treats
`HasComponent<Name>::Provider` as an elaborated dictionary: the context chooses
the provider once, and blanket consumer traits delegate through that explicit
selection. See `crates/codegen/vtcode-core/src/components.rs` and `crates/codegen/vtcode-core/src/llm/cgp.rs`.
## Model + Harness
VT Code treats the model as the reasoning engine and the harness as the runtime that makes that reasoning useful. Phase 1 of the
exec/full-auto runtime is built around that split rather than around a separate agent subsystem.
> **Capability is a composition.** The model is one of seven reinforcing
> subsystems (model · harness · context · tools · evals · sandbox · state)
> whose job is to keep the agent making *monotonic progress* on long-horizon
> tasks. See [`docs/guides/agent-capability-composition.md`](guides/agent-capability-composition.md)
> for the full mapping.
Harness primitives in VT Code map to the runtime like this:

# Zed Agent Client Protocol Integration
VT Code adopts [ACP (Agent Client Protocol) by Zed](https://agentclientprotocol.com/).
It took the reference from the official Zed implementations
([`zed-industries/claude-code-acp`](https://github.com/zed-industries/claude-code-acp),
[`cola-io/codex-acp`](https://github.com/cola-io/codex-acp)) and follows the
[Goose ACP client guidance](https://block.github.io/goose/docs/guides/acp-clients/). Use the steps
below to configure, launch, and validate the integration end to end.
## Setup overview
1. Build VT Code (`target/debug` is fine for local development; `target/release` is recommended for regular editor workflows).
2. Enable the ACP bridge in `vtcode.toml` or via environment overrides.
3. Wire either the VT Code binary or a small wrapper script into Zed's `settings.json` under `agent_servers`.
4. Start an external agent session in Zed and confirm ACP logs report healthy traffic.
## Prerequisites
- Rust toolchain pinned by `rust-toolchain.toml`.
- VT Code configuration with provider, model, and credentials.
- Zed `v0.201` or later with the Agent Client Protocol feature flag enabled.
- An ACP client that advertises the `fs.read_text_file` capability so VT Code can proxy
`read_file` requests. If the handshake omits it, the bridge keeps the tool disabled and reports a
reasoning notice.
## Build VT Code
```bash
cargo build --release
```
Record the resulting binary path (`target/release/vtcode`) or add it to your `PATH`.
For local repository development, this is also fine:
```bash
cargo build -p vtcode
```

# Agent Skills Guide
VT Code supports repository, user, admin, and bundled system skills using the open Agent Skills `SKILL.md` format.
## Discovery
VT Code discovers skills in this order:
1. Nearest ancestor `.agents/skills` from the current working directory up to the git repository root
2. `~/.agents/skills`
3. `/etc/codex/skills`
4. Bundled system skills
If multiple skills share the same name, the nearest repository skill wins, then user, then admin, then system.
VT Code also honors disabled entries from `~/.codex/config.toml`:
```toml
[[skills.config]]
path = "/path/to/skill/SKILL.md"
enabled = false
```
## Skill Structure
Each skill is a directory containing a required `SKILL.md` file.
```text
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
├── references/
└── assets/
```
`scripts/`, `references/`, and `assets/` are optional.

`disable-model-invocation` flag used to hide a skill from the model-facing startup catalog while

# JavaScript Workbook — Build the Fundamentals
Eight exercises that *use* every fundamental. Each has: the task, a hint ladder (read one hint at a time), a full solution, and a line-by-line explanation. Type the solutions out — don't paste.
---
## Exercise 1 — Shopping Cart Math (arrays, immutability)
**Task:** Given the cart below, write four functions — `addItem(cart, item)`, `removeItem(cart, id)`, `changeQty(cart, id, qty)`, `cartTotal(cart)` — **none of which mutate the input**.
```js
const cart = [
{ id: 1, name: "Mouse",    price: 25,  qty: 1 },
{ id: 2, name: "Keyboard", price: 80,  qty: 2 },
];
```
<details><summary>Hints</summary>
1. "Don't mutate" means every function returns a **new array** — which three array tools build new arrays?
2. Add → spread. Remove → `filter`. Update one → `map` with a conditional spread.
3. Total → `reduce` with a seed of `0`; each item contributes `price * qty`.
</details>
**Solution:**
```js
const addItem   = (cart, item)     => [...cart, item];
const removeItem = (cart, id)      => cart.filter(i => i.id !== id);
const changeQty = (cart, id, qty)  =>
cart.map(i => (i.id === id ? { ...i, qty } : i));
const cartTotal = (cart) =>
cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
```
**Why it works:** `[...cart, item]` copies the array and appends — the original is untouched (verify: `cartTotal(cart)` is the same before and after). `filter` returns only survivors. The `map` line is the most important idiom in the file: untouched items pass through *as-is*; the matching item is rebuilt with `{ ...i, qty }` — a new object with one field replaced. `reduce` starts at `0` and folds each line item in. These four shapes are 90% of state updates you'll ever write (and the *required* style in React).
**Check yourself:** after `const c2 = changeQty(cart, 2, 5)`, what is `cart[1].qty`? (Answer: still `2` — and if it isn't, your map is mutating `i` instead of spreading.)
---

Parts 1–5 cover the 25 fundamental JavaScript topics; Parts 6–9 extend the same format to Node.js, TypeScript, React, and SQL; Parts 10–18 form the **advanced track** — one companion file per part with the mid-senior-level material that comes up in interviews and code reviews. Parts 19–23 add the **C#/.NET track**: language and platform fundamentals, their advanced companions, and a `.NET Plus` ecosystem file (Entity Framework, testing libraries, logging, and the rest of what .NET interviews assume). 150 topics total. Each topic includes a definition, practical use cases, and code snippets with explanations.
## How to use this tutorial
Work through the parts in order — later topics build on earlier ones (React leans on closures and immutability; the SQL part ends by wiring queries into Express routes). Run the snippets in a browser console, Node.js REPL, or a scratch file. Don't just read: type the examples out and break them on purpose.

"Idempotency means safe-to-repeat — for example, the workflow engine I studied claims executions by row acquisition so duplicate queue deliveries can't double-run, at the cost of a DB round-trip per claim; the failure mode it guards is at-least-once delivery." That sentence pattern, everywhere.
Using this repo as your portfolio: you may say "a large open-source low-code platform I've studied in depth" or name NocoBase. # NocoBase Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from this repository for one learner: a **junior fullstack JS engineer** (React/Node/TS CRUD experience) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, its alternatives and failure modes, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is (the 30-second identity)
NocoBase is an open-source, plugin-driven **no-code/low-code platform**: users define data collections (tables) and drag-and-drop UI at runtime, and the platform persists both the data model and the UI as data. The backend is a **Koa application** ([application.ts](../packages/core/server/src/application.ts#L222)) where every HTTP endpoint is a generic **resource action** (`/api/<collection>:<action>`) resolved by a resource manager ([resourcer.ts](../packages/core/resourcer/src/resourcer.ts#L330)) and executed against a Sequelize-backed **Repository** layer ([repository.ts](../packages/core/database/src/repository.ts#L679)). The frontend is React 18 + Ant Design 5, with two runtimes: legacy v1 (`@nocobase/client`, schema-driven via Formily) and v2 (`@nocobase/client-v2`, `FlowEngine`). Nearly all product functionality — auth, ACL, workflow, file storage, even the collection manager itself — ships as one of 100+ **plugins** under [packages/plugins/@nocobase](../packages/plugins/@nocobase), each with the same server lifecycle ([plugin.ts](../packages/core/server/src/plugin.ts#L119-L131)). It is a Lerna/Yarn workspaces monorepo of ~30 core packages plus plugins.
Why it's a great training lab: it contains, in one repo, a real HTTP pipeline, a real ORM abstraction with transactions and mass-assignment guards, a real RBAC authorization engine, a real async job system (workflow engine with queues and idempotent execution acquisition), a plugin architecture, migrations, i18n, multi-app tenancy, and three tiers of tests (unit, integration, Playwright e2e).

# 01 — Architecture: One Image, Six Services, and an Events Table
## What it is and why it exists
The whole product — API, frontend assets, websockets, the collaborative
editing server, background workers, and cron — compiles into one deployable
unit. At boot, `server/index.ts` reads a `--services=` flag (or the `SERVICES`
env var) and starts whichever subset you asked for. The service registry is
`server/services/index.ts`, and each entry (`web.ts`, `websockets.ts`,
`collaboration.ts`, `worker.ts`, `cron.ts`, `admin.ts`) is just a function
that attaches itself to the shared Koa app and HTTP server.
Why a monolith with flags instead of separate deployables? Because we ship to
two audiences with opposite needs. Self-hosters want `docker run` and done —
one container, one Postgres, one Redis. Our cloud wants horizontal scale —
dozens of `web` pods, a couple of `worker` pods, isolated `collaboration`
pods. The services flag gives both from one build artifact. `throng` in
`server/index.ts` handles per-container process fan-out on top of that.
The second load-bearing idea is the **event spine**. Nearly every mutation
writes a row to the `events` table (`server/models/Event.ts`) inside the same
transaction as the mutation, and after commit the event is pushed onto a Bull
queue (`server/queues/`). Processors (`server/queues/processors/`) subscribe
by event name and fan out into tasks (`server/queues/tasks/`). Websocket
broadcasts (`WebsocketsProcessor.ts`), notifications
(`NotificationsProcessor.ts`), search indexing (`SearchIndexProcessor.ts`),
revision snapshots (`RevisionsProcessor.ts`), and webhooks are all *consumers
of events*, not code called inline from route handlers. This is why the API
stays fast and why adding a new side effect rarely touches existing code.
The third idea is **plugins** (`plugins/`, loaded by
`server/utils/PluginManager.ts`). Anything optional — Slack, OIDC, S3 vs local
storage, the Postgres search provider — registers itself against a typed

# fabledocs3 — Reverse-Engineered Architecture Decision Records
Nobody wrote ADRs for this codebase at the time. The decisions got made
anyway — in PRs, in migrations, in the shape of directories — and the code is
the only record. This pack reconstructs the ten most significant ones in
standard ADR format (Context, Decision, Alternatives Considered, Consequences,
Status), each grounded in specific files and classes you can open and verify.
"Status" here means: **Active** (still the law of the land), **Active-Eroding**
(still enforced but under visible pressure), or **Active-with-Scar-Tissue**
(the decision stands, and the code contains visible remediation for what it
cost).
## The ten decisions
| ADR | Title | Domain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [ADR-001](adr-001-modular-monolith-service-flags.md) | Modular monolith with runtime service composition | Structure / distributed |
| [ADR-002](adr-002-three-runtime-layering.md) | Three-runtime layering: `app` / `server` / `shared` (+ `plugins`) | Structure |
| [ADR-003](adr-003-rpc-post-api.md) | RPC-over-POST API contract (`noun.verb`), Zod at the boundary | API contract |
| [ADR-004](adr-004-policy-authorization.md) | Centralized CanCan policy layer, serialized to clients | API / security |
| [ADR-005](adr-005-sequelize-explicit-transactions.md) | Sequelize with decorators; explicit transaction-per-mutation | Data access |
