| [ADR-007](adr-007-crdt-triple-representation.md) | Yjs CRDT collaboration with triple document representation | Data / distributed |
| [ADR-008](adr-008-redis-horizontal-scale.md) | Redis as the horizontal-scale substrate (pub/sub, locks, limits, cache) | Distributed |
| [ADR-009](adr-009-error-philosophy.md) | Typed error factories, stable ids, `isReportable`, one funnel | Error handling |
| [ADR-010](adr-010-integration-first-testing.md) | Integration-first testing on real infrastructure | Testing |

# Architecture
Outline is composed of a backend and frontend codebase in this monorepo. As both are written in TypeScript, they share some code where possible. We utilize the latest ES6 language features, including `async`/`await`, and types. oxfmt formatting and Oxlint are enforced by CI.
## Frontend
Outline's frontend is a React application compiled with [Vite](https://vitejs.dev/). It uses [MobX](https://mobx.js.org/) for state management and [Styled Components](https://www.styled-components.com/) for component styles. Unless global, state logic and styles are always co-located with React components together with their subcomponents to make the component tree easier to manage.
```
app
├── actions     - Reusable actions such as navigating, opening, creating entities
├── components  - React components reusable across scenes
├── editor      - React components specific to the editor
├── hooks       - Reusable React hooks
├── menus       - Context menus, often appear in multiple places in the UI
├── models      - State models using MobX observables
├── routes      - Route definitions, note that chunks are async loaded with suspense
├── scenes      - A scene represents a full-page view that contains several components
├── stores      - Collections of models and associated fetch logic
├── types       - TypeScript types
└── utils       - Utility methods specific to the frontend
```
## Backend
The API server is driven by [Koa](http://koajs.com/), it uses [Sequelize](http://docs.sequelizejs.com/) as the ORM and Redis with [Bull](https://github.com/OptimalBits/bull) for queues and async event management. Authorization logic
is contained in [cancan](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cancan) policies under the "policies" directory.
Interested in more documentation on the API routes? Check out the [API documentation](https://getoutline.com/developers).
```
server
├── routes            - All API routes are contained within here
│   ├── api           - API routes
│   └── auth          - Authentication routes
├── commands          - Complex commands that perform actions across multiple models
├── config            - Database configuration
├── emails            - Transactional email templates
│   └── templates     - Classes that define each possible email template
├── middlewares       - Shared Koa middlewares

# Fabledocs: Outline as a Training Lab
A curriculum that turns this repository — [Outline](../README.md), a real-time collaborative knowledge base — into a structured path from junior fullstack JS engineer to mid-level, with senior judgment and interview readiness as explicit goals.
**Who this is for:** you can build CRUD features in React/Node/TypeScript, but you want to (1) navigate a large production codebase confidently, (2) develop the judgment mid-level and senior engineers are paid for, and (3) walk into a mid-level fullstack interview with concrete, evidence-backed answers instead of memorized trivia.
**The method:** every page pairs *codebase-specific knowledge* (where things live in Outline, how its real flows work) with *transferable skill* (why the pattern exists, what the alternatives are, how it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview). Interview readiness is a first-class goal — most pages end with an "Interview angle."
## What Outline is (the 60-second version)
Outline is a team wiki/knowledge base: documents organized into collections, edited collaboratively in real time. It is a TypeScript monorepo with three main source trees: [`app/`](../app) is a React 17 + MobX single-page client; [`server/`](../server) is a Koa API server using Sequelize over PostgreSQL, Redis + Bull for background work, socket.io for live updates, and Hocuspocus/Yjs for collaborative editing; [`shared/`](../shared) holds code used by both, including the entire ProseMirror-based editor. The API is RPC-over-POST (e.g. `POST /api/documents.update`), authorization is cancan-style policies, and every mutation emits an event onto a Redis-backed event bus that fans out to processors (revisions, notifications, websockets, search, webhooks). It ships as a single deployable that can run one or many of its services (`web`, `worker`, `websockets`, `collaboration`, `cron`, `admin`) per process — see [server/index.ts](../server/index.ts#L182-L190). It is multi-tenant: nearly every table has a `teamId`, and tenant isolation is a recurring security theme in this curriculum.

samples.opening:
# Onboarding: From the Engineer Who Built This Thing
Welcome. You're joining a codebase that is roughly ten years old in spirit — a
TypeScript monolith that serves a real-time collaborative wiki to teams, ships
as a single Docker image, and has to work equally well on our cloud and on some
ops person's Raspberry Pi. That dual life (SaaS + self-hosted) explains about
half of the weird decisions you're going to ask me about, so keep it in mind
as a lens for everything below.
This pack is written the way I'd explain the system over a week of coffee
chats: what each subsystem does, the decisions that were genuinely hard, the
alternatives we walked away from, and the scars. It is not marketing copy.
Where the design still bothers me, I say so.
## How to read this
In order. Each doc builds on the previous one, and each ends with three
questions. Don't skip the questions — if you can't answer them, re-read before
moving on, because the next doc assumes you can.
| Doc | Subsystem | The one-sentence version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [01-architecture.md](01-architecture.md) | Architecture | One process image, six services behind a flag, plugins for everything optional, and an events table as the spine. |
| [02-api-design.md](02-api-design.md) | API design | RPC-over-POST, not REST — on purpose — with Zod at the door, policies in the middle, and presenters at the exit. |
| [03-data-access.md](03-data-access.md) | Data access | Sequelize with decorators, a transaction-per-mutation middleware, and a document that exists in three representations at once. |
| [04-testing.md](04-testing.md) | Testing strategy | Vitest projects per runtime, factories over fixtures, and real HTTP through TestServer instead of mocked routers. |
| [05-error-handling.md](05-error-handling.md) | Error handling | Typed error constructors with an `isReportable` bit, one Koa onerror funnel, and graceful shutdown as a first-class concern. |
| [06-observability.md](06-observability.md) | Observability | Category-tagged Winston logs, StatsD counters, dd-trace spans via decorator, and Sentry only for what we chose to report. |
## Ground rules that will save you pain
1. **`shared/` runs in both the browser and Node.** Never import anything
server-only into it. The editor schema lives there precisely because both
sides must agree on it (`shared/editor/`).
2. **Mutations flow through commands and emit Events.** If you write to the
database from a route handler directly, you've probably skipped a step that
websockets, webhooks, notifications, and search indexing all depend on.
3. **Every API mutation runs

# fabledocs4 — Practice Pack: Drills, Capstones, Labs, and Retention
fabledocs2 told you the story. fabledocs3 gave you the decisions. This pack
is where you stop reading and start *doing* — because the difference between
"I understand the lock convoy incident" and "I can diagnose one at 3 a.m." is
reps, and the difference between knowing the outbox gap exists and being able
to close it is a capstone.
Everything here is grounded in the same seams the earlier packs identified:
the commit-to-publish gap in the event spine, the triple document
representation, the explicit-transaction discipline, the policy layer, the
missing collaboration harness, and the Redis-wears-five-hats topology.
## Contents
| File | What it is | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [01-fire-drills.md](01-fire-drills.md) | Six production-incident simulations. Symptoms first, escalating hints, then the resolution path. Practice being on-call for this system. | 45–60 min each |
| [02-capstone-outbox-relay.md](02-capstone-outbox-relay.md) | Close the event spine's commit-to-publish gap with a real relay. The system's most instructive missing piece, built by you. | 2–3 days |
| [03-capstone-collab-harness.md](03-capstone-collab-harness.md) | Build the multi-client collaboration test harness — the testing strategy's standing IOU (ADR-010). | 2–3 days |
| [04-sql-concurrency-lab.md](04-sql-concurrency-lab.md) | Reproduce the lock convoy with two psql sessions. `FOR UPDATE`, `SET LOCAL lock_timeout`, `SKIP LOCKED`, pool math. | half a day |
| [05-frontend-mobx-lab.md](05-frontend-mobx-lab.md) | The `app/` tree hands-on: stores, models, shipped policies, and adding a feature end-to-end through the RPC convention. | half a day |
| [06-flashcards.md](06-flashcards.md) | ~50 spaced-repetition cards covering fabledocs2 + fabledocs3. Question / answer format, import into Anki if you like. | ongoing |
| [07-four-week-plan.md](07-four-week-plan.md) | A schedule that sequences all three packs plus this one into four weeks of ~90 min/day. | 4 weeks |
## Rules of engagement
1. **Fire drills: no peeking.** Read the symptoms, write your hypothesis and
first three diagnostic moves *before* opening the first hint. The value is
in the gap between your guess and the answer.
2. **Capstones: design doc first.** One page, reviewed against the acceptance
criteria in the doc, before you write code. Both capstones are real
engineering — treat them like a PR you'd ship.
3. **Labs need a running system.** `yarn install`, `.env` from sample,
`yarn db:migrate`, `yarn dev:watch` (see fabledocs2 README). The SQL lab
additional

# Optimal Upskill Plan — Junior → Mid/Senior SWE (CRUD Web Dev)
Synthesized from all past planning sessions. The winner is the **merged master plan** (project-first spine + Socratic mobile hours + diagram discipline), run on the **project ladder**, with the best pieces of the .NET paths and interview prep folded in. The enterprise Net* specs and C1–C10 capstones are the post-plan senior track, not part of the core 16 weeks.
---
## Top priorities (in order)
1. **Shipping reps over reading.** Ticket → branch → code → tests → PR → review defense. This is the single activity that closes the gap; everything else supports it.
2. **You type the code.** Claude writes tickets and reviews like a strict senior, but your hands write the fix (except the one designated AI-delegation week).
3. **One stack deep first: TypeScript/React/Node + Postgres.** C# /.NET starts as a second track in Phase 3, not before.
4. **Testing and debugging by default** — every PR has tests; every bug gets root-caused, not patched.
5. **SQL before ORM; async correctness; auth/RBAC; tenant isolation** — the four recurring mid-level gaps across every discussion.
6. **Active recall everywhere** — daily log → Anki cards; Socratic sessions where you attempt answers first; Friday oral exams on weak areas.
7. **Diagrams or it didn't happen** — every feature starts with an ERD/sequence diagram, every PR keeps diagrams true.
8. **AI supervision as an explicit skill** — reviewing/interrogating AI diffs and catching planted bugs is trained deliberately, not absorbed.
## Daily structure (8 hrs, 6 days/wk)
- **6 hrs desk:** 2.5 hrs ticket work → 1 hr PR defense with Claude → 1.5 hrs second ticket → 30 min diagram updates → 30 min engineering log
- **2 hrs mobile (gig waiting time, interruptible):** 30 min Anki → 45 min reading (best-practices / worked-examples docs, JSTut/csharptut/antigravupskill) → 30 min Socratic quiz with Claude → 15 min read tomorrow's ticket
- Weekly: Friday 45-min viva on weak areas; one full rest day
## Order of study (16 weeks)
- **Phase 0 — Setup (Days 1–2)**
- Free disk space (`npx npkill`), install .NET SDK, archive empty/duplicate folders
- VS Code + Mermaid preview, Anki, Git host for PRs
- **Phase 1 — Honest baseline (Weeks 1–2) · Tier 0**
- Projects: **job track, .netpastebin,

samples.opening:
# Learner guide
For every sprint:
1. Read the milestone and issues before the code.
2. Read commits in order and predict the next design pressure.
3. Start at a failing business-rule test, then trace the use case, adapter, endpoint, and contract.
4. Read review comments as design evidence, not style instructions.
5. Change one invariant and confirm the test fails for a useful reason.
6. Explain the transaction, tenant, retry, and compatibility boundaries in your own words.
Ask continuously: what business fact must remain true, who owns it, which failure can be retried, and what evidence would justify another abstraction?

# MeterForge product and curriculum specification
## Product statement
MeterForge lets fictional SaaS businesses define products and prices, subscribe customers, ingest metered usage, calculate charges, issue invoices and credits, collect payments through replaceable providers, enforce entitlements, deliver webhooks, and reconcile financial records.
## Invariants
- Money carries an ISO currency and unlike currencies never combine implicitly.
- Every resource belongs to a tenant at every application and repository boundary.
- Issued invoices are immutable; corrections use credits or replacement documents.
- Usage ingestion, commands, payment attempts, and webhook delivery have stable idempotency identities.
- Effective-dated price versions never overlap.
- Aggregate writes use an expected version where concurrent decisions can conflict.
- Business state, audit evidence, and outbox messages commit atomically in a durable adapter.
- Public contracts do not expose domain or persistence types.
## Fifteen sprints
| Sprint | Outcome | Teaching focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | Product and fixed-price vertical slice | dependency direction, contracts, Problem Details |
| 02 | Customer subscriptions and trials | aggregates and explicit transitions |
| 03 | Effective-dated price versions | temporal modeling and immutable history |
| 04 | Idempotent usage ingestion | deduplication and tenant scope |
| 05 | Tiered usage rating; `v0.5.0` | algorithms, money, boundary tests |
| 06 | Invoice calculation and finalization | immutable financial provenance |
| 07 | PostgreSQL-shaped durable adapter | transactions, migrations, adapter contracts |
| 08 | Subscription amendments and concurrency | compare-and-swap and conflict responses |
| 09 | Discounts, tax boundary, and credits | policy composition and corrections |
| 10 | Payment-provider adapter | timeouts, retries, and idempotency |
| 11 | Transactional outbox and webhooks | eventual consistency and delivery identity |
| 12 | Entitlements and usage limits | commercial policy versus authorization |
| 13 | Reconciliation, refunds, and disputes | ledgers and compensating records |

# Integration guide
- All public teaching routes use `/api/v1/tenants/{tenantId}`. A path tenant is untrusted; production authorization must match authenticated tenant claims.
- Send `Idempotency-Key` for retryable usage/payment commands and reuse it for the same logical operation.
- Send `If-Match` with the version read before an amendment. On conflict, fetch current state and reconcile rather than overwriting.
- Parse Problem Details by status and stable `code`; do not branch on human `detail` wording.
- Record `X-Trace-Id` for support correlation without embedding PII or secrets.
- Treat `404` for a foreign tenant resource as intentional information minimization.
- Webhook consumers deduplicate stable message/delivery IDs and verify signatures/replay windows in a real implementation.
- Evolve v1 additively. Removing fields, changing meanings/requiredness, or altering idempotency/version semantics requires a new version and migration window.

# MeterForge
MeterForge is a complete fifteen-sprint C#/.NET teaching repository for a fictional multi-tenant usage-based subscription billing platform. It is designed to help a junior software engineer grow toward mid-level ownership through business rules, API design, persistence, concurrency, integrations, testing, and operations.
It is an original educational product—not a Stripe clone, payment processor, accounting system, or production financial service. All tenants, providers, money flows, and policies are synthetic fixtures.
## What the course teaches
- model money, subscriptions, effective prices, usage, invoices, credits, refunds, and entitlements without framework coupling;
- make tenant scope, idempotency, optimistic concurrency, and immutable financial provenance explicit;
- integrate PostgreSQL and external providers through narrow application ports;
- design versioned APIs with Problem Details, `Idempotency-Key`, `If-Match`, and trace correlation;
- reason about outbox/webhook delivery, retries, ambiguous failures, and reconciliation;
- choose tests by risk and recognize when architecture or delivery ceremony becomes over-engineered.
## Architecture
```text
HTTP / OpenAPI contracts
|
v
Application use cases ------> persistence, provider, time, and event ports
|
v
Domain rules and financial records
^
|
In-memory, PostgreSQL, and simulated provider adapters
```
The deployable shape is a modular monolith. MeterForge deliberately avoids MediatR, AutoMapper, generic repositories, microservices, and an internal framework.
## Course map
| Sprint | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Product and fixed-price vertical slice |
| 2 | Subscriptions, trials, and lifecycle |
| 3 | Effective-dated price versions |
| 4 | Idempotent usage ingestion |
| 5 | Tiered rating and `v0.5.0` |

# Fifteen-sprint retrospective
The model grew from one fixed-price product into subscriptions, temporal pricing, usage, rating, invoices, PostgreSQL, concurrency, adjustments, payments, outbox/webhooks, entitlements, and reconciliation without moving core rules into controllers or provider adapters.
The most valuable teaching moments were the five counterexamples. Each changed a concrete guarantee and stayed local: tenant-scoped deduplication, non-overlapping tier arithmetic, invoice immutability, atomic compare-and-swap, and stable payment retry identity.
The process history is deliberately expensive. A normal small team should reduce milestones, issues, review narration, and project boundaries to what coordination and risk require. Read [OEReadMe](../../OEReadMe.md) before copying the structure.
The best next exercise is to wire PostgreSQL for a complete invoice/outbox use case, add Testcontainers adapter contracts, introduce authenticated tenant claims, implement a webhook worker, then perform load and restore drills. Do not add microservices until deployment, scaling, ownership, or security evidence requires them.

# Aral Tagalog — standalone mobile app
A Duolingo-style app teaching **Tagalog to English speakers**, built with React Native + Expo.
Ported from the `tagalog` monorepo into a single self-contained project: no pnpm workspace, no
`@aral/*` packages, no build step needed before `expo start`.
```bash
npm install
npm start          # then press "a" for Android, "i" for iOS, or scan the QR in Expo Go
```
## It works with no backend
The compiled course ships inside the app (`src/content/bundle.json` — 15 units, 57 lessons, 480
exercises, 230 vocabulary entries). Play as a guest and everything works offline on first launch:
progress lives in SQLite on the device.
The API is **optional**, and only adds two things: syncing progress across devices (log in /
register) and pulling newer content than the shipped bundle. Point it somewhere real by editing
`extra.apiUrl` in `app.json`; leave it and the app simply stays local — every network path fails
soft.
## Audio
No clips are recorded yet, so every 🔊 falls back to the device's text-to-speech voice
(`expo-speech`, `fil-PH`, slowed to 0.85 for learners). The bundle carries the spoken text for each
audio ref, so this covers all 304 of them. Real recordings win automatically once they exist —
`playAudio` tries the cached file, then the network, then speech.
## Layout
```
app/                     expo-router screens
_layout.tsx            ThemeProvider > ProgressProvider > Stack
index.tsx              course map — continue hero, collapsible units, grammar tips
lesson/[lessonId].tsx  lesson route (unlock + practice gating)
stats.tsx              XP, level, streak, goal editor, 14-day chart, achievements, appearance

# Junior SaaS Clone Learning Workspace
This workspace contains five separate learning codebases generated from the pasted SaaS clone specs.
Each project is intentionally scaffolded as a production-shaped TypeScript/React/Node app, but it is not wired for installation or deployment. The goal is reading, tracing, and modifying the architecture.
## Projects
- `planr` - Linear-style issue tracker
- `bookr` - Cal.com-style scheduling app
- `payr` - Stripe-dashboard-style analytics and payments admin
- `blockr` - Notion-style page and block editor
- `helpkit` - Intercom-style support inbox and chat widget
## How To Study
Start with each project's `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md`, then read:
1. `src/domain/types.ts` for the nouns.
2. `src/domain/*` for the important business rules.
3. `src/server/routes.ts` for API boundaries.
4. `src/components/*` for how UI state connects to domain behavior.
## Enterprise Readiness Pass
Each project now includes production-shaped supporting modules and focused tests:
- Policy and tenant guards.
- Audit or lifecycle records.
- Idempotency, locking, retry, or rate-limit examples where relevant.
- Search, cursor pagination, webhook signing, SLA, and widget-auth examples.
- `vitest` test scripts and domain-level tests for the riskiest logic.
These projects still do not need to run or install dependencies to be useful. Treat the tests as executable documentation for how the important business rules should behave.

# Payr
Payr is a Stripe-dashboard-inspired admin product for mock payments. It focuses on data-dense UI, RBAC, audit logs, API keys, idempotency, cursor pagination, and webhook delivery logs.
## Folder Map
- `src/domain/types.ts` - organizations, members, payments, keys, events, webhooks.
- `src/domain/rbac.ts` - role permissions used by API and UI.
- `src/domain/idempotency.ts` - 24-hour response replay model.
- `src/domain/analytics.ts` - metrics and time-series aggregation.
- `src/server/routes.ts` - payment, refund, key, webhook, and dashboard route sketches.
- `src/components/DashboardHome.tsx` - dense metrics UI.
- `src/data/seedGenerator.ts` - realistic payment generator.
- `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md` - onboarding and architecture notes.

# Bookr
Bookr is a Cal.com-inspired scheduling app focused on availability, timezone correctness, booking race conditions, calendar integrations, and notification workflows.
## Folder Map
- `src/domain/types.ts` - users, event types, availability, bookings, integrations, webhooks.
- `src/domain/availabilityEngine.ts` - converts host rules into safe invitee-facing slots.
- `src/domain/bookingService.ts` - transaction-shaped booking flow with slot revalidation.
- `src/domain/calendarGateway.ts` - provider boundary for external busy times and event creation.
- `src/server/routes.ts` - public booking and host dashboard API sketches.
- `src/components/BookingFlow.tsx` - public booking page state machine.
- `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md` - senior engineer onboarding notes.

# Blockr — Study Syllabus
Ordered by dependency. Companions: `docs/traces/`, `docs/reference.md`, `docs/issues/` (triage
exercise — do NOT read `severity-list.md`).
Blockr's curriculum in one line: **trees are invariants wearing a data structure — ordering,
acyclicity, tenancy, and access all live or die on write-path discipline.**
---
## Module 1 — Data modeling: trees in flat storage
**Read**: `src/domain/types.ts` (all) → `src/data/seed.ts` → the "Data modeling audit" in
`docs/reference.md`.
**Principle**: a parent-pointer column is the cheapest tree and the most expensive everything-else.
Every recursive walk in this repo (`permissions.ts:30`, `pageLifecycle.ts:13`, `blockTree.ts:25`)
is the price of that choice.
**Self-check**:
1. Why do blocks carry both `pageId` and `parentBlockId`, and what consistency rule does that
denormalization create? Where can it be violated today?
2. `propertyValues` keyed by property name — walk through "rename Status → State" end to end.
3. Which correlation in `Permission` can the current type not express, and what union fixes it?
4. Seed check: `entries[0].pageId` is `"pg_task_1"` (`seed.ts:26`) — does that page exist? What
does that tell you about fixture hygiene?
## Module 2 — TypeScript in practice
**Read**: `src/server/routes.ts:9,43` (the `as Block["type"]` laundering) →
`src/domain/types.ts:52-59` (the untyped content bag) → `src/domain/searchIndex.ts:51-58` +
`src/components/PageEditor.tsx:32-47` (two consumers paying the sniffing tax) →
`src/domain/blockTree.ts:32-55` (generic tree + the `sortOrder` cast at line 50) → audit tables in
`docs/reference.md`.
**Principle**: blockr shows the *cost side* of loose typing better than any sibling project: one
`Record<string, unknown>` at the center (`Block.content`) forces runtime type-sniffing at every
consumer and forecloses features (content id remapping, trace 03).
**Self-check**:
1. Design `BlockContent` as a discriminated union for five of the fifteen block types. Which
consumers simplify, and what new compile errors appear (good ones)?
2. Why is `z.string()` + `as` *worse* than no validation at all, argumentatively?

# Bookr — Study Syllabus
Ordered by dependency. Companions: `docs/traces/` (walkthroughs), `docs/reference.md` (patterns),
`docs/issues/` (your triage exercise — do NOT read `severity-list.md`).
Bookr's curriculum in one line: **time is a domain, concurrency is a discipline, and unwired
modules are lies.**
---
## Module 1 — Data modeling: entities of a scheduling product
**Read**: `src/domain/types.ts` (all), `src/data/seed.ts` (all), then the "Data modeling audit"
in `docs/reference.md`.
**Principle**: in scheduling, the schema *is* the product: what's an instant (`Booking.startUtc`),
what's a clock time (`AvailabilityRule.startTime`), and what's a duration (`durationMinutes`) are
three different types wearing the same two (`string`, `number`).
**Self-check**:
1. Which fields are instants, which are local clock times, and which are durations? Which type
distinguishes them? (None.)
2. Why does `Booking` duplicate `hostUserId` when it's derivable through `eventTypeId`?
3. What can't you query because invitees aren't an entity?
4. Write the exclusion constraint that makes double-booking impossible at the DB layer, and the
CHECK constraint that would catch an inverted booking.
## Module 2 — TypeScript in practice
**Read**: `src/domain/notificationJobs.ts:3-6` (the good union) →
`src/domain/bookingService.ts:4-6` + `src/domain/calendarGateway.ts` (interface seams — find the
mock's parameter mismatch at `calendarGateway.ts:17` and explain why it compiles) →
`src/server/routes.ts:6-14` (what the schema checks and what it merely types) →
`src/components/BookingFlow.tsx:47` (`String(null)`).
Then the TypeScript audit in `docs/reference.md`.
**Principle**: `z.string()` is not a semantic type. The three inputs that later throw or corrupt
(`startUtc`, `timezone`, `monthStartUtc`) all pass validation, because the schema encodes *shape*
and the domain needs *meaning*.
**Self-check**:
1. Why does `MockCalendarGateway` compile with a narrower method parameter? What syntax change
makes TS reject it?

# FABLE Guide — Notes App
**Project 4: a deliberately small scaffold you upgrade yourself.** Projects 1–3 gave
you finished apps to read. This one flips the model: you get a *working but naive*
CRUD app, and the learning is in replacing its shortcuts with the real patterns —
markdown rendering, folders/tags, debounced autosave, and PostgreSQL full-text search.
Building on a scaffold is closer to real jobs than greenfield work: you inherit code,
find its weakest seam, and improve it without breaking what works.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get (working today):** an Express + Knex + Postgres API for `notes`
(list/get/create/update/delete/stats) with the standard envelope, and a single-page
React client (`client/src/App.jsx`) with a form, list, search box, and stats strip.
Notes already have `title`, `body`, `folder`, `status`, and `tags` fields.
**You build (the labs in §5):**
| Upgrade | Replaces this shortcut in the scaffold |
|---|---|
| Markdown rendering | `body` is displayed as plain text even though seeds contain markdown (`"# Draft"`). |
| Real search (Postgres FTS) | `model.js` searches with `CAST(notes AS TEXT) ILIKE '%term%'` — the whole row cast to text. Read that line and enumerate why it's wrong. |
| Debounced autosave | The form saves only on explicit submit. |
| Folder/tag navigation | `folder` and `tags` are stored but the UI filters by a client-side `JSON.stringify(record).includes(search)` — yes, really (see `App.jsx`). |
The gap between the scaffold and the target *is the curriculum.* The naive lines are
left visible on purpose so you can articulate what's wrong before fixing it.
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL / JavaScript.
Same layer rules as always: routes → controller → service → model.

# FABLE Guide — REST API Testing Tool (Postman-lite)
**Project 15: build the tool, understand the trade.** You've curl'd every project so
far; now you build the thing that replaces curl: collections of saved requests,
environments with `{{variable}}` interpolation, request history, a response viewer —
and the piece that makes it interesting: a **backend proxy** that executes arbitrary
user-specified HTTP requests, because the browser's CORS rules won't let the client
do it directly. Developer tools are a distinct engineering genre (your user is a
developer, your data is *requests themselves*), and the proxy is a security problem
wearing a feature's clothes.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| The proxy | `services/proxyService.ts`, `controllers/proxyController.ts` | Your server executes requests to URLs users typed. Timing, size, status capture — and SSRF risk, for real this time (Project 6's Lab 3 warned you). |
| Why a proxy at all | client can't fetch cross-origin | Being able to *explain CORS from both sides* — as the blocked client and as the API that sets the headers — is a permanent interview asset. |
| Template interpolation | `utils/interpolate.ts` | `{{baseUrl}}/users/{{id}}` — a tiny template engine: resolution order, missing variables, no infinite recursion. |
| Environments | environment model/service/controller | Named variable sets with one active — the mental model behind every deploy config system. |
| Trees in UI | collections → folders (one level) → requests, `CollectionTree.tsx` | Persisted tree with sort fields; import/export/duplicate of nested structures (Project 11's deep-copy again). |
| History as a log | history model + pagination + clear | Append-only request log with retention questions — a mini ledger (Project 10) for requests. |
| CodeMirror integration | `client/src/components/ui/CodeEditor.tsx` | Wiring a serious third-party editor widget into React — controlled-component friction included. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod + CodeMirror.

# FABLE Guide — Personal Task Manager
**One doc to take you from "I can read this code" to "I could have designed this code."**
This is Project 1 of the curriculum, and it teaches the single most reusable skill in
full-stack work: the **layered CRUD app**. Every project after this one is a variation
on the shape you learn here. Master this project slowly and every later project gets faster.
> The older docs (`architecture.md`, the `upskill/` folder) are still valid references.
> This guide is the recommended path *through* them: shorter, ordered, and hands-on.
---
## 1. What you are looking at
A task manager with create, edit, filter, sort, complete, and delete. Nothing exotic —
and that is the point. The value is in *how* it is built:
```
Browser (React)                    Server (Express)                 Database
─────────────────                  ────────────────                 ────────
TasksPage                          taskRoutes.js      ─ URLs only
└─ useTasks (hook)     HTTP      taskController.js  ─ HTTP in/out
└─ tasksApi.js  ────────►   taskService.js     ─ rules & validation
taskModel.js       ─ Knex queries  ──►  tasks table
```
Each layer has exactly one job. When you can say **why** a piece of logic belongs in one
layer and not another, you are thinking at mid level. When you can argue about the cost
of moving it, you are thinking at senior level.

# Upskill Curriculum
Project: **Personal Task Manager** (`01-task-manager`)
This curriculum turns this project into a training lab for full-stack JavaScript roles. It is for juniors who want to become mid-level, mid-level engineers learning ownership, and senior engineers practicing architecture critique.
## Repo Identity
Personal Task Manager is a self-contained React, Express, Knex, PostgreSQL learning app. The main learning surface is task CRUD, filtering, completion toggles, overdue highlighting. The browser entry lives at `client/src/App.jsx:7`; the API starts around `server/src/app.js:1`; persistence is introduced in `server/db/migrations/20260703000000_create_tasks_table.js:45`; seed data begins at `server/db/seeds/01_tasks.js:136`. The codebase uses a deliberate layered shape: UI calls API services, API routes call controllers, controllers delegate to services, services call models, and models own Knex queries.
## How To Use This
| Timeline | Path |
| --- | --- |
| One weekend | Read `00-fast-track.md`, trace one flow, make one tiny UI or validation change. |
| Two weeks | Work through cartography, stack mastery, and two code-reading drills. |
| Eight weeks | Add tests, complete good-first tickets, and write one mid-level design note. |
| Ongoing | Use contribution and career docs for PR practice, review practice, and interview prep. |
## Recommended Path
- Brand-new junior: start with `00-fast-track.md`, then `01-codebase-cartography/02-file-reading-order.md`.
- Junior with stack familiarity: trace `01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md`, then do annotation drills.
- Mid-level engineer: focus on `03-architecture-and-patterns`, `05-quality-engineering`, and mid-level tickets.
- Senior reviewer: start with `03-architecture-and-patterns/06-architecture-critique.md` and `08-reference/risk-register.md`.
## Conventions
- Anchors use `path:line` references, for example `server/src/services/taskService.js:17`.
- Fake code is always labeled as illustrative.
- Drills include self-grading so learners can judge progress without needing another AI prompt.
- Verification notes list commands, inspected files, and uncertainty.
## Senior Mindset
A junior asks, "How do I make it work?" A mid-level engineer asks, "Is this the right pattern for this codebase?" A senior asks, "What does this commit us to, who pays the cost, and how do we reduce risk?" Use this project to practice moving from implementation toward judgment.

- Brand-new junior: start with `00-fast-track.md`, then `01-codebase-cartography/02-file-reading-order.md`.
- Junior with stack familiarity: trace `01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md`, then do annotation drills.
- Mid-level engineer: focus on `03-architecture-and-patterns`, `05-quality-engineering`, and mid-level tickets.
- Senior reviewer: start with `03-architecture-and-patterns/06-architecture-critique.md` and `08-reference/risk-register.md`.
## Conventions
- Anchors use `path:line` references, for example `server/src/services/contactService.js:10`.
- Fake code is always labeled as illustrative.
- Drills include self-grading so learners can judge progress without needing another AI prompt.
- Verification notes list commands, inspected files, and uncertainty.
## Senior Mindset
A junior asks, "How do I make it work?" A mid-level engineer asks, "Is this the right pattern for this codebase?" A senior asks, "What does this commit us to, who pays the cost, and how do we reduce risk?" Use this project to practice moving from implementation toward judgment.

# FABLE Guide — Recipe Manager with User Accounts
**Project 5: the biggest single jump in the curriculum.** Three new dimensions land at
once: **TypeScript** end-to-end, **JWT authentication** (access token + HTTP-only
refresh cookie), and **multi-table writes in a transaction**. Plus the concept that
reshapes every layer: requests now have an *identity*, and some data has an *owner*.
Budget more time here than for Projects 1–4 combined. It's worth it — auth + ownership
+ transactions is the exact skill set the industry means by "mid-level backend."
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript everywhere | `server/src/**/*.ts`, `client/src/**/*.tsx`, shared shapes in `server/src/types/domain.ts` and `client/src/types/recipe.ts` | Types are the contract between layers; watch how they replace guesswork. |
| JWT access + refresh | `services/authService.ts`, `middleware/auth.ts` | Short-lived bearer token in memory, long-lived refresh token in an HTTP-only cookie. Learn *why the split exists*. |
| Route protection, two flavors | `middleware/auth.ts`: `requireAuth` vs. `optionalAuth` | Public browsing works logged-out; favorites/ownership light up when logged in. Read both — the asymmetry is the lesson. |
| Ownership checks | `recipeService.ts` update/delete paths | 403 vs. 404 vs. 401 — three different "no" answers, each meaning something. |
| Knex transactions | recipe create: recipe + ingredients + steps + categories in **one transaction** | Partial writes are corruption. This is the pattern Projects 9–10 build on. |
| React auth context | `client/src/context/AuthContext.tsx` + `services/api.ts` | Login state as app-wide context; token installed via `setAccessToken()`; `withCredentials: true` carries the refresh cookie. |
| Password hashing | `authService.ts` + `models/userModel.ts` | bcrypt, and why the users table must never leak `password_hash` in responses. |

**Project 6: your first TypeScript scaffold-upgrade project.** The theme is
**hardening an API's edges**: schema validation with Zod, API versioning, fetching
metadata from external URLs, and designing an endpoint that outside clients (a
bookmarklet) can call. Projects 1–5 taught you the layers; this one teaches you the
*boundaries* — every place data enters or leaves your process.
Like Project 4, this is a working-but-naive scaffold plus labs. The scaffold runs
today; the learning-focus features are yours to build.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get:** a TypeScript Express + Knex API for `bookmarks` (`title`, `url`,
`collection`, `status`, `tags`) with list/search/stats/CRUD, the standard envelope,
and a one-page React client (`client/src/App.tsx`). The whole server backbone is six

| Upgrade | Replaces this shortcut |
|---|---|

# FABLE Guide — Poll / Survey Builder
**Project 11: schema-driven software.** Until now, your apps knew their data shapes at
compile time — a task has a title, a recipe has steps. A survey builder's core object
is **a form defined by the user at runtime**: questions of different types, options,
ordering, and a public-facing renderer that draws UI from that definition. This
"data that describes structure" pattern is the same one behind form builders, CMS page
builders, and workflow designers — it's a genuinely mid-level modeling problem.
This is also the first project with a dedicated **validators layer**: Zod schemas in
`server/src/validators/` applied by `middleware/validate.ts`, and even the env config
(`config/env.ts`) is Zod-parsed. What you *built* in Project 6's Lab 1, you now get to
*read* as an established pattern.

| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Nested aggregate modeling | survey → questions → options tables | Editing a tree of rows: create/update/delete/reorder children without orphaning anything. |
| Zod validators as a layer | `validators/surveyValidators.ts` + `middleware/validate.ts` | Validation declared once, applied at the route edge — compare with Project 1's hand-rolled service checks. |
| Public vs. builder API split | public survey rendering + response submission with access codes | Two audiences, one database: the owner edits; anonymous respondents see a *published projection*. |

# FABLE Guide — Multi-User Chat (HTTP Polling)
**Project 12: real-time behavior with no real-time transport.** This chat app has
direct and group conversations, unread counts, read receipts, typing indicators,
presence, reactions, and search — built entirely on plain HTTP requests. That
constraint is the curriculum: you learn **cursor pagination**, **polling loops**, and
**ephemeral state modeling** so precisely that when you later add WebSockets
(Project 19's territory), you'll know exactly what the socket is and isn't buying you.
Most "real-time" features in production apps are, in fact, polling. Knowing when
that's fine is a senior judgment; this project gives you the data to make it.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Cursor pagination, both directions | `GET .../messages` with `before` (history) and `GET .../messages/new` with `after` (polling) | The fix for Project 2's offset-pagination bug, in its natural habitat: an append-heavy feed. |
| The polling loop | client `App.tsx` + `services/api.ts` | Interval fetch with a moving cursor: cheap requests that usually return `[]`. |
| Presence via heartbeat | `POST /api/presence/heartbeat` + `GET /api/presence/status` | "Online" = "heartbeat within N seconds" — presence is *derived from recency*, not stored as a boolean. |
| Ephemeral state with TTL | typing indicators + stale cleanup | State that must *expire*: who cleans it up, and when? |
| Read receipts & unread counts | `POST .../read`, unread math in the service | Per-user-per-conversation watermarks — a `last_read_message_id` beats a `read` flag per message. Verify which this app chose and why. |
| Membership-scoped access | conversation members table | Every message query must check "is the requester a member?" — your first data-access rule that isn't ownership. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod validators.

# FABLE Guide — Appointment Booking System
**Project 14: time is the boss fight.** Booking is the domain where correct-looking
code is wrong in ways users notice: a slot shown twice, a 9:00 that's actually 8:00
because of DST, two customers booked into the same chair. This project is fully built —
recurring weekly availability, date overrides, slot generation, conflict detection,
booking/cancellation/reschedule policies, timezone conversion via `date-fns-tz`, and
notifications as database rows. Your job is to read it like a skeptic: the algorithms
here (interval math, slot generation) are the most interview-transferable code in the
whole curriculum.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Slot generation | `server/src/services/slotService.ts` | Recurring weekly windows + per-date overrides + existing appointments + service duration → available start times. An algorithm, not a query. |
| Interval conflict detection | slot/appointment services | The overlap predicate `(startA < endB && startB < endA)` and its off-by-one edges (back-to-back bookings must NOT conflict). |
| Timezones done deliberately | `date-fns-tz` at the slot boundary; UTC `timestamptz` in Postgres | The golden rule demonstrated: store UTC, convert at the *edge*, keep "wall-clock" concepts (weekly availability) separate from instants. |
| Policy rules | cancellation with provider policy, reschedule flow | Business rules with time math: "cancel up to N hours before start" — computed against *whose* clock? |
| Roles via headers | `x-user-id` / `x-user-role: provider` | Customer vs. provider — first two-role API. Provider routes manage availability; customer routes book. |
| Notifications as rows | `models/notificationModel.ts` | The outbox idea in embryo: record the intent to notify in the same DB (and transaction?) as the booking. Real email comes later; the *pattern* is the point. |
| Multi-model backend | 5 models, 3 services, 2 controllers | The biggest layered backend yet that's still readable in a sitting. |

# FABLE Guide — Team Project Management
**Project 16: the enterprise pattern kit — read this one deeply.** Projects 16–20 are
five apps built from the same compact scaffold (~600 lines of server+client core), each
wearing a different domain. The scaffold's point is a set of patterns that separate
"app that works" from "app a company can operate": **soft delete, archive/restore,
audit logs, request context (actor + request id), saved views, bulk operations, role
gates, and a readiness endpoint.** This tasks app is the canonical instance — study it
here, then treat 17–20 as domain-specific labs.
Companion reading: `docs/journal.md` in this folder explains *why* each pattern was
chosen, with trade-offs. Read it after the code tour — it's the voice of the code
reviewer you want to become.
---
## 1. The pattern kit (what to actually learn here)
| Pattern | Where | The idea |
|---|---|---|
| Soft delete | `model.ts` — `softDeleteRecord`, `deleted_at` filtering | Delete hides, never destroys. The model owns the default filter so nobody forgets it. |
| Archive ≠ delete | `PATCH /:id/archive` / `/restore`, `includeArchived` query | Two lifecycles: archived is *done but reportable*; deleted is *hidden from operations*. Conflating them is a classic data-model smell. |
| Request context | `middleware/requestContext.ts` → `Context = {actor, requestId, role}` | Every write can answer "who did this, in which request?" — the prerequisite for audit, debugging, and support. |
| Audit log | model writes audit rows alongside mutations; `GET /api/tasks/audit` | The operational ledger (Project 10's idea applied to *actions* instead of stock). |
| Role gate | `service.ts#requireOperator` — operator/manager/admin | Authorization as an explicit, greppable check at the top of each mutating service function. |
| Saved views | `views` endpoints, filters stored as JSON | User-defined filter bundles — the feature that turns a list into a workflow tool. |
| Bulk operations | `POST /api/tasks/bulk/status` | N records, one request, one validation pass — and one audit story. |
| Bounded lists | `normalizeListQuery`: `pageSize` capped at 100, page at 10000, sort allow-listed | Every list input clamped. Compare with Project 2's pagination — same idea, now defensive by default. |
| Readiness | readiness endpoint in `app.ts`/routes | "Can I serve traffic?" as an endpoint — what load balancers and k8s actually call. |

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line where responsibility changes owners and assumptions must be re-checked. A layer is a boundary stacked horizontally. This repo's layers, what each owns, must not own, and where the leaks are.
## The layer contract
| Layer | Owns | Must NOT own | Enforced by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Nop.Core` | entities, cache/event abstractions, infrastructure primitives | business rules, data access, HTTP | project references (Core references nothing) |
| `Nop.Data` | query execution, schema, migrations, entity events | business decisions | references Core only |
| `Nop.Services` | ALL business logic, orchestration | HTTP types, view models | references Data+Core; no ASP.NET reference |
| `Nop.Web.Framework` | MVC plumbing: filters, DI wiring, work context | domain rules | — |
| `Nop.Web` | controllers, factories, view models, views | direct DB access, business rules | convention (not enforced!) |
The strongest wall is compiler-backed: `Nop.Services` cannot mention `IActionResult` because the assembly doesn't reference MVC. The weakest wall is Web→Services: nothing but convention stops a controller from composing raw queries or embedding business rules.
## Good boundaries, with receipts
- **Controller/service split done right:** [ShoppingCartController.AddProductToCart_Details](../../src/Presentation/Nop.Web/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs#L791-L874) does HTTP things (form parsing, JSON shapes) and delegates every decision to [AddToCartAsync](../../src/Libraries/Nop.Services/Orders/ShoppingCartService.cs#L1549). You could bolt a REST API onto the same service untouched — and the [WebApi plugin](../../src/Plugins/Nop.Plugin.Misc.WebApi.Frontend) does exactly that. That's the test of a real boundary: *a second consumer arrives and nothing has to move*.
- **Entity/view-model wall:** factories ([ProductModelFactory#L1502](../../src/Presentation/Nop.Web/Factories/ProductModelFactory.cs#L1502)) are the only place entities become models; views never see entities. This protects the DB shape from becoming a UI contract — the #1 coupling disease in CRUD apps.
- **Provider boundary:** three databases + SQLite-for-tests behind [INopDataProvider](../../src/Libraries/Nop.Data/INopDataProvider.cs) — an abstraction earning its keep (contrast with interfaces that merely mirror one class).
## Boundary leaks worth studying
1. **`IQueryable` through the repository.** [EntityRepository.Table#L525](../../src/Libraries/Nop.Data/EntityRepository.cs#L525) hands services raw query composition. Pragmatic (services can build efficient que

# 03 — Architecture and Patterns
The judgment module: not *what* the code does but *what it commits the project to*.
1. [01-boundaries-and-layers.md](01-boundaries-and-layers.md) — the layer rules and where they leak
2. [02-data-model-and-persistence.md](02-data-model-and-persistence.md) — schema, transactions, safe change
3. [03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md](03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md) — every gate, mapped
4. [04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md](04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md) — events, queues, retries, idempotency
5. [05-pattern-catalog.md](05-pattern-catalog.md) — 16 pattern cards (the module centerpiece)
6. [06-architecture-critique.md](06-architecture-critique.md) — strengths, risks, and what I'd change owning this
Vocabulary being trained (all defined in context as they appear, all interview-grade): *boundary, invariant, contract, ownership, idempotency, isolation, consistency, blast radius, migration, rollback, observability*. When you can use six of these accurately about code you've read, you interview differently.

# 08 — Interview Prep
Target: **mid-level fullstack loops**, using this repo as your portfolio of concrete evidence. Contents:
| File | Round | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [01-csharp-dotnet-deep-dive.md](01-csharp-dotnet-deep-dive.md) | language/runtime | 16 |
| [02-frontend-framework-questions.md](02-frontend-framework-questions.md) | frontend | 10 |
| [03-api-and-data-modeling-questions.md](03-api-and-data-modeling-questions.md) | API + data | 12 |
| [04-system-design-from-this-repo.md](04-system-design-from-this-repo.md) | system design | full walkthrough + 5 variations |
| [05-debugging-and-code-review-rounds.md](05-debugging-and-code-review-rounds.md) | practical rounds | 7 timed sims |
| [06-behavioral-star-stories.md](06-behavioral-star-stories.md) | behavioral | 8 worksheets |
| [07-two-week-cram-plan.md](07-two-week-cram-plan.md) | all | day-by-day |
## How mid-level loops are structured
Typically: recruiter screen → technical screen (language + small coding) → onsite: practical coding (build/debug in a real-ish codebase), a design conversation (scaled to mid: one feature or one service, not planet-scale), a code-review or debugging round, and behavioral. Mid-level is *not* graded on exotic algorithms — it's graded on: writes working code, reasons about tradeoffs with examples, debugs methodically, communicates while doing all three.
## The golden rule
**Answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff, and a failure mode — never with a definition.** Compare:
- "Cache invalidation is removing stale entries when data changes." (definition — junior)
- "In nopCommerce, every repository write publishes an entity event and a consumer evicts key prefixes — invalidation is systemic, so new caches are correct by default. The tradeoff is coarseness: one product update flushes whole prefix families, so hit rate dips during bulk edits. And it's memory-cache-per-node, so it silently breaks under load balancing unless you switch to the distributed cache." (evidence + tradeoff + failure mode — this is the mid-level sound)
Every card in this module is built to produce answers of the second kind. ≥60% are anchored to real code you can name — that specificity is *rare* among candidates and reads as seniority.
## How to practice
Out loud, timed (90s per card answer), anchors open on second monitor for checking *after* answering. Rotate: never two sessions on the same file. The [cram plan](07-two-week-cram-plan.md) schedules all of it.

# nopCommerce as a Training Lab
A learning curriculum built **from this repository** for one specific learner: a junior fullstack engineer (comfortable with CRUD web dev in .NET/C# or React/Node/TS) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, when it fails, and how to recognize and articulate it in any other repo or in an interview.
## What this repo is
nopCommerce is a full-featured open source e-commerce platform: ASP.NET Core MVC (`net10.0`), Razor views, a layered architecture of three class libraries — [Nop.Core](../src/Libraries/Nop.Core) (domain entities, caching, infrastructure), [Nop.Data](../src/Libraries/Nop.Data) (repositories, FluentMigrator migrations, Linq2Db data access), [Nop.Services](../src/Libraries/Nop.Services) (all business logic) — under two presentation projects: [Nop.Web](../src/Presentation/Nop.Web) (the storefront + `/Admin` area) and [Nop.Web.Framework](../src/Presentation/Nop.Web.Framework) (MVC plumbing: filters, DI startup, work context). It supports multi-store, multi-language, multi-vendor, ACL-per-entity, a plugin system (33 plugins in [src/Plugins](../src/Plugins)), scheduled background tasks, and a queued-email outbox. It has been in production at tens of thousands of stores for ~15 years, so it is a rare chance to study *mature* production tradeoffs — including some deliberate ugliness (see the named-mutex block in [OrderProcessingService.cs](../src/Libraries/Nop.Services/Orders/OrderProcessingService.cs#L1679-L1718)) that a tutorial codebase would never show you.

# Implicit ADRs — Reverse-Engineered from the eShop Codebase
Ten Architecture Decision Records the authors never wrote down but demonstrably made. Each is grounded in code read on 2026-07-16 at commit `9b4f943` (line anchors verified at read time; see `../fabledocs/09-reference/verification-log.md`). "Status" reflects what the code and its comments say, not an official record.
An ADR reconstructed from code is an inference: the *Decision* is fact (the code exists), the *Context* and *Alternatives Considered* are informed reconstruction. Where the authors left comments confirming intent, those are quoted.
---
## ADR-001: One repository, many deployables, with an Aspire AppHost as the composition root
**Context.** The system comprises 7+ runnable services (WebApp, Catalog, Basket, Ordering, Identity, Webhooks, two workers), three infrastructure dependencies (Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ), and cross-cutting concerns (telemetry, discovery, health). Developers need to run all of it locally with one command; the topology (who talks to whom, who waits for whom) must live somewhere authoritative.
**Decision.** Keep everything in a single solution (`eShop.slnx`, 19 projects) that deploys as independent services, and encode the entire runtime topology in a .NET Aspire AppHost project: `src/eShop.AppHost/Program.cs` declares every container, database, service, dependency edge (`WithReference`), startup ordering (`WaitFor` — e.g., OrderProcessor waits for Ordering.API "because that contains the EF migrations", L46-L49), and even the cyclic identity-callback wiring that references can't express (L96-L101). Cross-cutting defaults are centralized in `src/eShop.ServiceDefaults` (OTel, health endpoints, service discovery, default JWT auth), consumed by every service via `AddServiceDefaults()`.
**Alternatives considered.** (a) Polyrepo per service — maximal team autonomy, but for a system meant to be cloned and run whole, coordination costs dominate. (b) docker-compose + per-service config files — the pre-Aspire norm; topology scattered across YAML and connection strings duplicated per service. (c) A true monolith — abandons the microservices teaching goal.
**Consequences.**
- (+) `dotnet run --project src/eShop.AppHost` boots the world; the AppHost file doubles as an always-accur

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line where you can change one side without asking the other side's permission — as long as you honor the **contract** at the line. Layers are boundaries stacked vertically inside one service.
## The two boundary kinds in eShop
**Service boundaries (horizontal):** WebApp | Catalog | Basket | Ordering | Identity | Webhooks | workers. Contracts: REST routes, `basket.proto`, integration event classes, OIDC scopes. Enforced by: separate processes, separate databases.
**Layer boundaries (vertical, strongest in Ordering):**
| Layer | Project | Owns | Must not own | Evidence it's enforced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| API | `Ordering.API/Apis` | HTTP shapes, headers, status codes | business rules | `OrdersApi.cs` only builds commands and reads results |
| Application | `Ordering.API/Application` | orchestration, validation, transactions, event translation | domain invariants | handlers call aggregate methods, never set status fields |
| Domain | `Ordering.Domain` | invariants, state machine, domain events | HTTP/EF/RabbitMQ | its `.csproj` references neither EF nor ASP.NET (check it) |
| Infrastructure | `Ordering.Infrastructure` | EF mappings, repositories, idempotency store | deciding anything | `OrderingContext` + `EntityConfigurations/` |
## Boundaries done well (steal these)
1. **Domain purity.** `Ordering.Domain` compiles without EF Core. Persistence adapts to the domain via `EntityConfigurations/` (private field mapping for `_orderItems`), not vice versa. This is the Dependency Inversion everyone claims and few ship.
2. **Prices never trusted from the client.** Basket stores only (ProductId, Quantity) (`BasketService.cs:L93-L110`); the WebApp re-fetches prices from Catalog (`BasketState.cs:L117-L149`); the Order snapshots price at creation (`OrderItem`). Three boundaries each doing their part of one security property.
3. **Async-first coupling.** Ordering never calls Catalog. Stock validation happens via events (Flow 4). If Catalog is down, orders queue up in AwaitingValidation instead of checkout throwing 500s.
4. **ServiceDefaults as a shared kernel with discipline** — only cross-cutting infra (OTel, health, auth defaults), no business types (`src/eShop.ServiceDefaults/`).
## Boundary leaks (real, findable, discussable)
1. **OrderProcessor reads Ordering's database with raw SQL** — `GracePeriodManagerService.cs:L69-L74` queries `ordering.orders` directly, including string-matching the status `'Submitted'`. If Ordering renames a column or changes the enum-to-string conversion, OrderProcessor breaks *at ru

# 08 — Interview Prep (first-class module)
Target: **mid-level fullstack interviews** for a .NET/C# candidate (with React/Node crossover notes). Over 60% of the question cards here anchor to real code in this repo, so you practice answering with *evidence* instead of recited definitions.
## How mid-level loops are typically structured
1. **Screen** (30–45 min): language/runtime fundamentals, one small coding exercise.
2. **Technical deep-dive** (60 min): "walk me through a system you know well." *This repo is that system now.*
3. **Practical coding** (60 min): build/extend/debug something realistic.
4. **System design** (45–60 min): mid-level bar = a coherent design with named tradeoffs, not planet-scale.
5. **Behavioral** (45 min): STAR stories; for mid-level they probe ownership and collaboration.
## The golden rule
Every answer = **concept + concrete example + tradeoff + failure mode**. "The outbox pattern keeps DB writes and events consistent — in eShop, a price change writes the event to a log table in the same transaction (`CatalogApi.cs:L350-L356`), publishes after commit, and the gap is that a crash between commit and publish needs a sweeper, which that repo lacks." That is a mid-level answer. A definition alone is a junior answer.

samples.opening:
# fabledocs — eShop as a Training Lab
A codebase-specific curriculum that turns this repository into a training lab for a **junior fullstack engineer (.NET/C#, plus React/Node/TS experience)** who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This repo** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file:line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, what alternatives look like, how it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is (the 8-sentence version)
eShop is Microsoft's reference e-commerce application ("AdventureWorks"), built on .NET 9 and orchestrated with **.NET Aspire** (`src/eShop.AppHost/Program.cs`). It is a services-based system: a Blazor Server storefront (`src/WebApp`), a REST **Catalog.API** (PostgreSQL + pgvector for AI search), a gRPC **Basket.API** (Redis), and an **Ordering.API** built with DDD + CQRS (MediatR commands, an `Order` aggregate, EF Core with a Postgres database). Services never call each other's databases; they communicate asynchronously through **RabbitMQ integration events** (`src/EventBusRabbitMQ`), with a transactional **outbox** (`src/IntegrationEventLogEF`) to keep database writes and event publishing consistent. Two headless workers — **OrderProcessor** (grace-period polling) and **PaymentProcessor** (simulated payment) — drive the order state machine forward. Authentication is centralized in **Identity.API** (Duende IdentityServer, OpenID Connect); the WebApp signs users in with cookies+OIDC and forwards JWTs to the backend APIs. Tests exist at three levels: MSTest/xUnit unit tests, Aspire-hosted functional tests, and Playwright e2e specs in `e2e/`. It is deliberately a *teaching* codebase: some corners are simplified (simulated payments, no dead-letter queue, permissive auth in places) — those simplifications are themselves lesson material here.
## The learning tracks
| Track | Folder | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cartography | `01-codebase-cartography/` | System map, reading order, glossary, 6 end-to-end flow traces |
| Stack mastery | `02-stack-and-language-mastery/` | C#/.NET async model, ASP.NET Core + Blazor mental models, types & contracts, Aspire tooling |
| Architecture | `03-architecture-and-patterns/` | Layers, persistence, auth, async reliability, 14 pattern cards, a full critique |

---
This guide covers naming and formatting conventions. For visual design choices — icons, colours, buttons, and UX copy — see [design-choices.md](./design-choices.md).
---
### Naming Conventions
**Files**:
- Web components: `my-component.element.ts`
- Tests: `my-component.test.ts`
- Stories: `my-component.stories.ts`
- Controllers: `my-component.controller.ts`
- Contexts: `my-component.context.ts`
- Modals: `my-component.modal.ts`
- Workspaces: `my-component.workspace.ts`
- Repositories: `my-component.repository.ts`
- Index files: `index.ts` (barrel exports)
**Classes & Types**:
- Classes: `PascalCase` with `Umb` prefix: `UmbMyComponent`
- Interfaces: `PascalCase` with `Umb` prefix: `UmbMyInterface`
- Types: `PascalCase` with `Umb`, `Ufm`, `Manifest`, `Meta`, or `Example` prefix
- Exported types MUST have approved prefix
- Example types for docs: `ExampleMyType`
**Variables & Functions**:
- Public members: `camelCase` without underscore: `myVariable`, `myMethod`
- Private members: `camelCase` with leading underscore: `_myPrivateVariable`
- #private members: `camelCase` without underscore: `#myPrivateField`
- Protected members: `camelCase` with optional underscore: `myProtected` or `_myProtected`
- Constants (exported): `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` with `UMB_` prefix: `UMB_MY_CONSTANT`

# Contributing to the Umbraco Templates
If you're making changes to any of the templates in this folder, please note that installing them directly from this location to test will not work. You need to 'pack' the source into a nuget package (.nupkg) in a local folder, and install from there.
For example, using a folder location of `c:\nuget.local`:
```
# Pack the templates to a local folder
dotnet pack Umbraco.Templates.csproj -c Release --no-build -o "c:\nuget.local"
# Add this folder as a local nuget source
dotnet nuget add source "c:\nuget.local" --name "local nuget"
# Make sure you don't have the global templates installed
dotnet new uninstall Umbraco.Templates
# Install your version of the templates, having checked/updated the name of the generated .nupkg file
dotnet new install "c:\nuget.local\Umbraco.Templates.XXXX.nupkg"
```
You can now test your template changes using the appropriate `dotnet new` command.

# Architecture
---
### Technology Stack
> Exact versions are in `package.json` (root and workspace packages). Only major versions that affect API usage are listed here.
- **Runtime**: Node.js >=22, npm >=10 (see `engines` in `package.json`)
- **Language**: TypeScript 5.x (strict mode, ESM — all imports must use `.js` extensions)
- **Framework**: **Lit 3** — Web Components with reactive templates, decorators, and `html`/`css` tagged template literals
- **UI Library**: **@umbraco-ui/uui 2.x** — 80+ Web Components (`<uui-button>`, `<uui-input>`, `<uui-box>`, etc.). Always prefer UUI components over native HTML or custom implementations.
- **Rich Text**: **TipTap 3** — ProseMirror-based editor (see `src/packages/tiptap/`)
- **Build**: Vite 7 (config in `vite.config.ts`)
- **State**: RxJS 7 wrapped by UmbState classes — see [Core Primitives](./core-primitives.md)
- **Context/DI**: DOM-event-based Context API — see [Core Primitives](./core-primitives.md)
- **Testing**: @web/test-runner + Playwright, @open-wc/testing — see [Testing](./testing.md)
- **Mocking**: MSW 2 — see [Testing](./testing.md)
- **Code Quality**: ESLint 9 (flat config), Prettier
- **Key Libraries**: Luxon 3, Monaco Editor (code editing), DOMPurify 3 (sanitization — see [Security](./security.md)), Marked (Markdown→HTML), SignalR (real-time server events)
### Application Type
SPA packaged as npm library (`@umbraco-cms/backoffice`) for typings and built as a bundle copied to `src/Umbraco.Cms.StaticAssets/wwwroot/umbraco/backoffice`. Provides extensible Web Components, API libraries, TypeScript types, and a manifest-based extension system.
### Architecture Pattern
**Modular Package Architecture**:
```
src/
├── apps/              # Entry points (app, backoffice, installer, preview, upgrader)
├── libs/              # Core API libraries (context-api, controller-api, element-api, extension-api, observable-api, localization-api, etc.)
├── packages/          # Feature packages (50+)
│   ├── core/         # UI framework (auth, http, router, modals, notifications, etc.)
│   ├── documents/    # Document types & editing
│   ├── media/        # Media management
│   └── ...           # 30+ more domain packages
├── external/          # Dependency wrappers (lit, rxjs, luxon, monaco-editor, etc.)
├── mocks/             # MSW mock handlers & test data
└── assets/            # Static assets (fonts, images, localization)

# Jellyfin as a Training Lab: Codebase-to-Curriculum
A complete learning suite that turns the Jellyfin server codebase into a structured path from **junior CRUD developer** to **mid-level fullstack engineer with senior judgment** — and into a portfolio of concrete, evidence-backed interview answers.
## Who this is for
A junior fullstack engineer (C#/.NET, React/Node/TS, or similar CRUD web background) who wants to:
1. Learn how a large, real production codebase is shaped and why.
2. Build transferable judgment — the ability to recognize the same patterns in *any* repo.
3. Pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles using this repo as a portfolio of talking points.
Every module teaches two things at once: **where things live in Jellyfin** and **why the pattern exists anywhere**. Interview readiness is a first-class goal — most pages end with an "Interview angle."
## What Jellyfin is (the repo's identity in 7 sentences)
Jellyfin is a free, self-hosted media server — the open-source alternative to Plex/Emby — and this repository is its **backend server** only (the web client lives in the separate [jellyfin-web](https://github.com/jellyfin/jellyfin-web) repo). It is a .NET 10 / ASP.NET Core application ([README.md](../README.md#L79)) exposing a large REST API (59 controllers in [Jellyfin.Api/Controllers](../Jellyfin.Api/Controllers)), WebSocket real-time messaging, and HLS video streaming backed by ffmpeg transcoding. Media metadata is stored in SQLite through EF Core ([src/Jellyfin.Database](../src/Jellyfin.Database)), with a hybrid model: relational columns for queryable fields plus a serialized JSON blob per item. It descends from Emby 3.5.2, so it carries visible **legacy seams** — project names like `Emby.Server.Implementations`, a custom token auth scheme bridged into ASP.NET Core, and two parallel migration systems. Background work (library scans, transcodes, cleanup) runs through a custom scheduled-task engine with triggers and progress reporting. It is multi-user with per-user permissions, parental controls, and network-based access rules — a real authorization surface, not a toy one. That mix of modern ASP.NET Core idioms and battle-scarred legacy makes it an unusually honest teaching codebase: you see both what good looks like and what technical debt looks like when it's managed responsibly.

2. Read the sprint playbook, noting scope, teaching focus, and exclusions.
3. Read commits oldest-to-newest. The history is designed as schema → pure domain
core/tests → repository/API → UI → ADR/concept.
4. Read inline PR comments at the exact lines they discuss. Compare Author,
Reviewer, and Stakeholder priorities.
5. Read the design-debate thread and find the documented conclusion.
6. Run the gate, then attempt the PR exercises without reading later sprints.
7. After Sprint 15, revisit earlier reviews using the revealed flaw ledger and ask
which assumptions reviewers missed.
Do not begin with the final source tree. The teaching value is in how decisions and
invariants evolve across the review history.

# Perch Product and Course Specification
## Product thesis and personas
Perch is a CRUD-rich ATS. Recruiters own jobs, candidate flow, communication, and
offers. Hiring managers configure pipelines and make decisions. Interviewers see
only assigned candidates and submit scorecards. Administrators manage organization
access. Candidates browse the public careers surface and apply without a session.
The authenticated SPA favors dense list/detail workflows, keyboard-accessible forms,
optimistic interaction, stable pagination, and explicit authorization. The public
careers page exposes only open jobs and a validated application boundary.
## Data model
- `Organization` owns users, jobs, candidates, tags, and outbound events.
- `User`, `Membership`, and `Session` model identity plus admin, hiring-manager,
recruiter, and interviewer permissions.
- `Job` stores title, department, location, description, and draft/open/closed state.
- `PipelineStage` belongs to a job and uses a sortable fractional position.
- `Candidate` stores profile, resume text, source, and many-to-many tags.
- `Application` joins candidate to job, points at the current stage, and owns an
append-only `StageHistory` and general `Activity` stream.
- `Interview` stores schedule, stage, and panel assignments; `Scorecard` stores one
structured rating/feedback submission per interviewer.
- `Comment`, `Mention`, and `Notification` connect collaboration to candidate access.
- `Offer`, `OfferApproval`, and `OfferEvent` preserve draft/sent/accepted/declined
state and ordered approval decisions.
- `OutboundMessage` records fake email intent; Perch never sends real email.
All tenant-owned records carry `organizationId`. Mutable records carry timestamps
and version fields where optimistic concurrency matters. History/event records are
append-only. Production repositories target Prisma/Postgres; domain services depend
on interfaces and CI uses in-memory fakes.

# Perch
Perch is a Greenhouse/Lever-style applicant tracking system and a teaching repository for junior engineers. The working product and the engineering curriculum were built through fifteen sequential, reviewed pull requests.
It covers jobs, candidates, applications, configurable pipelines, interviews, scorecards, comments, mentions, notifications, search, stable pagination, bulk actions, CSV, offers, reporting, public careers, permissions, security hardening, accessibility, and operational readiness. Outbound mail, calendars, e-signature, object storage, and cloud deployment are intentionally represented as fake intent boundaries.
## Architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
Public[Public careers] --> API[Fastify API]
Team[React recruiter UI] --> API
API --> Core[Shared functional domain core]
API --> Policy[Capability + object policy]
API --> Ports[Repository ports]
Ports --> Memory[Deterministic in-memory adapters]
Ports -. production model .-> Postgres[(Prisma / Postgres)]
API --> Intent[Fake outbound intent log]
```
- `apps/web`: Vite, React, TanStack Query, accessible workflow states.
- `apps/api`: Fastify route boundaries, Zod validation, services, policy orchestration.
- `packages/shared`: pure domain transitions, parsers, reports, and tests.
- `packages/db`: repository contracts, in-memory adapters, Prisma schema, demo seed.
- `docs`: 15 sprint playbooks, ADRs, concepts, audits, runbooks, incident exercise, and retrospective.
Organization scope is established from the authenticated route context. Interviewer reads additionally follow stored panel → application → candidate relationships. Durable transitions use explicit state machines or version comparison; public retries reserve idempotency keys before writes.
## Run it
Requires Node 20+ and pnpm 9.12.3.
```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm seed
pnpm gate
pnpm dev

headings: ## Why the cook log isn't a "review"
samples.opening:
# 🧪 Recipe Lab
A local-first cooking journal built around a three-level hierarchy:
**Dish → Recipe → Cook Log**
- A **Dish** is what you want to make — *Pizza*, *Ramen*, *Chocolate chip cookies*. It's a container.
- A **Recipe** is one specific approach to that dish — *Neapolitan 65% hydration*, *Cast-iron pan pizza*. A dish has many recipes. Each has ingredients, steps, a source, and a verdict (keeper / needs work / abandoned / untested).
- A **Cook Log** is a single time you actually made that recipe. A recipe has many cook logs. This is the point of the app: the same recipe goes differently on different nights, and the log captures *why*.
This is a lab notebook, not Pinterest — dense, readable, keyboard-friendly, and fast to log a cook with messy hands.
## Why the cook log isn't a "review"
The tempting shortcut is to collapse cook logs into star ratings on the recipe. Recipe Lab deliberately doesn't. Each cook log keeps four things distinct:
- **What I changed** — the deltas from the base recipe (*"bread flour instead of 00 · fermented 72h"*). This is the headline of every entry.
- **Taste notes** and **process notes** — kept in separate fields, because bland dough and torn dough are unrelated problems.
- **Structured ratings** — taste, texture, effort, and would-make-again, each rated on its own axis.
- **Next time I should…** — one concrete change to try.
The result is the difference between *"this recipe is 4 stars"* and *"this recipe is 4 stars **when you cold-ferment it**."* The recipe page surfaces the single best cook and what made it best.
## Stack
- **Frontend** — React 18 + Vite + TypeScript, React Router. No component library; a small hand-rolled design system with light/dark themes.
- **Backend** — Express + Node's built-in `node:sqlite` (no native compilation). Full-text search via SQLite **FTS5**.
- **Storage** — a single SQLite file plus an uploaded-photos folder, both under `data/` (git-ignored). Fully local; no accounts, no network.
## Features
- Three-level navigation: home (dishes) → dish (recipes side by side with average ratings + verdicts) → recipe (full text + reverse-chronological cook-log feed).
- **Full-text search** across dishes, recipes, ingredients, steps, and every cook-log note. `⌘K` / `Ctrl-K` from anywhere; arrow keys + Ent

# net/ — The Proposed C# / .NET Rewrite
This folder is a **planning package, not code**. It proposes rewriting
Sarap & Ngon on the .NET platform, and — like `docs/` — it's written to
upskill a junior engineer while doing it. Nothing here has been
implemented; that's deliberate. Reading, critiquing, and *then* executing a
plan is a different (and rarer) skill than jumping straight to code.
## Why rewrite at all?
Be suspicious of rewrites. "Let's rewrite it" is the most expensive
sentence in software, and the current React app *works*. There are exactly
two honest justifications here, and you should hold the plan accountable to
both:
1. **Learning.** The React app taught frontend fundamentals. A .NET rewrite
teaches the other half of the profession: servers, databases, dependency
injection, migrations, integration testing, deployment of stateful
systems. Same familiar product, entirely new half of the stack — the
product knowledge you already have becomes free working memory for the
new material.
2. **The debts in `docs/IMPROVE.md` that the current architecture can't pay
down.** A static SPA fundamentally cannot fix SEO-invisible recipe pages
(#6), and it makes real persistence, migrations (#9), and stable
ingredient identity (#1) awkward. A server-rendered app with a real
database fixes those *by construction* — the rewrite is the payment
plan.
If neither of those applied — if this were a production system with users
and no learning goal — the correct proposal would be "don't rewrite;
incrementally fix IMPROVE.md items in place." Write that sentence on your
hand. Knowing when *not* to rewrite is the senior half of this lesson.
