# 08 — Interview Prep (first-class module)
Target: **mid-level fullstack interviews** for a .NET/C# candidate (with React/Node crossover notes). Over 60% of the question cards here anchor to real code in this repo, so you practice answering with *evidence* instead of recited definitions.
## How mid-level loops are typically structured
1. **Screen** (30–45 min): language/runtime fundamentals, one small coding exercise.
2. **Technical deep-dive** (60 min): "walk me through a system you know well." *This repo is that system now.*
3. **Practical coding** (60 min): build/extend/debug something realistic.
4. **System design** (45–60 min): mid-level bar = a coherent design with named tradeoffs, not planet-scale.
5. **Behavioral** (45 min): STAR stories; for mid-level they probe ownership and collaboration.
## The golden rule
Every answer = **concept + concrete example + tradeoff + failure mode**. "The outbox pattern keeps DB writes and events consistent — in eShop, a price change writes the event to a log table in the same transaction (`CatalogApi.cs:L350-L356`), publishes after commit, and the gap is that a crash between commit and publish needs a sweeper, which that repo lacks." That is a mid-level answer. A definition alone is a junior answer.

samples.opening:
# fabledocs — eShop as a Training Lab
A codebase-specific curriculum that turns this repository into a training lab for a **junior fullstack engineer (.NET/C#, plus React/Node/TS experience)** who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This repo** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file:line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, what alternatives look like, how it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is (the 8-sentence version)
eShop is Microsoft's reference e-commerce application ("AdventureWorks"), built on .NET 9 and orchestrated with **.NET Aspire** (`src/eShop.AppHost/Program.cs`). It is a services-based system: a Blazor Server storefront (`src/WebApp`), a REST **Catalog.API** (PostgreSQL + pgvector for AI search), a gRPC **Basket.API** (Redis), and an **Ordering.API** built with DDD + CQRS (MediatR commands, an `Order` aggregate, EF Core with a Postgres database). Services never call each other's databases; they communicate asynchronously through **RabbitMQ integration events** (`src/EventBusRabbitMQ`), with a transactional **outbox** (`src/IntegrationEventLogEF`) to keep database writes and event publishing consistent. Two headless workers — **OrderProcessor** (grace-period polling) and **PaymentProcessor** (simulated payment) — drive the order state machine forward. Authentication is centralized in **Identity.API** (Duende IdentityServer, OpenID Connect); the WebApp signs users in with cookies+OIDC and forwards JWTs to the backend APIs. Tests exist at three levels: MSTest/xUnit unit tests, Aspire-hosted functional tests, and Playwright e2e specs in `e2e/`. It is deliberately a *teaching* codebase: some corners are simplified (simulated payments, no dead-letter queue, permissive auth in places) — those simplifications are themselves lesson material here.
## The learning tracks
| Track | Folder | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cartography | `01-codebase-cartography/` | System map, reading order, glossary, 6 end-to-end flow traces |
| Stack mastery | `02-stack-and-language-mastery/` | C#/.NET async model, ASP.NET Core + Blazor mental models, types & contracts, Aspire tooling |
| Architecture | `03-architecture-and-patterns/` | Layers, persistence, auth, async reliability, 14 pattern cards, a full critique |
| Reading gym | `04-code-reading-gym/` | Annotation drills, trace tables, fake-code contrasts, review katas |
| Quality | `05-quality-engineering/` | Tes

# Style Guide

---
This guide covers naming and formatting conventions. For visual design choices — icons, colours, buttons, and UX copy — see [design-choices.md](./design-choices.md).
---
### Naming Conventions
**Files**:
- Web components: `my-component.element.ts`
- Tests: `my-component.test.ts`
- Stories: `my-component.stories.ts`
- Controllers: `my-component.controller.ts`
- Contexts: `my-component.context.ts`
- Modals: `my-component.modal.ts`
- Workspaces: `my-component.workspace.ts`
- Repositories: `my-component.repository.ts`
- Index files: `index.ts` (barrel exports)
**Classes & Types**:
- Classes: `PascalCase` with `Umb` prefix: `UmbMyComponent`
- Interfaces: `PascalCase` with `Umb` prefix: `UmbMyInterface`
- Types: `PascalCase` with `Umb`, `Ufm`, `Manifest`, `Meta`, or `Example` prefix
- Exported types MUST have approved prefix
- Example types for docs: `ExampleMyType`
**Variables & Functions**:
- Public members: `camelCase` without underscore: `myVariable`, `myMethod`
- Private members: `camelCase` with leading underscore: `_myPrivateVariable`
- #private members: `camelCase` without underscore: `#myPrivateField`
- Protected members: `camelCase` with optional underscore: `myProtected` or `_myProtected`
- Constants (exported): `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` with `UMB_` prefix: `UMB_MY_CONSTANT`

samples.opening:
# Contributing to the Umbraco Templates
If you're making changes to any of the templates in this folder, please note that installing them directly from this location to test will not work. You need to 'pack' the source into a nuget package (.nupkg) in a local folder, and install from there.
For example, using a folder location of `c:\nuget.local`:
```
# Pack the templates to a local folder
dotnet pack Umbraco.Templates.csproj -c Release --no-build -o "c:\nuget.local"
# Add this folder as a local nuget source
dotnet nuget add source "c:\nuget.local" --name "local nuget"
# Make sure you don't have the global templates installed
dotnet new uninstall Umbraco.Templates
# Install your version of the templates, having checked/updated the name of the generated .nupkg file
dotnet new install "c:\nuget.local\Umbraco.Templates.XXXX.nupkg"
```
You can now test your template changes using the appropriate `dotnet new` command.

# Architecture
---
### Technology Stack
> Exact versions are in `package.json` (root and workspace packages). Only major versions that affect API usage are listed here.
- **Runtime**: Node.js >=22, npm >=10 (see `engines` in `package.json`)
- **Language**: TypeScript 5.x (strict mode, ESM — all imports must use `.js` extensions)
- **Framework**: **Lit 3** — Web Components with reactive templates, decorators, and `html`/`css` tagged template literals
- **UI Library**: **@umbraco-ui/uui 2.x** — 80+ Web Components (`<uui-button>`, `<uui-input>`, `<uui-box>`, etc.). Always prefer UUI components over native HTML or custom implementations.
- **Rich Text**: **TipTap 3** — ProseMirror-based editor (see `src/packages/tiptap/`)
- **Build**: Vite 7 (config in `vite.config.ts`)
- **State**: RxJS 7 wrapped by UmbState classes — see [Core Primitives](./core-primitives.md)
- **Context/DI**: DOM-event-based Context API — see [Core Primitives](./core-primitives.md)
- **Testing**: @web/test-runner + Playwright, @open-wc/testing — see [Testing](./testing.md)
- **Mocking**: MSW 2 — see [Testing](./testing.md)
- **Code Quality**: ESLint 9 (flat config), Prettier
- **Key Libraries**: Luxon 3, Monaco Editor (code editing), DOMPurify 3 (sanitization — see [Security](./security.md)), Marked (Markdown→HTML), SignalR (real-time server events)
### Application Type
SPA packaged as npm library (`@umbraco-cms/backoffice`) for typings and built as a bundle copied to `src/Umbraco.Cms.StaticAssets/wwwroot/umbraco/backoffice`. Provides extensible Web Components, API libraries, TypeScript types, and a manifest-based extension system.
### Architecture Pattern
**Modular Package Architecture**:
```
src/
├── apps/              # Entry points (app, backoffice, installer, preview, upgrader)
├── libs/              # Core API libraries (context-api, controller-api, element-api, extension-api, observable-api, localization-api, etc.)
├── packages/          # Feature packages (50+)
│   ├── core/         # UI framework (auth, http, router, modals, notifications, etc.)
│   ├── documents/    # Document types & editing
│   ├── media/        # Media management
│   └── ...           # 30+ more domain packages
├── external/          # Dependency wrappers (lit, rxjs, luxon, monaco-editor, etc.)
├── mocks/             # MSW mock handlers & test data

samples.opening:
# Jellyfin as a Training Lab: Codebase-to-Curriculum
A complete learning suite that turns the Jellyfin server codebase into a structured path from **junior CRUD developer** to **mid-level fullstack engineer with senior judgment** — and into a portfolio of concrete, evidence-backed interview answers.
## Who this is for
A junior fullstack engineer (C#/.NET, React/Node/TS, or similar CRUD web background) who wants to:
1. Learn how a large, real production codebase is shaped and why.
2. Build transferable judgment — the ability to recognize the same patterns in *any* repo.
3. Pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles using this repo as a portfolio of talking points.
Every module teaches two things at once: **where things live in Jellyfin** and **why the pattern exists anywhere**. Interview readiness is a first-class goal — most pages end with an "Interview angle."
## What Jellyfin is (the repo's identity in 7 sentences)
Jellyfin is a free, self-hosted media server — the open-source alternative to Plex/Emby — and this repository is its **backend server** only (the web client lives in the separate [jellyfin-web](https://github.com/jellyfin/jellyfin-web) repo). It is a .NET 10 / ASP.NET Core application ([README.md](../README.md#L79)) exposing a large REST API (59 controllers in [Jellyfin.Api/Controllers](../Jellyfin.Api/Controllers)), WebSocket real-time messaging, and HLS video streaming backed by ffmpeg transcoding. Media metadata is stored in SQLite through EF Core ([src/Jellyfin.Database](../src/Jellyfin.Database)), with a hybrid model: relational columns for queryable fields plus a serialized JSON blob per item. It descends from Emby 3.5.2, so it carries visible **legacy seams** — project names like `Emby.Server.Implementations`, a custom token auth scheme bridged into ASP.NET Core, and two parallel migration systems. Background work (library scans, transcodes, cleanup) runs through a custom scheduled-task engine with triggers and progress reporting. It is multi-user with per-user permissions, parental controls, and network-based access rules — a real authorization surface, not a toy one. That mix of modern ASP.NET Core idioms and battle-scarred legacy makes it an unusually honest teaching codebase: you see both what good looks like and what technical debt looks like when it's managed responsibly.

This curriculum turns NetShopifyLite into a training lab for a junior engineer growing toward mid-level and senior judgment. The repo is a synthetic ecommerce scaffold, not an organically grown OSS project: Git has no commits, the entire project is untracked, there is no CONTRIBUTING/CHANGELOG issue history, and the style is very uniform. samples.opening:
# Junior SaaS Clone Learning Workspace
This workspace contains five separate learning codebases generated from the pasted SaaS clone specs.
Each project is intentionally scaffolded as a production-shaped TypeScript/React/Node app, but it is not wired for installation or deployment. The goal is reading, tracing, and modifying the architecture.
## Projects
- `planr` - Linear-style issue tracker
- `bookr` - Cal.com-style scheduling app
- `payr` - Stripe-dashboard-style analytics and payments admin
- `blockr` - Notion-style page and block editor
- `helpkit` - Intercom-style support inbox and chat widget
## How To Study
Start with each project's `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md`, then read:
1. `src/domain/types.ts` for the nouns.
2. `src/domain/*` for the important business rules.
3. `src/server/routes.ts` for API boundaries.
4. `src/components/*` for how UI state connects to domain behavior.
## Enterprise Readiness Pass
Each project now includes production-shaped supporting modules and focused tests:
- Policy and tenant guards.
- Audit or lifecycle records.
- Idempotency, locking, retry, or rate-limit examples where relevant.
- Search, cursor pagination, webhook signing, SLA, and widget-auth examples.
- `vitest` test scripts and domain-level tests for the riskiest logic.
These projects still do not need to run or install dependencies to be useful. Treat the tests as executable documentation for how the important business rules should behave.

# Payr
Payr is a Stripe-dashboard-inspired admin product for mock payments. It focuses on data-dense UI, RBAC, audit logs, API keys, idempotency, cursor pagination, and webhook delivery logs.
## Folder Map
- `src/domain/types.ts` - organizations, members, payments, keys, events, webhooks.
- `src/domain/rbac.ts` - role permissions used by API and UI.
- `src/domain/idempotency.ts` - 24-hour response replay model.
- `src/domain/analytics.ts` - metrics and time-series aggregation.
- `src/server/routes.ts` - payment, refund, key, webhook, and dashboard route sketches.
- `src/components/DashboardHome.tsx` - dense metrics UI.
- `src/data/seedGenerator.ts` - realistic payment generator.
- `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md` - onboarding and architecture notes.

# Bookr
Bookr is a Cal.com-inspired scheduling app focused on availability, timezone correctness, booking race conditions, calendar integrations, and notification workflows.
## Folder Map
- `src/domain/types.ts` - users, event types, availability, bookings, integrations, webhooks.
- `src/domain/availabilityEngine.ts` - converts host rules into safe invitee-facing slots.
- `src/domain/bookingService.ts` - transaction-shaped booking flow with slot revalidation.
- `src/domain/calendarGateway.ts` - provider boundary for external busy times and event creation.
- `src/server/routes.ts` - public booking and host dashboard API sketches.
- `src/components/BookingFlow.tsx` - public booking page state machine.
- `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md` - senior engineer onboarding notes.

# Blockr
Blockr is a simplified Notion-style page and block editor focused on recursive data, rich text blocks, database views, sharing, and inherited permissions.
## Folder Map
- `src/domain/types.ts` - workspaces, pages, blocks, databases, permissions.
- `src/domain/blockTree.ts` - block/page tree construction and fractional ordering.
- `src/domain/permissions.ts` - inherited page permission checks.
- `src/domain/databaseView.ts` - table and board view helpers.
- `src/server/routes.ts` - page, block, search, database, and permissions route sketches.
- `src/components` - editor and sidebar tree components.
- `docs/senior-engineer-journal.md` - onboarding journal.

# Flow: Database views (filter + board grouping)
Entry point:        None — `filterEntries` and `groupEntriesForBoard` (`src/domain/databaseView.ts:9-28`) have no route; consumed only by tests.
Auth/middleware:    None. Note `Database` has no `workspaceId` (`src/domain/types.ts:61-65`) — scoping would have to go entry → database → page → workspace.
Validation:         `groupEntriesForBoard` validates the property exists and is a select (`databaseView.ts:21-22`) — one of the few explicit domain validations in this repo. `filterEntries` validates nothing: filters naming unknown properties compare `undefined` and silently match/not-match.
Business logic:     1. Filter: every filter must pass (implicit AND, `databaseView.ts:11`); `is`/`is_not` use `===`/`!==` on `unknown`, `contains` stringifies both sides and lowercases (`databaseView.ts:13-15`).
2. Board grouping: one group per select option, entries matched by strict equality (`databaseView.ts:24-27`).
Invariant that should hold: every entry appears in exactly one group. **Doesn't**: an entry whose value is missing or not in `options` appears in *no* group — silently invisible on the board (Notion renders a "No Status" column for exactly this reason).
DB queries:         Entries would live as rows with a jsonb `property_values`; the filter is
`SELECT * FROM database_entries WHERE database_id = $1 AND property_values->>'Status' = 'Doing';`
and grouping is a client-side partition (or `GROUP BY property_values->>'Status'`).
Side effects:       None; pure.
Response:           Filtered entries / `{ option, entries }[]`.
Failure modes:      - `is` with `value: 5` against a stored `"5"` → false: `===` on `unknown` makes type mismatches silent filter misses. The property *type* metadata (`DatabaseProperty.type`, `types.ts:69`) exists and is never consulted during filtering — a number property could be compared numerically, dates chronologically; instead everything is identity-or-substring.
- Renaming a property in `Database.properties` orphans every value: `propertyValues` is keyed by property **name** (`types.ts:77`), not a stable id. This is the flow's data-modeling lesson — see the audit in `docs/reference.md`.
Why it's built this way: Filter-as-data (`DatabaseFilter`) mirrors planr's filter engine at smaller scale.

# Flow: Cancel booking
Entry point:        None — `cancelBooking` (`src/domain/bookingService.ts:60-62`) has no callers. There is no cancel route in `src/server/routes.ts`.
Auth/middleware:    n/a (would need one: only the host or the invitee should cancel — no identity model exists to express that).
Validation:         None. `reason` is any string; a booking already `cancelled` can be "cancelled" again with a new reason (idempotent-ish by accident, but the old reason is overwritten).
Business logic:     Returns `{ ...booking, status: "cancelled", cancellationReason: reason }` — a pure copy. Nothing writes it back to `BookingStore`, so even a hypothetical caller must remember to persist.
DB queries:         Would be: `UPDATE bookings SET status = 'cancelled', cancellation_reason = $1 WHERE id = $2;`
Side effects:       None — and three are missing by the repo's own design: no `webhook.delivery` job for `booking.cancelled` (the event type exists at `src/domain/types.ts:82` and `notificationJobs.ts:6`), no cancellation email, no calendar event deletion via `CalendarGateway`.
Response:           The new `Booking` object.
Failure modes:      No validation of current status: a `rescheduled` or already-`cancelled` booking transitions silently. A status state machine (which transitions are legal) is implied by `BookingStatus` (`types.ts:50`) and enforced nowhere.
Why it's built this way: Pure function + caller persists is a fine pattern (compare planr's syncEngine). The problem is the missing caller: cancellation is half a feature. A senior would either wire it or delete it — shipped dead code invites callers who assume the side effects happen.
Focus-area notes:   - **Business logic**: write the legal status-transition table for `BookingStatus`. Which transitions does the type allow that the domain should forbid? (e.g. `cancelled → confirmed`.)
- **System design**: freeing a slot is implicit — availability filters on status (`availabilityEngine.ts:20`), so cancelling *automatically* reopens the slot. Elegant or fragile? (Both: no cache to invalidate, but also nothing prevents the reminder job from still firing for a cancelled booking.)

# Helpkit
Helpkit is an Intercom-inspired support product with a multi-tenant inbox, real-time chat, inbound email, assignment routing, contact sidebar, canned responses, and a distributable widget.
## Folder Map
- `src/domain/types.ts` - organizations, agents, contacts, conversations, messages, notes, tags, email config.
- `src/domain/tenancy.ts` - org scoping helpers.
- `src/domain/routing.ts` - assignment and round-robin logic.
- `src/domain/realtime.ts` - event and room model.
- `src/domain/emailParser.ts` - inbound email normalization.
- `src/server/routes.ts` - agent, widget, and inbound email APIs.

# Flow: API key lifecycle
Entry point:        None — `createApiKey`/`verifyApiKey`/`revokeApiKey` (`src/domain/apiKeys.ts:9-45`) have no route callers; the RBAC permissions `api_keys.create`/`api_keys.revoke` (`src/domain/rbac.ts:9-10`) exist for routes that were never written.
Auth/middleware:    n/a (would be `requirePermission(member, "api_keys.create")`).
Validation:         None needed on create (inputs are enums/ids); `verifyApiKey` trusts the caller found the right record.
Business logic:     1. Create: 24 random bytes → base64url secret; prefix `pk|sk` + mode; plaintext returned **once**; record stores `keyHash` (SHA-256) and a display `keyPrefix` containing the first 8 chars of the secret (`apiKeys.ts:15-32`).
2. Verify: not revoked AND `sha256(plaintext) === keyHash` (`apiKeys.ts:39-41`).
3. Revoke: pure copy with `revokedAt` set (`apiKeys.ts:43-45`).
Invariants: plaintext never persisted — holds; revoked keys never verify — holds (`apiKeys.test.ts:13-18` pins it).
DB queries:         Would be: `INSERT INTO api_keys (id, org_id, key_prefix, key_hash, ...) VALUES (...);` and lookup at verify time: `SELECT * FROM api_keys WHERE key_hash = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL;` — note verification needs an index on `key_hash`, which is why hashing (deterministic) rather than salted-bcrypt (non-deterministic) is the industry pattern for high-entropy API keys.
Side effects:       None. Missing per the type model: no `api_key.created`/`api_key.revoked` events pushed (`types.ts:74` declares both), `lastUsedAt` (`types.ts:31`) is never updated by anything.
Response:           `CreatedApiKey` — the one shape that carries the plaintext (`apiKeys.ts:4-7`). Good: the type makes "show it once" explicit.
Failure modes:      - `verifyApiKey` compares hashes with `===` (`apiKeys.ts:40`) — not timing-safe, in the same repo where `webhooks.ts:24` carefully uses `timingSafeEqual`. For SHA-256 of high-entropy input the practical risk is negligible; the inconsistency is the finding.
- Unsalted SHA-256 is fine *only because* the secret has 192 bits of entropy; the same pattern copied to user passwords would be a serious flaw. Know why the entropy argument works.
- `keyPrefix` leaks the first 8 chars of the secret (`apiKeys.ts:24`) — standard practice (Stripe shows prefixes) but it d

# Flow: Command palette search
Entry point:        UI event — typing in the palette input → `src/components/CommandPalette.tsx:12-41` (rendered from `src/app/page.tsx:42-55`)
Auth/middleware:    None. Client-only; operates on whatever issues the page already holds.
Validation:         None. `query` is a raw string (`CommandPalette.tsx:24-25`). Nothing needs to be rejected here, but note there is no debounce or length guard — every keystroke re-filters the full list.
Business logic:     1. Parent owns `query` state (`page.tsx:16`) and passes it down.
2. `matches` = issues where `` `${identifier} ${title}`.toLowerCase() `` includes `query.toLowerCase()` (`CommandPalette.tsx:15-17`).
3. Render at most 8 matches (`CommandPalette.tsx:32`).
Invariant: results must come only from issues already scoped to the user's workspace — which holds here only because `page.tsx:13` seeds from a single-workspace fixture, not because anything enforces it.
DB queries:         None executed. The equivalent server-side query would be:
`SELECT * FROM issues WHERE workspace_id = $1 AND (identifier ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%' OR title ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%') LIMIT 8;`
Side effects:       None. Selecting a match calls `onOpenIssue`, which in `page.tsx:47-50` is a placeholder `alert()`.
Response:           n/a (rendered list). Empty query matches everything (every string includes `""`), so the palette shows the first 8 issues before you type.
Failure modes:      - `issues` empty → empty list, fine.
- Very large issue list → O(n) string build + filter per keystroke; no memoization (`matches` recomputed every render).
- No escaping issues since it's `includes`, not regex.
Why it's built this way: Substring match over `identifier + title` is the simplest thing that feels like Linear's palette. A senior would keep exactly this for a first pass but hoist the lowercased haystack out of the per-keystroke loop (or memoize), and make `onOpenIssue` real.

**Read**: `src/domain/types.ts` (all) → `src/data/seed.ts` → the "Data modeling audit" in

**Principle**: a parent-pointer column is the cheapest tree and the most expensive everything-else.

denormalization create? Where can it be violated today?

**Read**: `src/domain/types.ts` (all), `src/data/seed.ts` (all), then the "Data modeling audit"
in `docs/reference.md`.
**Principle**: in scheduling, the schema *is* the product: what's an instant (`Booking.startUtc`),
what's a clock time (`AvailabilityRule.startTime`), and what's a duration (`durationMinutes`) are
three different types wearing the same two (`string`, `number`).
**Self-check**:
1. Which fields are instants, which are local clock times, and which are durations? Which type
distinguishes them? (None.)
2. Why does `Booking` duplicate `hostUserId` when it's derivable through `eventTypeId`?
3. What can't you query because invitees aren't an entity?
4. Write the exclusion constraint that makes double-booking impossible at the DB layer, and the
CHECK constraint that would catch an inverted booking.
## Module 2 — TypeScript in practice
**Read**: `src/domain/notificationJobs.ts:3-6` (the good union) →
`src/domain/bookingService.ts:4-6` + `src/domain/calendarGateway.ts` (interface seams — find the
mock's parameter mismatch at `calendarGateway.ts:17` and explain why it compiles) →
`src/server/routes.ts:6-14` (what the schema checks and what it merely types) →
`src/components/BookingFlow.tsx:47` (`String(null)`).

and the domain needs *meaning*.

# 18. Real-Time Team Chat
Enterprise patterns demonstrated:
- Channels and direct-message conversations.
- Cursor-based message history backed by Postgres.
- Socket.IO lifecycle for joining rooms, sending messages, typing indicators, and receipts.
- Redis-backed online presence with short TTL heartbeats.
- Optimistic client messages reconciled with server-confirmed message IDs.
- Unread count model separated from message storage.
Redis stores volatile state only; Postgres remains the source of truth for users, conversations, messages, and read cursors.

# Real-Time Team Chat Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Use WebSockets or SignalR for live delivery, but keep message persistence in normal HTTP-backed application services.
- Store message history in Postgres with cursor pagination. Avoid offset pagination because active conversations mutate constantly.
- Track presence in Redis with connection IDs and short TTLs so disconnected clients disappear without manual cleanup.
- Treat typing indicators as ephemeral events with expiry timestamps.
- Reconcile optimistic messages using an idempotent `clientNonce`.
## Production checklist
- Authorize every conversation read/write against membership.
- Deduplicate sends by unique `(conversation_id, client_nonce)`.
- Persist read cursors per user and conversation.
- Fan out socket events only after the database commit succeeds.
- Add backpressure and reconnect logic on the client.
## Interview prompts
- How do you prevent duplicate messages when the client retries?
- Why is cursor pagination a better fit than offset pagination for chat?
- What belongs in Redis versus Postgres?
- How would you rebuild unread counts after a bug?

# 18. Real-Time Team Chat (.NET + React)
Learning clone of the team chat project using ASP.NET Core and React TypeScript. It is designed as an enterprise-ready reference scaffold, not a runnable production service.
## What is inside
- ASP.NET Core minimal API with channels, DMs, cursor pagination, unread tracking, typing state, and presence.
- React TypeScript client that models optimistic messages being reconciled with server truth.
- Documentation focused on WebSocket lifecycle, Redis-backed presence, and Postgres message persistence.
## Production architecture
- Use SignalR or raw WebSockets at the edge for message, typing, and presence fanout.
- Persist messages in Postgres with a monotonic cursor column and channel membership checks.
- Store presence and typing indicators in Redis with short TTL keys.
- Reconcile optimistic client messages by `clientNonce` so duplicate sends do not create duplicate UI rows.
## Suggested next steps
1. Replace in-memory stores with EF Core entities and migrations.
2. Add SignalR hubs for `JoinConversation`, `SendMessage`, `Typing`, and `PresenceChanged`.
3. Add JWT auth and conversation membership authorization.
4. Add integration tests for cursor pagination and unread count behavior.

## Core patterns
- Store prices, totals, discounts, and tax in integer minor units. Never use binary floating point for money.

# 20. Event Booking System
Enterprise patterns demonstrated:
- Organizer-owned events with multiple ticket types and capacity.
- Seat-count limits enforced by service validation.
- Concurrent booking safety using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
- QR-code ticket payload generation.
- Transactional email dispatch boundary.
- Waitlist promotion job when tickets are cancelled or capacity opens.
The booking transaction only locks the ticket type row long enough to allocate inventory and create tickets. Email work is deferred so external providers cannot hold database locks open.

# Event Booking Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Lock the ticket type row while checking and incrementing sold count.
- Keep booking creation, ticket issuance, and inventory mutation in one transaction.
- Send email after commit, ideally by writing an outbox record and letting a worker deliver it.
- QR codes should contain signed opaque ticket tokens, not raw user data.
- Waitlist promotion should be deterministic: oldest eligible entry first.
## Production checklist
- `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` around ticket capacity.
- Per-order seat limits enforced on the server.
- Idempotency key for payment and booking retries.
- Email retry strategy with dead-letter handling.
- Ticket scan endpoint validates status and prevents double check-in.
## Interview prompts
- What happens if two people book the last seat simultaneously?
- Why should QR payloads be signed?
- How do you promote waitlisted attendees fairly?
- Where would you place payment authorization in the transaction flow?

- Docs covering concurrency, transactional email, QR ticket validation, and waitlist jobs.
## Production architecture
- Keep ticket capacity in a row locked with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` during booking.
- Commit booking, ticket, and payment intent state in one transaction before sending email.
- Generate QR payloads as signed tokens that resolve to server-side ticket records.
- Promote waitlisted attendees from a background job after cancellation or capacity increase.
## Suggested next steps
1. Replace the in-memory lock with EF Core transaction boundaries.
2. Add Resend or SES behind an `IEmailSender`.
3. Add QR image rendering and ticket scan endpoints.

- Permission checks on both page reads and search results.

- How do recursive CTEs help with nested pages?
- What is the difference between a diff view and a restore action?

# 24. File Sharing App
Enterprise patterns demonstrated:
- Folder hierarchy modeled as parent-child records.
- Presigned S3 upload/download control-plane flows.
- Multi-file upload progress modeled on the client.
- Resumable upload session metadata.
- Per-user storage quota enforcement.

# File Sharing Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Presign upload URLs only after auth, ownership, file type, and quota checks.
- Complete uploads by verifying object existence and size before creating visible metadata.
- Use multipart upload sessions for large files.
- Keep share tokens opaque and high entropy.
- Hash optional share passwords with a password hash algorithm in production.
## Production checklist
- Never expose raw bucket credentials to the browser.
- Enforce quota before upload and after upload completion.
- Expire public links and signed download URLs separately.
- Scan uploaded files asynchronously before allowing downloads.
- Log share-link access for auditing.
## Interview prompts
- Why do presigned uploads still need server-side completion?
- How do you avoid quota bypass through parallel uploads?
- What should a share token reveal?
- How would resumable uploads recover after network failure?

## Production architecture

- Presign upload URLs server-side after quota and ownership checks.
- Track upload sessions and committed object sizes before making files visible.

7. [App.tsx](../client/src/App.tsx) - feed UI.
Fast win: add a comment count badge in the post card. Teach-back: explain why vote uniqueness belongs in the database schema.
## System Map
```text
React feed
-> post/comment/vote routes
-> rate limiter + ranking utility
-> Prisma transactions
-> unique vote constraints + materialized comment paths
```
| Layer | Owns | Anchors |

# 25. Discussion Forum
Enterprise patterns demonstrated:
- Communities, posts, and nested threaded comments.
- Materialized-path comment threading.
- Up/down votes with database-level deduplication.
- Hot/top/new sorting and user karma.
- Redis-backed rate limiting for posting.
The project is a compact learning scaffold for Reddit-like systems.

# Discussion Forum Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Adjacency lists are simple for writes; materialized paths make nested reads and ordering easier.
- Vote deduplication belongs in the database with a unique `(user_id, target_type, target_id)` index.
- Hot ranking combines score and age so new good posts can surface.
- Karma is derived from votes on authored posts/comments.
- Rate limits should live in Redis so every API node shares the same counters.
## Production checklist
- Transactionally update vote rows and cached scores.
- Prevent users from voting more than once on the same target.
- Paginate comments by path and depth.
- Enforce community membership/moderator permissions.
- Tune hot ranking for your product, not just a copied formula.
## Interview prompts
- What are the tradeoffs between adjacency lists and materialized paths?
- How do you keep vote counts correct under retries?
- Why is Redis useful for rate limiting?
- How would you migrate a comment tree model later?

# 25. Discussion Forum (.NET + React)

## Production architecture
- Store comments with `parent_id` and a materialized path for efficient nested reads.
- Enforce one vote per user per target with a unique database constraint.
- Cache hot feeds but recompute scores from canonical votes.
- Use Redis token buckets for post and comment creation limits.

# Restaurant Reservations Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Availability is a constrained-resource search over time intervals and table capacity.
- Interval overlap is `new_start < existing_end AND new_end > existing_start`.
- Try exact table fits before combinations to avoid wasting large tables.
- Public booking widgets should be embeddable and tenant-scoped.
- SMS should be queued after commit, not sent inside the transaction.
## Production checklist
- Index reservations by table and time range.
- Add buffers for turn time and cleaning time.
- Track no-shows and cancellation windows.
- Make widget origins configurable.
- Add host override flows with audit logging.
## Interview prompts
- How do you assign a party of six if only two two-tops and one four-top are free?
- Why is interval overlap easy to get wrong?
- What makes an embeddable widget different from an internal app?

# Headless CMS Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Content schemas define entry validation rules, so the schema model must be carefully versioned.
- Public API versions should be stable contracts for developers.
- API keys should be hashed at rest and plaintext should only be shown once.
- Rate limits should be tracked per key and endpoint family.
- Webhooks should be delivered from an outbox with retry and backoff.
## Production checklist
- Validate dynamic fields on every entry write.
- Support draft and published views separately.
- Document public API error formats and pagination.
- Sign webhook payloads.
- Keep webhook attempts observable for developers.
## Interview prompts
- What makes a schema-that-defines-schemas difficult?
- How would you version public APIs without duplicating every controller?
- Why hash API keys instead of encrypting them?
- How do webhook retries avoid duplicate side effects for receivers?

# Architecture Map
## Workspace
- `packages/shared` contains framework-agnostic helpers used by the APIs: RBAC, error handling, async Express wrappers, and cursor helpers.
- Every numbered app has a `server` package, a `client` package, a Prisma schema, seed data, and a project README.

## 16. Blog Platform

- `server/src/posts/service.ts` owns draft creation, transitions, public listing, author pages, and the editorial queue.
- `server/src/comments/service.ts` owns moderation queue behavior.
## 17. Kanban Board
- `server/src/boards/rank.ts` implements lexicographic ordering for drag-and-drop.
- `server/src/boards/service.ts` owns board membership checks, card movement, assignment, labels, due dates, and activity logs.
- `server/src/invitations/service.ts` owns token creation, hashing, expiration, and acceptance.
## 18. Team Chat

**Project 4: a deliberately small scaffold you upgrade yourself.** Projects 1–3 gave
you finished apps to read. This one flips the model: you get a *working but naive*
CRUD app, and the learning is in replacing its shortcuts with the real patterns —
markdown rendering, folders/tags, debounced autosave, and PostgreSQL full-text search.
Building on a scaffold is closer to real jobs than greenfield work: you inherit code,
find its weakest seam, and improve it without breaking what works.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get (working today):** an Express + Knex + Postgres API for `notes`
(list/get/create/update/delete/stats) with the standard envelope, and a single-page
React client (`client/src/App.jsx`) with a form, list, search box, and stats strip.
Notes already have `title`, `body`, `folder`, `status`, and `tags` fields.
**You build (the labs in §5):**
| Upgrade | Replaces this shortcut in the scaffold |
|---|---|
| Markdown rendering | `body` is displayed as plain text even though seeds contain markdown (`"# Draft"`). |
| Real search (Postgres FTS) | `model.js` searches with `CAST(notes AS TEXT) ILIKE '%term%'` — the whole row cast to text. Read that line and enumerate why it's wrong. |
| Debounced autosave | The form saves only on explicit submit. |
| Folder/tag navigation | `folder` and `tags` are stored but the UI filters by a client-side `JSON.stringify(record).includes(search)` — yes, really (see `App.jsx`). |
The gap between the scaffold and the target *is the curriculum.* The naive lines are
left visible on purpose so you can articulate what's wrong before fixing it.

# FABLE Guide — REST API Testing Tool (Postman-lite)
**Project 15: build the tool, understand the trade.** You've curl'd every project so
far; now you build the thing that replaces curl: collections of saved requests,
environments with `{{variable}}` interpolation, request history, a response viewer —
and the piece that makes it interesting: a **backend proxy** that executes arbitrary
user-specified HTTP requests, because the browser's CORS rules won't let the client
do it directly. Developer tools are a distinct engineering genre (your user is a
developer, your data is *requests themselves*), and the proxy is a security problem
wearing a feature's clothes.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| The proxy | `services/proxyService.ts`, `controllers/proxyController.ts` | Your server executes requests to URLs users typed. Timing, size, status capture — and SSRF risk, for real this time (Project 6's Lab 3 warned you). |
| Why a proxy at all | client can't fetch cross-origin | Being able to *explain CORS from both sides* — as the blocked client and as the API that sets the headers — is a permanent interview asset. |
| Template interpolation | `utils/interpolate.ts` | `{{baseUrl}}/users/{{id}}` — a tiny template engine: resolution order, missing variables, no infinite recursion. |
| Environments | environment model/service/controller | Named variable sets with one active — the mental model behind every deploy config system. |
| Trees in UI | collections → folders (one level) → requests, `CollectionTree.tsx` | Persisted tree with sort fields; import/export/duplicate of nested structures (Project 11's deep-copy again). |
| History as a log | history model + pagination + clear | Append-only request log with retention questions — a mini ledger (Project 10) for requests. |
| CodeMirror integration | `client/src/components/ui/CodeEditor.tsx` | Wiring a serious third-party editor widget into React — controlled-component friction included. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod + CodeMirror.

# FABLE Guide — Personal Task Manager
**One doc to take you from "I can read this code" to "I could have designed this code."**
This is Project 1 of the curriculum, and it teaches the single most reusable skill in
full-stack work: the **layered CRUD app**. Every project after this one is a variation
on the shape you learn here. Master this project slowly and every later project gets faster.
> The older docs (`architecture.md`, the `upskill/` folder) are still valid references.

A task manager with create, edit, filter, sort, complete, and delete. Nothing exotic —
and that is the point. The value is in *how* it is built:
```
Browser (React)                    Server (Express)                 Database
─────────────────                  ────────────────                 ────────
TasksPage                          taskRoutes.js      ─ URLs only
└─ useTasks (hook)     HTTP      taskController.js  ─ HTTP in/out
└─ tasksApi.js  ────────►   taskService.js     ─ rules & validation

```

layer and not another, you are thinking at mid level. When you can argue about the cost
of moving it, you are thinking at senior level.

# FABLE Guide — Recipe Manager with User Accounts
**Project 5: the biggest single jump in the curriculum.** Three new dimensions land at
once: **TypeScript** end-to-end, **JWT authentication** (access token + HTTP-only
refresh cookie), and **multi-table writes in a transaction**. Plus the concept that
reshapes every layer: requests now have an *identity*, and some data has an *owner*.
Budget more time here than for Projects 1–4 combined. It's worth it — auth + ownership
+ transactions is the exact skill set the industry means by "mid-level backend."
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript everywhere | `server/src/**/*.ts`, `client/src/**/*.tsx`, shared shapes in `server/src/types/domain.ts` and `client/src/types/recipe.ts` | Types are the contract between layers; watch how they replace guesswork. |
| JWT access + refresh | `services/authService.ts`, `middleware/auth.ts` | Short-lived bearer token in memory, long-lived refresh token in an HTTP-only cookie. Learn *why the split exists*. |
| Route protection, two flavors | `middleware/auth.ts`: `requireAuth` vs. `optionalAuth` | Public browsing works logged-out; favorites/ownership light up when logged in. Read both — the asymmetry is the lesson. |
| Ownership checks | `recipeService.ts` update/delete paths | 403 vs. 404 vs. 401 — three different "no" answers, each meaning something. |
| Knex transactions | recipe create: recipe + ingredients + steps + categories in **one transaction** | Partial writes are corruption. This is the pattern Projects 9–10 build on. |
| React auth context | `client/src/context/AuthContext.tsx` + `services/api.ts` | Login state as app-wide context; token installed via `setAccessToken()`; `withCredentials: true` carries the refresh cookie. |
| Password hashing | `authService.ts` + `models/userModel.ts` | bcrypt, and why the users table must never leak `password_hash` in responses. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + jsonwebtoken + bcrypt.

# FABLE Guide — Bookmark Manager
**Project 6: your first TypeScript scaffold-upgrade project.** The theme is
**hardening an API's edges**: schema validation with Zod, API versioning, fetching
metadata from external URLs, and designing an endpoint that outside clients (a
bookmarklet) can call. Projects 1–5 taught you the layers; this one teaches you the
*boundaries* — every place data enters or leaves your process.
Like Project 4, this is a working-but-naive scaffold plus labs. The scaffold runs
today; the learning-focus features are yours to build.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get:** a TypeScript Express + Knex API for `bookmarks` (`title`, `url`,
`collection`, `status`, `tags`) with list/search/stats/CRUD, the standard envelope,
and a one-page React client (`client/src/App.tsx`). The whole server backbone is six
small files under `server/src/` — the same generic scaffold as Projects 4 and 7–10
(routes → `controller.ts` → `service.ts` → `model.ts`).
**You build:**
| Upgrade | Replaces this shortcut |
|---|---|
| Zod validation | `service.ts#sanitizePayload` only allow-lists field *names* — a `url` of `"not a url"` or a 10MB `title` sails through. |
| API versioning | Routes mount at `/api/bookmarks` with no version; changing a response shape today breaks every client silently. |
| URL metadata fetch | Creating a bookmark stores whatever title you type; real bookmark apps fetch the page's `<title>`/description/favicon. |
| Bookmarklet endpoint | The API assumes the React client; a bookmarklet is a *hostile-environment* client (other people's pages, CORS, no build step). |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + TypeScript.
API on **:4106**, client on :5173.

# FABLE Guide — Blog Platform
**Project 7: user-authored content, done safely.** The theme is the most dangerous
boundary in web development: **storing HTML that users wrote and rendering it to other
users.** Around it: rich-text editor wiring, slug generation, nested comments, and RSS.
Get the sanitization story wrong and everything else is decoration — this project
exists so you get it wrong here, on seed data, instead of in production.
Like Projects 4 and 6, this is a working scaffold plus build-labs.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get:** a TypeScript Express + Knex API for `posts` (list/search/stats/CRUD,
standard envelope) and a one-page React client — the same six-file scaffold shape as
Projects 4, 6, and 8–10 (`routes.ts` → `controller.ts` → `service.ts` → `model.ts`).
**You build:**
| Upgrade | The lesson inside it |
|---|---|
| Rich-text editing + sanitization | Where exactly the trust boundary sits (spoiler: the server, on write AND the render path). |
| Slugs | Deriving URLs from titles: uniqueness, collisions, and what happens when a title changes after publication. |
| Nested comments | Modeling a tree in SQL (`parent_id`), fetching it efficiently, rendering it recursively. |
| RSS feed | Content negotiation — the same data as XML, and why standards-formatted output is fussier than JSON. |
| Draft → published workflow | The `status` column grows teeth: visibility rules per status. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL.

# FABLE Guide — Kanban Board
**Project 8: the frontend finally gets hard.** Until now the client was a form and a
list. A kanban board is **interaction-heavy UI state**: drag-and-drop, optimistic
updates with rollback, and the sneaky-deep problem of **ordering** — where does "card
position" live in a database, and what happens when two moves race?
Like Projects 4, 6, and 7, this is a working scaffold plus build-labs. The scaffold
gives you flat `cards` CRUD; you build the board on top.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get:** the standard six-file TypeScript scaffold (`routes.ts` → `controller.ts`
→ `service.ts` → `model.ts`) serving `cards` with list/search/stats/CRUD and the
response envelope, plus a one-page React client.
**You build:**
| Upgrade | The lesson inside it |
|---|---|
| Board → lists → cards data model | Modeling one-to-many-to-many hierarchy and shipping a nested `GET /api/board` payload. |
| Drag-and-drop | Wiring a DnD library (`@dnd-kit` recommended) and separating *gesture* state from *data* state. |
| Optimistic reorder | Update the UI instantly, reconcile with the server, roll back on failure — the pattern behind every snappy app. |
| Fractional indexing | Storing order as a sortable value between neighbors so a move is a 1-row `UPDATE`, not a renumber-everything. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL.
API on **:4108**, client on :5173.

# FABLE Guide — Job Application Tracker
**Project 9: business rules with teeth.** The theme is the **state machine** — the
pattern behind order fulfillment, ticket workflows, deployment pipelines, and every
"status" column that ever mattered. Around it: transactional history (audit trail of
every stage change), file upload wiring, and the KPI queries that turn a pipeline
into a dashboard.
Like Projects 4 and 6–8, this is a working scaffold plus build-labs. The scaffold
serves flat `applications` CRUD; the workflow engine is yours to build.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get:** the standard six-file TypeScript scaffold (`routes.ts` → `controller.ts`
→ `service.ts` → `model.ts`) for `applications` with list/search/stats/CRUD and the
envelope, plus a one-page React client. Crucially, the scaffold's `status` is just a
string anyone can set to anything — the "before" state of the whole project.
**You build:**
| Upgrade | The lesson inside it |
|---|---|
| Pipeline state machine | Legal transitions only (`applied → screening → interview → offer → accepted/rejected`, `withdrawn` from anywhere). The difference between a status *field* and a status *machine*. |
| Transactional stage history | Every transition writes the application AND a history row atomically — Project 5's transactions, now structural. |
| Resume upload | Multipart handling (`multer`), what goes in the DB vs. on disk, and validating files (the trap: trusting extensions). |
| KPI dashboard queries | Conversion rates per stage, time-in-stage, applications per week — SQL that answers manager questions. |

# FABLE Guide — Inventory Management
**Project 10: the capstone of Tier 1's first half — numbers that must never lie.**
The theme is the **ledger**: stock levels you never `UPDATE` directly, but derive from
an append-only trail of movements, written under transactions, and reported on with
real SQL. This is the mental model behind bank balances, warehouse systems, and
double-entry bookkeeping — and it composes everything from Projects 1–9: layers,
validation, transactions, state machines, and aggregate queries.
Like Projects 4 and 6–9, this is a working scaffold plus build-labs. The scaffold
serves flat `products` CRUD; the ledger, orders, and reports are yours to build.
---
## 1. What you get vs. what you build
**You get:** the standard six-file TypeScript scaffold (`routes.ts` → `controller.ts`
→ `service.ts` → `model.ts`) for `products` with list/search/stats/CRUD and the
envelope, plus a one-page React client. The scaffold's notion of stock — if you add a
quantity column and edit it freely — is exactly the anti-pattern this project cures.
**You build:**
| Upgrade | The lesson inside it |
|---|---|
| Stock movement ledger | Append-only `stock_movements`; on-hand quantity is a *derived* number. Why "just update the quantity" destroys auditability. |
| Purchase & sales orders | Multi-line documents with their own status machine (Project 9's pattern, reused) whose *fulfillment* writes ledger rows. |
| Knex transactions, seriously | An order receipt = order status + N movement rows + (maybe) a cached quantity, atomically. Plus your first real look at race conditions on decrement. |
| SQL report patterns | Stock-on-hand, valuation, low-stock alerts, movement history — reports as queries, not spreadsheets. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL.
API on **:4110**, client on :5173.

# FABLE Guide — Poll / Survey Builder
**Project 11: schema-driven software.** Until now, your apps knew their data shapes at
compile time — a task has a title, a recipe has steps. A survey builder's core object
is **a form defined by the user at runtime**: questions of different types, options,
ordering, and a public-facing renderer that draws UI from that definition. This
"data that describes structure" pattern is the same one behind form builders, CMS page
builders, and workflow designers — it's a genuinely mid-level modeling problem.
This is also the first project with a dedicated **validators layer**: Zod schemas in
`server/src/validators/` applied by `middleware/validate.ts`, and even the env config
(`config/env.ts`) is Zod-parsed. What you *built* in Project 6's Lab 1, you now get to
*read* as an established pattern.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Nested aggregate modeling | survey → questions → options tables | Editing a tree of rows: create/update/delete/reorder children without orphaning anything. |
| Zod validators as a layer | `validators/surveyValidators.ts` + `middleware/validate.ts` | Validation declared once, applied at the route edge — compare with Project 1's hand-rolled service checks. |
| Public vs. builder API split | public survey rendering + response submission with access codes | Two audiences, one database: the owner edits; anonymous respondents see a *published projection*. |
| Response aggregation | results endpoints: counts per option, rating averages, matrix totals | GROUP BY over answers, shaped for charts (Project 3's skill, harder shapes). |
| Deep copy | `POST /api/surveys/:id/duplicate` | Cloning an aggregate: new ids everywhere, relationships preserved. Sneaky-hard. |
| Demo auth header | `x-demo-user-id` (falls back to `DEMO_USER_ID`) | A deliberate stub. Know exactly what it fakes so you know what real auth (Project 5) would restore. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod.
API on **:4111** (see `server/src/config/env.ts`), client on :5173.

# Architecture
## Layers
- `client/` is a React 18 Vite app using TypeScript, Axios, React Query, and CSS Modules.
- `server/src/routes` maps HTTP endpoints to thin controllers.
- `server/src/controllers` extracts request data and returns the standard response envelope.
- `server/src/services` owns business rules such as activation, response limits, aggregation, duplication, and CSV export.
- `server/src/models` contains Knex-only database access.
- `server/src/middleware` centralizes validation and error formatting.
## Data model
Surveys own ordered questions. Choice questions own options. Responses are split into `responses` and `response_answers` so each question type can store the answer shape it needs while preserving relational joins.
The `questions.config` JSONB column stores type-specific settings such as rating ranges, matrix rows and columns, and numeric bounds. This avoids creating many sparse columns while keeping the core question fields queryable.
## API conventions
Every successful response uses:
```json
{ "success": true, "data": {} }
```
Every error response uses:
```json
{ "success": false, "error": { "message": "Readable message", "code": "ERROR_CODE" } }
```
## Tradeoffs
This educational app uses a `x-demo-user-id` header instead of full authentication. Drag-and-drop is represented with up/down reorder buttons so the behavior is understandable without another package.

# FABLE Guide — Multi-User Chat (HTTP Polling)
**Project 12: real-time behavior with no real-time transport.** This chat app has
direct and group conversations, unread counts, read receipts, typing indicators,
presence, reactions, and search — built entirely on plain HTTP requests. That
constraint is the curriculum: you learn **cursor pagination**, **polling loops**, and
**ephemeral state modeling** so precisely that when you later add WebSockets
(Project 19's territory), you'll know exactly what the socket is and isn't buying you.
Most "real-time" features in production apps are, in fact, polling. Knowing when
that's fine is a senior judgment; this project gives you the data to make it.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Cursor pagination, both directions | `GET .../messages` with `before` (history) and `GET .../messages/new` with `after` (polling) | The fix for Project 2's offset-pagination bug, in its natural habitat: an append-heavy feed. |
| The polling loop | client `App.tsx` + `services/api.ts` | Interval fetch with a moving cursor: cheap requests that usually return `[]`. |
| Presence via heartbeat | `POST /api/presence/heartbeat` + `GET /api/presence/status` | "Online" = "heartbeat within N seconds" — presence is *derived from recency*, not stored as a boolean. |
| Ephemeral state with TTL | typing indicators + stale cleanup | State that must *expire*: who cleans it up, and when? |
| Read receipts & unread counts | `POST .../read`, unread math in the service | Per-user-per-conversation watermarks — a `last_read_message_id` beats a `read` flag per message. Verify which this app chose and why. |
| Membership-scoped access | conversation members table | Every message query must check "is the requester a member?" — your first data-access rule that isn't ownership. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod validators.

# Architecture
## Layers
- `client/` uses React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Axios, React Query, and CSS Modules.
- `server/src/routes` defines endpoint surfaces.
- `server/src/controllers` stays thin and delegates to services.
- `server/src/services` contains polling rules, DM dedupe, read receipts, ownership checks, and presence calculations.
- `server/src/models` contains Knex queries only.
- `server/src/middleware` owns validation and centralized error responses.
## Polling model
The active conversation polls `/messages/new?after=messageId` every two seconds. The conversation list polls every five seconds. Presence heartbeat runs every thirty seconds and stores `last_seen_at`. Typing indicators are upserted and treated as expired after five seconds.
## Cursor pagination
Message history uses `before=messageId&limit=30`. The query orders by newest for efficient pagination, then reverses the page so the UI renders oldest first.
## Tradeoffs
This project intentionally avoids WebSockets and full authentication. It uses a demo user header so the data modeling and polling behaviors stay easy to inspect.

# FABLE Guide — E-Commerce Storefront
**Project 13: the transaction becomes the product.** A storefront looks like CRUD with
nicer CSS, but three problems here are qualitatively harder than anything in a task
app: **guest identity** (a cart for someone with no account), **the checkout
transaction** (order + stock deduction + cart clear, atomically), and **two-sided
APIs** (shopper routes and admin routes over the same data). Plus it quietly reuses
half the curriculum: catalog filters (P2), aggregates (P3), stock (P10), reviews (P7's
user content).
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Guest sessions | `x-session-id` header; client persists a session id in `localStorage` | Identity without auth. The cart belongs to a *browser*, not a user. |
| Cart merge | `POST /api/cart/merge` | The classic flow: guest fills a cart, then logs in — now two carts exist. Merge rules are product decisions encoded in a service. |
| Checkout transaction | `POST /api/checkout` in `storeService.ts` | Create order + order lines, deduct stock, clear cart — one transaction, with stock races handled (Project 10's lab, now load-bearing). |
| Catalog filtering | `GET /api/products` with category/price/rating/stock/sort | Compound filters over joins (rating is an aggregate!) — the hardest list query in the curriculum so far. |
| Two audiences | `/api/products...` vs `/api/admin/...` routes | Same tables, different projections and permissions. `x-demo-user-id` stubs the auth. |
| Slug-based detail + related products | `/products/:slug` | URLs from Project 7's slug lab, in a catalog context. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod validators.
API on **:4113** (`server/src/config/env.ts`), client on :5173.

# Architecture
## Layers
- `client/` is a React 18 Vite app using TypeScript, Axios, React Query, and CSS Modules.
- `server/src/routes` maps endpoints to thin controllers.
- `server/src/controllers` extracts ids, headers, params, and bodies.
- `server/src/services` owns cart merge rules, checkout transactions, stock checks, review verification, and admin stats.
- `server/src/models` contains Knex-only data access.
- `server/src/middleware` handles validation and error responses.
## Checkout transaction
Checkout validates cart contents and stock, snapshots product names and prices, creates the order and order items, decrements stock, and clears the cart inside one Knex transaction.
## Cart persistence
Guest carts are stored server-side by `session_id`; the browser keeps only the session id in `localStorage`. Logged-in users use `user_id`. The merge endpoint combines guest and user cart items by keeping the larger quantity for duplicates.

# FABLE Guide — Appointment Booking System
**Project 14: time is the boss fight.** Booking is the domain where correct-looking
code is wrong in ways users notice: a slot shown twice, a 9:00 that's actually 8:00
because of DST, two customers booked into the same chair. This project is fully built —
recurring weekly availability, date overrides, slot generation, conflict detection,
booking/cancellation/reschedule policies, timezone conversion via `date-fns-tz`, and
notifications as database rows. Your job is to read it like a skeptic: the algorithms
here (interval math, slot generation) are the most interview-transferable code in the
whole curriculum.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Slot generation | `server/src/services/slotService.ts` | Recurring weekly windows + per-date overrides + existing appointments + service duration → available start times. An algorithm, not a query. |
| Interval conflict detection | slot/appointment services | The overlap predicate `(startA < endB && startB < endA)` and its off-by-one edges (back-to-back bookings must NOT conflict). |
| Timezones done deliberately | `date-fns-tz` at the slot boundary; UTC `timestamptz` in Postgres | The golden rule demonstrated: store UTC, convert at the *edge*, keep "wall-clock" concepts (weekly availability) separate from instants. |
| Policy rules | cancellation with provider policy, reschedule flow | Business rules with time math: "cancel up to N hours before start" — computed against *whose* clock? |
| Roles via headers | `x-user-id` / `x-user-role: provider` | Customer vs. provider — first two-role API. Provider routes manage availability; customer routes book. |
| Notifications as rows | `models/notificationModel.ts` | The outbox idea in embryo: record the intent to notify in the same DB (and transaction?) as the booking. Real email comes later; the *pattern* is the point. |
| Multi-model backend | 5 models, 3 services, 2 controllers | The biggest layered backend yet that's still readable in a sitting. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod + date-fns-tz.
API on **:4214**, client on **:5174**. DB: `appointment_booking`.
## 2. Run it (10 minutes)

createdb appointment_booking
cd 14-a

# Architecture
## Backend
The Express app follows the required controller/service/model split:
- Controllers parse validated Express requests and return the standard `{ success, data }` envelope.
- Services own business rules: slot calculation, cancellation policy, conflict checks, and notification creation.
- Models contain Knex queries only.
- Middleware handles request context, Zod validation, and centralized error envelopes.
## Data model
Core tables are `users`, `provider_profiles`, `services`, `availability`, `availability_overrides`, `appointments`, and `notifications`.
Appointments store `start_time` and `end_time` as `timestamp with time zone`. Weekly availability stores local `time` values and a provider `timezone` decides how those local times become UTC instants.
## Slot calculation
`slotService.getAvailableSlots` implements the key booking algorithm:
1. Load provider policy and requested service.
2. Pick custom override hours for the date, or recurring weekly availability for the weekday.
3. Convert provider-local date/time windows to UTC.
4. Step through windows by `service.duration_minutes + provider.booking_buffer_minutes`.
5. Exclude past slots and any slots returned by the SQL overlap query.
The conflict query is intentionally explicit:
```sql
select *
from appointments
where provider_id = ?
and status = 'confirmed'
and start_time < ?
and end_time > ?
```
## Frontend
The React app uses Vite, TypeScript, CSS Modules, Axios, and React Query. The first screen is the real provider browsing experience, not a marketing page. The provider settings page demonstrates recurring availability and overrides, while dashboards show the two-sided marketplace views.

# Architecture
## Backend
The Express backend uses thin controllers, service-level business logic, Knex models, Zod validation, centralized error middleware, and a consistent response envelope.
Key services:
- `proxyService`: interpolates environment variables, normalizes params/headers/auth, sends the request with Axios, measures total time, and writes history.
- `collectionService`: manages collection trees, folders, saved requests, duplicate, import, and export.
- `environmentService`: manages active environments and bulk variable replacement.
- `historyService`: provides paginated execution history.
## Data model
The schema includes `users`, `environments`, `env_variables`, `collections`, `folders`, `saved_requests`, and `request_history`. JSON-like request data is stored in `jsonb` columns for headers, params, auth config, request headers, and response headers.
Secret variables stay in the database and are masked in the UI. Collection export intentionally exports saved request data, not environment secrets.
## Variable interpolation
The shared interpolation pattern is:
```ts
template.replace(/\{\{(\w+)\}\}/g, (match, key) => variables[key] ?? match)
```
The backend applies this to URL, query params, header values, body content, and auth fields before dispatching the proxy request.
## Frontend
The React app is a dense tool UI built for repeated use:
- Left panel: collections tree or request history.
- Center panel: tabbed request builder with URL, params, headers, body, and auth.
- Right panel: response status, body, headers, and timing.
CodeMirror is mounted directly in a reusable `CodeEditor` component so JSON request bodies and response bodies use the same editor wiring.

# FABLE Guide — Team Project Management
**Project 16: the enterprise pattern kit — read this one deeply.** Projects 16–20 are
five apps built from the same compact scaffold (~600 lines of server+client core), each
wearing a different domain. The scaffold's point is a set of patterns that separate
"app that works" from "app a company can operate": **soft delete, archive/restore,
audit logs, request context (actor + request id), saved views, bulk operations, role
gates, and a readiness endpoint.** This tasks app is the canonical instance — study it
here, then treat 17–20 as domain-specific labs.
Companion reading: `docs/journal.md` in this folder explains *why* each pattern was
chosen, with trade-offs. Read it after the code tour — it's the voice of the code
reviewer you want to become.
---
## 1. The pattern kit (what to actually learn here)
| Pattern | Where | The idea |
|---|---|---|
| Soft delete | `model.ts` — `softDeleteRecord`, `deleted_at` filtering | Delete hides, never destroys. The model owns the default filter so nobody forgets it. |
| Archive ≠ delete | `PATCH /:id/archive` / `/restore`, `includeArchived` query | Two lifecycles: archived is *done but reportable*; deleted is *hidden from operations*. Conflating them is a classic data-model smell. |
| Request context | `middleware/requestContext.ts` → `Context = {actor, requestId, role}` | Every write can answer "who did this, in which request?" — the prerequisite for audit, debugging, and support. |
| Audit log | model writes audit rows alongside mutations; `GET /api/tasks/audit` | The operational ledger (Project 10's idea applied to *actions* instead of stock). |
| Role gate | `service.ts#requireOperator` — operator/manager/admin | Authorization as an explicit, greppable check at the top of each mutating service function. |
| Saved views | `views` endpoints, filters stored as JSON | User-defined filter bundles — the feature that turns a list into a workflow tool. |
| Bulk operations | `POST /api/tasks/bulk/status` | N records, one request, one validation pass — and one audit story. |
| Bounded lists | `normalizeListQuery`: `pageSize` capped at 100, page at 10000, sort allow-listed | Every list input clamped. Compare with Project 2's pagination — same idea, now defensive by default. |

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line where responsibility changes owners and assumptions must be re-checked. A layer is a boundary stacked horizontally. This repo's layers, what each owns, must not own, and where the leaks are.
## The layer contract
| Layer | Owns | Must NOT own | Enforced by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Nop.Core` | entities, cache/event abstractions, infrastructure primitives | business rules, data access, HTTP | project references (Core references nothing) |
| `Nop.Data` | query execution, schema, migrations, entity events | business decisions | references Core only |
| `Nop.Services` | ALL business logic, orchestration | HTTP types, view models | references Data+Core; no ASP.NET reference |
| `Nop.Web.Framework` | MVC plumbing: filters, DI wiring, work context | domain rules | — |
| `Nop.Web` | controllers, factories, view models, views | direct DB access, business rules | convention (not enforced!) |
The strongest wall is compiler-backed: `Nop.Services` cannot mention `IActionResult` because the assembly doesn't reference MVC. The weakest wall is Web→Services: nothing but convention stops a controller from composing raw queries or embedding business rules.
## Good boundaries, with receipts
- **Controller/service split done right:** [ShoppingCartController.AddProductToCart_Details](../../src/Presentation/Nop.Web/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs#L791-L874) does HTTP things (form parsing, JSON shapes) and delegates every decision to [AddToCartAsync](../../src/Libraries/Nop.Services/Orders/ShoppingCartService.cs#L1549). You could bolt a REST API onto the same service untouched — and the [WebApi plugin](../../src/Plugins/Nop.Plugin.Misc.WebApi.Frontend) does exactly that. That's the test of a real boundary: *a second consumer arrives and nothing has to move*.
- **Entity/view-model wall:** factories ([ProductModelFactory#L1502](../../src/Presentation/Nop.Web/Factories/ProductModelFactory.cs#L1502)) are the only place entities become models; views never see entities. This protects the DB shape from becoming a UI contract — the #1 coupling disease in CRUD apps.
- **Provider boundary:** three databases + SQLite-for-tests behind [INopDataProvider](../../src/Libraries/Nop.Data/INopDataProvider.cs) — an abstraction earning its keep (contrast with interfaces that merely mirror one class).
## Boundary leaks worth studying
1. **`IQueryable` through the repository.** [EntityRepository.Table#L525](../../src/Libraries/Nop.Data/EntityRepository.cs#L525) hands services raw query composition. Pragmatic (services can build efficient que

# 03 — Architecture and Patterns
The judgment module: not *what* the code does but *what it commits the project to*.
1. [01-boundaries-and-layers.md](01-boundaries-and-layers.md) — the layer rules and where they leak
2. [02-data-model-and-persistence.md](02-data-model-and-persistence.md) — schema, transactions, safe change
3. [03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md](03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md) — every gate, mapped
4. [04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md](04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md) — events, queues, retries, idempotency
5. [05-pattern-catalog.md](05-pattern-catalog.md) — 16 pattern cards (the module centerpiece)
6. [06-architecture-critique.md](06-architecture-critique.md) — strengths, risks, and what I'd change owning this
Vocabulary being trained (all defined in context as they appear, all interview-grade): *boundary, invariant, contract, ownership, idempotency, isolation, consistency, blast radius, migration, rollback, observability*. When you can use six of these accurately about code you've read, you interview differently.

# 08 — Interview Prep
Target: **mid-level fullstack loops**, using this repo as your portfolio of concrete evidence. Contents:
| File | Round | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [01-csharp-dotnet-deep-dive.md](01-csharp-dotnet-deep-dive.md) | language/runtime | 16 |
| [02-frontend-framework-questions.md](02-frontend-framework-questions.md) | frontend | 10 |
| [03-api-and-data-modeling-questions.md](03-api-and-data-modeling-questions.md) | API + data | 12 |
| [04-system-design-from-this-repo.md](04-system-design-from-this-repo.md) | system design | full walkthrough + 5 variations |
| [05-debugging-and-code-review-rounds.md](05-debugging-and-code-review-rounds.md) | practical rounds | 7 timed sims |
| [06-behavioral-star-stories.md](06-behavioral-star-stories.md) | behavioral | 8 worksheets |
| [07-two-week-cram-plan.md](07-two-week-cram-plan.md) | all | day-by-day |
## How mid-level loops are structured
Typically: recruiter screen → technical screen (language + small coding) → onsite: practical coding (build/debug in a real-ish codebase), a design conversation (scaled to mid: one feature or one service, not planet-scale), a code-review or debugging round, and behavioral. Mid-level is *not* graded on exotic algorithms — it's graded on: writes working code, reasons about tradeoffs with examples, debugs methodically, communicates while doing all three.
## The golden rule
**Answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff, and a failure mode — never with a definition.** Compare:
- "Cache invalidation is removing stale entries when data changes." (definition — junior)
- "In nopCommerce, every repository write publishes an entity event and a consumer evicts key prefixes — invalidation is systemic, so new caches are correct by default. The tradeoff is coarseness: one product update flushes whole prefix families, so hit rate dips during bulk edits. And it's memory-cache-per-node, so it silently breaks under load balancing unless you switch to the distributed cache." (evidence + tradeoff + failure mode — this is the mid-level sound)
Every card in this module is built to produce answers of the second kind. ≥60% are anchored to real code you can name — that specificity is *rare* among candidates and reads as seniority.
## How to practice
Out loud, timed (90s per card answer), anchors open on second monitor for checking *after* answering. Rotate: never two sessions on the same file. The [cram plan](07-two-week-cram-plan.md) schedules all of it.

# nopCommerce as a Training Lab
A learning curriculum built **from this repository** for one specific learner: a junior fullstack engineer (comfortable with CRUD web dev in .NET/C# or React/Node/TS) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, when it fails, and how to recognize and articulate it in any other repo or in an interview.
## What this repo is
nopCommerce is a full-featured open source e-commerce platform: ASP.NET Core MVC (`net10.0`), Razor views, a layered architecture of three class libraries — [Nop.Core](../src/Libraries/Nop.Core) (domain entities, caching, infrastructure), [Nop.Data](../src/Libraries/Nop.Data) (repositories, FluentMigrator migrations, Linq2Db data access), [Nop.Services](../src/Libraries/Nop.Services) (all business logic) — under two presentation projects: [Nop.Web](../src/Presentation/Nop.Web) (the storefront + `/Admin` area) and [Nop.Web.Framework](../src/Presentation/Nop.Web.Framework) (MVC plumbing: filters, DI startup, work context). It supports multi-store, multi-language, multi-vendor, ACL-per-entity, a plugin system (33 plugins in [src/Plugins](../src/Plugins)), scheduled background tasks, and a queued-email outbox. It has been in production at tens of thousands of stores for ~15 years, so it is a rare chance to study *mature* production tradeoffs — including some deliberate ugliness (see the named-mutex block in [OrderProcessingService.cs](../src/Libraries/Nop.Services/Orders/OrderProcessingService.cs#L1679-L1718)) that a tutorial codebase would never show you.
