# Upskill: The Expense Management Training Lab
This is a self-directed curriculum that turns **this** repository — a small ASP.NET Core
(C#) + React expense-management system — into a training lab. It teaches two things at
once:
1. **This codebase specifically** — where things live, how a request flows, why each
pattern was chosen.
2. **Transferable engineering judgment** — runtime fundamentals, framework mental models,
architecture, testing, debugging, performance, security, code review, and how to
contribute to a real project.
## Repo identity (read this first)
This is a learning clone of Ramp / Expensify / Brex expense workflows. An **employee**
creates an expense, attaches a receipt, and submits it; a **manager** approves or rejects
it; **finance** reimburses it (payment completes asynchronously). The backend is an
ASP.NET Core 8 Web API with **zero NuGet dependencies** — everything (auth, hashing,
background queue, JSON) uses the bundled framework, by design, so the moving parts are
visible rather than hidden in libraries. Persistence is an **in-memory store** (a
singleton of `ConcurrentDictionary`s) that resets on restart; this keeps the focus on the
domain (a state machine, a policy engine, role-scoped authorization) instead of a
database. The frontend is a Vite + React SPA that talks to the API over `fetch` with a
bearer token. The whole thing is intentionally readable in an afternoon — which is exactly
what makes it a good lab.
> ⚠️ **Status caveat (verify before trusting):** at the time these docs were written the
> code had **not been compiled or run** in this environment (no .NET SDK installed). The
> code is complete and written to be correct, but treat "it builds / it runs" as
> *unverified* until you run it yourself. See [08-reference/verification-log.md](08-reference/verification-log.md).
## Who this is for
A junior engineer who wants to reach mid-level (and start thinking like a senior). It also
works for a mid-level engineer who is new to ASP.NET Core, React, or to this repo.

# Orchard Core Upskill Curriculum
A training lab built from the real Orchard Core codebase, for one specific learner: a **junior fullstack engineer** (CRUD web dev — .NET/C#, React/Node/TS or similar) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, when it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repo is
Orchard Core (v3.0.1) is an open-source, **modular, multi-tenant application framework and CMS for ASP.NET Core**, maintained by the Orchard Core team under the .NET Foundation. It is two products in one repository: a framework for building modular multi-tenant ASP.NET Core apps (`src/OrchardCore/*`), and a full CMS built on that framework as ~95 pluggable modules (`src/OrchardCore.Modules/*`). Each tenant gets its **own dependency-injection container and request pipeline**, built lazily from that tenant's enabled features. Persistence is **YesSql** — a document store over SQL Server/SQLite/MySQL/Postgres where documents are JSON and queries run against explicit *index tables*. UI is rendered through a **display-management** system (drivers produce "shapes", placement files position them, templates can be overridden per theme). It is one of the most instructive large .NET codebases in the wild: real multi-tenancy, real modularity, real versioned-content invariants, real background scheduling — all things interviews probe.

## Status
Accepted
## Context
As we want to base inter-modular communication on asynchronous communication in the form of event-driven architecture, we need some "events bus" to do that.

### 1. In Memory Events Bus
In memory Publish/Subscribe implementation without any external component.

- very easy to implement

#### Cons
- does not support more advanced integration scenarios, everything needs to be implemented
- does not have configuration
- does not have other features (who have messaging brokers)

External middleware component. It could be a low-level broker (like RabbitMQ) or a high-level broker (like MassTransit, NServiceBus).

- only integration with platform code needed

# Interlude
A local Pomodoro timer and Chrome extension with art breaks and customizable messages.
## Try the app
The preview is at http://127.0.0.1:43210. To start it again, run `npm.cmd start` from this folder. If that port is occupied, the server chooses a free port and prints the URL.
## Install the Chrome extension
1. Open `chrome://extensions` and enable **Developer mode**.
2. Click **Load unpacked** and select this project's `extension` folder.
3. Open Interlude from Chrome's extensions menu and click **Start focus**.
The extension folder is self-contained and already built. It does not need the preview server or Node.js. The toolbar icon opens its dashboard.
## Behavior
- Defaults to 60 minutes of focus followed by a 5-minute art break. Settings include 25/5 and 50/10 presets, custom durations, and automatic return to focus.
- Opens a focused full-screen Chrome window for each break. Turn off full screen to use a maximized window. Snooze delays the break five minutes; closing the break returns to focus.
- Edit the message below the artwork, select a painting, rotate the collection, or upload a JPG, PNG, or WebP. Uploaded images are resized locally; no upload leaves the device.
- Chrome alarms and stored deadlines keep the extension running when the dashboard closes. Chrome must remain running. Sleeping computers may delay an alarm; on return, Interlude provides a complete break instead of replaying every missed interval.
- The website preview requires its tab to stay open. It can show an in-page takeover automatically; browser full screen is available through the Preview break button. Install the extension for automatic full-screen windows.
- This is a dismissible Chrome break window, not an operating-system lock. It does not block other apps or cover every monitor.
- All settings, messages, artwork, and daily counters stay in local storage. The website and extension have separate storage.
## Development and checks
`npm.cmd install` installs dependencies; `npm.cmd run build` bundles the UI into `extension/app.js`. `npm.cmd test` covers the timer and service worker with a simulated Chrome API. `node tests/browser-check.mjs` checks the website in an isolated headless Chrome browser with the local server running and writes screenshots to `artifacts`.

# 16. Multi-User Blog Platform
Enterprise patterns demonstrated:
- Registration/login boundary with role-aware session middleware.
- RBAC for `author`, `editor`, and `admin` access.
- State machine for draft -> review -> approved/rejected -> published content workflow.
- Comment moderation queue with approve/reject actions.
- Per-author public page data model and API.

newcodex3/apps/18-team-chat-net/docs/ups.opening:
# Real-Time Team Chat Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Use WebSockets or SignalR for live delivery, but keep message persistence in normal HTTP-backed application services.
- Store message history in Postgres with cursor pagination. Avoid offset pagination because active conversations mutate constantly.
- Track presence in Redis with connection IDs and short TTLs so disconnected clients disappear without manual cleanup.
- Treat typing indicators as ephemeral events with expiry timestamps.
- Reconcile optimistic messages using an idempotent `clientNonce`.
## Production checklist
- Authorize every conversation read/write against membership.
- Deduplicate sends by unique `(conversation_id, client_nonce)`.
- Persist read cursors per user and conversation.
- Fan out socket events only after the database commit succeeds.
- Add backpressure and reconnect logic on the client.
## Interview prompts
- How do you prevent duplicate messages when the client retries?
- Why is cursor pagination a better fit than offset pagination for chat?
- What belongs in Redis versus Postgres?
- How would you rebuild unread counts after a bug?

# E-Commerce Storefront Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Store prices, totals, discounts, and tax in integer minor units. Never use binary floating point for money.
- Model guest carts with a durable anonymous cart ID stored in a cookie.
- Merge guest cart lines into the authenticated user's cart after login.
- Decrement inventory inside a transaction and lock the relevant variant rows.
- Fulfill paid orders from verified Stripe webhooks, not from client redirects.
## Production checklist
- Unique idempotency key per checkout attempt.
- Unique processed webhook event ID table.
- Product variant inventory checked again at checkout time.
- Order status transitions are explicit and audited.
- Admin product writes require elevated roles.

- How do you prevent overselling the last item?
- Why should the webhook create fulfillment side effects instead of the frontend?
- How would you reconcile a payment that succeeded after your server timed out?

# Discussion Forum Upskill Notes
## Core patterns
- Adjacency lists are simple for writes; materialized paths make nested reads and ordering easier.
- Vote deduplication belongs in the database with a unique `(user_id, target_type, target_id)` index.
- Hot ranking combines score and age so new good posts can surface.
- Karma is derived from votes on authored posts/comments.
- Rate limits should live in Redis so every API node shares the same counters.
## Production checklist
- Transactionally update vote rows and cached scores.
- Prevent users from voting more than once on the same target.
- Paginate comments by path and depth.
- Enforce community membership/moderator permissions.
- Tune hot ranking for your product, not just a copied formula.
## Interview prompts
- What are the tradeoffs between adjacency lists and materialized paths?
- How do you keep vote counts correct under retries?
- Why is Redis useful for rate limiting?
- How would you migrate a comment tree model later?

## Core patterns
- Availability is a constrained-resource search over time intervals and table capacity.

- API keys should be hashed at rest and plaintext should only be shown once.
- Rate limits should be tracked per key and endpoint family.
- Webhooks should be delivered from an outbox with retry and backoff.
## Production checklist
- Validate dynamic fields on every entry write.
- Support draft and published views separately.
- Document public API error formats and pagination.
- Sign webhook payloads.
- Keep webhook attempts observable for developers.
## Interview prompts
- What makes a schema-that-defines-schemas difficult?
- How would you version public APIs without duplicating every controller?
- Why hash API keys instead of encrypting them?
- How do webhook retries avoid duplicate side effects for receivers?

| Step | Owner | File | What happens | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Check role | API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Requires Owner role | Needs granular permission model |
| Validate value | API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Accepts unknown setting value | Setting-specific schemas needed |
| Version setting | Domain | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Increments version and audits diff | Race without optimistic locking |
### Flow: Check Permission
| Step | Owner | File | What happens | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Resolve roles | Auth | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Reads user roles from request | Header/auth scaffold only |
| Match action | API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Checks role permissions | No resource scoping |
| Return decision | UI/API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Sends allowed boolean | Must not replace server enforcement |
## Stack Mastery
**Granular permissions:** Roles are bundles; permissions are specific resource/action pairs.

## Core patterns
- Enforce permissions server-side even when the UI hides controls.
- Model permissions as resource/action pairs, not only broad role names.
- Version settings and audit every admin mutation.
- Add optimistic locking to prevent stale admin screens from overwriting changes.
## Production checklist
- Derive role membership from authenticated organization context.
- Validate setting values per key.
- Add audit log search and export.
- Add custom role builder and permission tests.

## Key Flows
### Flow: Queue Manual Sync
| Step | Owner | File | What happens | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Choose connection | UI/API | [App.tsx](../client/src/App.tsx), [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Operator queues sync | Needs permission control |
| Create run | API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Adds queued run | Should be persistent job |
| Process cursor | Worker | Future | Reads provider changes | Cursor bugs cause skipped data |
### Flow: Ingest Webhook
| Step | Owner | File | What happens | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Receive event | Public API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Accepts provider payload | Signature verification missing |
| Idempotency | API | [index.ts](../server/src/index.ts) | Returns event id key | Needs durable dedupe |
| Queue sync | Future worker | N/A | Processes event asynchronously | Provider retries require 2xx fast |

**OAuth token storage:** [schema.prisma](../server/prisma/schema.prisma) stores cipher fields. Real systems encrypt provider tokens.

**Project 3: the layered skeleton from Projects 1–2, now with the skill that quietly
separates juniors from mids — aggregation SQL and dashboard endpoints.** CRUD moves
rows; aggregation answers questions ("how much did I spend on food this month, and am
I over budget?"). This project is where the database stops being a filing cabinet and
becomes a calculator.
Prerequisites: Project 1's FABLE guide (layers, envelope) and Project 2's (filters,
list-state). New here: GROUP BY endpoints, per-category budgets with status math,
date-range filtering, Recharts on the client, and money handling.

| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregation endpoints | `server/src/routes/statsRoutes.js` → `statsController.js` | `/monthly`, `/weekly`, `/by-category`, `/daily-trend` — each one is a GROUP BY you can read. |
| Multiple resources | `expenseRoutes` / `categoryRoutes` / `budgetRoutes` / `statsRoutes` | Four route modules mounted side by side; the app is now big enough that organization pays. |
| Budgets with derived status | budget controller/service | Budget vs. actual → `ok` / `warning` / `exceeded`. Business rules computed from aggregates. |
| Date-range filtering | expense list | `?from=&to=` — inclusive/exclusive boundaries, month edges, timezone traps. |
| Charts | client + Recharts | Turning API aggregates into a bar/pie/line chart, and shaping API responses *for* charts. |

# FABLE Guide — Recipe Manager with User Accounts
**Project 5: the biggest single jump in the curriculum.** Three new dimensions land at
once: **TypeScript** end-to-end, **JWT authentication** (access token + HTTP-only
refresh cookie), and **multi-table writes in a transaction**. Plus the concept that
reshapes every layer: requests now have an *identity*, and some data has an *owner*.
Budget more time here than for Projects 1–4 combined. It's worth it — auth + ownership
+ transactions is the exact skill set the industry means by "mid-level backend."
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript everywhere | `server/src/**/*.ts`, `client/src/**/*.tsx`, shared shapes in `server/src/types/domain.ts` and `client/src/types/recipe.ts` | Types are the contract between layers; watch how they replace guesswork. |
| JWT access + refresh | `services/authService.ts`, `middleware/auth.ts` | Short-lived bearer token in memory, long-lived refresh token in an HTTP-only cookie. Learn *why the split exists*. |
| Route protection, two flavors | `middleware/auth.ts`: `requireAuth` vs. `optionalAuth` | Public browsing works logged-out; favorites/ownership light up when logged in. Read both — the asymmetry is the lesson. |
| Ownership checks | `recipeService.ts` update/delete paths | 403 vs. 404 vs. 401 — three different "no" answers, each meaning something. |
| Knex transactions | recipe create: recipe + ingredients + steps + categories in **one transaction** | Partial writes are corruption. This is the pattern Projects 9–10 build on. |
| React auth context | `client/src/context/AuthContext.tsx` + `services/api.ts` | Login state as app-wide context; token installed via `setAccessToken()`; `withCredentials: true` carries the refresh cookie. |
| Password hashing | `authService.ts` + `models/userModel.ts` | bcrypt, and why the users table must never leak `password_hash` in responses. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + jsonwebtoken + bcrypt.
API on **:4005**, client on **:5175**.
---

# FABLE Guide — Poll / Survey Builder
**Project 11: schema-driven software.** Until now, your apps knew their data shapes at
compile time — a task has a title, a recipe has steps. A survey builder's core object
is **a form defined by the user at runtime**: questions of different types, options,
ordering, and a public-facing renderer that draws UI from that definition. This
"data that describes structure" pattern is the same one behind form builders, CMS page
builders, and workflow designers — it's a genuinely mid-level modeling problem.
This is also the first project with a dedicated **validators layer**: Zod schemas in
`server/src/validators/` applied by `middleware/validate.ts`, and even the env config
(`config/env.ts`) is Zod-parsed. What you *built* in Project 6's Lab 1, you now get to
*read* as an established pattern.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Nested aggregate modeling | survey → questions → options tables | Editing a tree of rows: create/update/delete/reorder children without orphaning anything. |
| Zod validators as a layer | `validators/surveyValidators.ts` + `middleware/validate.ts` | Validation declared once, applied at the route edge — compare with Project 1's hand-rolled service checks. |
| Public vs. builder API split | public survey rendering + response submission with access codes | Two audiences, one database: the owner edits; anonymous respondents see a *published projection*. |
| Response aggregation | results endpoints: counts per option, rating averages, matrix totals | GROUP BY over answers, shaped for charts (Project 3's skill, harder shapes). |
| Deep copy | `POST /api/surveys/:id/duplicate` | Cloning an aggregate: new ids everywhere, relationships preserved. Sneaky-hard. |

# Architecture
## Layers
- `client/` is a React 18 Vite app using TypeScript, Axios, React Query, and CSS Modules.
- `server/src/routes` maps HTTP endpoints to thin controllers.
- `server/src/controllers` extracts request data and returns the standard response envelope.
- `server/src/services` owns business rules such as activation, response limits, aggregation, duplication, and CSV export.
- `server/src/models` contains Knex-only database access.
- `server/src/middleware` centralizes validation and error formatting.
## Data model
Surveys own ordered questions. Choice questions own options. Responses are split into `responses` and `response_answers` so each question type can store the answer shape it needs while preserving relational joins.
The `questions.config` JSONB column stores type-specific settings such as rating ranges, matrix rows and columns, and numeric bounds. This avoids creating many sparse columns while keeping the core question fields queryable.
## API conventions
Every successful response uses:
```json
{ "success": true, "data": {} }
```
Every error response uses:
```json
{ "success": false, "error": { "message": "Readable message", "code": "ERROR_CODE" } }
```
## Tradeoffs
This educational app uses a `x-demo-user-id` header instead of full authentication. Drag-and-drop is represented with up/down reorder buttons so the behavior is understandable without another package.

# FABLE Guide — Multi-User Chat (HTTP Polling)
**Project 12: real-time behavior with no real-time transport.** This chat app has
direct and group conversations, unread counts, read receipts, typing indicators,
presence, reactions, and search — built entirely on plain HTTP requests. That
constraint is the curriculum: you learn **cursor pagination**, **polling loops**, and
**ephemeral state modeling** so precisely that when you later add WebSockets
(Project 19's territory), you'll know exactly what the socket is and isn't buying you.
Most "real-time" features in production apps are, in fact, polling. Knowing when
that's fine is a senior judgment; this project gives you the data to make it.
---
## 1. What is new in this project
| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Cursor pagination, both directions | `GET .../messages` with `before` (history) and `GET .../messages/new` with `after` (polling) | The fix for Project 2's offset-pagination bug, in its natural habitat: an append-heavy feed. |
| The polling loop | client `App.tsx` + `services/api.ts` | Interval fetch with a moving cursor: cheap requests that usually return `[]`. |
| Presence via heartbeat | `POST /api/presence/heartbeat` + `GET /api/presence/status` | "Online" = "heartbeat within N seconds" — presence is *derived from recency*, not stored as a boolean. |
| Ephemeral state with TTL | typing indicators + stale cleanup | State that must *expire*: who cleans it up, and when? |
| Read receipts & unread counts | `POST .../read`, unread math in the service | Per-user-per-conversation watermarks — a `last_read_message_id` beats a `read` flag per message. Verify which this app chose and why. |
| Membership-scoped access | conversation members table | Every message query must check "is the requester a member?" — your first data-access rule that isn't ownership. |
**Stack:** React 18 + Vite + TypeScript / Express + Knex + PostgreSQL + Zod validators.

## Polling model
The active conversation polls `/messages/new?after=messageId` every two seconds. The conversation list polls every five seconds. Presence heartbeat runs every thirty seconds and stores `last_seen_at`. Typing indicators are upserted and treated as expired after five seconds.
## Cursor pagination
Message history uses `before=messageId&limit=30`. The query orders by newest for efficient pagination, then reverses the page so the UI renders oldest first.
## Tradeoffs
This project intentionally avoids WebSockets and full authentication. It uses a demo user header so the data modeling and polling behaviors stay easy to inspect.

**Project 13: the transaction becomes the product.** A storefront looks like CRUD with
nicer CSS, but three problems here are qualitatively harder than anything in a task
app: **guest identity** (a cart for someone with no account), **the checkout

| Pattern | Where it lives | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|

# Architecture
## Layers
- `client/` is a React 18 Vite app using TypeScript, Axios, React Query, and CSS Modules.
- `server/src/routes` maps endpoints to thin controllers.
- `server/src/controllers` extracts ids, headers, params, and bodies.
- `server/src/services` owns cart merge rules, checkout transactions, stock checks, review verification, and admin stats.
- `server/src/models` contains Knex-only data access.

## Checkout transaction
Checkout validates cart contents and stock, snapshots product names and prices, creates the order and order items, decrements stock, and clears the cart inside one Knex transaction.

**Project 14: time is the boss fight.** Booking is the domain where correct-looking
code is wrong in ways users notice: a slot shown twice, a 9:00 that's actually 8:00

# Architecture
## Backend
The Express app follows the required controller/service/model split:
- Controllers parse validated Express requests and return the standard `{ success, data }` envelope.
- Services own business rules: slot calculation, cancellation policy, conflict checks, and notification creation.
- Models contain Knex queries only.
- Middleware handles request context, Zod validation, and centralized error envelopes.
## Data model
Core tables are `users`, `provider_profiles`, `services`, `availability`, `availability_overrides`, `appointments`, and `notifications`.
Appointments store `start_time` and `end_time` as `timestamp with time zone`. Weekly availability stores local `time` values and a provider `timezone` decides how those local times become UTC instants.
## Slot calculation
`slotService.getAvailableSlots` implements the key booking algorithm:
1. Load provider policy and requested service.
2. Pick custom override hours for the date, or recurring weekly availability for the weekday.
3. Convert provider-local date/time windows to UTC.
4. Step through windows by `service.duration_minutes + provider.booking_buffer_minutes`.
5. Exclude past slots and any slots returned by the SQL overlap query.
The conflict query is intentionally explicit:
```sql
select *
from appointments
where provider_id = ?
and status = 'confirmed'
and start_time < ?
and end_time > ?
```
## Frontend
The React app uses Vite, TypeScript, CSS Modules, Axios, and React Query. The first screen is the real provider browsing experience, not a marketing page. The provider settings page demonstrates recurring availability and overrides, while dashboards show the two-sided marketplace views.

# Architecture
## Backend
The Express backend uses thin controllers, service-level business logic, Knex models, Zod validation, centralized error middleware, and a consistent response envelope.
Key services:
- `proxyService`: interpolates environment variables, normalizes params/headers/auth, sends the request with Axios, measures total time, and writes history.
- `collectionService`: manages collection trees, folders, saved requests, duplicate, import, and export.
- `environmentService`: manages active environments and bulk variable replacement.
- `historyService`: provides paginated execution history.
## Data model
The schema includes `users`, `environments`, `env_variables`, `collections`, `folders`, `saved_requests`, and `request_history`. JSON-like request data is stored in `jsonb` columns for headers, params, auth config, request headers, and response headers.
Secret variables stay in the database and are masked in the UI. Collection export intentionally exports saved request data, not environment secrets.
## Variable interpolation
The shared interpolation pattern is:
```ts
template.replace(/\{\{(\w+)\}\}/g, (match, key) => variables[key] ?? match)
```
The backend applies this to URL, query params, header values, body content, and auth fields before dispatching the proxy request.
## Frontend
The React app is a dense tool UI built for repeated use:
- Left panel: collections tree or request history.
- Center panel: tabbed request builder with URL, params, headers, body, and auth.
- Right panel: response status, body, headers, and timing.
CodeMirror is mounted directly in a reusable `CodeEditor` component so JSON request bodies and response bodies use the same editor wiring.

# FABLE Guide — Team Project Management
**Project 16: the enterprise pattern kit — read this one deeply.** Projects 16–20 are
five apps built from the same compact scaffold (~600 lines of server+client core), each
wearing a different domain. The scaffold's point is a set of patterns that separate
"app that works" from "app a company can operate": **soft delete, archive/restore,
audit logs, request context (actor + request id), saved views, bulk operations, role
gates, and a readiness endpoint.** This tasks app is the canonical instance — study it
here, then treat 17–20 as domain-specific labs.
Companion reading: `docs/journal.md` in this folder explains *why* each pattern was
chosen, with trade-offs. Read it after the code tour — it's the voice of the code
reviewer you want to become.
---
## 1. The pattern kit (what to actually learn here)
| Pattern | Where | The idea |
|---|---|---|
| Soft delete | `model.ts` — `softDeleteRecord`, `deleted_at` filtering | Delete hides, never destroys. The model owns the default filter so nobody forgets it. |
| Archive ≠ delete | `PATCH /:id/archive` / `/restore`, `includeArchived` query | Two lifecycles: archived is *done but reportable*; deleted is *hidden from operations*. Conflating them is a classic data-model smell. |
| Request context | `middleware/requestContext.ts` → `Context = {actor, requestId, role}` | Every write can answer "who did this, in which request?" — the prerequisite for audit, debugging, and support. |

| Saved views | `views` endpoints, filters stored as JSON | User-defined filter bundles — the feature that turns a list into a workflow tool. |

# Flow: Database views (filter + board grouping)
Entry point:        None — `filterEntries` and `groupEntriesForBoard` (`src/domain/databaseView.ts:9-28`) have no route; consumed only by tests.
Auth/middleware:    None. Note `Database` has no `workspaceId` (`src/domain/types.ts:61-65`) — scoping would have to go entry → database → page → workspace.
Validation:         `groupEntriesForBoard` validates the property exists and is a select (`databaseView.ts:21-22`) — one of the few explicit domain validations in this repo. `filterEntries` validates nothing: filters naming unknown properties compare `undefined` and silently match/not-match.
Business logic:     1. Filter: every filter must pass (implicit AND, `databaseView.ts:11`); `is`/`is_not` use `===`/`!==` on `unknown`, `contains` stringifies both sides and lowercases (`databaseView.ts:13-15`).
2. Board grouping: one group per select option, entries matched by strict equality (`databaseView.ts:24-27`).
Invariant that should hold: every entry appears in exactly one group. **Doesn't**: an entry whose value is missing or not in `options` appears in *no* group — silently invisible on the board (Notion renders a "No Status" column for exactly this reason).
DB queries:         Entries would live as rows with a jsonb `property_values`; the filter is
`SELECT * FROM database_entries WHERE database_id = $1 AND property_values->>'Status' = 'Doing';`
and grouping is a client-side partition (or `GROUP BY property_values->>'Status'`).
Side effects:       None; pure.
Response:           Filtered entries / `{ option, entries }[]`.
Failure modes:      - `is` with `value: 5` against a stored `"5"` → false: `===` on `unknown` makes type mismatches silent filter misses. The property *type* metadata (`DatabaseProperty.type`, `types.ts:69`) exists and is never consulted during filtering — a number property could be compared numerically, dates chronologically; instead everything is identity-or-substring.
- Renaming a property in `Database.properties` orphans every value: `propertyValues` is keyed by property **name** (`types.ts:77`), not a stable id. This is the flow's data-modeling lesson — see the audit in `docs/reference.md`.
Why it's built this way: Filter-as-data (`DatabaseFilter`) mirrors planr's filter engine at smaller scale.

newcodecjs2/bookr/docs/traces/01-cancel-.opening:
# Flow: Cancel booking
Entry point:        None — `cancelBooking` (`src/domain/bookingService.ts:60-62`) has no callers. There is no cancel route in `src/server/routes.ts`.
Auth/middleware:    n/a (would need one: only the host or the invitee should cancel — no identity model exists to express that).
Validation:         None. `reason` is any string; a booking already `cancelled` can be "cancelled" again with a new reason (idempotent-ish by accident, but the old reason is overwritten).
Business logic:     Returns `{ ...booking, status: "cancelled", cancellationReason: reason }` — a pure copy. Nothing writes it back to `BookingStore`, so even a hypothetical caller must remember to persist.
DB queries:         Would be: `UPDATE bookings SET status = 'cancelled', cancellation_reason = $1 WHERE id = $2;`
Side effects:       None — and three are missing by the repo's own design: no `webhook.delivery` job for `booking.cancelled` (the event type exists at `src/domain/types.ts:82` and `notificationJobs.ts:6`), no cancellation email, no calendar event deletion via `CalendarGateway`.
Response:           The new `Booking` object.
Failure modes:      No validation of current status: a `rescheduled` or already-`cancelled` booking transitions silently. A status state machine (which transitions are legal) is implied by `BookingStatus` (`types.ts:50`) and enforced nowhere.
Why it's built this way: Pure function + caller persists is a fine pattern (compare planr's syncEngine). The problem is the missing caller: cancellation is half a feature. A senior would either wire it or delete it — shipped dead code invites callers who assume the side effects happen.
Focus-area notes:   - **Business logic**: write the legal status-transition table for `BookingStatus`. Which transitions does the type allow that the domain should forbid? (e.g. `cancelled → confirmed`.)
- **System design**: freeing a slot is implicit — availability filters on status (`availabilityEngine.ts:20`), so cancelling *automatically* reopens the slot. Elegant or fragile? (Both: no cache to invalidate, but also nothing prevents the reminder job from still firing for a cancelled booking.)

newcodecjs2/payr/docs/traces/01-api-key-.opening:
# Flow: API key lifecycle
Entry point:        None — `createApiKey`/`verifyApiKey`/`revokeApiKey` (`src/domain/apiKeys.ts:9-45`) have no route callers; the RBAC permissions `api_keys.create`/`api_keys.revoke` (`src/domain/rbac.ts:9-10`) exist for routes that were never written.
Auth/middleware:    n/a (would be `requirePermission(member, "api_keys.create")`).
Validation:         None needed on create (inputs are enums/ids); `verifyApiKey` trusts the caller found the right record.
Business logic:     1. Create: 24 random bytes → base64url secret; prefix `pk|sk` + mode; plaintext returned **once**; record stores `keyHash` (SHA-256) and a display `keyPrefix` containing the first 8 chars of the secret (`apiKeys.ts:15-32`).
2. Verify: not revoked AND `sha256(plaintext) === keyHash` (`apiKeys.ts:39-41`).
3. Revoke: pure copy with `revokedAt` set (`apiKeys.ts:43-45`).
Invariants: plaintext never persisted — holds; revoked keys never verify — holds (`apiKeys.test.ts:13-18` pins it).
DB queries:         Would be: `INSERT INTO api_keys (id, org_id, key_prefix, key_hash, ...) VALUES (...);` and lookup at verify time: `SELECT * FROM api_keys WHERE key_hash = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL;` — note verification needs an index on `key_hash`, which is why hashing (deterministic) rather than salted-bcrypt (non-deterministic) is the industry pattern for high-entropy API keys.
Side effects:       None. Missing per the type model: no `api_key.created`/`api_key.revoked` events pushed (`types.ts:74` declares both), `lastUsedAt` (`types.ts:31`) is never updated by anything.
Response:           `CreatedApiKey` — the one shape that carries the plaintext (`apiKeys.ts:4-7`). Good: the type makes "show it once" explicit.
Failure modes:      - `verifyApiKey` compares hashes with `===` (`apiKeys.ts:40`) — not timing-safe, in the same repo where `webhooks.ts:24` carefully uses `timingSafeEqual`. For SHA-256 of high-entropy input the practical risk is negligible; the inconsistency is the finding.
- Unsalted SHA-256 is fine *only because* the secret has 192 bits of entropy; the same pattern copied to user passwords would be a serious flaw. Know why the entropy argument works.

# Flow: Command palette search
Entry point:        UI event — typing in the palette input → `src/components/CommandPalette.tsx:12-41` (rendered from `src/app/page.tsx:42-55`)
Auth/middleware:    None. Client-only; operates on whatever issues the page already holds.
Validation:         None. `query` is a raw string (`CommandPalette.tsx:24-25`). Nothing needs to be rejected here, but note there is no debounce or length guard — every keystroke re-filters the full list.
Business logic:     1. Parent owns `query` state (`page.tsx:16`) and passes it down.
2. `matches` = issues where `` `${identifier} ${title}`.toLowerCase() `` includes `query.toLowerCase()` (`CommandPalette.tsx:15-17`).
3. Render at most 8 matches (`CommandPalette.tsx:32`).
Invariant: results must come only from issues already scoped to the user's workspace — which holds here only because `page.tsx:13` seeds from a single-workspace fixture, not because anything enforces it.
DB queries:         None executed. The equivalent server-side query would be:
`SELECT * FROM issues WHERE workspace_id = $1 AND (identifier ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%' OR title ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%') LIMIT 8;`
Side effects:       None. Selecting a match calls `onOpenIssue`, which in `page.tsx:47-50` is a placeholder `alert()`.
Response:           n/a (rendered list). Empty query matches everything (every string includes `""`), so the palette shows the first 8 issues before you type.
Failure modes:      - `issues` empty → empty list, fine.
- Very large issue list → O(n) string build + filter per keystroke; no memoization (`matches` recomputed every render).
- No escaping issues since it's `includes`, not regex.
Why it's built this way: Substring match over `identifier + title` is the simplest thing that feels like Linear's palette. A senior would keep exactly this for a first pass but hoist the lowercased haystack out of the per-keystroke loop (or memoize), and make `onOpenIssue` real.
Focus-area notes:   - **TypeScript**: `CommandPaletteProps` (`CommandPalette.tsx:3-10`) is a clean example of a fully-typed component contract — compare with the `unknown`-typed payloads in flow 07.
- **System design**: search lives in the component, not the domain layer. `blockr` (sibling project) has a dedicated `searchIndex.ts`; planr does not. Ask:

# Expense Management System
A learning-oriented clone of Ramp / Expensify / Brex expense workflows, built with
**ASP.NET Core (C#)** and **React**. It demonstrates file uploads, validation,
background processing, a state machine, security, and reporting — with a deliberately
small dependency footprint.
> **Status:** the source is complete but has not been compiled/run in this environment
> (the .NET SDK isn't installed here). Install the .NET 8 SDK to build and run.
---
## What it does
- **Employees** create expenses, attach receipts, and submit them for approval.
- **Managers** approve or reject their direct reports' expenses.
- **Finance** reimburses approved expenses (payment completes in the background).
- **Policy checks** flag or block expenses (receipt required over $25, category limits,
future dates, high-value spend).
- **Reports** summarise spend by status and category, scoped to your role.
### Expense state machine
```
Draft ──submit──▶ Submitted ──approve──▶ Approved ──reimburse──▶ Reimbursing ──(system)──▶ Reimbursed
▲                   │
│                   └──reject──▶ Rejected ──submit──▶ Submitted
└──────── edit (while Draft or Rejected)
```
All transitions go through a single `ExpenseStateMachine` that enforces both the legal
edges and which **role** may trigger each one. Every change is recorded in an audit trail.
---
## Architecture
```
backend/                 ASP.NET Core Web API (.NET 8) — ZERO NuGet packages
Domain/                Entities, enums, the state machine, domain exceptions
Storage/               In-memory DataStore (singleton) + demo seeding
Security/              PBKDF2 hashing, token sessions, custom auth handler
Services/              PolicyEngine, ExpenseService, ReceiptService, Reporting, mappings

A learning-oriented Stripe Billing / Chargebee style dashboard built with C#, .NET minimal APIs, and React.
The implementation focuses on enterprise billing fundamentals:

Frontend:

cd src/Billing.Web
npm install

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line across which things are decoupled: code on one side can change without forcing changes on the other. A **layer** owns a responsibility and depends only inward. Finding boundaries — and spotting where they *leak* — is the core architecture skill.
## The four layers
| Layer | Project | Owns | Must NOT own |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Domain | `ApplicationCore` | Entities, invariants, use-case services, query specs, the interfaces it needs | EF, ASP.NET, HTTP, JSON |
| Infrastructure | `Infrastructure` | EF mappings, migrations, Identity, email, concrete `IRepository` | Business rules |
| Presentation | `Web`, `PublicApi`, `BlazorAdmin` | HTTP, view models/DTOs, auth wiring, rendering | Domain invariants, direct SQL |
| Contracts | `BlazorShared` | Shapes shared client↔API | Behavior |
The dependency rule: **arrows point inward.** `Infrastructure` and the UIs depend on `ApplicationCore`; `ApplicationCore` depends on nothing internal. Proof: [ApplicationCore.csproj](../../src/ApplicationCore/ApplicationCore.csproj) references only small helper libraries (Ardalis.*), never EF Core or ASP.NET.
## Where the boundaries are clean (good examples)
- **Domain ↔ persistence:** the domain declares `IRepository<T>` ([IRepository.cs](../../src/ApplicationCore/Interfaces/IRepository.cs)); `Infrastructure` implements it ([EfRepository.cs](../../src/Infrastructure/Data/EfRepository.cs)). Swap SQL for in-memory by changing one registration ([Dependencies.cs:19-38](../../src/Infrastructure/Dependencies.cs#L19-L38)).
- **Domain ↔ UI shape:** `CatalogViewModelService` explicitly calls itself "a UI-specific service … does not contain any business logic" ([CatalogViewModelService.cs:14-17](../../src/Web/Services/CatalogViewModelService.cs#L14-L17)) and maps entities to view models — keeping presentation concerns out of the domain.
- **Network boundary:** BlazorAdmin runs in the browser and *cannot* reach the DbContext; it must call the API over HTTP ([HttpService.cs](../../src/BlazorAdmin/Services/HttpService.cs)). The compiler + runtime enforce this boundary.
- **Client ↔ API contract:** shared DTOs live in `BlazorShared` so both sides compile against the same shapes without sharing domain internals.
## Where boundaries leak or bend (teachable weak spots)
- **UI decides a domain value:** the checkout's shipping address is constructed in the *page* ([Checkout.cshtml.cs:57](../../src/Web/Pages/Basket/Checkout.cshtml.cs#L57)) and handed to the domain. Address *should* be user input flowing into the domain, not a presentation-layer

# 08 — Interview Prep
This module is first-class, not an afterthought. Target: **mid-level fullstack interviews** (.NET/C# primary; the transferable concepts map to any stack). At least 60% of the question cards here are anchored to real code in this repo, so you practice answering with concrete evidence — "in eShopOnWeb, the `OrderService` does X at line Y" — instead of reciting definitions.
## How mid-level fullstack loops are usually structured
| Round | What they probe | This repo's prep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recruiter/technical screen | Can you talk about your work coherently? | [06-behavioral-star-stories.md](06-behavioral-star-stories.md) |
| Language/runtime deep-dive | Do you understand your tools below the surface? | [01-js-ts-node-deep-dive.md](01-js-ts-node-deep-dive.md) (C#/.NET edition) |
| Frontend | Rendering, state, data-fetching, a11y | [02-frontend-framework-questions.md](02-frontend-framework-questions.md) |
| API / data modeling | REST design, schema, transactions, caching | [03-api-and-data-modeling-questions.md](03-api-and-data-modeling-questions.md) |
| System design | Can you design and reason about tradeoffs? | [04-system-design-from-this-repo.md](04-system-design-from-this-repo.md) |
| Practical coding / debugging / review | Can you actually do the work? | [05-debugging-and-code-review-rounds.md](05-debugging-and-code-review-rounds.md) |
| Behavioral | Judgment, collaboration, ownership | [06-behavioral-star-stories.md](06-behavioral-star-stories.md) |
## The golden rule
**Answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff, and a failure mode — not a definition.**
- Weak: "Clean Architecture separates concerns."
- Strong: "In this repo, `ApplicationCore` defines `IRepository<T>` and `Infrastructure` implements it, so I can unit-test `BasketService` with a fake repo — the tests do exactly that. The cost is more mapping code and indirection; for a thin CRUD app I'd skip it."
The second answer proves you've read and reasoned about real code. That's the mid-level signal.
## How to use this repo as your portfolio of talking points
You may not be able to discuss your employer's proprietary code in an interview. You *can* discuss a public reference app you studied deeply. Treat eShopOnWeb as a shared codebase you can point at: it gives you concrete anchors for architecture, auth, caching, testing, and at least one real security bug you found ([the Flow 7 IDOR](../01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md#flow-7-view-my-order-details-read--the-idor-lesson)).

# eShopOnWeb Upskill Curriculum
A codebase-to-curriculum training lab built on Microsoft's **eShopOnWeb** reference application. It teaches two things at once, always paired:
1. **This repo**: where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill**: why these patterns exist, when they fail, how to recognize them in any codebase — and how to articulate them in a mid-level fullstack interview.
## Who this is for
A junior fullstack engineer (CRUD web dev in .NET/C#, or React/Node/TS moving to .NET) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
## What this repo is (identity in 7 sentences)
eShopOnWeb is Microsoft's official reference application for the free eBook *Architecting Modern Web Applications with ASP.NET Core and Azure* ([README.md](../README.md#L18)). It is a deliberately **monolithic** e-commerce store — catalog, basket, checkout, orders, admin — built on .NET 8 ([global.json](../global.json)). It demonstrates **Clean Architecture**: a dependency-free domain project (`ApplicationCore`), an EF Core data layer (`Infrastructure`), and three UI surfaces — a Razor Pages storefront (`Web`), a JWT-secured minimal-API backend (`PublicApi`), and a Blazor WebAssembly admin panel (`BlazorAdmin`). Persistence is SQL Server via EF Core with two separate DbContexts (catalog vs. identity). It is a *teaching* app: some things are intentionally simplified or deliberately flawed (hardcoded JWT secret, hardcoded checkout address, a `Task.Delay(1000)` in an API endpoint), which makes it an outstanding lab for developing senior judgment — you get to find real flaws in a professionally structured codebase. Development moved to [dotnet/eShop](https://github.com/dotnet/eShop); this repo is stable and safe to dissect. # JavaScript Workbook — Build the Fundamentals
Eight exercises that *use* every fundamental. Each has: the task, a hint ladder (read one hint at a time), a full solution, and a line-by-line explanation. Type the solutions out — don't paste.
---
## Exercise 1 — Shopping Cart Math (arrays, immutability)
**Task:** Given the cart below, write four functions — `addItem(cart, item)`, `removeItem(cart, id)`, `changeQty(cart, id, qty)`, `cartTotal(cart)` — **none of which mutate the input**.
```js
const cart = [
{ id: 1, name: "Mouse",    price: 25,  qty: 1 },
{ id: 2, name: "Keyboard", price: 80,  qty: 2 },
];
```
<details><summary>Hints</summary>
1. "Don't mutate" means every function returns a **new array** — which three array tools build new arrays?
2. Add → spread. Remove → `filter`. Update one → `map` with a conditional spread.
3. Total → `reduce` with a seed of `0`; each item contributes `price * qty`.
</details>
**Solution:**
```js
const addItem   = (cart, item)     => [...cart, item];
const removeItem = (cart, id)      => cart.filter(i => i.id !== id);
const changeQty = (cart, id, qty)  =>
cart.map(i => (i.id === id ? { ...i, qty } : i));
const cartTotal = (cart) =>
cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
```
**Why it works:** `[...cart, item]` copies the array and appends — the original is untouched (verify: `cartTotal(cart)` is the same before and after). `filter` returns only survivors. The `map` line is the most important idiom in the file: untouched items pass through *as-is*; the matching item is rebuilt with `{ ...i, qty }` — a new object with one field replaced. `reduce` starts at `0` and folds each line item in. These four shapes are 90% of state updates you'll ever write (and the *required* style in React).
**Check yourself:** after `const c2 = changeQty(cart, 2, 5)`, what is `cart[1].qty`? (Answer: still `2` — and if it isn't, your map is mutating `i` instead of spreading.)
---

A production-grade Calendly-style booking SaaS built with C# / .NET 9 and React.
## Architecture
```
src/
NetCalendy.Domain/        # Aggregates, Value Objects, Domain Events, Repository interfaces
NetCalendy.Application/   # CQRS commands & queries (MediatR), validators (FluentValidation)
NetCalendy.Infrastructure/ # EF Core + PostgreSQL, repository implementations, services
NetCalendy.Api/           # ASP.NET Core controllers, JWT auth, middleware
tests/
NetCalendy.Domain.Tests/        # Pure domain unit tests (xUnit + FluentAssertions)
NetCalendy.Application.Tests/   # Handler unit tests (NSubstitute mocks)
NetCalendy.Integration.Tests/   # End-to-end API tests (WebApplicationFactory + Testcontainers)
web/                        # React + TypeScript + Vite frontend
```
### Key design decisions
| Concern | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture | Clean Architecture / DDD | Domain is dependency-free; infra depends inward |
| CQRS | MediatR | Decoupled handlers, pipeline behaviors for cross-cutting concerns |
| Multi-tenancy | Tenant ID per row | Simple, performant, no schema management overhead |
| Validation | FluentValidation pipeline behavior | Validated before handlers execute; clean error surface |
| Domain events | `IHasDomainEvents` + MediatR `IPublisher` | Events dispatched after `SaveChanges` succeeds |
| Auth | JWT Bearer | Stateless; tenant + user claims in token |
| Integration tests | Testcontainers (real Postgres) | No mock/real divergence risk |

# Tier 1: Junior Missions
Welcome to Tier 1. Your goal is to map the physical terrain of the codebase. You are not building anything yet; you are learning how to read the map.
---
### Mission 1: The App's Heartbeat
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 10 minutes
**Goal:** Prove that you know how the server determines "who" is looking at the screen.
**The Concept:** Every interaction in this app requires a "badge scan." The server must know who you are before it shows you data or lets you change it. In a normal app, this is a complex JWT validation middleware. Here, it is drastically simplified for training.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:**
We expect to find a function that reads a cookie from the incoming request, looks up a user in the database matching that cookie, and returns their profile. If they don't have a cookie, it should probably default to someone safe so the app doesn't crash during local dev.
**Find It In The Code:**
Open `src/packages/shared/auth.ts`.
Read the `getActiveUser` function (Lines 18-51).
*Annotations to follow:*
- Notice `cookies().get('mock_user_id')`. This relies heavily on Next.js server context.
- Notice the fallback: `where: { username: 'admin' }`. This is a deliberate choice to make local onboarding frictionless, avoiding login screens entirely.
**The Aha Moment:** The server *pretends* someone is logged in if they don't have a cookie, ensuring the developer can immediately see the UI.
**Socratic Checkpoint:**
1. What happens if the `admin` user is deleted from the SQLite database?
2. Does this function run in the user's browser, or on the server?
3. What is the return type of `getActiveUser`?
*How to self-grade:*
1. The app will throw a fatal error: `❌ Critical Setup Error: No admin user found`.
2. It runs entirely on the server. `cookies()` from `next/headers` is a server-only API.
3. It returns a Promise resolving to `ActiveSession`, which contains the `UserRole` and `profileId`.
**Connects To:** Mission 2 (Your First React Component) heavily relies on calling `getActiveUser()`.
---
### Mission 2: Your First React Component
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 15 minutes
**Goal:** Understand how a page fetches data and renders it without any loading spinners.
**The Concept:** Imagine going to a restaurant where the chef already knows what you want, cooks it before you sit down, and hands you the plate the second you pull out your chair. That's a React Server Component.

# Architecture Overview
This project is an internal education operations and learning management platform. It models records and workflows for teachers, students, courses, class sections, enrollments, assignments, submissions, grades, attendance, support notes, intervention plans, jobs, structured logs, audit events, and mock agent analysis.
## Major Modules
- `apps/web`: Next.js App Router UI, route handlers through server actions, layout, pages, and application workflows.
- `packages/db`: Prisma schema, Prisma Client singleton, and deterministic seed data.
- `packages/domain`: business rules, validations, calculations, and risk scoring.
- `packages/agents`: deterministic local mock agent framework and initial agent implementations.
- `packages/observability`: structured log helpers, audit metadata helpers, and anomaly scoring utilities.
- `packages/ui`: small reusable UI primitives and CSS-variable design system.
- `packages/shared`: shared enums, labels, role helpers, and formatting utilities.
## Modular Monolith
The app is intentionally one deployable system with clear internal module boundaries. That makes it easier to learn than microservices while still teaching production ideas:
- domain logic is isolated from React
- data access is centralized through Prisma
- agents are replaceable components with stable interfaces
- UI pages compose services rather than owning business rules
- audit, logs, and jobs are first-class operational concepts
## Data Flow
Typical write flow:
1. User submits a form in `apps/web/app/**`.
2. A server action in `apps/web/lib/actions.ts` parses form data.
3. Zod schemas and domain rules validate the request.
4. Prisma writes to PostgreSQL.
5. Audit events are written for important actions.
6. Next.js revalidates affected routes.
## Request Flow
Pages are React Server Components. They query Prisma directly for read-heavy views and call pure domain functions for derived values such as grade summaries, risk scores, attendance summaries, and workload scores.
## Where Logic Lives
- Business logic: `packages/domain/src`
- Agent logic: `packages/agents/src`
- Database schema and seed: `packages/db/prisma`
- Database client: `packages/db/src/index.ts`

# Phase 1: Architecture Stabilization
Phase 1 was about making the existing MVP easier to extend safely. The product surface stayed mostly the same, but the internal architecture changed from "pages and one giant server-action file orchestrate everything" to a cleaner request path:
`page -> server action -> application service -> domain rule/db/audit`
## Why This Phase Matters
The original codebase had good package boundaries for domain logic and agents, but `apps/web/lib/actions.ts` had become a large coordination file. That is common in early Next.js apps: server actions start small, then slowly absorb validation, authorization, database writes, audit logging, agent orchestration, and redirect behavior.
That pattern is fine for a prototype, but it becomes harder to evolve because:
- authorization is easy to forget
- multi-write operations are not consistently transactional
- pages duplicate read-model calculations
- agent persistence is mixed with UI concerns
- tests have fewer stable seams
- future features require editing one central file too often
Phase 1 creates those seams.
## What Changed
### Added `packages/application`
New package:
```text
packages/application
src/context.ts
src/errors.ts
src/audit.ts
src/services/*
src/queries/*
```
This package owns application use cases. It is intentionally different from `packages/domain`:
- `domain` decides business rules using pure functions.
- `application` coordinates workflows using domain rules, Prisma, permissions, transactions, audit events, and agents.
This is still a modular monolith. Nothing became a microservice.
## Service Layer
The previous `actions.ts` implementation contained all write workflows. These now live in services:
- `teacherService`
- `studentService`

# Learning Guide for Junior to Mid-Level Engineers
Welcome to GlobalWorkforce OS! If you are a junior engineer looking to level up your architectural understanding, this project is designed for you.
## How to Read This Codebase
Don't read it top-to-bottom. Start with the data model (`apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma`). Understand the relationship between `Tenant`, `Company`, and `Worker`.
Next, look at the authentication flow: `apps/api/src/auth`. Understand how a user logs in and receives a JWT.
Then, pick one feature (like `Workers`) and trace a request from the frontend UI (`apps/web/src/pages/Workers`), to the API Client, to the NestJS Controller, down to the Service, and finally to the Prisma query.
## Key Concepts to Master
1. **Multi-Tenancy**: How do we ensure Client A cannot see Client B's data? Look at `TenantGuard` and how `tenantId` is passed into Prisma `where` clauses.
2. **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**: How do we prevent a `WORKER` from approving a payroll cycle? Look at `RolesGuard`.
3. **Validation Boundary**: Where is data validated? Look at the Zod schemas in `packages/shared` and how they are used by React Hook Form (frontend) and validation pipes (backend).
## 10 Learning Tasks to Modify the App
1. **Add a new field**: Add a `middleName` field to the Worker model. Update the DB, backend DTOs, and frontend forms.
2. **Enhance Audit Logs**: Currently, audit logs might only trigger on a few actions. Add an interceptor to automatically log whenever an entity is updated.
3. **Build a Workflow Engine**: When a contract is signed, automatically mark the associated onboarding task as DONE.
4. **Implement Soft Delete**: Instead of deleting workers, implement a `deletedAt` field and update queries to ignore deleted records.
5. **Add Pagination**: The worker list currently returns all workers. Add limit/offset parameters to the API and a paginated table component on the frontend.
6. **Feature Flags**: Introduce a simple feature flag service to hide the "Benefits" tab from certain tenants.
7. **File Uploads**: Replace the simulated document upload with a real integration to AWS S3.
8. **Email Notifications**: Add an event emitter when a support case is created, and simulate sending an email.
9. **Extract a Microservice**: The `SupportCases` domain is fairly isolated. Try extracting it into a separate NestJS app.
10. **Write an E2E Test**: Add a new Playwright test for the payroll approval flow.

# Extension Roadmap
This MVP serves as a learning foundation. A real EOR platform would need the following extensions:
## 1. Real Document Storage
Currently, document uploads are simulated metadata updates. This needs to be integrated with AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage, along with pre-signed URLs for secure access.
## 2. Background Jobs & Workflow Engine
Payroll generation, report compilation, and sending bulk emails should not happen synchronously. A message queue (RabbitMQ, Redis + BullMQ, Kafka) is needed to process these jobs in the background.
## 3. Webhooks & Integrations
Client companies need to synchronize data with their internal HRIS (Workday, BambooHR). We need an outbound webhook system and public API keys.
## 4. Advanced Compliance Engine
Instead of static rules, the compliance engine should be a rule-based system (e.g., using a rules engine library) that evaluates worker country, visa status, and role to dynamically generate required documents.
## 5. Analytics & Reporting
Integrate a proper analytics pipeline (e.g., Snowflake, dbt, Looker) or build materialized views in PostgreSQL for complex payroll and workforce reporting.
## 6. Microservice Extraction
As the team grows, the `Payroll` module is the most likely candidate for extraction into a separate microservice, as it has high security and performance isolation requirements.

# MarketForge
MarketForge is a production-style multi-vendor marketplace codebase. It models a buyer storefront, seller operations portal, and platform admin console with shared domain rules, typed API routes, Prisma persistence, Redis-backed security primitives, and Stripe Connect payment boundaries.
This repository is intentionally scaffolded without installing dependencies or running services. The code is written as if it were a corporate production application, but Docker, npm install, database provisioning, and third-party credentials are left to the learner.
## Stack
- Next.js App Router with React Server Components
- TypeScript with strict compiler settings
- Prisma with PostgreSQL
- Redis for rate limits, refresh-token families, sessions, and cache
- Stripe Connect for marketplace payments and seller payouts
- Zod-style request validation
- Pino-style structured logging
- Vitest and Playwright test targets
## Project Layout
- `app/`: Next.js routes, route handlers, and web entry points.
- `src/components/`: reusable UI components for marketplace, seller, admin, and shell surfaces.
- `src/domain/`: pure business rules: checkout splitting, order state machines, seller approval rules, RBAC.
- `src/server/`: infrastructure adapters for database, auth, payments, cache, validation, logging, and API responses.
- `prisma/`: production-grade relational data model.
- `tests/`: unit, integration, and E2E test targets.
- `docs/`: architecture notes, ADRs, and the older static prototype.
## Learning Order
1. Read `src/domain/orders/order-state.ts` and `src/domain/checkout/pricing.ts`.
2. Read `app/api/v1/checkout/sessions/route.ts` and `src/server/payments/stripe-connect.ts`.
3. Read `src/server/auth/session.ts`, `src/server/security/rate-limit.ts`, and `src/server/auth/rbac.ts`.
4. Read `prisma/schema.prisma`.
5. Read `tests/unit/order-state.test.ts` and `tests/integration/checkout.test.ts`.

npm install
npm run db:migrate
npm run dev

### Mission 1: The App's Heartbeat
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 25 minutes
**Goal:** Identify how a request becomes a rendered page.
**The Concept:** The app heartbeat is like a shopper entering the storefront: the front door is the root layout, the market desk is the localized layout, and the aisles are route files.

# Tier 2: Mid-Level Missions
### Mission 9: State Has a Home and a Reason
**Tier:** Mid-Level
**Time Estimate:** 45 minutes
**Goal:** Decide where each kind of state belongs.
**The Concept:** Storefront state is like inventory paperwork: Spree owns the official order, cookies hold the claim ticket, React Context shows the clerk's current screen, and URLs label the aisle.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:** Read cart context, cart cookies, and listing params. Poor state placement causes stale carts, broken back buttons, or wrong market prices.
**Find It In The Code:** Open `src/contexts/CartContext.tsx:39-184`, `src/lib/spree/cookies.ts:43-60`, and `src/lib/utils/listing-search-params.ts:1-13`.
```ts
const [cart, setCart] = useState<Cart | null>(null); // Browser session view.
const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false); // Pure UI state.
const itemCount = useMemo(() => cart?.items?.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.quantity, 0) ?? 0, [cart]); // Derived state.
```
**The Aha Moment:** Bugs shrink when you can name the rightful owner of every value.
**Socratic Checkpoint:** 1. Who owns durable cart data? 2. Who owns drawer open state? 3. Who owns listing filters? 4. Why is item count derived? 5. Why do cookies matter?

| Cart line items | Spree plus `src/lib/data/cart.ts` | They must persist and remain consistent with checkout. |
| Cart drawer open state | `CartContext` | Multiple header/cart components need the same UI state. |

# Architecture Journal
## 2026-05-04 - Initial System Start
The repository starts as an empty workspace, so the first decision is to create the architecture and documentation structure before code. This mirrors real product work: before a team creates routes, models, and screens, it should agree on the main boundaries and vocabulary.
The initial architecture uses a TypeScript monorepo with a modular monolith backend. A modular monolith is a good learning shape because it teaches service boundaries, domain ownership, authorization, database modeling, and background jobs without introducing distributed systems complexity too early.
The first code pass will create:
- Shared domain helpers in `packages/domain`.
- An Express API in `apps/api`.
- A Next.js frontend in `apps/web`.
- A BullMQ-ready worker in `apps/worker`.
- Prisma schema and seed data for the LMS domain.
- Documentation and walkthroughs written for a junior developer growing toward mid-level engineering.
## 2026-05-04 - Initial Expanded Build
The first implementation pass now has the major product boundaries in place. The most important design decision was keeping definitions separate from activity:
- Course content lives under `CourseVersion`.
- Learner state lives under `Enrollment`, `LessonProgress`, `QuizAttempt`, and `AssignmentSubmission`.
- Certificates are generated records, not booleans.
This matters because real enterprise training systems need historical accuracy. If an employee completed version 1 of compliance training, version 2 should not silently rewrite their record.
The frontend is intentionally a product workspace, not a landing page. It has learner, instructor, admin, reporting, settings, catalog, course, and verification screens. The backend has matching routes for the real workflows. The worker gives the system a place for slow or retryable operations.
The backlog features were implemented as a mix of complete vertical workflows and realistic extension points. This keeps the codebase learnable while still showing how a larger SaaS system grows.

# Initial Architecture Plan
This document comes before the first implementation pass. The point is to make the codebase easier to reason about for a junior developer learning how larger systems are shaped.
## Product Shape
The application is an enterprise learning management and certification platform. Companies create courses, publish structured learning content, enroll learners, track progress, assess learners with quizzes and assignments, issue certificates, and report on compliance or training completion.
The first version is a modular monolith. That means one deployable backend owns the product workflows, but the code is organized into clear modules so it could later be split into services if there were a real operational need.
## System Boundaries
- `apps/api`: Express API, Prisma database access, authentication, authorization, audit logging, and product workflows.
- `apps/web`: Next.js frontend for learners, instructors, admins, and organization admins.
- `apps/worker`: background processors for certificate generation, notification reminders, video processing mocks, and outbox dispatch.
- `packages/domain`: shared TypeScript business rules, policy helpers, completion calculations, quiz scoring, transcript helpers, and feature flag utilities.
- `docs`: architecture plans, architecture journal, feature plans, build journals, walkthroughs, and final system design.
## Architectural Principles
- Content and learner state are separate. A lesson definition is not a learner's progress through that lesson.
- Authoring and publishing are separate. Draft content can change without rewriting the version a learner is enrolled in.
- Quiz definitions and quiz attempts are separate. Attempts are historical records.
- Assignment definitions and submissions are separate. Submissions can be graded, returned, and audited.
- Certificates are generated artifacts. They have identifiers, verification codes, issue dates, and revocation state.
- Reporting is a product module, not a collection of random SQL queries.
- Backend authorization is the source of truth. Frontend checks are only for navigation and experience.
- Audit logs capture security-sensitive and compliance-sensitive events.
- Domain events and an outbox give the codebase a realistic path toward asynchronous workflows.
## Data Model Overview
The core model groups are:
- Identity: users, organizations, memberships, roles, API keys, impersonation sessions.
- Learning content: courses, course versions, modules, lessons, quiz definitions, assignment definitions, rubrics, question banks, content packages, video as

# Architecture Journal
This journal is written for a junior developer who wants to grow into mid-level and senior-level engineering habits quickly. The goal is not only to explain what was built, but to explain why each piece exists, what tradeoffs it creates, and how to keep evolving the codebase without letting it become a pile of unrelated features.
## 2026-05-03 - Project Framing
We are building a fictional Employer of Record platform called GlobalWork. An EOR platform lets client companies hire workers in countries where the client may not have a local legal entity. That domain is useful for growth because it contains many real production concerns:
- Multi-tenant data access: one client must never see another client's workers, payroll, documents, or invoices.
- Workflow state: hires, documents, payroll cycles, expenses, and invoices all move through controlled states.
- Sensitive data: identity documents, compensation, tax details, and bank details require careful permissions and auditing.
- Operational queues: internal teams need dashboards for work that is pending, blocked, overdue, or risky.
- Background work: notifications, payroll cycle generation, invoice creation, document reminders, and email retries cannot all happen inline in HTTP requests.
- Country-specific rules: required onboarding fields, document types, payroll frequency, leave policy, and contract requirements vary by jurisdiction.
The project is intentionally a modular monolith. That means one deployable backend application, but code is organized into domain modules with explicit boundaries. This gives us the learning benefits of enterprise architecture without the accidental complexity of microservices.
## System Shape
The repository is a monorepo:
```txt
apps/
api/      NestJS HTTP API
web/      Next.js web application
worker/   BullMQ background worker process
packages/
config/   shared environment/config parsing

# 01 - Prisma Schema
Source: `packages/database/prisma/schema.prisma`
## Why This File Matters
This is the backbone of the application. When you enter a business-heavy codebase, the database schema is often the fastest way to understand what the product really does. UI labels can be vague and services can hide complexity, but tables and relationships reveal the domain.
In GlobalWork, this file defines the core nouns of an Employer of Record platform: organizations, users, hire requests, workers, documents, employments, payroll cycles, invoices, notifications, audit logs, and internal notes.
## Line-By-Line Reading Notes
Lines 1-8 configure Prisma itself. The `generator client` block tells Prisma to generate a TypeScript client. The `datasource db` block says PostgreSQL is the backing database and the connection string comes from `DATABASE_URL`.
Lines 10-103 define enums. These are not just type niceties. They are business vocabulary. For example, `HireRequestStatus` gives the hiring workflow a controlled set of states. `PayrollCycleStatus` gives payroll a controlled lifecycle. A senior habit is to notice where status fields exist and then ask, "Where are transitions enforced?"
Lines 105-118 define `User`. This model supports both platform users and client users. `platformRole` is optional because a normal client user should not automatically be an internal admin. The relation fields at the bottom show that users can belong to organizations, act in audit logs, review documents, own internal notes, and receive notifications.
Lines 120-138 define `Organization`. This is the tenant boundary for the app. Almost every business record eventually points back to an organization. When learning a multi-tenant system, always identify the tenant key early. Here that key is usually `organizationId`.
Lines 140-151 define `OrganizationMember`. This is the join model between users and organizations. The `@@unique([organizationId, userId])` rule prevents the same user from being added twice to the same organization. The `role` field models client-side roles such as owner, finance, manager, and worker.
Lines 153-166 define `CountryProfile`. This is where country-specific configuration lives. The interesting fields are `requiredWorkerDocuments`, `requiredContractFields`, `annualPtoDays`, and `employerCostRateBps`. This keeps early country logic data-driven instead of scattering `if country === "GB"` checks everywhere.
Lines 168-196 define `HireRequest`. This is the pre-employment workflow object. It captures the proposed worker, job, country, salary, manager, and status. Th

# Architecture Planning: Multi-Tenant Billing Platform
## Product Goal
Build a realistic modular monolith for SaaS billing: organizations can manage plans, customers subscribe to plans, invoices are generated, payments are simulated, and the system records audit trails and background work.
This project is intentionally shaped like an enterprise codebase. The first version is more than a toy MVP, but it still avoids distributed-system complexity that would distract from learning core backend engineering.
## Initial Scope
- Organizations, users, memberships, and role-based permissions.
- Product catalog with plans, prices, coupons, and tax rates.
- Customers, subscriptions, trials, invoices, invoice lines, and payments.
- Mock payment provider with webhook ingestion.
- Idempotency keys for risky write operations.
- Audit logs for important business actions.
- Domain events persisted through an outbox table.
- Background worker for invoice finalization and payment simulation.
- Admin dashboard and customer portal screens.
- Tests for money math, subscription state transitions, and authorization helpers.
## Architecture Style
The app is a modular monolith:
- One deployable API process owns HTTP, authorization, transactions, and domain workflows.
- One worker process consumes background jobs and outbox events.
- The database is PostgreSQL through Prisma.
- Redis and BullMQ provide background job queues.
- The frontend is a React app that talks to the API.
This teaches realistic boundaries without prematurely splitting services. The modules are still designed so that a future team could split them later if scale or ownership demanded it.
## Repository Shape
- `apps/api`: Express API, module routers, request validation, auth middleware, and transaction orchestration.
- `apps/worker`: BullMQ workers for background billing jobs and outbox processing.
- `apps/web`: React dashboard/customer portal.
- `packages/domain`: Shared domain rules, money helpers, state machines, and permission helpers.
- `packages/db`: Prisma schema, migrations, seed data, and Prisma client export.
- `docs`: Architecture, feature plans, build journals, walkthroughs, and final system design.

# Architecture Journal
## 2026-05-04 - Initial System Spine
The first implementation creates the product spine rather than a toy screen. The important choice is that ticket workflow rules live in `packages/domain`, not inside React components or Express route callbacks. A junior developer should notice that this makes the rules testable without a web server or database.
The API is organized by product module: tickets, customers, notifications, and admin. The ticket module owns the highest-risk workflow because ticket updates touch status transitions, assignment, SLA, audit logging, and outbox events. That is why the route file is thin and the service file carries orchestration.
Tenant isolation is represented by `tenantId` on operational tables. The current auth layer resolves a demo user from `x-tenant-slug` and `x-user-email`, then every module uses `req.auth.tenantId`. This is not production authentication, but it teaches the correct data-access habit: queries should be scoped by tenant as close to the persistence layer as possible.
The outbox table was added early because notifications and integrations are common places where enterprise apps become unreliable. Creating the ticket and event in one transaction means the worker can be retried independently without losing the fact that something happened.
The frontend is intentionally dense and workflow-oriented. It is not a marketing page. The first screen is the working queue because support agents live in queues, filters, details, status changes, and replies.
## 2026-05-04 - Verification Discipline
The first tests cover ticket transition rules, SLA state, and authorization helpers. These tests do not prove the whole app works, but they protect the rules most likely to create product bugs when future features arrive.
CI runs typecheck, tests, and build. Database-backed integration tests are deferred until migrations are stabilized, because the first local setup should remain approachable.

# System Design Summary
## Repo Structure
- `apps/api`: Express API for tenant-scoped product workflows
- `apps/web`: React frontend for support agents, managers, and admins
- `apps/worker`: background outbox consumer
- `packages/domain`: framework-independent business rules
- `packages/shared`: validation schemas and DTO types
- `prisma`: PostgreSQL schema and seed data
- `docs`: architecture plan, journal, feature plans, backlog, and walkthroughs
- `tests`: domain-level verification
## Major Module Connections
The frontend calls API endpoints through `apps/web/src/lib/api.ts`. The API resolves a demo actor in auth middleware, then route modules call service functions. Services use Prisma to read/write tenant-scoped data and domain helpers to enforce ticket rules. Important writes create audit logs and outbox events. The worker processes pending outbox events.
## Key Workflows
- Ticket queue: filter tickets, select a ticket, inspect customer/company context.
- Ticket update: validate input, enforce transition and assignment rules, update record, audit, emit outbox event.
- Commenting: create internal notes or public replies; public replies set first response time and emit notification events.
- Email ingestion: receive inbound email, upsert customer, create ticket, store email, emit integration event.
- Audit review: managers/admins inspect recent actions.
## Design Decisions
- Modular monolith over microservices to keep learning focused on boundaries inside one codebase.
- Domain package for reusable business rules.
- Zod schemas for API input validation.
- Prisma schema with tenant IDs on operational tables.
- Outbox pattern from the first version because notifications and integrations are realistic support-desk concerns.
- Dense frontend UI because internal tools are used repeatedly by trained users.
## Tradeoffs
- Header-based demo auth is intentionally temporary.
- Polling worker is simpler than a real queue.
- Search is database filtering, not full-text search.
- Tests currently focus on domain rules instead of database-backed integration.
- The frontend is a single app component to keep the first walkthrough approachable; it should be split as more features land.
