# Auth and Permissions
## Roles
- `support_agent`
- `support_lead`
- `support_manager`
- `observer`
- `customer_portal_user`
## Permission design principles
- permissions are explicit, not inferred from UI
- roles define broad capability
- queue membership narrows operational visibility
- customer-facing access is isolated from internal access
- write actions require server-side policy checks
## Early examples
- agents can view and update tickets in permitted queues
- leads can reassign and escalate within broader scope
- managers/admins can manage queues, policies, and staff settings
- observers can read permitted data but cannot mutate
- customer portal users can only access their own visible tickets and replies
## Current implementation
- Auth uses a signed HTTP-only session cookie.
- Login validates seeded internal user credentials against hashed passwords.
- Every API route resolves the current user on the server.
- Permissions are checked with `assertPermission`.
- Queue visibility is checked with `assertQueueAccess`.
- Managers are global by role.
- Agents, leads, and observers are queue-scoped by membership.
- Reassignment and escalation are reserved for leads and managers in the current implementation.

# Auth And Permissions
Support Hub uses lightweight cookie-based demo auth so the codebase can teach RBAC and workflow boundaries without hiding them behind an external auth SDK.
## Session flow
- Session cookies are read and written in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`.
- `readSession()` reads the `support-hub-session` cookie and parses it into a `SessionUser`.
- `requireSession()` throws `unauthorized()` from `src/lib/http/errors.ts` when no cookie exists.
- `writeSessionCookie()` persists the acting user after `switchSessionUser()` in `src/services/session-service.ts`.
- `src/app/page.tsx` calls `readSession()` and falls back to `getOrCreateSessionPayload()` so the first page request creates a usable demo session.
## Centralized authorization
- Role and visibility checks live in `src/lib/permissions/policies.ts`.
- `assertCanViewTicket()` enforces the customer-portal ownership rule by comparing `session.email` to `ticket.requester.email`.
- `assertCanAddInternalNote()` blocks non-internal users from writing private support notes.
- `assertCanReassignTicket()` restricts assignment and queue transfer to leads and managers.
- `assertCanEscalateTicket()` and `assertCanChangeStatus()` protect operational workflow endpoints.
- `assertCanViewDashboards()` restricts internal reporting access.
## Where permission checks fire
- Session is verified in `src/lib/http/route-helpers.ts` function `requireRouteSession()` before route handlers call services.
- Ticket visibility is re-checked in `src/services/ticket-service.ts` function `getTicketDetail()` after loading the actual ticket detail shape.
- Public replies are checked in `src/services/ticket-service.ts` function `addPublicReply()` with both `assertCanReplyPublicly()` and `assertCanViewTicket()`.
- Internal notes are checked in `src/services/ticket-service.ts` function `addInternalNote()` through `assertCanAddInternalNote()`.
- Reassignment is checked in `src/services/ticket-service.ts` function `reassignTicket()` through `assertCanReassignTicket()`.
- Dashboard access is checked in `src/services/dashboard-service.ts` function `getOverviewDashboard()`.

# Junior SWE Onboarding Guide
This guide is for a junior engineer opening the Support Hub codebase for the first time and trying to answer a practical question:
How does this app actually work, and where should I look when I need to change something?
The short answer is:
1. The UI starts in `src/app/page.tsx`
2. The main client workspace lives in `src/components/support-hub-client.tsx`
3. The client talks to REST endpoints through `src/hooks/use-support-hub.ts`
4. API route handlers live in `src/app/api`
5. Those handlers validate requests and call service functions in `src/services`
6. Services call repositories in `src/repositories`
7. Repositories call Prisma models defined in `prisma/schema.prisma`
If you keep that pipeline in your head, the rest of the repo becomes much easier to navigate.
## What this app is
Support Hub is an internal support-operations app for one company. It is not just CRUD. The important behaviors are:
- tickets move through workflow states
- permissions differ by role
- customer-visible replies and internal notes are separated
- SLA deadlines are tracked and recalculated
- escalations are first-class records
- operational history is written on purpose, not inferred later
That is why the codebase has more layers than a small demo app.
## The mental model to use while reading
When you read this repo, think in terms of responsibilities:
- UI files render data and trigger actions
- route handlers accept HTTP requests
- validation files reject bad input
- auth files identify the acting user
- permission files decide what that user may do
- service files decide how the business workflow changes
- repository files decide how data is loaded and written
- Prisma schema files decide what data can exist at all
If you ever see business rules drifting upward into the UI, that is usually a smell in this codebase.

Session signing and verification live in [src/lib/auth/session.ts](/c:/Users/Owner/Desktop/zz4/src/lib/auth/session.ts). `createSignedSessionToken()` signs the JWT cookie after [src/services/authService.ts](/c:/Users/Owner/Desktop/zz4/src/services/authService.ts) authenticates the password, and `getServerSession()` plus `requireServerSession()` are the shared entry points used by API routes such as [src/app/api/requests/route.ts](/c:/Users/Owner/Desktop/zz4/src/app/api/requests/route.ts) and [src/app/api/approvals/queue/route.ts](/c:/Users/Owner/Desktop/zz4/src/app/api/approvals/queue/route.ts).

# Auth And Permissions
Auth flow:
- Login input is validated in `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts` by `loginSchema`.
- Credentials are checked in `src/services/authService.ts` inside `login()`.
- User lookup and session creation happen in `src/repositories/authRepository.ts` through `findUserForLogin()` and `createSession()`.
- The session cookie name and security flags are defined in `src/lib/auth/cookies.ts`.
- Session resolution for later requests happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `resolveActorFromRequest()`.
Permission enforcement:
- The role matrix is centralized in `src/lib/permissions/policy.ts` in `permissions`, `hasPermission()`, and `assertPermission()`.
- API routes call `src/lib/middleware/withPermission.ts`, which first authenticates through `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts` and then calls `assertPermission()`.
- Billing routes enforce billing permissions in:
`src/app/api/billing/accounts/route.ts`
`src/app/api/billing/invoices/route.ts`
`src/app/api/billing/subscriptions/[subscriptionId]/status/route.ts`
- Onboarding routes enforce onboarding permissions in:
`src/app/api/onboarding/employees/route.ts`
`src/app/api/onboarding/tasks/[taskId]/complete/route.ts`
- Internal job routes enforce operational permissions in:
`src/app/api/internal/jobs/route.ts`
`src/app/api/internal/jobs/run-pending/route.ts`
Why permission checks appear in both middleware and services:
- The first check happens at the route boundary in `src/lib/middleware/withPermission.ts` so unauthorized requests are rejected before business logic runs.
- Sensitive services such as `src/services/billingService.ts` and `src/services/onboardingService.ts` call `assertPermission()` again near the top of their methods so the service layer stays safe if another caller is added later.
Ownership and data isolation:
- This project does not implement multi-tenancy in v1. The app is modeled as one company operating one internal tool.
- Ownership scoping still exists for employee self-service reads. The scoping logic lives in `src/repositories/onboardingRepository.ts` inside `buildEmployeeProfileAccessWhere()`.
- `listEmployeeProfilesForActor()` in `src/repositories/onboardingRepository.ts` uses that helper before issuing the Prisma query, which prevents an `EMPLOYEE` actor from listing another employee's onboarding profile.
- Task mutation ownership is enforced in `src/services/onboardingService.ts` inside `completeTask()`, where the service compares `task.employeeProfile.userId` to `actor.userId` before allowing self-service updates.

Session flow:
- Session resolution starts in `src/lib/auth/session.ts`.
`getSessionContext()` reads the `compliance_portal_demo_session` cookie and calls `resolveSessionContext()`.
- `resolveSessionContext()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` finds the selected `SessionProfile`, active `Tenant`, `User`, and optional `Membership`.

`src/app/api/policies/route.ts`

RBAC enforcement:
- The permission vocabulary is centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`.
`permissions` defines the allowed actions.
`orgRolePermissions` maps org roles to allowed actions.
`platformRolePermissions` grants `PLATFORM_ADMIN` a platform override.
- `hasPermission()` in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` first checks platform permissions, then falls back to the active tenant membership role.
- `requirePermission()` in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` throws `AppError(403, "FORBIDDEN", ...)` before the service performs the mutation.
Where authorization actually fires:
- Policy creation and publication are gated in `src/services/policy-service.ts`.

- Reporting is gated in `src/services/report-service.ts`.

# Auth And Permissions
Authentication starts in `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, which parses `loginRequestSchema` from `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts` and then calls `authService.login()` in `src/services/authService.ts`. Password verification happens in `verifyPassword()` in `src/lib/auth/password.ts`. Session issuance uses `createOpaqueSessionToken()`, `hashSessionToken()`, and `signSessionToken()` from `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, and the signed token is written as the `procureflow_session` cookie in the login route.
Session resolution is centralized, not spread across pages and routes:
- API requests go through `withRouteAuth()` in `src/lib/http/route.ts`.
- `withRouteAuth()` calls `resolveSessionFromRequest()` in `src/services/authService.ts`.
- `resolveSessionFromRequest()` reads the cookie and delegates to `resolveSessionFromSignedToken()` in the same file.
- `resolveSessionFromSignedToken()` verifies the JWT, hashes the embedded opaque token, loads the backing session row through `authRepository.findSessionByTokenHash()` in `src/repositories/authRepository.ts`, and then reloads membership through `authRepository.findMembershipForUser()`.
- Server-rendered pages use `requirePageSession()` in `src/lib/auth/page-session.ts`, which shares the same `resolveSessionFromSignedToken()` path instead of inventing a second auth mechanism.
Role-based access control is explicit and centralized:
- The source permission vocabulary lives in `requirePermission()` and `rolePermissionMatrix` in `src/lib/validation/authSchemas.ts`.
- App-facing guards adapt that contract in `assertPermission()` inside `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`.
- Route-level checks happen in `withRouteAuth()` in `src/lib/http/route.ts`, which accepts `options.permission` such as `"vendor.read"`, `"purchaseOrder.approve"`, or `"report.export"`.

This folder is a permanent learning layer for this repository. It does not replace the existing README, architecture notes, or training docs. It gives you four different ways to study the same codebase so you can build stronger engineering judgment instead of only memorizing file names.

# Product User Stories For ApplyPilot
This folder contains 25 implementation-ready user stories for ApplyPilot. They are written as if a product owner were assigning progressively harder work to a mid-level engineer, but each implementation plan is detailed enough for a junior developer to follow carefully.
No story in this folder has been implemented. These are plans only.
## How To Use These Stories
For each story:
1. Read the product goal.
2. Open every file listed under "Files You Will Likely Touch."
3. Write your own one-paragraph implementation plan before reading the provided plan.
4. Compare your plan to the provided plan.
5. Implement in a branch only when you are ready.
6. Run the listed tests or verification steps.
7. Ask for code review before merging.
## Difficulty Progression
- Stories 1-5: small CLI, text, parser, or validation improvements.
- Stories 6-10: reporting and read-only features that use existing data.
- Stories 11-17: medium features that add command options, helper functions, or artifact metadata.
- Stories 18-22: hard features involving new state, recovery behavior, privacy, or workflow checkpoints.
- Stories 23-25: expert-level product features with architectural implications.
## Important Product Rule
ApplyPilot automates job applications. That means safety, privacy, and user trust are product requirements, not optional engineering polish. Any feature that changes auto-apply behavior should be reviewed for:
- accidental submissions
- repeated submissions
- leaked personal data
- unsafe domains
- retry loops
- poor failure visibility

- CLI commands: `src/applypilot/cli.py`
- Pipeline stages: `src/applypilot/pipeline.py`
- SQLite state: `src/applypilot/database.py`
- Apply workflow: `src/applypilot/apply/launcher.py`
- Agent result parsing: `src/applypilot/apply/agents/parsing.py`

# Store Selection and Render Controls: Zustand State Architecture
As an application grows, managing state solely within local components leads to prop-drilling hell and fragmented business logic. Selecting the right architectural home for each piece of state (local, lifted, URL, global, server) is a key senior skill.
---
## Global State Modeling with Zustand
Zustand is a lightweight, hook-based state management library that uses pure closure stores. Unlike React Context, Zustand bypasses the Context provider boundary completely, allowing components to subscribe to precise slices of global state and avoid unnecessary re-renders.
Let's inspect our authentication store:
[frontend/src/stores/authStore.ts:36-43](frontend/src/stores/authStore.ts#L36-L43):
```typescript
export const useAuthStore = create<AuthState>()(
persist(
(set, get) => ({
user: null,
accessToken: null,
isAuthenticated: false,
```
### Why This Architecture Works:
1. **Direct Subscriptions**: Components can subscribe to the exact fields they need. If a component reads only `isAuthenticated`, it will not re-render when `accessToken` changes.
2. **Outside React Scope**: The store's set/get closures exist independently of React component life-cycles, allowing you to read state outside React components (such as inside Axios interceptors).
3. **Built-in Persistence**: Using the `persist` middleware automatically syncs the state object with standard localStorage, maintaining user sessions across page reloads.
---
## Using Precise Selectors to Limit Re-renders
A common junior mistake is importing the entire store object inside components:
```ts
// Illustrative — not from the repo
const state = useAuthStore(); // Bad! Component will re-render on ANY store changes!
```
To limit renders, you must utilize precise **Selector Functions** to pull only the required slice:
```typescript
// Illustrative — not from the repo
const user = useAuthStore((state) => state.user); // Good! Re-renders ONLY if user changes!
```
> **Senior aside:** *Always define custom hooks or precise selectors when reading from Zustand stores. This decouples components from the store's internal layout, allowing you to refactor store fields without modifying every UI file.*

# Extension Roadmap - GlobalWorkforce OS
GlobalWorkforce OS is designed to be easily extensible. Below is the strategic technical roadmap outlining future architecture enhancements, scaling patterns, and product feature integrations.
---
## 1. Production Document Storage
* **Current State**: Document metadata is stored in PostgreSQL, and files are referenced using local path placeholders.
* **Production Path**: Integrate **AWS S3** or **Google Cloud Storage** bucket managers:
* Generate signed upload URLs on backend: `GET /api/documents/signed-url`.
* Upload directly from the React client to bucket vaults to keep API traffic light.
* Encrypt files at rest (SSE-KMS) to meet HIPAA / GDPR criteria.
## 2. Distributed Workflow & Compliance Rule Engine
* **Current State**: Compliance checklists are statically defined per country, and task completion is handled inline.
* **Production Path**:
* Integrate **Temporal.io** or a BPMN engine (such as Camunda) to orchestrate complex onboarding tasks (e.g. background checks, local tax submissions, physical laptop shipments).
* Build a regional rules engine utilizing a DSL (Domain Specific Language) to dynamically evaluate local statutory laws (such as calculating overtime rates based on regional work hours in California vs. France).
## 3. Background Processing & Distributed Tasks
* **Current State**: Automation occurs synchronously inside HTTP requests.
* **Production Path**:
* Implement **BullMQ** (powered by Redis) or **RabbitMQ** to handle background queues.
* Offload long-running tasks: generating PDF payslip files, verifying bank accounts, emailing onboarding notifications, and syncing payroll sheets to external systems.
## 4. Feature Flags & Progressive Rollouts
* **Current State**: Features are toggle-locked purely by user role.
* **Production Path**: Integrate **LaunchDarkly** or an open-source alternative like **Unleash**:
* Allow client companies to selectively toggle features (such as retirement benefit enrollment modules) or test new payroll aggregators for specific departments.
## 5. Observability & Telemetry
* **Current State**: Logs are logged to stdout using NestJS Logger.
* **Production Path**:
* Integrate **OpenTelemetry** to export traces and metrics.
* Setup Prometheus & Grafana to monitor DB queries, API response latencies, and transaction error rates.
* Stream audit logs to SIEM systems (like Datadog, ELK, or Splunk) for immutable corporate audit tracking.

A local, personal Chrome extension that fills in the repetitive parts of job application forms — name, email, phone, links, education, work history — from a profile you control. - No backend, API keys, analytics, or app-initiated network uploads. Values filled into a website are visible to that website and may be transmitted by it before submission.
- Saved profiles live in `chrome.storage.local`; editor drafts use extension-local storage. Audio stays in the extension's local IndexedDB until you download it.
- It never clicks Submit, Apply, Continue, Next, or Finish.
- It only runs on a tab after you click the extension icon — it doesn't run in the background on every page you visit.
## 1. Install it
```sh
npm ci
npm run build
```
Then in Chrome:
1. Go to `chrome://extensions`.
2. Turn on **Developer mode** (top right).
3. Click **Load unpacked**.
4. Select the `dist` folder (created by `npm run build`).
5. Pin **eli apply mate** to your toolbar so it's one click away.
Whenever you pull code changes later, run `npm run build` again and click the reload icon on the extension's card in `chrome://extensions`.
Requires Node.js 22.12+ to build and desktop Chrome 120+ to run. Keep the same unpacked extension folder when updating to retain local data. Back up profiles and download important recordings before uninstalling.
## 2. Set up your real profile
The extension starts with a **blank draft and autofill disabled**. Existing profiles also need review after upgrading from v0.2:
1. Right-click the extension icon → **Options** (or find it from the extension's card in `chrome://extensions`).
2. Enter contact information and US authorization using the guided fields. Edit education, work history, optional EEO answers, and skill years in the full JSON editor.
3. Review your details, select **I reviewed this profile...**, then **Save**. Invalid dates, email/URLs, and sample contact details cannot be enabled for autofill.
**Multiple versions:** if you keep more than one resume (e.g. frontend vs. backend), create a separate profile version for each:
- **New version** starts blank.
- **Duplicate** copies the current editor contents, including valid unsaved edits.
- **Import JSON file** reads a local `.json` profile (validated first) and makes it active. New, imported, and duplicated profiles require review before autofill.
- **Export** downloads the visible editor contents, including an unfinished draft. Tr

# Current implementation: v0.3
Updated September 4, 2026. This is the maintained implementation map. The onboarding, Fable, and training materials describe earlier versions. See [README](../README.md) for installation and usage, and [fix verification](app-review-2026-09-04/FIXES.md) for evidence and remaining checks.
## Runtime and entry points
This is a desktop Chrome Manifest V3 extension using React 18 and TypeScript. Node 22.12+ builds it with Vite 7 and esbuild. Chrome 120+ is the declared runtime minimum.
| Entry | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `popup.html` / `src/popup/Popup.tsx` | Profile selection; explicitly triggered fill, detect, undo, and review; recorder launcher |
| `options.html` / `src/options/Options.tsx` | Guided contact/authorization editing, full profile JSON, version management, draft protection, recovery import/export |
| `recorder.html` / `src/recorder/Recorder.tsx` | Persistent recorder tab, source selection and permissions, input meter, recording controls, local audio library |
| `src/background/serviceWorker.ts` | Sender-checked profile messages and installation metadata |
| `src/background/profileStore.ts` | Serialized initialization, migration, reads, mutations, revision checks, and recovery |
| `src/content/contentScript.ts` | Injected on demand; serialized scan/fill/review/undo requests |
| `src/content/scanner.ts`, `domLabels.ts` | Visible native controls, scoped labels and groups, stable private element identities, accessible frames/open shadow roots |
| `src/shared/fieldMatchers.ts` | Deterministic, conservative field-to-profile matching |
| `src/content/filler.ts` | Native setters/events, eligibility and acceptance checks, last-batch undo |
| `src/sidebar/renderSidebar.ts` | Review counts, field navigation, focus handling, structural debug export |
| `src/recorder/engine.ts`, `database.ts` | Recording state machine and transactional audio chunk storage |
`manifest.json` requests only `activeTab`, `storage`, and `scripting` by default. `tabCapture` is optional and requested from the recorder's Start action. Microphone access uses Chrome's ordinary `getUserMedia` permission prompt. There are no persistent host permissions, static content-script registrations, offscreen pages, external messaging entries, or backend services.
## Profiles and drafts
Saved profiles use `chrome.storage.local.profileStore`, schema version 2. Each version has a name, ID, timestamps, `configured` flag, and revision. The schema version stays at 2 for compatible existing profile data; missing new metadata is normalized conservatively. First-run/

# Fable Code Review — eli apply mate
Review date: 2026-07-03 · Reviewed by: Claude (Fable 5) · Scope: full codebase at `v0.1.0`
This folder documents a full read-through of the extension source: architecture notes,
concrete findings (bugs and risks, each with file/line references), and suggested
improvements ordered by value.
## Contents
| File | What's in it |
| --- | --- |
| [01-codebase-overview.md](./01-codebase-overview.md) | How the extension is put together — data flow, module map, design strengths |
| [02-findings.md](./02-findings.md) | Bugs, correctness risks, and privacy notes found during review |
| [03-improvements.md](./03-improvements.md) | Suggested improvements, prioritized |
## TL;DR
The codebase is small (~1,200 lines of TypeScript), deterministic, and genuinely cautious —
the "never submit, review first, local only" promises in the README are honored by the code.
Types are clean, module boundaries are sensible, and the escape-hatch behaviors (rollback,
review sidebar, confidence gating) are real, not decorative.
The most important findings:
1. **Shallow profile validation can crash the matcher** — `validateCandidateProfile` never
checks inside the `education`/`experience` arrays, so a hand-edited profile with a
malformed entry throws inside `formatDate` during autofill (findings #1).
2. **Rollback entries are recorded for selects that were never changed**, inflating the
"Cleared N" count and re-dispatching events on untouched fields (findings #2).
3. **Years-of-experience skill matching uses substring `includes`**, so a saved skill
`java` would match a "years of JavaScript" question with high confidence (findings #3).
4. **`<all_urls>` content-script injection contradicts the extension's own privacy story** —
`activeTab` + on-click injection would fit the "explicit click" model better
(improvements #1).

This document explains the live-chat project in detail: architecture choices, data flow, and a build-from-scratch path for junior developers.
## 1. Product Goal
Build a real-time support platform with:
- multi-room chat
- typing indicators
- read receipts

## 2. System Architecture
## 2.1 Components
- Express API (`server/src/server.js` + routes)
- Socket.IO realtime server (`server/src/socket.js`)
- SQLite persistence (`server/src/db/database.js`)
- React client (`client/src/App.jsx`)

- REST endpoints for CRUD/read models/uploads
- websocket events for realtime collaboration
Why single server:
- easiest local setup

- SQLite is source of truth for users, rooms, messages, read receipts.

Tables:

- `rooms`
- `room_participants`
- `messages`

# 06 — Exercises Against This Codebase
Reading reviews doesn't build skill; fixing the code does. These exercises are ordered by
difficulty and target the live `.NET` implementation (plus the migrated web app) unless
noted. Each has acceptance criteria — treat them as the PR description you'd write.

## Exercise 0 — Put the project under real version control (30 min)
1. Create a git repo **at the project root** (`globalhire-lite/`), not your home directory.
2. Write a `.gitignore` covering `node_modules/`, `bin/`, `obj/`, `*.log`,
`*.tsbuildinfo`, `.env` (keep `.env.example`).
3. Commit the current state. Then, in a second commit, **delete every commented-out
original file** (`apps/`, `packages/`) — they live in commit #1 forever.
4. From now on, every exercise below is its own branch + commit(s) with messages that
explain *why*.
**Acceptance:** `git log` tells the story; `grep -r "MIGRATION_NOTE" .` returns nothing;
no log/env/build files tracked.

### 1.1 Fix the stuck `useLoad` hook
In `GlobalHireLite.Web/src/App.tsx`: reset `error` when a reload starts, add a `loading`
flag, and add effect cleanup (a `cancelled` flag or `AbortController`) so a slow response
for worker A can't overwrite worker B's page.
**Acceptance:** navigating quickly between two worker detail pages always shows the right
worker; a failed request followed by a successful reload clears the error; no React
"setState on unmounted component" warnings.
### 1.2 Stop swallowing activation errors
`api.activateWorker(worker.id).catch(() => undefined)` hides messages like "Employment
contract must be SIGNED before activation."
**Acceptance:** failed activation shows the server's message to the user; the Activate

# Fable — A Guided Review of GlobalHire Lite
This folder is a structured code review of the `globalhire-lite` codebase, written with a
specific goal: **take a junior software engineer and pull them toward mid/senior level for
CRUD web-app development jobs.** Every observation about this codebase is paired with the
general principle behind it, so you can carry the lesson to any Express/ASP.NET/Rails/Django
job you land.
## What you're looking at
GlobalHire Lite is an Employer-of-Record (EOR) demo app: hire international workers, run
onboarding, approve leave/timesheets, calculate payroll, generate invoices, offboard.
It's a genuinely good domain for learning because it has everything a real CRUD job has:
multi-tenancy, role-based access, workflow state machines, money math, and audit trails.
The repo contains **two complete implementations** of the same product:
| | Original | Migration |
|---|---|---|
| Location | `apps/api` + `apps/web` | `migrated-dotnet/` |
| Backend | Node, Express, TypeScript, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Zod | C#, ASP.NET Core Minimal API, in-memory store |
| Frontend | React, TanStack Query, React Hook Form, Tailwind | React, hand-rolled `useLoad` hook, plain CSS |
| Status | **Entirely commented out** (every line prefixed with `//`) | **The live code** |
That migration decision — commenting out 88 files instead of using version control — is
itself one of the biggest lessons in this repo. See `04-overengineering-and-complexity.md`.
## Reading order
1. **[01-codebase-overview.md](01-codebase-overview.md)** — the domain, the architecture of both implementations, and how a request flows through each. Read this first.
2. **[02-what-is-done-well.md](02-what-is-done-well.md)** — the patterns worth stealing: state machines, tenant scoping, idempotency, business-rule tests, batched queries.
3. **[03-what-needs-improvement.md](03-what-needs-improvement.md)** — real bugs and gaps: broken auth, missing authorization checks, mass assignment, float money, thread safety, validation. Each one is a category of bug you WILL meet on the job.
4. **[04-overengineering-and-complexity.md](04-overengineering-and-complexity.md)** — where the code is more complicated than the problem: the comment-out migration, stringly-typed errors, anonymous response shapes, over-fetching list endpoints.
5. **[05-junior-to-senior-playbook.md](05-junior-to-senior-playbook.md)** — the general skills this codebase illustrates, organized as "what a junior does / what a senior does" for each CRUD competency.
6. **[06-exercises.md](06-exercises.md)** — concrete refactoring and feature

# Architecture
## System Overview
GlobalHire Lite is an npm-workspace monorepo:
- `apps/api`: Express API, Prisma, auth, workflow services
- `apps/web`: React dashboard app
- `packages/shared`: shared Zod schemas and TypeScript types
The API follows `routes -> controller/service -> Prisma`. Controllers and route handlers stay thin; business rules live in service files such as `workers.service.ts`, `payroll.service.ts`, and `leave.service.ts`.
## Database Model
Most business entities are scoped to `Organization` either directly or through `Worker`. This supports multi-tenant behavior:
- Organization owns workers, payroll runs, invoices, users, and audit logs.
- Worker owns employment, onboarding tasks, documents, leave, timesheets, payroll items, and offboarding cases.
- CountryRule stores demo compliance/payroll assumptions.
## Auth and RBAC
Auth uses JWTs stored in HTTP-only cookies. Middleware exposes:
- `requireAuth()`
- `requireRole([...])`
- `requireOrgAccess()`
I intentionally kept authorization explicit and readable. In a real EOR product, I would likely move toward policy-based authorization or Postgres row-level security, but for this project I wanted understandable code and testable route guards.
## Multi-Tenant Scoping
Client users are scoped by `organizationId`. Platform admin and EOR specialist can operate across organizations. Workers can only access their own worker record and related data.
The backend is the source of truth for scoping. The UI also hides irrelevant navigation to make demos cleaner.
## Workflow Design
The app uses enum statuses and service-level transition checks:
- Onboarding: `NOT_STARTED -> SUBMITTED -> APPROVED/REJECTED`
- Payroll: `DRAFT -> CALCULATED -> APPROVED -> LOCKED`
- Offboarding: `REQUESTED -> APPROVED -> COMPLETED`
I did not add a state-machine library because the workflows are small. If the product grew, I would introduce a formal state-machine or policy layer.
## Payroll Design
Payroll calculation lives in `payroll.service.ts` because it has important business rules:
- Only `ACTIVE` workers are included.
- Only approved timesheets affect overtime.
- Payroll cannot be approved before calculation.

# Pure JS/TS/React Rewrite System Architecture
This document outlines the conceptual system architecture for rewriting the Review Board application purely with modern JavaScript/TypeScript, React, and adjacent enterprise web frameworks.
---
## 🛠️ Complete Technology Stack Selection
### 1. Front-End / Client Layer
*   **Framework**: **Next.js App Router** (React 19 ecosystem) for hybrid Server-Side Rendering (SSR), static site generation, and optimized client bundles.
*   **Styling**: **Tailwind CSS** + **shadcn/ui** (Radix UI primitives) to build a beautiful, accessible, responsive, premium glassmorphism interface.
*   **State Management**: **Zustand** for global client states (dashboard configs, panel collapse flags) and **React Query (TanStack Query)** for robust server-state caching, prefetching, and automatic mutations syncing.
*   **Rich Text Editor**: **Lexical** or **TipTap** for editing markdown fields with real-time bracket-matching and auto-save capabilities.
### 2. Back-End / API Layer
*   **Runtime & Framework**: **Node.js** running **NestJS** (TypeScript) to construct a clean, highly structured, modular, dependency-injected enterprise REST API.
*   **Database ORM**: **Prisma ORM** for fully type-safe schema modeling, database relations mapping, and lightning-fast database migrations.
*   **Real-time Communication**: **Socket.io** or **native WebSockets** for push synchronization (e.g. comment additions, review publishing events, and issue state updates across active user sessions).
### 3. Asynchronous Task Worker Layer
*   **Background Jobs & Queues**: **BullMQ** (Node.js/Redis backed) to run intensive non-blocking operations asynchronously (e.g. parsing massive Myers diff file uploads, preparing email payloads, triggering outgoing webhook dispatches).
### 4. Database & Infrastructure Services
*   **Primary Database**: **PostgreSQL** for relational schemas, composite indexes, JSONB fields, and transaction isolations.
*   **In-Memory Store / Cache**: **Redis** for rate-limiting, session states, BullMQ job metadata, and short-term API response caching.
*   **Object Storage**: **AWS S3** (or local **MinIO** clusters) to house raw diff patches and uploaded screenshots/attachments.
*   **Containerization**: **Docker** + **Docker Compose** for local dev pipelines, and **Kubernetes** for cloud deployments.
---
## 📐 Service Architecture Layout
Our JS/TS rewrite is partitioned into core decoupled services communicating via a central API Gateway:

# 04 — Junior → Senior Roadmap
The review as a training plan: what's missing entirely, the habits that separate levels, and exercises on *this* repo (you level up by fixing real flawed code, not reading about it).
## Missing entirely (absences, not bugs)
- **Tests — zero.** No file. No unit tests on the tax math (the riskiest code), no integration test on the tenant boundary. This is why every [02](02-bugs-and-security.md) bug survives. Start: unit-test the pure functions (`computeProgressiveTax`, `toMinorUnits`, the CSV mapper — no DB needed, exposes the float bugs immediately); integration-test the invariants that are broken ("Org A can't read Org B," "approve DRAFT rejected," "concurrent leave requests don't over-draw"); a couple of Playwright E2E on the golden path. Learn the **test pyramid** and be able to draw it.
- **Migrations.** Only `db push` — no `prisma/migrations/`, so no versioned, reviewable, reversible schema history. Unacceptable once real data exists. Switch to `migrate dev`/`deploy`.
- **CI.** No workflow. A test not run on every PR rots. install → lint → typecheck → test → build is a half-day with huge leverage.
- **Observability & config validation.** `console.error` is the whole story — add structured logs + request IDs + error tracking. Validate `process.env` once at startup (Zod) and refuse to boot if a secret is missing — turning the [silent-fallback bug](02-bugs-and-security.md) into an impossible state.
## The habit shifts (portable to any CRUD codebase)
| Junior instinct | Senior instinct | Seen here |
|---|---|---|
| Make it work | Make it work, prove it stays working, prove it can't be bypassed | tenant checks exist but skipped ([02·A3](02-bugs-and-security.md#a3)) |
| A pattern I applied | A pattern that's impossible to skip | `withRoute` (good) vs per-entity tenant checks (skipped) |
| Add capability / abstraction | Remove what I don't need yet | half the schema unused ([03](03-scope-and-quality.md#unused)) |
| Validate field types | Validate legal *states of the world* | no `endDate>=startDate`, trusted `totalDays` ([02·B4](02-bugs-and-security.md)) |
| Worked in the demo | Works at 100× data & under concurrency | no pagination; leave-balance race |
| Safe default on error | Fail loud — wrong answer > crash | silent `0`/passthrough on bad money/crypto |
| Code is the deliverable | The *system* is: tests, migrations, CI, docs | all absent |
| DRY every line | One authority per *fact* | permissions defined twice |
Throughline: **juniors optimize "does it work now"; seniors optimize "will it still be correct after 100 commit

# Fable Review — Velocity Grid
An honest code review of this EOR platform (Next.js App Router + Prisma + Postgres), doubling as a **junior→mid/senior training guide** for CRUD web app work. Every claim below is tied to a real file and line, and the load-bearing ones were verified against the code, not assumed.
This differs from the `docs/` folder: those are the author's feature writeups ("completed for MVP scope"). This is what's actually true when you run the code.
| Doc | Contents |
|---|---|
| [01-architecture.md](01-architecture.md) | How a request flows, the layering, and the patterns worth keeping |
| [02-bugs-and-security.md](02-bugs-and-security.md) | Verified defects — tenant leaks, authz gaps, the payroll 500, money math, races — with fixes |
| [03-scope-and-quality.md](03-scope-and-quality.md) | Unused half of the schema, dead deps, missing pagination, duplication, the TS case |
| [04-roadmap.md](04-roadmap.md) | What's missing (tests/CI/migrations), the junior→senior habits, exercises on this repo |
## Verdict
**Strong skeleton, unreliable enforcement.** The bones are good: thin routes → services → Prisma, one wrapper (`withRoute`) for auth/validation/errors, money as integer minor units, audit + outbox rows written in the same transaction as the mutation. Many production apps do worse.
The recurring flaw is **a good pattern applied once, then not enforced everywhere**: tenant scoping exists but several paths accept foreign IDs unchecked; status enums define state machines but transitions aren't guarded; money is *stored* as integers but *computed* in floats. And there are **zero tests**, so none of it gets caught. That gap — "I know the pattern" vs "the pattern holds on every path, and a test proves it" — is exactly the junior→senior gap.
## Fix these five first
1. **Payroll 500** — Calculate/Approve/Process commit to the DB, then crash serializing a `BigInt` to JSON; the user sees failure on a success and retries. [02](02-bugs-and-security.md#a1)
2. **Payslip endpoint** — path traversal via `params.id` + no tenant check; any org can read any org's payslip. [02](02-bugs-and-security.md#a2)
3. **Cross-tenant IDs** — `createContract`/`createLeaveRequest` trust foreign `employeeId`/`templateId`/`policyId`. [02](02-bugs-and-security.md#a3)
4. **No transition guards** — you can approve a DRAFT payroll run or re-sign a SIGNED contract. [02](02-bugs-and-security.md#a5)
5. **Disabled users log in** — `UserStatus` LOCKED/DISABLED is never checked. [02](02-bugs-and-security.md#a4)

# Auth And Permissions
Session verification starts in `src/lib/middleware/withAuth.ts`. The route passes a required permission, `withAuth()` calls `getSessionContext()` from `src/lib/auth/session.ts`, and then `assertPermission()` from `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` runs before the request body is parsed.
Session lookup happens in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` inside `getSessionContext()`. It reads the bearer token and `x-tenant-id` header, hashes the token, loads `AuthSession` with the user's membership filtered by the requested tenant, and returns `AuthContext`. The important tenant check is the membership filter in the Prisma include: only the membership for the active tenant is loaded.
Roles are defined in `prisma/schema.prisma` as `PlatformRole` and `OrgRole`. Platform role is separate from org role so a platform admin does not automatically bypass tenant permissions. The actual CRM permissions are centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` in `rolePermissions`.
Visibility is assigned by `visibilityForRole()` in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts`. `SALES_REP` gets `owned`; `SALES_MANAGER` gets `team`; `OWNER`, `ADMIN`, and `READ_ONLY` get `tenant`. `getSessionContext()` in `src/lib/auth/session.ts` computes `visibleOwnerIds` and `visibleTeamIds` from `Team` and `TeamMembership` rows. Repositories apply owner visibility with `ownerVisibilityScope()` from `src/lib/tenant/scope.ts`, and forecast quotas use `visibleTeamIds` in `src/repositories/forecastRepository.ts`.
Record-level sharing expands visibility in `recordAccessScope()` from `src/lib/tenant/scope.ts`. Lead, contact, and deal repositories use `recordAccessScope(context)` for reads and `recordAccessScope(context, RecordShareAccess.WRITE)` for mutable workflows such as `src/repositories/dealRepository.ts` `findDealForUpdate()`. Shares are created only through `src/services/recordShareService.ts`, which calls `assertEntityWriteAccess()` from `src/services/entityAccessService.ts` and verifies the recipient through `src/repositories/membershipRepository.ts` or `src/repositories/teamRepository.ts`.
Tenant isolation is enforced in repositories. Examples:
- `src/repositories/leadRepository.ts` uses `tenantScope(context)` in `listLeads()`, `findLeadById()`, `findLeadInTenant()`, and `updateLead()`.
- `src/repositories/dealRepository.ts` uses `tenantScope(context)` in `buildDealWhere()`, `findDealForUpdate()`, `updateDealStage()`, and `getDealAfterWrite()`.
- `src/repositories/reportRepository.ts` uses `buildDealWhere()` for deal aggregates and `tenantScope(context)` for stage lookup inside `pipelineReport()`.

# Auth And Permissions
## Session Resolution
Session resolution is centralized in `backend/app/core/auth.py`.
Ordered path:
1. FastAPI injects headers into `get_actor_context`.
2. `get_actor_context` uses `AuthRepository` from `backend/app/repositories/auth_repository.py`.
3. The repository loads `User`, `Tenant`, and the matching `TenantMembership`.
4. `get_actor_context` returns an `ActorContext` with `user`, `tenant`, and optional `membership`.
Headers used:
- `x-demo-user-id`
- `x-demo-tenant-id`
Why this matters: services do not trust raw headers. They operate on a typed actor object that was resolved against the database.
## Platform Roles vs Tenant Roles
The separation lives in `backend/app/core/enums.py` and `backend/app/core/permissions.py`.
- Platform roles: `PlatformRole`
- `PLATFORM_ADMIN`
- `PLATFORM_SUPPORT`
- `NONE`
- Tenant roles: `TenantRole`
- `TENANT_ADMIN`
- `HR_ADMIN`
- `MANAGER`
- `EMPLOYEE`
- `INTEGRATION_ADMIN`
The main guard helpers are:
- `require_platform_role`
- `require_tenant_role`

- `EmployeeService.list_employees`

# Tier 1: Junior Missions
### Mission 1: The App's Heartbeat
**Tier:** Junior
**Time Estimate:** 35 minutes
**Goal:** Trace one cron ping from URL to database mutation.
**The Concept:** A ping is like a scheduled train checking in at the station. If the train reports on time, the board stays green; if it reports failure or stops reporting, the board changes.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:** `hc/api/urls.py` owns public ping routes, `hc/api/views.py` owns request parsing, and `hc/api/models.py` owns check mutation. If implemented poorly, duplicate or concurrent pings could corrupt status.
**Find It In The Code:** Open `hc/api/urls.py:75-78`, `hc/api/views.py:180-243`, and `hc/api/models.py:485-565`.
```python
path("ping/<uuid:code>", views.ping)      # UUID ping URL enters here.
path("ping/<uuid:code>/", include(uuid_urls))  # /fail, /start, /log variants delegate.
```
```python
@csrf_exempt                              # Cron jobs are not browser forms.
@never_cache                              # A ping should always reach the app.
def ping(request, code, check=None, action="success", exitstatus=None):
check = Check.objects.get(code=code)  # URL identity selects the monitored job.
body = request.body[: settings.PING_BODY_LIMIT]  # Store only bounded evidence.
if exitstatus is not None and exitstatus > 0:
action = "fail"                   # Shell exit code becomes domain action.
check.ping(remote_addr, scheme, method, ua, body, action, rid, exitstatus)
```
```python
with transaction.atomic():                # Check update and Ping creation stay together.
self = Check.objects.select_for_update().get(id=self.id)  # Lock hot row.
self.last_ping = frozen_now            # Successful/failure pings update latest evidence.
self.n_pings = models.F("n_pings") + 1 # Count atomically in the database.
ping = Ping(owner=self)                # History row records this request.
ping.save()
```
**The Aha Moment:** The view decides what happened, but the model owns how a check changes.
**Socratic Checkpoint:** 1. Why is this view CSRF-exempt? 2. Why is `never_cache` used? 3. What turns an exit status into failure? 4. Where is the database lock? 5. Which object stores the history row?

### Mission 9: State Has a Home and a Reason
**Tier:** Mid-Level
**Time Estimate:** 45 minutes
**Goal:** Explain where check status lives and why it is also computed.
**The Concept:** The dashboard is like a live departures board: stored state is the last official event, computed state accounts for time passing.
**Design Intent Before You Read the Code:** `Check.status` stores durable state, while `get_status()` calculates time-sensitive display state. Poor design would require a background write every second.
**Find It In The Code:** Open `hc/api/models.py:208-215` and `hc/api/models.py:347-372`.
```python
status = models.CharField(max_length=6, choices=STATUSES, default="new")  # Stored state.
def get_status(self, *, with_started=False):
if self.last_start and frozen_now >= self.last_start + self.grace:
return "down"              # Time can turn running into down.
if self.status in ("new", "paused", "down"):
return self.status         # Some states are durable.
if frozen_now >= grace_start:
return "grace"             # Late but not down yet.
```
**The Aha Moment:** Not all visible state must be stored.

# 01 — Ownership-based concurrency: the slot, the Gate, and exactly-once release
**Concept.** In most codebases, "clean up exactly once" is a discipline: every
exit path must remember to call `release()`, and a code review is the only
thing standing between you and a double-free or a leaked slot. Ownership-based
design turns the discipline into a type-system consequence: the resource *is a
value*, taking it out of its container consumes it, and a second taker finds
nothing. You cannot forget what you cannot express.
**Where this repo stakes its life on it.** The session machine
(`src-tauri/core/src/session/machine.rs`) runs one question/answer pipeline at
a time, and §5.11 of the spec demands: *whatever the outcome (done, error,
abort), the active slot is released exactly once*. Six paths can end a session
— completion, provider error, STT death, timeout, cancel, supersession — and
any two of them can race. Nobody coordinates them. The types do.
## The one-slot registry
```rust
// machine.rs:36-46
/// The one-slot session registry. `Mutex<Option<Active>>` rather than a map:
/// the product rule is "one live pipeline", and encoding it in the type means
/// supersession cannot be forgotten on any path.
pub struct SessionManager {
inner: Arc<Inner>,
}
struct Inner {
slot: Mutex<Option<Active>>,
next_id: AtomicU64,
}
```
The product rule ("one live pipeline") is not a comment on a map — it *is* the
data structure. A `HashMap<SessionId, Active>` would make "two live sessions"
representable, and everything representable eventually happens. With

# Learn: a code-reading curriculum
Ten lessons that teach intermediate-to-senior systems concepts *through this
repo*. Each lesson takes one concept, shows where this codebase stakes its
correctness on it, quotes the real code, and names the tests that pin the
behavior. Every lesson ends with exercises: reading exercises (answers
included) and one **break it** exercise — a specific edit to make, the test
that catches it, and why that test exists.
The repo is small enough to actually read and hostile enough to be worth
reading: realtime audio, two streaming wire protocols, a race-heavy state
machine, untrusted input at three boundaries (settings file, provider frames,
model output), and a ~1 s latency promise that every timeout serves. The spec
is [`docs/SPEC.md`](../SPEC.md); lessons cite its § numbers the same way the
code does.
## How to use it
1. Read the lesson with the cited file open. Citations are `path:line` against
the current tree — if a file has drifted, the named test is the stable
anchor.
2. Run the named test before and after any break-it edit:
```sh
# core lessons (from src-tauri/)
cd src-tauri && cargo test -p app-core <test_name>
# frontend lessons (from the repo root)
npm test -- -t "<test name>"
```
3. Revert the break-it edit (`git checkout -- <file>`). Nothing in these
lessons should ever be committed.

# Learn this codebase — a curriculum for a junior software engineer
AI Call Assistant v3 is a small app with senior-grade problems inside it:
real-time streaming, cross-thread async, race conditions that were each
"purchased with a real bug", untrusted input at three boundaries, and a
latency budget measured in milliseconds. That makes it an unusually good
training ground: every pattern here exists for a reason you can trace to a
concrete failure — and the failures are real, proved by measurement, a
mutation-testing pass, and four adversarial audit rounds recorded in the
git log.
The curriculum is thirteen documents in two layers: a **core sequence**
(01–06, six different learning methods — do these in order the first time
through) and **deep dives** (07–13, one topic each — read on demand, in

# Recall — Engineering practice, in your pocket
A complete, local-first spaced-repetition web app for the spare minutes in your day. Open it and start studying: **13,609 practical web development flashcards across 75 decks** are included. The library is 4.86 times the v6 size: 2,799 base cards plus 10,810 related recall variations. No API key or account is required. The library focuses on forms, APIs, SQL, authentication, validation, testing, and shipping CRUD apps. LeetCode and DSA exercises are excluded.
## Start the app
Requires Node 22.13+ (or Node 24+) and npm.
```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
```
For the production app, including offline support:
```sh
npm run build
npm start
```
Open the printed address (normally `http://localhost:4173`). `dist/` contains the complete prebuilt website; it needs a web server and cannot be opened by double-clicking `index.html`.
## Use it on your phone, anywhere
1. Publish `dist/` to an HTTPS static host. Netlify and Vercel configuration is included. Run `python scripts/package-release.py` after building to create the portable `release/recall-web.zip` archive and its SHA-256 checksum.
2. Open the hosted URL on your phone while online and let the app finish loading once.
3. **iPhone:** Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen. **Android:** Chrome → menu → Install app / Add to Home screen.
4. Pick a 2-, 5-, or 10-minute session. Think of the answer, reveal it, and rate your recall. You can stop at any time; each rating is saved immediately.
5. Reopen and review even without a connection. Offline behavior is tested against the production build, including rating and reloading.
The development server also prints your local network address for testing on the same Wi-Fi. A LAN HTTP address is for previewing: reliable PWA installation and service workers require **HTTPS** outside localhost. A localhost URL will not work on your phone when you are away from this computer. Publishing is a separate step; the project does not automatically upload your code or study data.

# Helios Interplanetary
A persistent station and enterprise operations simulation for practicing AI-assisted engineering. Mission Control handles telemetry and incidents; the Operations hub connects maintenance, inventory, procurement, cargo, crew, energy, bounded advisers, knowledge, billing, support and durable background work.
The [local milestone contract](docs/exec-plans/002-complete-local-program.md) defines the delivered program. Start the separate learning track with [Learn by replaying the build](upskilling/retrospective/README.md); it follows the actual contracts, failures, checks and implementation decisions. Your learning assessment remains pending until you attempt the exercises.
## Run locally
Prerequisites: Node.js 22.16 or newer, npm, Docker Desktop running Linux containers, and available loopback ports 3000 and 5438.
```sh
npm ci
npm run setup
npm run dev
```
In a second terminal, start the persistent worker:
```sh
npm run worker
```
Open **http://127.0.0.1:3000**, select **Enter Mission Control**, then **Operations hub**. Setup creates a random local session secret, starts PostgreSQL, applies checksummed migrations and adds missing fixtures. Existing configuration and simulation data are preserved. For a production-mode preview use `npm run build` followed by `npm start`. A [container preview](deploy/README.md) includes the app, migration job and worker at port 3002.
The development database is `helios`; automated integration and browser suites reset only `helios_test`. The fixture contains two organizations, 200 crew members, station assets, warehouses, budgets, vessels, energy systems and approved procedure documents. The virtual clock starts paused in 2042. Manual controls advance it; a running worker advances a resumed clock and processes events and timers. Audit and retry timestamps use actual wall time.
## Explore six connected demonstrations
For a populated review world, stop the worker and run `npm run showcase`, then restart the worker. This **resets the local disposable development fixtures** and builds a completed repair history, recovered solar crisis, uncertain payment, investigation, adviser traces and evaluation evidence through the real domain services. The [deployment guide](deploy/README.md) includes the exact worker and container commands.
Follow [the step-by-step scenario guide](docs/runbooks/demo-scenarios.md).

# BorrowBox
BorrowBox is a beginner-friendly fifteen-sprint C#/.NET teaching repository for lending campus equipment such as laptops, cameras, calculators, and lab kits.
The repository is designed for a new graduate with limited .NET experience. It starts with plain C# and one HTTP slice, then gradually introduces validation, LINQ, dependency injection, SQLite, background work, authorization concepts, testing, and operations.
## Deliberately small architecture
```text
BorrowBox.Api             HTTP routes and request/response models
BorrowBox.Core            equipment, borrowers, loans, and simple services
BorrowBox.Infrastructure  in-memory and SQLite storage
```
BorrowBox does not use microservices, MediatR, CQRS, generic repositories, AutoMapper, or a message broker.
```powershell
dotnet restore BorrowBox.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/BorrowBox.Api
dotnet test BorrowBox.slnx
```
## Run it
Requires the .NET 10 SDK.
```powershell
dotnet restore BorrowBox.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/BorrowBox.Api
```
OpenAPI is available at `/openapi/v1.json` in Development. Inventory reads and health endpoints are public. Mutating inventory uses the teaching header `X-Demo-Role: Staff`; borrowing accepts `Student` or `Staff`. This header is not production authentication.
## Course map
| Sprints | Theme | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–3 | C# and HTTP foundations | equipment CRUD, validation, search, pagination |
| 4–6 | Business workflows | borrowers, checkout, return, v0.5 release |
| 7–10 | Data and state | SQLite adapter, reservations, expiry, inspections |
| 11–13 | Policies and API design | lending limits, authorization, reports |
| 14–15 | Engineering judgment | bug harvest, threat model, operations, v1.0 |
Each sprint has a focused lesson in [`docs/sprints`](docs/sprints). Start with the [learner guide](LEARNER-GUIDE.md) and [course specification](docs/curriculum/SPEC.md). Then use [TESTREADME.md](TESTREADME.md) to practice testing and [OEReadMe.md](OEReadMe.md) to discuss which complexity is justified.

borrowbox/docs/curriculum/RETROSPECTIVE..opening:
# Course retrospective
## Progression
The course began with one class, one store, and one endpoint slice. Each later concept answered a problem already visible: SQLite answered persistence, policies answered lending limits, an injected clock answered nondeterministic time, and atomic checkout answered a reproduced race.
## What a learner should now be able to do
- Trace an HTTP request through a use case into an adapter.
- Place business rules in objects or services rather than controllers.
- choose unit, integration, or API tests based on the boundary being proved.
- Read a CI failure, create a regression test, and make a scoped repair.
- Explain 401 versus 403, persistence versus memory, and liveness versus readiness.
- Push back on speculative architecture while naming evidence that would justify it.
## Suggested capstone
Choose one production-readiness gap, write an architecture decision record, implement the smallest vertical slice, and demonstrate it with tests and an updated runbook. Good options are durable loan persistence, idempotent checkout, or real token validation in a local identity test environment.

# Event Ticketing Platform
TypeScript monorepo for a ticketing platform with a Next.js frontend, Fastify API, Prisma/PostgreSQL data layer, Redis-backed jobs, Stripe checkout hooks, signed QR tickets, and mobile check-in.
## Apps And Packages
- `apps/web`: Next.js App Router UI for event discovery, event detail, ticket selection, organizer event creation, checkout, tickets, and scanner screens.
- `apps/api`: Fastify API with authentication, event management, reservations, checkout, tickets, seating, waitlist, and check-in routes.
- `packages/shared`: shared types, constants, and Zod schemas.
- `packages/ticket-renderer`: signed QR payload and QR image generation.
## Local Setup
```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d
npm run db:push
npm run db:seed
npm run dev
```
Default seeded users:
- `organizer@example.com / Password123!`
- `attendee@example.com / Password123!`
- `staff@example.com / Password123!`
## Concurrency Strategy
Ticket reservations use optimistic locking on `TicketTier.version`. The API reads the tier version, validates availability, and increments `reservedCount` only when the version still matches. A mismatch means another checkout changed inventory first, so the reservation retries with jitter. Confirmed payment moves inventory from `reservedCount` to `soldCount`; expiry jobs release old pending orders.
## Useful Scripts
```bash
npm run build
npm run typecheck
npm run test
npm --workspace @ticketing/api run db:push
npm --workspace @ticketing/api run db:seed
```

# CampusOps
CampusOps is a fifteen-sprint teaching repository for learning business-heavy C#/.NET API development and React/TypeScript integration through a university facilities platform.
## Architecture
```text
CampusOps.Api             HTTP composition and security
CampusOps.Core            business modules and use cases
CampusOps.Infrastructure  in-memory, SQLite, and integration adapters
CampusOps.Contracts       stable public request/response contracts
CampusOps.Worker          scheduled maintenance and delivery work
CampusOps.Web             React and TypeScript operations console
```
The backend is a modular monolith. Module boundaries organize code without adding network calls, distributed transactions, or separate deployments.
```powershell
dotnet restore CampusOps.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/CampusOps.Api
npm ci --prefix web/CampusOps.Web
npm run build --prefix web/CampusOps.Web
```
## Course map
| Sprints | Theme | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–5 | Operational foundations | locations, assets, requests, work orders, technicians |
| 6–10 | Reliability and time | audit history, SQLite, stock, worker scheduling, SLAs |
| 11–13 | Integration surfaces | procurement, authorization, React dashboard |
| 14–15 | Engineering ownership | idempotency, concurrency, reporting, operations, release |
Development OpenAPI is at `/openapi/v1.json`. Mutations use teaching-only `X-Demo-Role` and `X-Demo-Campus` headers. The API default is non-durable; `/health/ready` reports that fact.
Read [LEARNER-GUIDE.md](LEARNER-GUIDE.md), the [curriculum specification](docs/curriculum/SPEC.md), [TESTREADME.md](TESTREADME.md), and [OEReadMe.md](OEReadMe.md).

# ADR-001: start as a modular monolith
CampusOps uses one backend deployment with module-oriented code inside `CampusOps.Core`. Facilities workflows share transactions and evolve together. In-process calls keep failure modes visible to a learner.
Revisit only when a module has independent ownership and release cadence, measured scaling needs, and a clear data boundary that outweighs network and operational costs.

campusops/docs/curriculum/RETROSPECTIVE..opening:
# Curriculum retrospective
CampusOps begins with one vertical slice and introduces complexity only after a visible need: SQLite for persistence, a worker for scheduled work, `IClock` for deterministic time, policies for permissions, React for an actual consumer, and idempotency/concurrency controls for reproduced integration failures.
A learner finishing the course should be able to trace requests across layers, model state and policy, choose an appropriate test boundary, publish compatible contracts, diagnose CI, review security and operational gaps, and argue against speculative architecture with concrete evidence.
Suggested capstone: choose one production-readiness gap—durable outbox, token validation, or transactional work-order persistence—write an ADR, implement one tested vertical slice, and update the runbook.

# Boundaries and Layers
A **boundary** is a line across which things are decoupled: code on one side can change without forcing changes on the other. A **layer** owns a responsibility and depends only inward. Finding boundaries — and spotting where they *leak* — is the core architecture skill.
## The four layers
| Layer | Project | Owns | Must NOT own |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Domain | `ApplicationCore` | Entities, invariants, use-case services, query specs, the interfaces it needs | EF, ASP.NET, HTTP, JSON |
| Infrastructure | `Infrastructure` | EF mappings, migrations, Identity, email, concrete `IRepository` | Business rules |
| Presentation | `Web`, `PublicApi`, `BlazorAdmin` | HTTP, view models/DTOs, auth wiring, rendering | Domain invariants, direct SQL |
| Contracts | `BlazorShared` | Shapes shared client↔API | Behavior |
The dependency rule: **arrows point inward.** `Infrastructure` and the UIs depend on `ApplicationCore`; `ApplicationCore` depends on nothing internal. Proof: [ApplicationCore.csproj](../../src/ApplicationCore/ApplicationCore.csproj) references only small helper libraries (Ardalis.*), never EF Core or ASP.NET.
## Where the boundaries are clean (good examples)
- **Domain ↔ persistence:** the domain declares `IRepository<T>` ([IRepository.cs](../../src/ApplicationCore/Interfaces/IRepository.cs)); `Infrastructure` implements it ([EfRepository.cs](../../src/Infrastructure/Data/EfRepository.cs)). Swap SQL for in-memory by changing one registration ([Dependencies.cs:19-38](../../src/Infrastructure/Dependencies.cs#L19-L38)).
- **Domain ↔ UI shape:** `CatalogViewModelService` explicitly calls itself "a UI-specific service … does not contain any business logic" ([CatalogViewModelService.cs:14-17](../../src/Web/Services/CatalogViewModelService.cs#L14-L17)) and maps entities to view models — keeping presentation concerns out of the domain.
- **Network boundary:** BlazorAdmin runs in the browser and *cannot* reach the DbContext; it must call the API over HTTP ([HttpService.cs](../../src/BlazorAdmin/Services/HttpService.cs)). The compiler + runtime enforce this boundary.
- **Client ↔ API contract:** shared DTOs live in `BlazorShared` so both sides compile against the same shapes without sharing domain internals.
## Where boundaries leak or bend (teachable weak spots)
- **UI decides a domain value:** the checkout's shipping address is constructed in the *page* ([Checkout.cshtml.cs:57](../../src/Web/Pages/Basket/Checkout.cshtml.cs#L57)) and handed to the domain. Address *should* be user input flowing into the domain, not a presentation-layer

This module names the structures that hold eShopOnWeb together and teaches you to **recognize them anywhere**. Pattern recognition — not pattern memorization — is what separates a mid-level engineer from a junior in design discussions and interviews.

This module is first-class, not an afterthought. Target: **mid-level fullstack interviews** (.NET/C# primary; the transferable concepts map to any stack). At least 60% of the question cards here are anchored to real code in this repo, so you practice answering with concrete evidence — "in eShopOnWeb, the `OrderService` does X at line Y" — instead of reciting definitions.

## The golden rule
**Answer with a concrete example, a tradeoff, and a failure mode — not a definition.**
- Weak: "Clean Architecture separates concerns."
- Strong: "In this repo, `ApplicationCore` defines `IRepository<T>` and `Infrastructure` implements it, so I can unit-test `BasketService` with a fake repo — the tests do exactly that. The cost is more mapping code and indirection; for a thin CRUD app I'd skip it."
The second answer proves you've read and reasoned about real code. That's the mid-level signal.

# eShopOnWeb Upskill Curriculum
A codebase-to-curriculum training lab built on Microsoft's **eShopOnWeb** reference application. It teaches two things at once, always paired:
1. **This repo**: where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file/line anchors.
2. **Transferable skill**: why these patterns exist, when they fail, how to recognize them in any codebase — and how to articulate them in a mid-level fullstack interview.
## Who this is for
A junior fullstack engineer (CRUD web dev in .NET/C#, or React/Node/TS moving to .NET) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
## What this repo is (identity in 7 sentences)
eShopOnWeb is Microsoft's official reference application for the free eBook *Architecting Modern Web Applications with ASP.NET Core and Azure* ([README.md](../README.md#L18)). It is a deliberately **monolithic** e-commerce store — catalog, basket, checkout, orders, admin — built on .NET 8 ([global.json](../global.json)). It demonstrates **Clean Architecture**: a dependency-free domain project (`ApplicationCore`), an EF Core data layer (`Infrastructure`), and three UI surfaces — a Razor Pages storefront (`Web`), a JWT-secured minimal-API backend (`PublicApi`), and a Blazor WebAssembly admin panel (`BlazorAdmin`). Persistence is SQL Server via EF Core with two separate DbContexts (catalog vs. identity). It is a *teaching* app: some things are intentionally simplified or deliberately flawed (hardcoded JWT secret, hardcoded checkout address, a `Task.Delay(1000)` in an API endpoint), which makes it an outstanding lab for developing senior judgment — you get to find real flaws in a professionally structured codebase. Development moved to [dotnet/eShop](https://github.com/dotnet/eShop); this repo is stable and safe to dissect. Everything here was verified against the code on 2026-07-16; see the [verification log](09-reference/verification-log.md).

# Recall
Recall is a local-first spaced-repetition PWA with quick capture, inbox triage, and offline study. IndexedDB is the source of truth on the device; Supabase is an optional sync target.
## Run locally
```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```
The app works without Supabase credentials in local-only mode.
## Supabase setup
1. Create a Supabase project.
2. Run `supabase/migrations/0001_init.sql` in the SQL editor or via the Supabase CLI.
3. Enable email OTP magic links in Supabase Auth.
4. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set:
```bash
VITE_SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=your-anon-key
```
## Scripts
```bash
npm run dev
npm test
npm run build
npm run preview
```
## Deploy
Build with `npm run build` and deploy `dist/` to any static host. Service workers and the share target require HTTPS outside local development.
## Notes
- Capture, study, rating, undo, export, and import all operate on local IndexedDB.
- Sync is disabled when signed out or when Supabase env vars are absent.
- The PWA manifest includes a GET share target at `/capture`.

# BorrowBox
BorrowBox is a beginner-friendly fifteen-sprint C#/.NET teaching repository for lending campus equipment such as laptops, cameras, calculators, and lab kits.
The repository is designed for a new graduate with limited .NET experience. It starts with plain C# and one HTTP slice, then gradually introduces validation, LINQ, dependency injection, SQLite, background work, authorization concepts, testing, and operations.
## Deliberately small architecture
```text
BorrowBox.Api             HTTP routes and request/response models
BorrowBox.Core            equipment, borrowers, loans, and simple services
BorrowBox.Infrastructure  in-memory and SQLite storage
```
BorrowBox does not use microservices, MediatR, CQRS, generic repositories, AutoMapper, or a message broker.
```powershell
dotnet restore BorrowBox.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/BorrowBox.Api
dotnet test BorrowBox.slnx
```
## Run it
Requires the .NET 10 SDK.
```powershell
dotnet restore BorrowBox.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/BorrowBox.Api
```
OpenAPI is available at `/openapi/v1.json` in Development. Inventory reads and health endpoints are public. Mutating inventory uses the teaching header `X-Demo-Role: Staff`; borrowing accepts `Student` or `Staff`. This header is not production authentication.
## Course map
| Sprints | Theme | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–3 | C# and HTTP foundations | equipment CRUD, validation, search, pagination |
| 4–6 | Business workflows | borrowers, checkout, return, v0.5 release |
| 7–10 | Data and state | SQLite adapter, reservations, expiry, inspections |
| 11–13 | Policies and API design | lending limits, authorization, reports |
| 14–15 | Engineering judgment | bug harvest, threat model, operations, v1.0 |
Each sprint has a focused lesson in [`docs/sprints`](docs/sprints). Start with the [learner guide](LEARNER-GUIDE.md) and [course specification](docs/curriculum/SPEC.md). Then use [TESTREADME.md](TESTREADME.md) to practice testing and [OEReadMe.md](OEReadMe.md) to discuss which complexity is justified.

# Course retrospective
## Progression
The course began with one class, one store, and one endpoint slice. Each later concept answered a problem already visible: SQLite answered persistence, policies answered lending limits, an injected clock answered nondeterministic time, and atomic checkout answered a reproduced race.
## What a learner should now be able to do
- Trace an HTTP request through a use case into an adapter.
- Place business rules in objects or services rather than controllers.
- choose unit, integration, or API tests based on the boundary being proved.
- Read a CI failure, create a regression test, and make a scoped repair.
- Explain 401 versus 403, persistence versus memory, and liveness versus readiness.
- Push back on speculative architecture while naming evidence that would justify it.
## Suggested capstone
Choose one production-readiness gap, write an architecture decision record, implement the smallest vertical slice, and demonstrate it with tests and an updated runbook. Good options are durable loan persistence, idempotent checkout, or real token validation in a local identity test environment.

# CampusOps
CampusOps is a fifteen-sprint teaching repository for learning business-heavy C#/.NET API development and React/TypeScript integration through a university facilities platform.
## Architecture
```text
CampusOps.Api             HTTP composition and security
CampusOps.Core            business modules and use cases
CampusOps.Infrastructure  in-memory, SQLite, and integration adapters
CampusOps.Contracts       stable public request/response contracts
CampusOps.Worker          scheduled maintenance and delivery work
CampusOps.Web             React and TypeScript operations console
```
The backend is a modular monolith. Module boundaries organize code without adding network calls, distributed transactions, or separate deployments.
```powershell
dotnet restore CampusOps.slnx --locked-mode
dotnet run --project src/CampusOps.Api
npm ci --prefix web/CampusOps.Web
npm run build --prefix web/CampusOps.Web
```
## Course map
| Sprints | Theme | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–5 | Operational foundations | locations, assets, requests, work orders, technicians |
| 6–10 | Reliability and time | audit history, SQLite, stock, worker scheduling, SLAs |
| 11–13 | Integration surfaces | procurement, authorization, React dashboard |
| 14–15 | Engineering ownership | idempotency, concurrency, reporting, operations, release |
Development OpenAPI is at `/openapi/v1.json`. Mutations use teaching-only `X-Demo-Role` and `X-Demo-Campus` headers. The API default is non-durable; `/health/ready` reports that fact.
Read [LEARNER-GUIDE.md](LEARNER-GUIDE.md), the [curriculum specification](docs/curriculum/SPEC.md), [TESTREADME.md](TESTREADME.md), and [OEReadMe.md](OEReadMe.md).

# ADR-001: start as a modular monolith
CampusOps uses one backend deployment with module-oriented code inside `CampusOps.Core`. Facilities workflows share transactions and evolve together. In-process calls keep failure modes visible to a learner.
Revisit only when a module has independent ownership and release cadence, measured scaling needs, and a clear data boundary that outweighs network and operational costs.

The goal of this template is to provide a straightforward and efficient approach to enterprise application development, leveraging the power of Clean Architecture and ASP.NET Core. Using this template, you can effortlessly create a new app with Angular, React, or Web API only, powered by ASP.NET Core and Aspire. # fabledocs — A Training Lab Built From This Codebase
This is a learning curriculum generated from the code in this repository. It is written for one specific learner: **a junior fullstack engineer** (comfortable with CRUD web dev in .NET/C# and React/TypeScript or similar) who wants to reach mid-level fast, build senior judgment, and pass interviews for mid-level fullstack roles.
Every page teaches two things at once:
1. **This codebase** — where things live, how its real flows work, with exact file-and-line anchors.
2. **The transferable skill** — why the pattern exists, what the alternatives are, how it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.
## What this repository is
This is [jasontaylordev/CleanArchitecture](../README.md) — the source of the `Clean.Architecture.Solution.Template` NuGet template (`dotnet new ca-sln`). It is a **.NET 10 solution template** demonstrating Clean Architecture with:
- **Domain** layer: entities, value objects, domain events — almost no external dependencies ([ADR-003](../docs/decisions/ADR-003-MediatR-Contracts-In-Domain.md)).
- **Application** layer: CQRS use cases via MediatR, FluentValidation, AutoMapper, and a pipeline of cross-cutting behaviours (logging, exception handling, authorization, validation, performance).
- **Infrastructure** layer: EF Core 10 (`ApplicationDbContext`), ASP.NET Core Identity, save-changes interceptors for auditing and domain-event dispatch.
- **Web** layer: Minimal API endpoint groups, OpenAPI + Scalar, ProblemDetails error mapping, and two SPA clients (Angular 21 and React 19) whose API clients are **generated** from the OpenAPI spec by NSwag.
- **Aspire** orchestration: `AppHost` runs the full stack; `TestAppHost` runs just the database for functional tests ([ADR-002](../docs/decisions/ADR-002-Aspire-For-Orchestration-And-Testing.md)).
- Four test layers: domain unit tests, application unit tests, functional tests against a real database (Respawn resets), and Playwright/Reqnroll acceptance tests.
The sample domain is deliberately small — todo lists and todo items — so the architecture is the star. That makes it an ideal gym: every enterprise pattern is present, but no page of business logic gets in your way.
**One caveat you must internalize early:** this repo is a *template*. You will see `#if (UseApiOnly)` / `#if (UsePostgreSQL)` conditional blocks in C# and `<!--#if ... -->` in XML — these are template preprocessor directives, not normal code (e.g. [Program.cs](../src/Web/Program.cs#L40-L49), [DependencyInjection.cs](../src/Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs#L26-L32)). The other three doc sets in this repo are things you *read*. This one is things you *do*.
- **fabledocs** — the full curriculum (maps, patterns, drills, interview prep).

# ADR-0002: Add Storefront Cache Layers Only When Measured
- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-07-12
## Context
Catalog reads will eventually traverse CDN, Next.js ISR, Redis, and Postgres. Each
layer can reduce origin load, but every layer also creates a new place where a
price or availability value can become stale. Starting with all layers would hide
which one provides value and make invalidation failures difficult to teach.
## Decision
Start with the separate storefront read seam and add layers in measured stages:
1. Sprint 3 selects SSG, ISR, or dynamic rendering per route.
2. Sprint 5 adds Redis read-through caching and records hit rate, p95, and origin load.
3. Sprint 6 adds tag invalidation, TTL backstops, single-flight, and SWR.
4. Sprint 12 tunes keys and warming from measurements; Sprint 13 stress-tests them.
Every cached surface must name its audience and staleness tolerance. Storefront
catalog pages initially tolerate 60 seconds; cart, checkout, inventory mutation,
and all admin reads tolerate zero and never use the catalog page cache as truth.
## Consequences
Each layer arrives with a baseline and a removal criterion. Event invalidation will
provide precision, TTL will self-heal missed events, and transactional operations
will always revalidate price and inventory against the authoritative store.
